al-masudi-meadows-of-gold-sprenger-1841:
Al-Masudi was a traveler from Baghdad. He saw India, Africa, and the Caspian lands in the tenth century, and he wrote the Muruj al-Dhahab, the Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems. Aloys Sprenger gave the first part of it English form in 1841. Only this first volume of his version ever appeared.

The Meadows is a cabinet of the world. It holds the making of the earth, the kings of Persia and India, the seas, the wonders, and the tales told in ports. Al-Masudi asks questions everywhere he goes and writes down what he hears, gold and dross together. Sprenger's volume lets English readers taste the great Arab Herodotus. The full French version stands in the library beside it.
arxiv-2510-00041:
Yuchen Song and colleagues argue that current cultural awareness benchmarks for multimodal language models are too easy. Because real-world photos usually contain a single culture and tasks lack rising difficulty or cross-lingual depth. Their new answer is C3B, a Comics Cross-Cultural Benchmark built from full comic pages that pack several cultures into one frame together. With over 2,000 images and over 18,000 question-answer pairs in multiple languages for evaluation.

Three tasks climb in difficulty from basic visual recognition, through understanding cultural conflicts, to generating cultural content. And evaluating 11 open-source multilingual multimodal models exposes a significant reported gap against human performance. Models also especially lack proficiency with less well-known cultures and with processing genuine cultural conflicts. Precisely the abilities the benchmark was designed to stress, giving developers a harder target for culturally aware systems in the future.
arxiv-2510-00141:
Dipankar Shakya and colleagues at New York University and the University of Southern California published this 2025 paper on wireless data standards. Engineers measure how radio signals travel in each new frequency band planned for 6G networks. Those campaigns are costly, yet every lab archives results in its own format. The team proposes one shared, machine-readable point-data format for all such measurements.

Each record in the format holds key channel values tied to a spot on an environment map. A metadata table sums up the campaign behind the records. The authors prove the format by merging two independent campaigns, at 142 gigahertz in New York and 145 gigahertz in Los Angeles. A joint path-loss fit then refined the shared estimates across both sites. The standard could let labs pool data worldwide instead of repeating costly measurement trips.
arxiv-2510-00441:
Yiyuan Pan and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on NeuRO, a framework for robots that navigate by sight under uncertainty. Navigation policies trained on scarce data tend to overfit and fail in new places. Simply making the network bigger backfires when samples are few. NeuRO instead welds a perception network directly to a robust optimization planner.

Noisy visual predictions become convex uncertainty sets through a special network design plus conformal calibration. Those sets parameterize the constraints the planner must respect. Planning under partial observability is then solved as one robust optimization problem. On multi-object navigation tasks, both unordered and sequential, NeuRO set new best results. Its edge was largest when generalizing to environments never seen in training. The authors argue the same fusion of learning and optimization suits other embodied tasks.
arxiv-2510-00641:
Liu and a large team of co-authors describe how they made and tested aluminium-manganese alloy films in this 2025 arXiv paper. The films are the sensing core of transition edge sensors, detectors planned for searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay. That rare decay could show whether neutrinos are their own antiparticles. The sensors must switch to superconductivity within a narrow band near ten to twenty millikelvin.

The team varied film thickness, manganese content, and annealing temperature, then measured the switching temperature of each sample. They found that annealing can tune that temperature into the required range, and that higher annealing spreads manganese more evenly through the film. A magnetic field across the film lowered the temperature, while a field along it had little effect. The results set the fabrication window for detectors at China's Jinping underground laboratory.
arxiv-2510-00841:
Chiang, Ishida, and Sugiyama recast language model routing as a dueling bandit problem in this 2025 arXiv paper. A router picks which model answers each query, trading off quality, expertise, and cost. Absolute scores for answers are expensive to collect, while pairwise preferences are cheap and natural. The authors learn the router from that relative feedback, which also lets it adapt as models and tastes change.

Their Category-Calibrated Fine-Tuning builds embeddings for each candidate model from offline data, using contrastive learning with quality-and-cost aware weighting. Those embeddings feed a Feel-Good Thompson Sampling algorithm with guarantees for contextual dueling bandits. On RouterBench and MixInstruct the approach reached lower cumulative regret and faster convergence than strong baselines. It beat routers built on general-purpose OpenAI embeddings, with a better performance-cost balance. The authors note that weighting less sometimes beat weighting more, a puzzle for future work.
arxiv-2510-01141:
Radhakrishna and a large team at the Apriel project argue that careful mid-training beats sheer scale, in this 2025 arXiv paper introducing Apriel-1.5-15B-Thinker. Their open-weights multimodal reasoning model has fifteen billion parameters and starts from Pixtral-12B rather than from scratch. The recipe has three stages: depth upscaling to add reasoning capacity, staged continual pretraining for text and vision, then text-only supervised fine-tuning on selected instruction data with explicit reasoning traces. No reinforcement learning or preference optimization is used anywhere.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index the model scores 52, matching DeepSeek-R1-0528 while using far less compute. Across ten image benchmarks it lands within about five points of Gemini-2.5-Flash and Claude Sonnet-3.7 on average. It also runs on a single GPU, and continual pretraining alone added large gains on visual mathematics. Checkpoint, recipes, and evaluation protocols are released under the MIT license.
arxiv-2510-01241:
Hu Wei and Ze Xu lead a technical report introducing harder mathematics benchmarks as public test suites saturate. Leading models now cluster near the ceiling of popular math sets, hiding real differences. The SKYLENAGE report answers with two deliberately tougher instruments.

A hundred-item diagnostic set tracks length, numeric density, and symbolic complexity per problem. A hundred-fifty contest problems span high school through doctoral levels across seven subjects. Fifteen current models faced both suites under one setup. Even the strongest reached well under half marks on the contest set, while the reasoning set exposed robustness gaps. Retention from high school to doctoral level near four-fifths marks the top systems. Subject-by-model breakdowns expose where training data runs thin. Calibrated difficulty is the design goal, not mere hardness. Mid-tier models fell away sharply on the hardest slices. Ceiling effects end where these suites begin.
arxiv-2510-01341:
Nagai revisits a family of vanishing sum identities for Bernoulli polynomials and explains them from two directions at once. The Sun-Pan cyclic identities look like combinatorial accidents, sums that cancel in perfect rotation. Minimal axioms for Appell-type sequences turn out to force them analytically.

The same relations drop out of modular symmetry on the other side. Period polynomials of Eisenstein series encode the identities through the modular group's own rotation. Quantum analogues extend the whole picture to q-deformed sequences. The crossroads position links the identities to zeta values and deeper motivic structures. Bernoulli numbers sit underneath the polynomials as the constant special case. Umbral calculus supplies the algebraic dialect for the analytic side. Polylogarithms and mixed Tate motives mark the promised deeper connections. Two pillars, one identity family, is the paper's architecture. Symmetry explains what computation only verifies.
arxiv-2510-01441:
da Silva and colleagues at NASA Goddard generate the Sun's three-dimensional coronal magnetic field with a diffusion model trained on physics simulations. The corona shapes space weather, yet its full field resists direct measurement. Structures recur daily and cycle over years, giving a generative model patterns to learn.

Their architecture works in spherical harmonics, matching the geometry of the problem. The scalar it synthesizes is the magnetic potential itself, keeping outputs physically meaningful. Training data spans nearly twelve years of daily coupled simulations. Space weather forecasting gains a new source of plausible coronal states. Air Force flux-transport simulations supplied the training corpus. Spherical Fourier operators shape the network's inductive bias. Power grids and navigation systems feel coronal tantrums downstream. Inverse problems in heliophysics are the stated next target. Generative models meet a classical physics problem head-on here.
arxiv-2510-01641:
Liu and co-authors deblur motion-blurred photographs in a single diffusion step by redefining what a timestep means. Diffusion restorers produce superb quality but iterate too slowly and drift from the original image. Their model treats each timestep as a progressively more blurred version of the same scene.

A consistency objective aligns every blur level to the same clean target. Training pairs follow matched blur trajectories, teaching temporal consistency directly. A kernel-estimating control branch injects the specific blur into the generation. Adaptive timestep prediction then picks the right starting point per image. Full-reference metrics place the model above earlier diffusion restorers. One-step inference removes the deployment bottleneck entirely. Foundation-model priors supply the true-world modeling strength. Kernel estimation adapts restoration to each image's actual blur. Fidelity and speed stop trading against each other. Blur trajectories themselves become the whole curriculum.
arxiv-2510-01841:
Kim and five co-authors borrow knowledge from image generators to find people in raw scenes in this 2025 computer vision paper. Person search must locate a person and then match that person against a query identity. Standard systems start from ImageNet-trained backbones, which miss scene context and fine identity cues. One shared backbone also serves two tasks whose goals conflict.

Their framework, DiffPS, starts instead from a pre-trained diffusion model. Three modules divide the work cleanly. A proposal network guided by diffusion features improves person localization. A frequency refinement network reduces the shape bias that hurts matching. A semantic aggregation network uses text-aligned diffusion features for identity cues. The system set a new state of the art on the CUHK-SYSU and PRW benchmarks. The results argue diffusion priors deserve a central place in recognition pipelines.
arxiv-2510-01941:
Koskela, Karvonen, Łatuszyński, and Spanò build an unbiased estimator for a transformed probability in this 2025 statistics paper. The setup gives only coin flips with an unknown bias, plus a known function of that bias. The goal is an estimate of the function's value with no systematic error. Classical Bernoulli factories attack a cousin of this problem by manufacturing new coins from old ones.

Their estimator debiases a sequence of ever-better approximations by truncating the series at a random point. The consistent approximations come from coefficients of a tailor-made Bernoulli factory for the function. That construction yields provable upper and lower bounds on the resulting estimator. A notable bonus is that the number of coin flips consumed does not depend on their outcomes. The result doubles as a constructive example of an f-factory. It supplies exact, bias-free estimates for simulation methods that cannot tolerate approximation error.
arxiv-2510-02041:
Xiong and co-authors derive explicit upper bounds for the derivative of the Riemann zeta function on its critical line in this 2025 number theory paper. Bounds for the zeta function itself are plentiful, but effective estimates for its derivative have barely moved since Titchmarsh's 1985 result. Explicit constants matter because computer-assisted work needs numbers, not just growth rates. The authors attack the problem with exponential sum methods.

Their machinery produces a flexible formula whose parameters can be tuned for different ranges. One theorem gives a concrete bound built from the square root of the height times its logarithm, with explicit constants. A second theorem trades that shape for a sixth-root growth rate multiplied by logarithmic powers. The authors concede their bounds may not be optimal. Even so, the work refines a forty-year-old benchmark and supplies usable estimates for analytic number theory.
arxiv-2510-02241:
Gwon, Jedidi, and Lin test whether small open language models can generate training queries for search in this 2025 information retrieval paper. The Promptagator recipe uses a big proprietary model to write synthetic queries for a niche domain. A dense retriever then fine-tunes on those queries. Privacy rules and access limits block that recipe for many teams.

The authors swap in open-source models at accessible scales, up to fourteen billion parameters. Even a three-billion-parameter model proved an effective query generator in their study. Fine-tuned retrievers trained on its output performed competitively for domain-specific search. That finding frees the recipe from proprietary APIs and their data exposure. Practitioners with sensitive corpora, from hospitals to law firms, get a workable alternative. Synthetic supervision turns out to need far less model than folklore assumed.
arxiv-2510-02341:
Wang and co-authors train chatbots from the complaints users already leave behind. Their 2025 machine learning paper studies real deployment feedback. Users rarely praise answers outright. They rephrase, correct, and push back instead. Those moves signal dissatisfaction, which the authors call DSAT. Happy signals, called SAT, stay scarce by comparison. Classic preference training wants costly human labels or many positives. Their method, DRIFT, anchors learning on real dissatisfaction cases. It samples fresh positive answers from the improving model itself. Training then repeats in rounds as the model evolves.

The team trained models on the real world WildFeedback data. Synthetic tests added a second check on the approach. Learning from abundant complaints beat ignoring them. The setup matches how deployed systems actually earn feedback. Product teams sit on piles of correction traces today. DRIFT turns that waste stream into training fuel.
arxiv-2510-02641:
Croon, Linden, and Sakstein predict that dark matter should erase a class of pulsing stars near the galactic center. Their 2025 astrophysics paper studies Cepheid variables. Cepheids pulse with clocklike periods and anchor distance scales. The innermost parsec of the Milky Way packs dark matter densely. Captured dark matter annihilates inside stars there. That heat changes how the stars evolve. Stellar models show the blue loop phase gets suppressed. Without that phase, low mass stars never become short period Cepheids. The missing stars would span one to six day periods.

No Cepheids have been found close enough to test this. New infrared facilities will see through the dust. JWST and the coming ELT change the search completely. A dearth of these variables would hint at heating. The signal appears at lower densities than main sequence effects. Stars become particle detectors in this picture. Galaxy centers gain a dark matter probe.
arxiv-2510-02841:
Coggan and co-authors study fairness in a children's emergency department. They reviewed records from about three hundred forty thousand visits. The visits took place at one large United States center from 2019 to 2024. The team compared care across racial and ethnic groups. They adjusted for the reason for the visit, insurance, income level, and other illness. Matching methods kept the comparisons as fair as the data allowed.

Clear gaps in admission remained after those adjustments. Black children were admitted less often than white children with like profiles. Hispanic children showed a like gap in admission odds. Black children also got top-urgency triage scores less often. The gaps grew sharpest when vital signs looked normal. A machine learning model trained on the records picked up the same skew. It leaned harder on triage scores for Black patients. The authors warn that decision tools can inherit these hidden biases.
arxiv-2510-02941:
Trepella and co-authors ask whether numbers can replace people in judging social robots. A social robot must move among humans with care. Comfort, safety, and clarity of intent all matter. Surveys capture how people feel about a robot's path. Surveys are costly, slow, and hard to repeat. Numeric metrics are cheap and easy to compare. No standard set of them exists yet, though.

The team compared metric scores with survey scores across runs. A clustering step grouped runs in the metric space. Correlation checks then hunted for links metric by metric. Chosen metric sets did sort good runs from bad ones. Their trends matched human judgment more clearly than the full set did. Some inner factors still escaped the numbers. Mixed or partly sound runs proved hardest to grade. The authors call for new metrics aimed at those gaps. For now, surveys cannot be fully retired.
arxiv-2510-03041:
Gryb and Friederich offer a new account of why time seems to flow one way. Cups shatter but never unshatter, yet the deep laws allow both. Built-in lopsided laws lack independent support. A special low-entropy start, the Past Hypothesis, raises puzzles of its own. Their account needs neither fix. It starts from what observers can actually measure. The universe's overall scale, they argue, is not measurable at all.

What can be measured is how fast that scale changes. Removing the useless scale reshapes the dynamics. A drag-like variable appears, yet time symmetry stays intact. The space of possible histories then has universal attractors. It also has Janus points, where arrows point outward both ways. Observers near such states feel an arrow like ours. Tests on cosmic and N-body gravity models followed. The scheme explained the early universe's fast cooling and smoothness.
arxiv-2510-03341:
Li and a team at Opus AI Research present a 2025 arXiv paper on making animated charts with large multimodal models. Their task, dynamic chart generation, asks a model to write code that renders a moving chart. Static charts are well studied, but motion adds timing and change over time. The team built DCG-Bench, the test suite for this skill, plus a data set of eight thousand chart examples with code and video.

The tests cover simple text prompts, detailed text prompts, and turning a video back into chart code. Leading models did worst on the video task, the study found. The authors then trained an expert model with a two stage recipe and a joint reward for code and visuals. Their three billion parameter model beat the best open rival by an average margin across tasks. It matched closed models while staying far smaller and cheaper to run.
arxiv-2510-03441:
Islam and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on teaching vision language models to reason about space. Models that mix sight and words still stumble on questions like which object sits left of another in 3D scenes. Their system, SpatialViLT, learns from extra tasks that rebuild depth maps, edge maps, and 3D coordinates alongside the main task. A masked variant trains on partly hidden object regions. An ensemble joins both variants for the final scores.

On the Visual Spatial Reasoning data set, the models shone in direction, closeness, and containment categories. The ensemble reached state of the art accuracy in the reported tests, beating the strong LXMERT baseline by a clear margin in the study. Learning to rebuild spatial maps seems to sharpen the encoder's sense of layout. Better spatial sense matters for robots, drivers, and assistants that must talk about the physical world without mixing up where things are.
arxiv-2510-03541:
Halterman and Keith present a 2025 arXiv paper warning social scientists who use language models to label texts. Before any prompting, someone must define the concept at stake, such as what counts as a protest. Models make labeling feel so easy that teams skip that codebook work. The authors show through simulations that a sloppy concept definition bakes bias into every later estimate. Worse, neither a more accurate model nor after the fact correction formulas can wash that bias out.

The trap springs because human reference labels inherit the same fuzzy definition. Corrections tuned against those labels then lock the error in place. The authors urge a pragmatist path: pair expert built gold labels with model predictions and careful correction. They also advise heavy expert input during early codebook drafts and more generous test time computing. In the model era, defining the thing still matters more than labeling speed.
arxiv-2510-03941:
Suresh and Yoshida, at the University of Oxford, wrote this 2025 conference paper on verifying message-passing systems when communication fails. Programs whose parts exchange messages over unbounded channels are hard to verify, and most questions about them are undecidable. Two restricted subclasses, called rsc and k-mc, restore decidability and have working tools. Both assume perfect channels, and real protocols break once failures occur.

The authors study two failure types: interference, where messages get corrupted or reordered, and crash-stop failures, where a participant halts. For interference, they relax both subclasses and prove the key checks stay decidable at the same complexity. For crashes, they define a new crash-handling system that captures more behavior than existing session type frameworks. They also show both properties remain decidable there. Tests on known protocols confirmed the relaxed systems tolerate failures better. The work brings formal verification closer to messy real networks.
arxiv-2510-04041:
Saxena and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on giving robot control models the ability to look ahead before acting. Vision-language-action models turn instructions into single control steps, but they cannot plan, and small errors compound on long tasks. The authors wrap such models in a planning loop inspired by model predictive control. 

Their framework, SITCOM, asks the model to propose several candidate actions at each step. A learned dynamics model, trained on the large BridgeV2 dataset and fine-tuned for the simulator, rolls each candidate forward in imagination. A reward function scores the imagined outcomes, and the robot executes the best plan. In the SIMPLER evaluation environment, task completion rose from under half to nearly three-quarters of attempts. The study shows inference-time search can turn one-shot robot policies into more robust long-horizon planners.
arxiv-2510-04141:
Ravishankara and Persad Maharaj present this 2025 arXiv survey tracing how evaluation of multimodal AI grew from recognition tests into reasoning examinations. Early benchmarks asked only what a model sees, and models quickly saturated them while hiding weaknesses like shortcut learning. The authors frame the history as a series of cognitive examinations of rising difficulty. Each generation of tests was designed to expose the previous generation's blind spots.

The survey moves from ImageNet-era knowledge tests to diagnostic benchmarks like GQA and Visual Commonsense Reasoning, built to catch compositional failures. It then covers today's expert-level suites such as MMBench, SEED-Bench, and MMMU, which grade the reasoning process itself. A final section explores untested territory: abstract, creative, and social intelligence. The authors warn of a whack-a-mole cycle where patching one bias amplifies another. Evaluation design, they argue, quietly defines what the field calls intelligence.
arxiv-2510-04241:
Ahn and Kim present this 2025 arXiv paper on compressing self-supervised graph neural networks into plain multilayer perceptrons. For large-scale deployment, simple MLPs are far cheaper to run than graph networks, and knowledge distillation can transfer the skill. Self-supervised distillation is harder than the supervised kind because success hinges on the model's inductive bias, and the capacity gap between teacher and student is huge. The authors insert an assistant between them.

Their method, DAD-SGM, employs a denoising diffusion model as a teacher assistant during distillation. The diffusion model reshapes the teacher's knowledge into a form the small student can absorb. Extensive experiments showed the method distilling self-supervised graph networks more effectively than state-of-the-art alternatives. The code is publicly available. Cheap graph inference matters wherever graph models must run at industrial scale, from recommendation to fraud detection.
arxiv-2510-04841:
Jihong Huang, Tommy Ohlsson, Sampsa Vihonen, and Shun Zhou wrote this 2025 physics paper on a correction with big consequences for neutrino science. Neutrinos change flavor as they travel through matter, and the effect steers precision measurements. Quantum loop corrections shift that matter potential by about two percent. Two percent sounds minor, yet the authors argue it cannot be ignored. Searches for new physics live at that level of precision.

They simulated the DUNE experiment, a long baseline neutrino facility. With corrections included, oscillation probabilities and event rates shifted in the presence of interactions. Leaving the corrections out could lead experimenters to claim a discovery that is not there. Or it could hide an effect behind a modeling error. The team traced effects on measuring the neutrino mass ordering. Constraints on the interaction strengths moved as well. Future long baseline experiments must budget for loop matter effects from the start.
arxiv-2510-05141:
Byung-Doh Oh and Tal Linzen argue that better language models make worse models of the human mind in this 2025 arXiv paper. People predict upcoming words while reading, and surprising words slow them down. Early language models predicted those slowdowns well. Newer models predict text far better than people do, so their difficulty estimates drift away from human data.

The authors blame two superhuman memories. Models retain far more facts and training examples than any person. They also hold previous words in perfect short-term memory. The paper advocates training models with human-like limits on both kinds of memory. It also warns that current human datasets cannot measure progress toward that goal. New reading experiments are needed to benchmark genuinely human-like prediction.
arxiv-2510-05841:
Popa examines gravitational wave fingerprints of warm dark matter in a left-right symmetric model. The extension adds a heavy right-handed gauge boson and three right-handed neutrinos. A keV sterile neutrino serves as the dark matter candidate. Her 2025 paper asks what early-universe history makes its abundance match observations.

Heavier right-handed neutrinos briefly dominate the universe, then decay and dilute everything. That entropy release reconciles the sterile neutrino density with measurements. The type-II seesaw in the model generates the active neutrino masses. The dilution pins the lightest active neutrino mass to a narrow window. Early matter domination suppresses the gravitational wave background frequency by frequency. Suppression depth is set by the heavy neutrinos' masses and lifetimes. A blue-tilted primordial tensor spectrum can lift the signal back up. Future detectors like LISA could then detect it with strong significance.
arxiv-2510-06441:
Benjamini, Blachar, and Yadin introduce stationary random walks on lamplighter groups, finding a recurrence phase transition in a 2025 probability paper. A lamplighter walks along a base group, switching lamps at visited sites. In their stationary variant, each step switches the current lamp, moves with drift toward the identity, then switches the new lamp.

The homeward drift competes with the lamp configurations left behind. Returning requires coming home and restoring the original lamp pattern. The authors prove a sharp dichotomy across group families. When the base is virtually the integers and the lamp group is finite, a phase transition separates recurrence from transience. Otherwise, with larger base or infinite lamp group, the walks are always transient. For the integer base case they go further. They identify the exact critical parameter and describe the transition quantitatively.
arxiv-2510-06541:
Nicholas Kroeger and Vincent Bindschaedler tackle a trust problem with modern neural networks. Their 2025 paper notes that vision models score well but hide how they reach decisions. Hidden reasoning can conceal bias, shortcuts, and likely failures. The authors propose a method called cluster paths to make those decisions easier to inspect.

The method groups the activations inside a network at chosen layers. Each input then becomes a path, recorded as its sequence of group labels. Four new metrics score each path for clarity, class alignment, faithfulness, and stability. In one test, the paths exposed a model that relied on color as a shortcut. On a hair-color task with five classes, the paths reached 90 percent faithfulness. They also held 96 percent agreement when noise was added. The paths can even flag unusual inputs before the model answers.
arxiv-2510-06641:
He-Da Wang, Bo Wang, Qun-Li Lei, and Yu-Qiang Ma revisit an idea about how materials jam. Their 2025 paper studies particles under repeated shearing, a stand-in for grains or powders. Many researchers had linked the jamming transition to an absorbing-state transition. In that picture, motion dies out below a critical density, in a known universality class.

The team re-examines the minimal model behind that conjecture. At high densities, they find critical behavior that clashes with the expected class. In three-dimensional systems of identical spheres, crystallization interrupts the transition. In dense mixtures of two particle types, a different transition appears, from absorbing states to an active glass. That points to a brand-new universality class. Near the jamming point, frozen disorder in the contact network smears the transition. The results complicate a story about jamming, and they replace it with a richer one.
arxiv-2510-06741:
Zi-Yuan Wang leads a team modeling pairs of a black hole and a Wolf-Rayet star. Their 2025 paper studies three X-ray binary systems, including IC 10 X-1 and Cygnus X-3. A Wolf-Rayet star is a hot, massive star blowing off its outer layers. The black hole companion feeds on that wind. Their tight orbits, under a day and a half, make them promising sources of gravitational waves.

The team built evolution models. A new prescription governs how efficiently the black hole captures the wind. A corrected treatment handles the tides the pair raise. Matching observations capped the black hole mass near twenty-five solar masses for two systems. For Cygnus X-3, the black hole's spin cannot exceed a set fraction of its maximum. Tides mattered only for starting periods under about one day. The models map how these systems could end as merging black holes.
arxiv-2510-06941:
Ricardo Campos and Bruno Vallette apply their new integration theory to the deformation problems of bialgebra-type structures. Their 2025 paper covers structures governed by properads, a broader form of operads. Examples include associative and Lie bialgebras, Frobenius bialgebras, and double Poisson algebras. Each such structure has deformations that mathematicians organize into a groupoid.

Using their Lie-graph algebra machinery, the authors describe that Deligne groupoid in full. The description respects the flexible sameness notions of the theory. They also settle the Koszul hierarchy at the properad level, a ladder of dual structures. The twisting procedure, which produces new structures from old, gets the same treatment. The transfer theorem gets a clean construction through gauge actions. That theorem moves algebraic structure along weak links, a daily need in the field. Together, the results extend formulas long known for operads to the wider properad world.
arxiv-2510-07141:
Amouyal, Meltzer-Asscher, and Berant compare how humans and language models read tricky sentences. Their 2025 study uses seven sentence types known to strain human readers. Garden path sentences are the hardest kind. They lead readers down a wrong parse, then force a restart. The team gathered answers from people and from five families of top models under one shared setup.

Models did well on most structures but stumbled badly on garden path items. The strongest model scored near perfect on plain structures, yet below half on garden path ones. The gap between hard and matched easy sentences mirrored the human gap in most cases. Bigger models ranked the structures more like humans did. The authors credit the model edge on plain items to stronger memory and logic. The work shows that fluent chat does not mean human-like reading.
arxiv-2510-07241:
Iyer and Sharma test whether a generalized entropy can certify how useful a quantum state is for teleportation. Their 2025 paper studies the Kaniadakis entropy, a one-parameter cousin of the standard entropy. The authors link that signal to the fully entangled fraction, a score that predicts teleportation quality. They examine four benchmark states with highly mixed parts, including Werner and Weyl states in two and higher dimensions.

For each state, they derive implicit bounds that the entangled fraction must obey when the entropy goes negative. Meeting those bounds can prove a state useless for teleportation, outside small exception regions where the test stays silent. The Weyl case adds conditions tied to its correlation pattern. Such entropy-based certificates could let labs screen states for communication tasks without full state reconstruction.
arxiv-2510-07341:
Jahns, Moreno, and Kinsy let spiking neural networks learn the behavior of their own neurons. Their 2025 paper targets an energy-saving breed of networks that communicate in brief spikes. Standard spiking neurons follow a simple leak-and-fire rule. That simplicity caps accuracy, while richer neuron models need fiddly hand tuning. The team's Learnable Neuron Models replace the fixed rule with a flexible formula whose shape is learned during training. Simple polynomials keep the formula cheap and stable.

Deep spiking networks built on these neurons set new best scores. Benchmarks included standard image sets and an event-camera variant. Learned dynamics adapt the neuron's memory and firing threshold to the data at hand. The result narrows the performance gap between frugal spiking hardware and ordinary networks. It points toward chips that tune themselves to each workload.
arxiv-2510-07641:
Weaver wrote this 2025 paper in mathematical logic on how formal systems handle truth. The paper builds a system with three special predicates. One marks statements that can be constructively asserted. One marks statements that are meaningful. The third is a truth predicate that applies to the system's own sentences and follows the classic truth scheme. Combining such ideas risks paradox, so consistency is the central question.

Weaver proposes axioms that govern how the three predicates interact. He then proves that the resulting system is consistent, so no contradiction can be derived. The proof uses the idea that dangerous self-referential sentences can be kept outside each partial truth collection. Extending that collection creates new problem sentences, and the construction handles them in turn. The result shows that constructive assertibility can support a classical notion of truth without collapse into paradox.
arxiv-2510-07941:
Basu and five coauthors wrote this 2025 study of security flaws in automotive system-on-chip software. Modern cars run connected, automated functions on single chips that mix processors, radios, and AI accelerators. The AUTOSAR standard organizes that software into layers for reuse. Yet reported chip vulnerabilities keep surging, and nobody had mapped their causes inside this architecture. The authors analyzed one hundred eighty automotive SoC vulnerabilities against a representative AUTOSAR-aligned model.

They found sixteen root causes spread across fifty-six software modules. The Wi-Fi module concentrated a striking share of the flaws. Missing size and length checks recurred as a leading weakness. Some weakness classes and layers also suffered long patch delays. The authors turn those patterns into guidance for detection, prioritization, and hardening. Testers can aim audits at the riskiest modules first. As car software centralizes further, such maps become essential for keeping vehicles safe.
arxiv-2510-08041:
Watanabe and four coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper confirming a rare form of methanol in the Orion KL star-forming region. Methanol seeds the chemistry of complex organic molecules between the stars. Its oxygen-17 variant had only a tentative detection before. The team searched archival ALMA data at two methanol emission peaks, comparing sky spectra against laboratory frequencies.

Six emission lines of the oxygen-17 methanol were identified at both peaks. Their profiles matched the better-known oxygen-18 variant, showing the molecules share the same gas. The abundance ratio between the rare variants landed between three and four, matching carbon monoxide values in the region. The main methanol form proved over two thousand times more abundant. The authors propose methanol isotopologues as new tracers of oxygen isotopes, and through them, of the Galaxy's star-formation history.
arxiv-2510-08341:
Pál Zsámboki and co-authors study why transformers fail on longer inputs than they trained on, in a 2025 arXiv paper. They use set complement, a task in which a model must name the tokens absent from an input. This skill matters for board-game reasoning. Length generalization, handling longer sequences than seen in training, is the core challenge.

Their main theory result gives tight bounds on embedding and value sizes for one-layer attention models. If such a model balances its outputs at lengths one and two, it must generalize to longer inputs, but with less precision. The reason is that softmax squashes score gaps as more tokens compete for attention. Training adds a second obstacle: noise grows when many next tokens are valid. Tests confirmed that dropout counters the first effect and exponential moving averages the second. They verified the moving average gain on OthelloGPT.
arxiv-2510-08441:
Haider Abidi and co-authors measure when silicon sensors crack under cold stress in a 2025 arXiv paper for the ATLAS detector. ATLAS's new Inner Tracker glues silicon strip sensors onto carbon fibre supports with soft gel. Cooling tests below minus thirty-five degrees Celsius cracked several sensors unexpectedly. The cause was mismatched thermal expansion between silicon and attached circuit boards.

Comparable modules failed across a wide range, from minus thirty-five to minus seventy degrees. That spread pointed to hidden variation inside the silicon wafers themselves. The team built a test program using representative wafer cutoffs from sensor production. They measured the fracture stress of the silicon sensors directly. Such data helps set safe assembly and cooling limits for tracker modules. It also tells builders how much module-to-module variation to expect from the material itself.
arxiv-2510-08641:
Mathias Boulanger and Ericmoore Jossou rebuild moving X-ray scans with neural networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Dynamic X-ray tomography pictures objects that change while they are scanned, which makes rebuilding the images hard. Interlaced scan schemes spread the shots over time to catch that motion. Their method uses networks that store the moving volume as a function of space and time.

The solver mixes ADMM, a split-and-swap optimization method, with INCODE, a scheme that feeds knowledge into the network. Tests varied how sparse the shots were, how complex the scenes were, and how much noise was present. The method beat TIMBIR, a top model-based solver, in every setting. The network's built-in bias gave strength at mild noise levels. Adding a noise model through weighted least squares helped in harsher, noisier cases. The design corrects ring flaws from the detector inside the rebuild.
arxiv-2510-08741:
Masis and O'Connor tackle a hard version of geocoding in this 2025 arXiv paper. Geocoding means linking a place mentioned in text to real map coordinates. Their focus is descriptions built from other places, such as a spot described as lying midway between two towns. Tools that look places up in a database cannot handle such phrases, because the spot itself has no database entry.

The authors test whether large language models, programs trained to work with text, fail from weak map knowledge or from weak reasoning. They find the models know less about where places are than their reasoning skills would suggest. Their fix pairs model reasoning with knowledge from older geocoding tools and marks each answer as a box on the map. The approach beats earlier methods, and a small tuned model matches far larger ones.
arxiv-2510-08841:
Mallu studies how spread out a directed network can be, in this 2025 arXiv paper in graph theory. A digraph is a web of points joined by one-way links, like one-way streets between intersections. For each point, the average distance counts the mean steps needed to reach every other point. The remoteness of the whole web is the largest of those averages, a measure of its worst-served corner.

The author proves a sharp upper bound on remoteness for strongly connected digraphs, webs where every point can reach every other. The bound depends on three given facts: how many points there are, how many links, and how many points must be removed to break the web apart. The paper also pinpoints exactly which digraphs hit the bound. As a last step, it shows that known bounds for ordinary undirected graphs carry over to a wider family called Eulerian digraphs.
arxiv-2510-09241:
Ferreira and Jové give one unified account of the wild boundaries that arise in complex dynamics when a region maps into itself with holes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Iterating a transcendental map splits the plane into the calm Fatou set and the chaotic Julia set. A Fatou component is one calm region, and multiply connected ones wrap around holes, making their boundaries intricate. Earlier work treated stable components and wandering domains, regions that never repeat, with separate toolkits.

The authors approach both through universal covering maps, which unroll a holed region onto a disk, and the inner functions those maps induce. Their treatment covers invariant components of every type alongside wandering domains. The central theorem says every Fatou component carries a harmonic measure supported on its entire boundary. They then connect the boundary's geometry, the dynamics on it, and the inner function's analytic properties.
arxiv-2510-09341:
Hanlin Sun, Filippo Radicchi, and Ginestra Bianconi extend a network model in a 2025 arXiv paper on percolation, which studies how a connected cluster spreads through a network. Their focus is triadic interactions, where a third regulator node strengthens or weakens the link between two other nodes. On a single network layer, such rules already turn percolation into a dynamical system that can tip into chaos.

The authors generalise the model to multilayer networks, where nodes connect across several layers at once, and call it multilayer triadic percolation. The richer setup shows behaviour the single-layer version lacks. It produces a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation, a change that creates oscillations of very long or uneven period. It also allows steady two-step oscillations without any negative regulation. The authors link the model to brain networks, climate, and ecosystems.
arxiv-2510-09541:
Chenyu Wang and eleven co-authors, among them Tommi Jaakkola and Yuandong Tian, tackle preference training for diffusion language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion models generate several tokens in parallel, making them an efficient rival to autoregressive models. Aligning them with human preferences through reinforcement learning is hard, because their true log-likelihood cannot be computed, and standard policy gradient methods need it.

Existing work uses one-sided approximations such as the evidence lower bound, which can bias the training signal. The authors propose the Sandwiched Policy Gradient, which uses both an upper and a lower bound on the log-likelihood to bracket the truth. In experiments, their method clearly beat baselines built on the lower bound or one-step estimates. Gains over the best rival reinforcement learning methods reached three point six percent on GSM8K, eighteen point four on Countdown, and twenty-seven percent on Sudoku puzzles.
arxiv-2510-09641:
Lei Wu, the sole author, models a laser-based flow measurement in a 2025 arXiv paper. Coherent Rayleigh-Brillouin scattering probes dilute gas flows with high signal quality and nanosecond time resolution. To read the measurements, experimental spectra must be matched against theory derived from the Boltzmann equation, the master equation of gas kinetics.

Wu develops a MATLAB code that solves the Boltzmann equation deterministically and produces a theoretical spectrum in about a minute per line shape. Two findings stand out. The computed spectrum proves highly sensitive to the intermolecular potential, the force law between molecules, so the choice of that law shapes any flow inferred from data. Rapid chirping of the laser, meaning a fast sweep of its frequency, generates fine ripples around the central Rayleigh peak together with spectral asymmetries. Both effects matter for anyone extracting flow information from such spectra.
arxiv-2510-09741:
Dwip Dalal and eight co-authors, among them Svetlana Lazebnik and Heng Ji, improve visual perception by warping images in a 2025 arXiv paper. Multimodal language models often miss the small details and the spatial relations in cluttered scenes, which leads to errors when grounding language in pictures. Their method, AttWarp, spends the image's resolution where it matters most.

At test time, the model's own cross-modal attention guides a rectilinear warping of the input. Regions the model deems important for the query gain resolution, while less informative areas compress, and no image information is thrown away. The global layout survives, so the same model simply reads a better-organised picture, with no change to its weights or architecture. Across five benchmarks and four different models, including LLaVA and Qwen-VL, AttWarp consistently raised accuracy, strengthened compositional reasoning, and reduced hallucinations, beating four rival test-time image manipulations.
arxiv-2510-09841:
Samantha Hasler, Leonid Pogorelyuk, Riley Fitzgerald, Kerri Cahoy, and Rhonda Morgan tackle a mix-up problem for future exoplanet missions in a 2025 arXiv paper. Telescopes such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory will image Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars in reflected light. In a multi-planet system, a detection does not announce which planet it is, and that confusion can misplace a planet inside or outside the habitable zone.

Their deconfuser tool ranks candidate orbits for each detection. This work adds a photometry model to the ranking, using how a planet's brightness varies with phase around its orbit. Tested on deliberately confused simulated systems across three inclination groupings, the ranking read previously confused orbits correctly in more than half of these hard cases.
arxiv-2510-10041:
Han and co-authors present FOSSIL in this 2025 arXiv paper on medical image diagnosis. FOSSIL is a curriculum learning framework for diagnosing Mpox from images, designed for settings with little data and no metadata. Deep learning on small, imbalanced medical datasets often trains unstably and generalizes poorly.

FOSSIL weights each training sample by its difficulty, shifting emphasis adaptively as training proceeds. The authors describe this as regret-minimizing: the weighting keeps balancing so that no group of samples is badly neglected. It is, they report, the first biomedical use of this framework. Metadata-free design matters because clinical images often arrive without the labels and records that many pipelines quietly assume.
arxiv-2510-10341:
Chen, Ningyuan Huang, and Soledad Villar learn from graphs at several scales in this 2025 arXiv paper on graph neural networks. Such networks scale with the number of edges, which suits sparse graphs but not dense ones like point clouds or molecular interactions. The usual fix sparsifies the graph at one chosen scale and discards the rest.

The authors introduce a multi-view graph-tuple framework that keeps several scales at once. Each view of the tuple captures interactions at a different range, and the model learns across them jointly. No single threshold decides what counts as a neighbor. Keeping all scales should preserve information that one-scale pruning loses, at a manageable cost.
arxiv-2510-10441:
Oem Trivedi explores what follows if black holes and the edge of the universe obey different heat laws, in this 2025 arXiv paper. His Thermodynamic Split Conjecture holds that black hole thermodynamics and cosmological horizon thermodynamics are not the same thing. Earlier work stated the idea. Here Trivedi traces its effects through the Gibbons-Hawking temperature, the temperature tied to the cosmic horizon, across the history of the universe.

He shows that several known results could change under the split. These include claims about eternal inflation, vacuum tunneling, quantum breaking, and black holes formed in the early universe. He also finds that small corrections to horizon thermodynamics, of the kind the split motivates, can subtly alter the Friedmann dynamics that govern cosmic expansion. Those shifts might help ease the Hubble constant and S8 tensions, two stubborn measurement clashes. Trivedi closes by calling for tests of the thermal laws of the universe.
arxiv-2510-10641:
Wu-Long Xu, Jin Min Yang, and Jun Zhao study how the physical size of particles changes the way they scatter, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most scattering theory treats particles as points. The team instead considers non-relativistic particles with different finite sizes. They first calculate the interaction potential, then apply the partial wave method to obtain the scattering cross section. Their central finding is that particle size can significantly affect the scattering outcome.

They then apply the analysis to direct detection of puffy dark matter, a hypothetical form with extended size. The finite size of the target nucleus can introduce non-perturbative effects unlike the point-like case. For large dark matter particles, this regime effectively disappears. For small ratios of size to interaction range, it can persist. For nugget type puffy dark matter, stability conditions on bound state formation can constrain the predicted detection cross section.
arxiv-2510-10741:
H M Maridi models the inner geometry of light atomic nuclei with packed spheres, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The work belongs to the NUCLEI-PACK project. Its semi-classical framework arranges nucleons and clusters by an optimized sphere packing algorithm. From those explicit coordinates, the model directly gives charge, matter, and core valence radii. That allows quantitative study of clustering and of halo nuclei, whose outer nucleons drift far from the core.

The study covers one neutron halo nuclei such as beryllium-11 and carbon-19, and two neutron halo systems such as helium-6 and lithium-11. For halos, a fitted geometric offset grows as the nucleon separation energy falls, reflecting how weakly bound nucleons decouple from the core. The framework also reproduces neutron pair separations and opening angles in Borromean nuclei, and captures alpha cluster arrangements in lithium and carbon isotopes. Maridi argues simple geometry links binding and observed radii surprisingly well.
arxiv-2510-11141:
Spotting abnormal points in streams of measurements matters for modern digital infrastructure, yet detection methods are rarely compared across domains in one frame. Mohammad Karami, Mostafa Jalali, and Fatemeh Ghassemi build such a frame in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their forecasting-based pipeline unifies classical methods such as Holt-Winters and SARIMA with deep learning models such as LSTM and Informer under one residual-based detection interface.

The authors ran the first complete evaluation on the Numenta Anomaly Benchmark, covering 58 datasets in seven categories with 232 training runs and 464 detection evaluations. LSTM performed best, reaching an F1 score of 0.688 and ranking first or second on 81 percent of the datasets tested. Informer was nearly as accurate and trained 30 percent faster. Forecasting quality mattered more than the choice of detector, and the authors give guidance on when each model family is the right pick.
arxiv-2510-11441:
The doubling map is the simplest chaotic map, and perturbing it with a kinked sine-like term creates a family. Anubrato Bhattacharyya and Kuntal Banerjee analyze that family, which they call piecewise linear perturbations of the doubling map, in this 2025 arXiv dynamical systems paper. 

The authors prove that whenever the map has an attracting cycle, that cycle is unique. They define tongues and eyes as regions of parameter space where an attracting cycle exists. Tongues are the regions that touch the top boundary along an interval. They prove that tongues of all types exist. They also show how the combinatorics of the attracting orbit decides whether its parameter region is a tongue or an eye. Outside the closure of these regions, the map is conjugate to the plain doubling map. Computer experiments support the existence of eyes for several combinatorics.
arxiv-2510-11641:
Atomic nuclei can be spherical, stretched like a rugby ball, or triaxial, stretched differently along all three axes, and germanium-70 is a contested case of shape coexistence. T. M. Kowalewski and a large collaboration measured its low-lying states in this 2025 arXiv nuclear physics paper. At Argonne's ATLAS facility they fired a germanium-70 beam at a lead-208 target and used multi-step Coulomb excitation to map the transitions between states.

From the measured cross sections they extracted twenty-seven transitional and six diagonal matrix elements coupling eleven low-lying states, yielding transition rates, quadrupole moments, and rotational-invariant shape values with enhanced precision. Rotor, shell-model, and density-functional calculations all agreed well with the data. Together with a two-state mixing analysis, the results support clear triaxiality and strong mixing between the two lowest zero-spin states, whose deformations are more similar than previously observed.
arxiv-2510-11941:
Rebecca Lin, Michal Lukáč, and Mackenzie Leake redesign clothing as a kit of reusable parts. Store-bought garments come in fixed sizes and styles, while bodies and fashions keep changing. Alterations can adjust a garment only slightly, need sewing, and cannot be undone. Their system, Refashion, was presented at the UIST 2025 conference in Busan and posted on arXiv the same year.

Refashion starts from a compact set of fabric modules and connectors that serve as building blocks. An integer linear programming method decomposes a target garment into those modules automatically. A digital design tool lets users plan garments and simulate how they drape before cutting cloth. In the team's demonstration, one module set became trousers, then resized, then transformed entirely into a sleeveless dress. A user evaluation suggested the approach supports a wide range of garments, reusing the same blocks.
arxiv-2510-12241:
Li and colleagues propose Ivan-ISTD, a method for spotting tiny infrared targets when conditions change between datasets, in a 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Infrared small target detection supports drone based sensing, but models trained in one domain often fail in another. Noise that varies in strength across the image, called heteroscedastic noise, makes the problem harder still.

The framework works in two stages guided by wavelets, which split an image by frequency. First, wavelet guided synthesis creates training samples aligned with the target domain by separating the background across frequency bands. Second, real domain noise invariance learning builds a dynamic library of actual noise patterns from the target domain, and the model learns to ignore them through a self supervised loss. The authors also built a benchmark dataset that simulates real distribution shifts. Ivan-ISTD outperformed leading methods on many measures and proved especially robust across domains.
arxiv-2510-12341:
Thomson-Paressant and colleagues expand the known list of magnetic pulsating stars of a specific type and ask how magnetism affects their pulsations, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Delta Scuti stars pulsate with typical frequencies, but only a handful were known to also host strong surface magnetic fields. The team set out to find more by combining several target sources.

They gathered archival and new polarization data and analyzed them with the Least Squares Deconvolution method to measure line of sight fields. They also mined photometry from the TESS satellite for pulsation frequencies and rotation signals. The compiled list now holds thirteen confirmed magnetic delta Scuti stars, the largest such database so far. Most lie outside the usual instability strip where pulsations are expected, and no clear correlation with field strength emerged. The authors conclude that strong global fields shape stellar interiors and must enter sound stellar models.
arxiv-2510-12441:
Maeta proves that a class of geometric solitons on Sasakian manifolds collapses to the trivial case under one condition, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Einstein type manifolds unify several soliton concepts, including Ricci solitons and Yamabe solitons, under four constants that tune the defining equation. Sasakian manifolds are odd dimensional spaces with a rich contact structure, common in geometry and physics.

Maeta studies gradient Einstein type structures on Sasakian manifolds and focuses on the case where the first constant, alpha, equals zero. He shows that every such manifold is trivial, meaning the soliton structure reduces to the underlying Einstein like geometry with no genuine soliton behavior. As a result, many geometric solitons that might have lived on Sasakian manifolds are forced to be trivial as well. The result clears up the landscape the unifying framework of Catino and co-authors opened up, within this parameter slice.
arxiv-2510-12541:
Freudenberg and colleagues evaluate preprocessing methods for electrocardiogram signals so analysis can run in real time on edge devices, in a 2025 arXiv paper connected to the FACE project. Long term heart recordings are increasingly captured by portable systems, where privacy rules and energy limits favor processing at the point of acquisition rather than in the cloud. Edge processing also cuts latency.

The work examines various preprocessing steps for ECG signals and judges their suitability for the project's edge component. Selection criteria center on processing capability, energy efficiency, and real time capability, alongside the accuracy the later machine learning stages require. The FACE project aims to combine edge and cloud strengths in one system for long term electrocardiogram analysis. By screening preprocessing methods against edge constraints early, the authors aim to keep the final system responsive and privacy compliant without sacrificing signal quality.
arxiv-2510-12741:
Tupper and Gagné fine tune vision foundation models across hospitals without pooling patient data, personalizing what each site learns, in a 2025 arXiv medical machine learning paper. Foundation models still need task specific fine tuning for healthcare uses, and no single hospital may hold enough data. Privacy rules block simply aggregating data, so federated learning, training across sites that keep their data, is the natural route.

Their personalized federated method learns orthogonal adapter modules, in the low rank adaptation style, that disentangle general knowledge from client specific knowledge. Orthogonality keeps the two kinds of knowledge from interfering, so each client can exploit both its own data and everyone else's. Preliminary findings on real world federated medical imaging tasks show the approach is competitive with current federated fine tuning methods. The authors present the disentanglement idea as a way to balance shared learning against the real differences between clinical sites.
arxiv-2510-13241:
Zhou simulates how the way a star cluster forms decides its black holes in this 2025 arXiv paper. Open clusters expel their leftover gas early in life, and that violent phase shapes everything after. Recent Gaia discoveries of dormant black holes in binaries make cluster black hole retention a live observational question.

Zhou ran N-body simulations of individual clusters and of subcluster coalescence, comparing gas expulsion modes and formation channels. Faster expulsion caused greater mass loss, and a broad degeneracy linked initial mass, expulsion timescale, and formation channel in both evolutionary paths and black hole production. With slower expulsion, progressively lower-mass clusters could still retain central black holes inside their tidal radius, while the fraction of high-velocity stars fell. Slowly expanding clusters kept more black holes and multiple systems, making them prime targets for Gaia black hole searches.
arxiv-2510-13341:
Korre and Pavlopoulos analyze sentiment in Greek proverbs in this 2025 arXiv paper. Proverbs carry cultural wisdom across generations, mostly through oral tradition, leaving much of the world's proverb landscape unmapped. The authors start from an annotated dataset of Greek proverbs and extend it to local dialects, charting where different sentiments live.

They show how large language models can classify proverb sentiment accurately enough when the task is treated as non-conventional sentiment polarity rather than ordinary opinion mining. Combining geography, dialect, and topic, they produce a map of Greece showing the distribution of sentiment across regions. Negative sentiment proved more prevalent in most areas. The study is computational folkloristics: language technology applied to folk sayings as cultural data, with the map and combined analysis as its main results.
arxiv-2510-13441:
Webber and co-authors adapt diffusion-based reconstruction of PET scans to handle domain shift. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns positron emission tomography, a scan that maps tracer activity in the body. Models trained on one anatomy or protocol can invent false structures on different data. That risk, called hallucination, blocks clinical trust in learned reconstruction. The work builds on the group's own earlier PET-LiSch method.

The team adds steerable conditional diffusion to their earlier likelihood-scheduled framework. At scan time, low-rank adaptation nudges the model's prior toward the target subject at each step. This steering happens on the fly, with no retraining of the base model. Tests use realistic synthetic two-dimensional brain phantoms with deliberate domain shift. The method suppressed hallucinated structure that the shifted prior produced. It beat both a standard iterative method and plain diffusion baselines on quality measures.
arxiv-2510-13641:
Waschitz, Stern, and Oreg show how a quantum twisting microscope could read how electrons pair up in flat materials. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds the theory for this tunnelling tool. A graphene tip turns against a flat sample, and matching motion rules steer which electrons tunnel across. How pairing strength varies with motion direction can reveal how electrons bind in odd superconductors.

The tool would read the paired state's spectrum along set paths in motion space. The balance of electron-like and hole-like signals encodes the pairing size through known factors. Three tunnelling paths, linked by threefold rotation, can expose broken rotational symmetry in the sample. They can also pinpoint the spots where pairing drops to zero. The authors test the scheme on two models of twisted bilayer graphene. One skips how electrons push on each other; the other, a heavy fermion model, includes that push.
arxiv-2510-13941:
Vijay Balasubramanian and Charlie Cummings build tensor networks, mathematical constructions for assembling quantum states, that respect the symmetries of three-dimensional gravity, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Tensor networks are prized in holography, the idea that gravity in a volume can be described by a theory on its boundary, Standard versions are not invariant under diffeomorphisms, though. Those are the smooth reshapings of coordinates that gravity must allow.

Earlier work fixed similar problems for networks based on topological field theories with finite or compact symmetry groups. The authors generalize the construction to groups that may be discrete or continuous, compact or not. Applied to Chern-Simons theory, a standard reformulation of gravity, with the group relevant to negatively curved space, their networks prepare states satisfying the theory's constraints. In ordinary metric language, the states solve the Wheeler-DeWitt equation and the momentum constraints, making them genuinely diffeomorphism invariant.
arxiv-2510-14141:
Teale Masrani and co-authors report fieldwork on how frontline shelter staff use data when making high-stakes decisions about people facing homelessness, in this 2025 paper published in the PACM Human-Computer Interaction journal. Staff at emergency shelters face vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue, and burnout, and their software is rarely designed for their needs; research usually focuses on automating their decisions instead.

From 2022 to 2024, the team co-designed, built, and deployed an interactive interface with staff at a large Canadian emergency shelter, supporting collaborative decisions rather than replacing them. They unpack why staff resist outsourcing decisions about people to data systems. They propose a 'data-outsourcing continuum' for how much judgment staff are willing to hand over. Their findings guide designers toward tools that support data-informed decision-making in nonprofit settings instead of handing it to software.
arxiv-2510-14441:
Francesco De Paolis, Faryal Naseem, and Noraiz Tahir test a candidate cause of a temperature asymmetry seen in the microwave background toward galaxies, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The candidate is anomalous microwave emission from dust in the halo of the Andromeda galaxy, M 31. The asymmetry matters because it might reveal the missing baryons, regular matter unaccounted for in halos, but only if its cause is understood.

With halo dust grains of amorphous carbon and silicates across a range of sizes and masses, the authors estimated the dust's mass and distribution. They estimated its emission in the hundred-micron band, and the asymmetry its rotation would induce. They then compared the result with Planck data. That emission falls far short: it can account for at most seven percent of the measured asymmetry. More mechanisms must be responsible for the signal, and the missing-baryon reading of the asymmetry remains unproven.
arxiv-2510-14741:
Carnemolla and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a framework that explains an image classifier's behavior in plain words, without ever seeing its training data. Understanding what a vision model has learned matters for trust, but most explanation tools need the original data or labels. Their system, DEXTER, instead interrogates the classifier by generating pictures and watching what excites it.

DEXTER optimizes text prompts so a diffusion model synthesizes images that strongly activate the classifier for a chosen class. A large language model then studies those synthetic samples and writes a report on the class-specific patterns and biases it finds. The authors demonstrate three uses: activation maximization, discovering and fixing weak slices of data, and explaining bias. On ImageNet, Waterbirds, CelebA, and FairFaces, plus a user study, DEXTER outperformed existing approaches at global explanation and class-level bias reporting.
arxiv-2510-14941:
Hazra tests, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether dark energy might be a scalar field coupled to gravity, in light of the latest cosmic data. The model pairs an exponential potential with a non-minimal coupling, and is analyzed in the Palatini formulation of gravity, where the connection is treated independently. Phase space analysis comes first, before any data fitting.

The dynamics contain a late-time stable de Sitter attractor, an accelerating state, whenever the coupling constant is negative, regardless of the potential's slope. Fitted against microwave background data, DESI baryon acoustic oscillations, and the DESY5 supernova sample, the model beat the standard cosmological constant picture with a log Bayes factor of 5.52 in the comparison, which counts as strong evidence. The data preferred dynamical dark energy at over three sigma, and a phantom crossing at two to three sigma. Palatini gravity fit marginally better than the metric formulation.
arxiv-2510-15041:
Li, Li, Zhang, Feng, and Torralba present GDGen, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a framework that simulates rigid objects, jointed bodies, and squishy materials under one set of rules. Digital twins that agents can interact with need all three at once, but simulators specialize, and stitching them together is painful. GDGen starts from an energy principle: the potential energy of any stable physical system should be low.

Taking that perspective lets the system treat the world as one whole and infer hidden physical traits from simple motion observations. The authors extend elastodynamics with directional stiffness, a material description spanning soft elastic, articulated, and rigid behavior. A specialized network models the material properties, while a neural field represents deformation in a geometry-free way. Experiments show the system unifies the three simulation paradigms, offering a foundation for interactive virtual worlds and for training robotic agents in complex settings.
arxiv-2510-15141:
Zelong Bi and Pierre Lafaye de Micheaux tackle a basic question about complex data: how many true dimensions does it live on? Their 2025 arXiv paper, published in Pattern Recognition, concerns manifolds, the curved surfaces that high-dimensional data often hug. Knowing that hidden dimension helps analysts simplify data without losing its real structure, and local PCA, a standard method, estimates it by flattening small patches.

The authors build a broader framework that reads a manifold's local graph structure by mixing PCA with regression fits, which follow curvature instead of assuming each patch is flat. From that framework they draw two new estimators, called quadratic embedding and total least squares. In tests on both synthetic and real datasets, the new estimators matched or beat the leading alternatives across many settings. The work extends a line of curvature-aware methods that had already improved on plain local PCA.
arxiv-2510-15441:
I. Sultana, A. Estradé, B. S. Meyer, and H. Schatz hunt for the nuclear reactions that most distort models of x-ray bursts on neutron stars. Their 2025 arXiv paper explains that these bursts are thermonuclear runaways in fuel piled onto an accreting neutron star. Proton and alpha captures on neutron-poor nuclei power them, but many of those reaction rates are poorly measured.

The team varied rates across a wide grid of accretion rates and fuel mixes. They found forty-one reactions that change the burst light curve and one hundred eighty-seven that change the final ashes. Bottleneck reactions on the main capture paths hit both observables at once. Most captures on medium and heavy nuclei changed only the final composition. Some rates also move the carbon yield in helium-rich bursts, which matters for igniting far larger superbursts. The list names targets for lab measurements.
arxiv-2510-15541:
Saumya B checks whether an uncertainty trick flags where a medical AI is wrong, in this solo 2025 paper. The task is outlining brain tumors in two-dimensional MRI slices with a U-Net model. Monte Carlo dropout, which runs the model many times with random parts switched off, is widely used to estimate where the model is unsure.

Saumya computed uncertainty from fifty stochastic passes and compared it with the model's actual errors. Four training setups varied the data augmentation, from none to flips, rotations, and scaling. Global correlations between uncertainty and error were weak, around a third at best. Near tumor boundaries, where errors hurt most, the correlation nearly vanished. Augmentation differences were statistically significant yet practically tiny. The author concludes that Monte Carlo dropout gives clinicians poor guidance about boundary errors and urges alternative or hybrid uncertainty methods.
arxiv-2510-15641:
Fusion reactors line their walls with tungsten, which slowly forms mixed deposits under plasma attack. S. Kodate, Y. Hayashi, and S. Kajita study such deposits in this 2025 arXiv experimental paper. They combined pulsed laser deposition with helium and argon plasma in a linear plasma device. This setup mimics brief, intense deposition events like those from plasma instabilities in reactors. Under co-deposition conditions, micron-sized spherical tungsten particles formed on the substrate surface.

The authors suggest the spheres grew from nanoparticles before landing on the surface. Plasma ions gathered electrostatically in the plume, feeding particle growth during flight. Surface microscopy supports this picture of how the co-deposition layer forms.
arxiv-2510-15741:
Ondřej Faltus and colleagues report a materials result in a 2025 paper. They switched the stiffness of a rubber honeycomb with air pressure. No mechanical squeezing was needed. Honeycombs with round voids are known to snap into set patterns. This happens when the material is strained. The team asked if air could trigger the same patterns. They inflated or emptied chosen voids.

Simulations showed the pattern depends on pressure ratios. Different voids received different suction levels. Tests on silicone samples confirmed the effect. The samples were cast in printed moulds. During pattern formation, stiffness changed by about a factor of two. Its direction also changed. The work points to soft structures with tunable stiffness.
arxiv-2510-15841:
Jiayi Lin, Jiabo Huang, and Shaogang Gong wrote a 2025 paper on image segmentation. The task labels every pixel in an image. Open-vocabulary systems use categories they never trained on. Vision-language models match image patches to candidate labels. But they grasp spatial relations poorly. A cat to the right of a person may be missed. It may also be confused with another object.

Their system is called RelateSeg. It extracts spatial relations from a scene on its own. It encodes them as first-order logic rules. The rules sit inside a neural network. The authors present this as a first for the task. Neuro-symbolic spatial reasoning replaces pure correlation. The constraints it adds can be checked.
arxiv-2510-16041:
Xiang Chen, Ce Xu, and Jianing Zhou evaluate a family of integrals whose integrands use only hyperbolic cosine functions. Integrals of Berndt type hide surprising closed forms. This class is approached in clear stages. Contour integration first turns the integral into a Ramanujan-type hyperbolic series. That name marks its likeness to series Ramanujan studied.

An auxiliary function with a free parameter is then added. The residue theorem simplifies mixed denominators, where cosine and sine terms were tangled. The result is a clean series with single-term denominators. Jacobi elliptic functions, Fourier expansions, and Maclaurin expansions finish the job together. The final answer is an explicit rational polynomial built from two named constants. One constant comes from the Gamma function, the other from pi. The work also links the integral to Barnes multiple zeta functions. That link opens a new route for related problems.
arxiv-2511-00041:
Yingzhao Jian, Zhongan Wang, Yi Yang, and colleagues present BiBo, a system that lets off-the-shelf vision-language models such as GPT-4 control humanoid robots. Training a dedicated model on massive datasets is the usual route and is prohibitively expensive. Instead, their bridge connects a general model's open-world generalization to a humanoid body, reducing the need for robot-specific data collection.

Humanoid agents struggle with flexible, diverse interactions in open environments, which is exactly where large vision-language models are strong. Robotics readers get an alternative architecture: reuse general perception and reasoning, and engineer the interface to physical action. The approach trades training cost for systems design.
arxiv-2511-00141:
Janghoon Cho, Jungsoo Lee, and Munawar Hayat present FLoC, a visual token compression method that makes long video understanding by multimodal models affordable. Extended videos generate overwhelming numbers of visual tokens, which limits how much video such models can process. Facility location, a principled selection objective, picks a compact subset of tokens that stays representative and diverse within a fixed budget.

Selected tokens carry the video's varied content without near-duplicates wasting context. Multimodal AI readers get a scalable preprocessing step for hour-scale video. Compression quality decides whether long video models reason about the whole story or only its beginning.
arxiv-2511-00341:
Mihir Sahasrabudhe points out a hidden symmetry in how language models are trained. The standard training goal, predicting the next token, gives a text and its exact reversal the same likelihood. In that sense the goal is direction-blind, even though human language and reasoning are strongly time-ordered. The symmetry helps explain a curious finding: models trained on reversed text can perform about as well as models trained on normal text.

Sahasrabudhe argues this is a real limitation, not a harmless quirk. If word order carries phonological, morphological, and causal information, a symmetric goal may miss it.
