He proposes judging pretraining by temporal asymmetry, and calls for losses and architectures that model the arrow of language while keeping standard modeling skill.
arxiv-2511-00441:
Yin-Long Yang, Fang-Ping Peng, Yan-Ting Yang, Hai-Bing Fu, and Sheng-Quan Wang calculate a rare decay of the charmed D meson, spurred by fresh measurements from the BESIII experiment. In the decay, a D meson turns into an omega meson plus a lepton and a neutrino. Their tool is the QCD light-cone sum rule, a method that connects quark-level theory to measurable form factors.

A right-handed chiral current makes one ingredient dominate: the omega meson's transverse twist-2 distribution amplitude, which they model with a light-cone harmonic oscillator. From it they extract form factor values at large recoil and two key ratios, then extend the results across the full decay range. Predicted branching fractions agree well with BESIII and CLEO measurements. They also forecast asymmetries and polarization measures for future tests.
arxiv-2511-00541:
Omar Hatem and Daoud Siniora settle a long-open puzzle in group theory. Can a finite group have exactly one element that is not a commutator, a product built from pairs of elements and their inverses? The question had resisted direct attack, so the authors turn to computation guided by theory, using a classic result of Frobenius and necessary properties any such group must have.

Working with the GAP computer algebra system and an extensive enumeration of finite perfect groups, they searched systematically up to a chosen order. Two non-isomorphic groups of order three hundred sixty-eight thousand six hundred forty pass the test, and no smaller group does. The answer resolves a problem from the Kourovka Notebook, and a structural description of one group is included.
arxiv-2511-00641:
Swapnil Bhosale and nine co-authors give early-exit networks a sense of hierarchy by moving them into hyperbolic space. Early-exit models let easy inputs leave a network early, saving computation on small devices, but their early predictions can be unreliable because nothing enforces order between layers. Event detection on constrained hardware is the motivating use case.

Their framework, HypEE, trains exits so deeper layers geometrically refine shallower ones, using a new entailment loss that imposes a partial order on representations. Across several audio event detection tasks and backbones, HypEE beat standard Euclidean early-exit baselines, with the largest gains at the earliest, most cost-critical exits. The learned geometry doubles as an uncertainty measure, powering a principled trigger that decides when to exit, making the system both cheaper and more accurate.
arxiv-2511-00741:
Pedro Felzenszwalb and Heon Lee study an unfashionable problem: maximizing a convex function over a convex set in a Hilbert space. Maximization usually hunts concave goals, so convex maximization, where the best points hide at extremes, needs its own theory. The authors analyze projected subgradient ascent, the simple loop that steps uphill and projects back into the allowed set.

For linear functions, one orthogonal projection already yields an approximate solution. For continuous convex functions, the ascent converges to a first-order stationary point even with arbitrarily large step sizes, a surprising license to stride. Sending step sizes to infinity produces a deterministic variant of the conditional gradient algorithm, with iterated linear optimization as a special case. Simple geometry, pushed hard, turns out to organize several known methods at once.
arxiv-2511-01441:
Hong-Gang Yang, Marcos Pellejero, John Peacock, and Romeel Dave compare galaxy assembly bias in two flagship cosmological simulations. Assembly bias is the dependence of galaxy clustering on properties beyond halo mass, and it complicates efforts to read cosmology from galaxy maps. Baryonic physics, the messy part simulations model differently, might strengthen or wash it out.

They measure the effect in the largest SIMBA and IllustrisTNG runs by comparing real clustering with shuffled samples where galaxies are reassigned among similar mass halos. In both simulations the bias grows from near zero early on to about a five percent clustering change by redshift two. After that the two diverge: it keeps rising in IllustrisTNG toward ten percent today, while in SIMBA it fades back to nearly zero, with environment density driving most of the signal.
arxiv-2511-01541:
Arthur Hubert, Gamal Elghazaly, and Raphaël Frank work on making rare, dangerous driving scenarios. Such scenarios are used to test self-driving cars. The events that matter most almost never happen on real roads. They organize each scenario in a structured five-layer model, extended so every agent in the scene carries its own subclasses and traits.

Large base models then generate new scenarios by augmenting data within that structure. The layer-based embedding lets scenarios be compared directly. Two scores judge the output: a diversity score, measuring how much scenarios differ from each other, and an originality score, measuring how close a synthetic set stays to real reference data. The team shows both scores at work across setups for making new scenarios. They also add a look at the quality of synthetic videos made from the structured forms.
arxiv-2511-01641:
Xiaopeng Ke and six colleagues estimate treatment effects when treatments are not yes-or-no. Treatments here come in multiple categories with multiple values each. That is common in medicine and online testing. Existing causal methods handle it poorly. Combinations of interventions interact, and the interactions are exactly what decision-makers need to know.

Their network, XTNet, separates basic effects from cross-treatment interactions and uses a dynamic masking module to capture those interactions without restrictive structural assumptions, which keeps the combinatorial space in check. A companion metric, MCMV-AUCC, scores methods while accounting for treatment costs and interaction effects. On synthetic and real-world data XTNet beat the leading baselines in ranking accuracy and estimation quality, and a real-world A/B test confirmed the advantage.
arxiv-2511-01841:
Dmitry Pushin and a large team report a new visual phenomenon inside the eye itself. Boehm's brushes are entoptic patterns, faint two-lobed shapes a person sees when polarized light hits the retina. Projecting spin-orbit coupled light, beams that entangle circular polarization with orbital angular momentum, transformed the pattern into a multi-lobed structure.

The effect arises from polarization-dependent scattering in the retina, not from the dichroic absorption behind the better-known Haidinger's brushes. Where retinal scattering centers' orientations converge, their contributions reinforce, sharpening lobes whose number and orientation track the light's topology. Measurements in eleven participants found detection thresholds falling exponentially with distance from the visual center. The fitted midpoint came out near one degree. That fits scattering by isotropic structures outside the fovea.
arxiv-2511-02141:
Solange Bridgitte Difo, a mathematician in operator theory, supplies a detailed proof of a theorem due to Xia about operators on a Fock space. The setting is the space of analytic functions square-integrable against a measure on complex n-dimensional space. Within it sits a class of weakly localized operators, defined by how their action concentrates, and the C-star algebra those operators generate.

Xia's theorem identifies that generated algebra exactly: it coincides with a specific algebra denoted T with superscript one in the literature. Results of this kind matter because they pin down the global structure created by a concrete class of operators, which then constrains everything built on top of them. Difo's contribution is the full, careful verification, written out over a twenty-three page argument rather than sketched.
arxiv-2511-02241:
Brennen Hill proposes a neural network that learns the way living tissue does, by moving its own parts around. Conventional networks train through global backpropagation, which brains do not use. Hill's Structurally Adaptive Predictive Inference Network places processing cells on a two-dimensional grid, where each cell works to minimise its own local prediction error, following the active inference principle from neuroscience.

Two learning mechanisms run together: a Hebbian-like rule adjusting connections based on the gap between a cell's activity and its expectation. A structural rule that physically migrates cells to improve what they can sense. On the classic CartPole balancing task, the network's drive to minimise error and stay in balance was enough to discover a stable policy. Locking the parameters after success kept the policy stable, with locked networks averaging an eighty-two percent success rate.
arxiv-2511-02441:
Adriano Barra, Martino Centonze, Michela Marra Solazzo, and Daniele Tantari ask how the brain's navigation system stores so many places. Place cells, which fire for specific locations, are usually modelled with pairwise connections. In such networks, the number of stored patterns grows only linearly with size, far too little for mapping two-dimensional surfaces at fine resolution, let alone three-dimensional space. The authors build a two-layer model pairing place cells with grid-like units like the brain's grid cells.

Each place cell interacts with pairs of grid cells, and the team proves the model is equivalent to a dense Hebbian network with four-body interactions, a class known for much larger memory. Statistical mechanics analysis shows analytically that these higher-order assemblies support more than linearly many stored continuous attractors. Numerical experiments confirm the network can recognise places and navigate on general surfaces embedded in three-dimensional space.
arxiv-2511-02941:
Stefan Teufel, Marius Wesle, and Tom Wessel prove that quantum lattice systems keep well-defined dynamics even when the driving terms grow with position. The dynamics are generated by derivations, sums of commutators with local terms at each site. Older results needed those terms to stay uniformly bounded across the lattice, a strong restriction. Their 2025 paper relaxes it to growth that is at most linear in space.

Global existence and uniqueness of the time evolution still hold under that weaker rule, much like the classic result for first-order differential equations. The authors also prove Lieb-Robinson bounds with exponential light cones for these dynamics, limiting how fast influence spreads. The proof leans on known linear light cone bounds for the bounded case, which hold for finite-range or rapidly decaying terms.
arxiv-2511-03141:
Rohit Satish Patil, Zhilin Han, and Sofia Mogilevskaya solve a mechanics problem: how an elastic solid strains around a thin open material surface embedded in it. Such surfaces, from cracks to coatings, change the solid's response, and the Gurtin-Murdoch model describes their own stiffness. Their 2025 paper builds an isogeometric boundary element method for the plane strain case, with the surface in any shape.

The method rewrites the problem as singular boundary integral equations in two unknown parts of the surface stress. NURBS curves, the same shapes used in design software, approximate those unknowns. Benchmark tests on a straight segment and a circular arc under uniform load validated the code. Further examples probe how surface curvature steers the effect.
arxiv-2511-03241:
Gang Bao and Yaohua Zang introduce IGNO, a generative framework for working backward from sparse measures to the hidden causes behind them. Many science problems governed by flow and field equations face exactly that backward task, often with noisy data and sharp jumps in the unknown fields. Older learning methods tend to need huge labeled sets or handle only one kind of measure.

IGNO squeezes wide, uneven fields into a compact hidden code, then rebuilds both the fields and the field solutions from that code. Training leans on physics rules alone, with no paired examples required. The same setup handles point readings and richer operator data. The authors present it as a broad tool for hard inverse problems across science and engineering.
arxiv-2511-03441:
Doria Bonzi and colleagues introduce CareMedEval, a test set for judging how well language models critique biomedical studies. Critical reading is a core medical skill, and model help there is promising yet still shaky in specialist areas. Questions come from real exams taken by French medical students, not from synthetic prompts.

Five hundred thirty-four questions rest on thirty-seven genuine articles. Unlike older benchmarks, every item demands appraisal grounded in the study at hand. Top general and medical models were tried under varied context setups, and none cleared a modest exact-match bar. The gap shows that fluent summary is not the same as sound critical judgment in medicine.
arxiv-2511-03541:
S S Agaev, K Azizi, and H Sundu calculate the traits of two hypothetical scalar molecules built from heavy quarks in uneven mixes. Each molecule binds two heavy mesons with mismatched charm and bottom content. A sum rule method from quantum chromodynamics supplies their masses and coupling strengths.

Both molecules prove unstable under the strong force and fall apart into ordinary meson pairs. One splits mainly into its named parent pair, while the other favors two decay routes, one of them with an excited partner. Total widths are estimated from those routes plus annihilation channels. Such predictions guide collider searches, since an unstable molecule still leaves a bump that detectors can hunt.
arxiv-2511-03741:
Xiachong Lin and colleagues survey five years of work on modeling the charging load that electric vehicles place on power grids. Planners need those forecasts to place chargers and reinforce wires, yet driver behavior brings deep randomness. Older reviews, the authors note, skip a systematic look at how models fuse information.

Methods sort into statistical, simulated, and data-driven families, each weighed for strengths and flaws. Three levels of information fusion inside the models get their own analysis, from raw data blending to decision blending. Trends, open challenges, and chances for better hybrids close the survey. Grid operators facing steep vehicle growth gain a structured pick among forecasting schools rather than a pile of single studies.
arxiv-2511-03841:
Yedidel Louck, Ariel Stulman, and Amit Dvir carry out a security analysis of the protocols AI agent systems use. They test the official CORAL system and a high-fidelity ACP system directly, and judge the A2A protocol from published work, using a fourteen-point checklist of flaws.

Checks cover authentication, authorization, integrity, confidentiality, and availability. CORAL showed strong design in message checks and session isolation, yet critical flaws at its gateway let login and access checks fail. ACP's flexible design, above all its optional signature checks, opened high-impact trust and privacy gaps. A hybrid that pairs CORAL's design with mandatory per-message integrity checks is recommended as the safer path forward.
arxiv-2511-04141:
Adam Bacsi and Balazs Dora study how electron interactions reshape altermagnetism in a general Hatsugai-Kohmoto model with a set momentum-space symmetry. Catalog evidence carried a different title focused on spin susceptibility; the arXiv record gives the interaction-centred title used here, and that record governs.

As interaction strength grows, a many-body Lifshitz transition removes doubly filled regions from the Fermi surface, leaving almost all momentum states fully spin polarized, an interaction-enhanced altermagnet. The dynamical response develops a gap that grows with coupling and a sharp peak that moves to the gap edge past the transition. Static susceptibility stays unchanged, while altermagnetism reduces the static transverse response.
arxiv-2511-04241:
Maksym Chaudkhari, Christian Gorski, and Eduardo Silva prove a central limit theorem for the drift of a random walk on a lamplighter group. That group is a wreath product, where a moving lamplighter switches lamps indexed by a base group. The base here is a non-elementary, acylindrically hyperbolic group, and the lamp group is a non-trivial finite group.

Finite exponential moment on the walk is assumed. Upper bounds on the central moments of the drift accompany the limit theorem. Results extend to finitely generated lamp groups, finite or infinite. Drift governs how fast the walk escapes, and a Gaussian limit with controlled moments sharpens probabilistic understanding of these richly structured groups.
arxiv-2511-04341:
Nick Oh and Fernand Gobet formalise metacognition for language model reasoning in a Monitor-Generate-Verify framework. Popular test-time setups generate and then verify, skipping the monitoring step that decides when and how reasoning should begin. The authors link that omission to early commitment to poor reasoning paths and sizable accuracy loss.

Monitoring before generation captures difficulty ratings and confidence judgments, drawn from classic metacognitive theories of Flavell and of Nelson and Narens. Verification feedback then refines future monitoring. No hands-on validation is claimed; what it adds is a diagnostic vocabulary and concrete structural fixes, plus links to resource-rational analysis. Component-level failure in such systems becomes easier to name and target.
arxiv-2511-04541:
Baptiste Bonin and two colleagues test whether language models can stand in for users in slate A/B tests. Slate recommenders show ordered sets of items, like playlists, that interact with each other. Classic offline tests need large logs of past user behavior.

The authors ask models to state pairwise preferences between slates. A validation protocol checks those preferences against classic metrics and basic preference rules. Joined with the generalized Rao-Kupper model, the synthetic tests recover stable rankings across weightings. Off-policy estimators only matched that when the target matched the logged behavior. The method is offered as a screening stage before costly live tests.
arxiv-2511-04641:
Hans Harder leads five authors comparing fast probabilistic surrogates for large dynamical systems. The systems come from partial equations, such as the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid flow. Flow matching can forecast them, but sampling often takes too many steps.

Variants under review include direct and progressive distillation, adversarial diffusion methods, and rectified flows. GANs join the comparison as well. Experiments run on a set of hard systems throughout. One task predicts two-dimensional slices of full three-dimensional runs, a route toward cheap inflow generation for solvers that need boundary data fast.
arxiv-2511-04741:
Roberto Carrasco leads nine authors reporting square moiré patterns in stacked graphene, steered by strain. They call the combined twist-and-strain control twistraintronics. Moving native wrinkles selectively flips the pattern from its usual trigonal order to square.

Scanning tunneling microscopy shows elliptically shaped AA domains in the square state. Spectroscopy finds narrow bands with split Van Hove singularities near the Fermi level, signs of strong correlation. A continuum model with electrostatic interactions reproduces the pattern at the energy-minimizing twist-strain mix. New moiré geometries like this widen the design space for correlated electron devices.
arxiv-2511-05141:
Ana Isaković proves that a family of groups built from triangles, with non-positive curvature and a k-fold twist, is automatic. Automatic groups have a finite machine that lists their elements along geodesic paths, which makes many group tasks solvable by algorithm.

She shows these groups have only finitely many cone types, so all geodesics form a regular language. The set of first-in-order geodesics is also regular and meets the fellow traveller rule. That pair of facts yields the automatic structure, a strong finiteness trait for an infinite group family today.
arxiv-2511-05341:
Khedidja Djeha revives quadratic inflation, an early-universe model long ruled out by sky data, with one small change from a field redefinition. The plain quadratic form gives a tilt and a wave share that clash with Planck satellite bounds.

With the added high-order term, the tilt stays near its old value while the gravitational wave share drops to a level that fits Planck 2018 bounds. The change also shifts the reheating phase that follows inflation. Djeha checks that phase for consistency too, so the revived model stands on both sky data and its own next step.
arxiv-2511-05441:
John Joseph Carrasco and co-authors present a modular way to build four-point contact amplitudes with higher-derivative terms, for particles that may include fermions. Amplitudes are the core inputs to scattering forecasts, and hand builds grow messy as terms pile up.

Their LEGO-like frame joins gauge-safe kinematic blocks, color weights, and scalar polynomials in the Mandelstam values. Bose and Fermi symmetry rules act as filters on which blocks can join. The frame works in full dimension count, keeps evanescent terms that loops need, and scales to higher mass dimension in a controlled way.
arxiv-2511-05541:
Usha Bhalla and co-authors argue that tools for reading AI minds miss a simple fact: meaning in language changes slowly. Sparse autoencoders are a popular way to find clear features inside a language model. Yet they often return noisy features tied to single tokens rather than broad ideas.

Their Temporal Sparse Autoencoders add a loss that rewards steady feature use across nearby tokens. That push helps split meaning features from grammar features, with no direct teaching signal about meaning. Across several data sets and models, the new features were smoother and easier to read. Reconstruction quality stayed intact, which the authors see as a path to cleaner model insight.
arxiv-2511-05941:
Jinyan Chen and co-authors test a general recovery recipe for light lost in optical quantum systems. Photons scatter into unmonitored paths, and that loss is the main enemy of optical quantum processing. The loss is modeled as a beam splitter mixing the signal with empty space. Perfect repair using only Gaussian operations is known to be impossible.

The Petz recovery map offers a principled approximation. For single-mode loss with Gaussian reference states, the authors find the map reduces to either a beam splitter or an amplifier, depending on settings. It beat re-preparing the reference state and rival protocols on their examples. But it loses to doing nothing when the reference state strays far from the true one, a caution they state plainly.
arxiv-2511-06241:
M. R. Ahmadi Zand and N. Baimani study transitivity for maps on generalized topological spaces, a looser setting than ordinary topology. Several flavors are compared: orbit-transitivity, strict orbit-transitivity, omega-transitivity, and transitivity defined through generalized open sets. The paper also introduces points that are quasi-isolated in this generalized sense.

One result characterizes those quasi-isolated points exactly, using dense subsets in which the point becomes isolated. When a space has no such points, the authors prove that orbit-transitivity and strict orbit-transitivity each coincide with omega-transitivity for a self-map. The findings tie together notions that could otherwise drift apart in this general framework.
arxiv-2511-06341:
Nikolaus Vertovec and co-authors speed up the safety checking of neural control barrier functions. A barrier function certifies that a control system stays inside safe states, and neural versions are flexible but hard to verify. Checking that a trained network truly works as a barrier function has capped the network sizes people can use.

Their framework builds piecewise linear upper and lower bounds on the barrier conditions. Linear bound propagation, extended to network gradients and paired with McCormick relaxation, replaces costly exact checks. An adaptive refinement step splits regions in parallel to reduce looseness. Experiments show the method verifies larger networks than leading procedures, across broad system and activation types.
arxiv-2511-06441:
Mayank Saini and Arit Kumar Bishwas route each incoming query to the cheapest model that can handle it well. Frontier language models now serve vision, audio, and document tasks, but running them on everything is too costly for real-time use. Small open models are cheaper yet stumble on complex or mixed-media questions.

A learned routing network reads each query and picks a fitting expert, balancing price against quality. Vision jobs pass through a two-stage open pipeline that revives classical methods where they still lead. On standard language and visual question benchmarks, the system matched or beat always-premium setups while cutting reliance on costly models by more than two thirds.
arxiv-2511-06641:
Mohammadreza Kalan, Yuyang Deng, Eitan Neugut, and Samory Kpotufe extend Neyman-Pearson classification to learning from a shifted source population. Neyman-Pearson classification caps one error type below a set threshold while minimizing the other, a natural fit for imbalanced problems. Transfer learning for it had handled shifts in the positive distribution only, though real sources drift on both sides.

Their adaptive procedure improves both error types when the source carries useful information. When the source turns out uninformative, the method detects that and avoids negative transfer, falling back safely instead of absorbing harm. Matching computational guarantees show the procedure also runs efficiently, rounding out the statistical promises.
arxiv-2511-06741:
Wenbo Huang and colleagues recognize actions in wide-angle video from only a few examples, where backgrounds threaten to swamp the performer. Few-shot action recognition must learn new moves from a handful of clips, and wide lenses pack in distracting scenery. A sequence architecture called RWKV models global context well but, applied plainly, lets background detail drown the subject.

Their system, Otter, adds a segmentation module that emphasizes the key patches of each frame and a temporal module that rebuilds time relations through bidirectional scanning. Blending a regular prototype with a time-enhanced one sharpens both subject focus and timing. Benchmarks in sports and general action datasets placed Otter at the state of the art.
arxiv-2511-07141:
Humaira Zafar and Mauro Fernandes Pereira design mid-infrared waveguide arrays that can be packed closer than a wavelength without their signals leaking into each other. Their bends use Euler-shaped curves whose widths taper asymmetrically, with neighboring waveguides tapered in complementary fashion. Earlier designs kept widths constant, which limited how tightly arrays could be integrated on a chip.

Fabricated on a silicon-on-insulator platform, the array holds crosstalk below thirty decibels to both first and second neighbors across the 3.1 to 3.6 micron wavelength band. Three-dimensional simulations show negligible coupling and low insertion loss, and the design tolerates fabrication width variations gracefully. The result is a CMOS-compatible building block for mid-infrared photonic circuits and for optical phased arrays needing a large field of view.
arxiv-2511-07441:
Ye Zheng, Yimin Chen, and Yidan Hu tackle a trust problem with AI agents. Agents can gather or share private user data while doing tasks, sometimes without clear consent. Their privacy policies promise certain practices, but users cannot easily check whether real behavior matches the promises.

Their tool, AudAgent, watches agent behavior live and flags policy violations. It turns policy text into formal rules through voting across several language models, then labels data flows with a privacy analyzer. Continuous checking replaces one-time review. The system aims to give users and developers ongoing proof that an agent handles sensitive data as stated.
arxiv-2511-07541:
Samiur Mir and colleagues use neutrino detectors to probe where neutrino mass comes from. Mixing between neutrino types shifts slowly as energies change, an effect called running. In the plain Standard Model that running is tiny, but light new particles tied to neutrinos can amplify it below the electroweak scale.

Amplified running changes the flavor mix arriving from the sky. At IceCube, tau neutrinos can make double bang events, two cascades from one particle. Rates of such events then reveal the running. Combining air-shower and cosmic fluxes sharpens the test. The approach turns a giant Antarctic detector into a tool for mass-model hunting.
arxiv-2511-08041:
Vittorio Franzese and Matteo El Hariry estimate a spacecraft rotation rate from an event based camera watching stars. Event cameras record brightness changes pixel by pixel, so moving stars leave timed trails of events. The pattern and polarity of those events encode the apparent motion field across the sensor.

From that field, the method infers angular velocity in the camera frame, then converts it to spacecraft rates when attitude is known. Simulations with random pointings and rates test the accuracy of the approach. The authors argue such sensing could complement or even replace conventional rate sensors on spacecraft that already carry event cameras.
arxiv-2511-08141:
A Chmeruk, D Jones, R Balducci, and J Ebad-Allah study how pressure cuts magnetism in the compound Co3Sn2S2, a compound whose band shape depends on its magnetic state. Driving magnetism can switch charge phases and create new quantum effects. The team tracked the ferromagnetic state under pressures up to about eleven gigapascals, combining test with theory.

Standard density functional calculations with relaxed ions greatly overestimated magnetization under pressure. Moving sulfur atoms while preserving symmetry fixed the match with measured values. Certain exchange and correlation choices also reproduced magnetization, structure, and optical spectra. Pressure dependent magnetism in this compound clearly demands careful theoretical handling.
arxiv-2511-08741:
Kai Yun and Navid Azizan make learned perception safer for robots and vehicles that must act on what their sensors suggest. Perception networks fail quietly on inputs unlike their training data, and a controller that trusts them blindly can steer into danger.

Their framework, ATOM-CBF, builds a control barrier function that measures its own doubt. An adaptive margin grows when incoming measurements look out of distribution, with no need for ground-truth labels or advance knowledge of how the data shifted. A safety filter then uses that margin to tune its caution in real time, staying permissive when perception is trustworthy and conservative when it is not. Simulations with a small race car reading LiDAR and a quadruped reading camera images show safety maintained throughout.
arxiv-2511-09341:
Weiran Yang, Yiqi Cai, Handi Deng, and Cheng Ma model an entire photoacoustic imaging readout chain to squeeze out more sensitivity. Photoacoustic imaging listens for ultrasound created when tissue absorbs light pulses, and detector sensitivity limits image quality. Earlier studies treated the acoustic front end or the electronics alone, missing their coupling.

The authors rederive the KLM transducer model from first principles, then extend it with cable and receiver models as lumped elements. The resulting circuit yields transfer functions showing how element area, cable length, and receiver impedance interact. Experiments validate the model with average error below five percent. They also identify a low-frequency tailing effect that appears when the one-dimensional vibration assumption breaks down.
arxiv-2511-10041:
José Reyes Castillo, Saúl Aguilar Salazar, and Diego Mauricio Gomez Coral test how temperature affects the timing precision of a plastic scintillator detector read out by silicon photomultipliers. Balloon and space cosmic-ray devices rely on such detectors for picosecond-level timing used in triggering and particle ID, and flight temperatures swing widely. Their prototype pairs a BC418 scintillator bar with Onsemi sensors inside a controlled thermal chamber.

Electrons from a strontium-90 source served as the test beam, with a dedicated differential preamplifier and coincidence triggering. The best time resolution reached was about 160 picoseconds at three volts of overvoltage. Crucially, that resolution stayed stable from minus twenty to plus twenty degrees Celsius and uniform along the bar, which is what flight devices need.
arxiv-2511-10241:
Jinxuan Li, Yi Zhang, Jian-Fang Hu, Chaolei Tan, Tianming Liang, and Beihao Xia localize, in space and time, the video tube matching a language query, without using fine-grained training annotations. Weakly supervised methods before them fused text and video late, generating tubes blind to the description, which caused wrong targets and drifting tracks. Their framework, TubeRMC, generates text-conditioned candidate tubes with pre-trained grounding models first.

Three reconstruction strategies then refine the candidates from temporal, spatial, and combined perspectives, each using a tube as the condition to rebuild key clues in the query. Mutual constraints between spatial and temporal proposals raise their quality further. On the VidSTG and HCSTVG benchmarks, TubeRMC beat existing methods, and visualizations showed fewer identification and tracking failures.
arxiv-2511-10541: Eve Shaw works in geometric analysis. She extends an earlier result about pseudotangents of Lipschitz curves, which describe the limiting shapes a rough curve can resemble when magnified at a point. Shaw shows the set of points where every pseudotangent actually occurs can be any compact, uniformly disconnected set that admits a Lipschitz capture.
arxiv-2511-10741:
R. Fisher leads an 18-author team measuring how fast twelve massive galaxies were forming stars when the universe was under a billion years old. The galaxies, drawn from the ALMA REBELS survey, were observed with JWST spectroscopy and ALMA, giving an unusually complete view of star formation tracers at redshift around seven.

Comparing rates from ultraviolet light, hydrogen emission, and far-infrared emission, with careful dust corrections, the team finds half to four-fifths of the star formation is hidden by dust. Total rates sit systematically above standard main-sequence relations, and the reconstructed histories rise more steeply than those of lower-mass galaxies. Because of those rising histories, standard conversion factors overestimate the hundred-million-year average rate by about a factor of three, so the authors provide updated calibrations.
arxiv-2511-10841:
YongKyung Oh, Dong-Young Lim, and Sungil Kim present FlowPath, a method for classifying time series that arrive sparsely and at uneven times. Neural controlled differential equations handle such data in principle. Their accuracy depends heavily on the path drawn between readings, and fixed schemes for filling the gaps impose geometry the data may not follow.

FlowPath learns that path's geometry instead, using an invertible neural flow to build a continuous, data-adaptive manifold through the observations. Invertibility acts as a built-in discipline, keeping the change information-preserving and well behaved, which sets the method apart from free learnable paths. Across eighteen benchmark datasets and a real-world case study, FlowPath delivered statistically significant accuracy gains over fixed-interpolation and non-invertible baselines. The gains were largest under heavy missingness.
arxiv-2511-11141:
Udo Schlegel, Franziska Weeber, and their colleagues introduce PRSM, a measure of how well the CLIP model holds its ranking when a text query is reworded. CLIP links images and text, and small wording changes should not scramble what it retrieves. Steady behavior matters most in sensitive social settings, where wobbly results can deepen demographic bias.

The measure is tested on a data set built to expose social and demographic bias. Robustness shifted with the rewording style used, and small but steady gaps appeared between queries tied to men and those tied to women. The authors discuss what that means for fair use of such models.
arxiv-2511-11541:
Joseph Onuegbu and four co-authors built a pipeline that spots nova explosions in data from the WISE infrared space telescope. Novae are sudden stellar outbursts that fade over time, and their infrared colors change in ways that can separate them from other brightening objects.

Applying clear infrared criteria to the WISE catalog turned up forty-one novae already confirmed by optical telescopes. The color gap between the optical V band and the WISE band at 3.4 microns proved a strong diagnostic, and a model of that color difference is proposed for future hunts. Results also support a theory linking slower mass loss to larger ejected envelopes in these systems.
arxiv-2511-11641:
Jinqi Xiao and ten co-authors introduce EcoSpa, a sparse training method for transformers that respects how weight matrices work in coupled pairs. Attention and feed-forward layers multiply matrices together, yet most sparsification methods prune each matrix alone and break those interactions, hurting quality at high sparsity.

EcoSpa judges and prunes coupled pairs together, removing aligned rows and columns so the interaction pattern survives. A new granularity for scoring structural importance supports both pretraining and fine-tuning runs. The payoff sought is real efficiency, training large models with far fewer active weights, without the accuracy collapse that naive pruning causes when sparsity grows aggressive.
arxiv-2511-11941:
Delmar G. A. Cabral and eight co-authors run quantum simulations of molecules with quantum nuclei. Electrons and nuclei are both treated as quantum particles. The Born-Oppenheimer approximation, which freezes nuclei in place, is dropped. Light nuclei, above all protons, tunnel and spread out. The approximation distorts their chemistry.

A multicomponent unitary coupled cluster method is built for the task. It rests on the nuclear-electronic orbital formalism. Targets include positronium hydride and hydrogen with a quantum proton. Resource costs are mapped for distinct excitation levels. A compact variant ran on IBM's Heron hardware. Error mitigation kept energies within chemical accuracy. Chemistry beyond Born-Oppenheimer, on real quantum hardware, is the milestone.
arxiv-2511-12141:
Caroline Guinet, Sepideh Mirrahimi and Jean-Michel Roquejoffre analyze a model of evolution for a population spread across a trait, such as body size. Individuals reproduce without sex, compete, are selected, and mutate with small effects. The governing equation tracks the density of each trait over time.

A logarithmic change turns the problem into a Hamilton-Jacobi equation with a constraint, a standard route for studying such models. When reproduction is a concave function of the trait, the authors derive a first-order expansion of the solution. That expansion lets them approximate moments of the trait density, linking the Hamilton-Jacobi picture to biological quantities that modelers can measure directly.
arxiv-2511-12541:
Benjamin-Feir instability, the tendency of a steady wave train to break up under small modulations, is studied here for waves on the interface between two fluid layers where surface tension acts. Olga Avramenko and Volodymyr Naradovyi present the second part of a study, now treating surface tension as a freely adjustable parameter.

Using a nonlinear Schrödinger reduction and long-wave approximations, they trace how the borders between stable and unstable regimes move as surface tension, depth ratio and density contrast change. The long-wave picture is organized by two density values and by a classic Bond threshold where dispersive and nonlinear singularities meet. Loop-shaped stability regions appear only when the lower layer is the deeper one.
arxiv-2511-12641:
Caleb Cheung and Bryan Shader study patterns of zeros and nonzeros in rectangular matrices. Their question is which patterns force every real matrix with that pattern to have all distinct singular values, meaning no two of them repeat. They work with patterns whose term rank equals the number of rows, and they give a full characterization of the patterns with this property.

The result extends an older theorem by Fiedler about symmetric matrices and repeated eigenvalues. Fiedler had shown that paths are the only graphs for which every symmetric matrix with that graph avoids repeated eigenvalues. Cheung and Shader prove the matching statement for singular values in the rectangular case. The paper is a compact piece of matrix theory that pins down exactly when a pattern rules out repetition.
arxiv-2511-12741:
Aritro Pathak bounds the Green's function for an elliptic operator that pairs the Laplacian with a drift term growing near the boundary. The Green's function measures how the solution at one point responds to a source at another, so pointwise upper and lower bounds are a basic tool for understanding such equations. Here the drift diverges like a power of the inverse distance to the boundary, and it need not be coercive, a setting where the usual energy methods break down.

Pathak's estimates hold inside the unit ball, with constants uniform on smaller balls. The drift can be any locally smooth function below an integrable radial majorant. He notes these appear to be the first such bounds for non-coercive drifts, and new even for smooth ones. The technique may extend to singular potentials and other problems where energy arguments fail.
arxiv-2511-12841:
Shuning Zhang and seven co-authors compare what academics propose for smart home privacy with what manufacturers actually document. Smart home devices collect data constantly, and protection mechanisms only work if users know about and adopt them. The study pairs a systematic review of one hundred seventeen academic papers with an audit of the public documentation of eighty-six commercial devices. The study asks what protections each side offers buyers.

Academics favor novel system and algorithm protections but rarely test them in real homes or study cost, compatibility, and legal issues. Manufacturers, meanwhile, barely mention the advanced academic ideas. Their documented protections are reactive, centered on after-the-fact data management such as deletion, and converge on simple mechanisms like physical buttons and local processing. The authors call for deployable designs and field validation.
arxiv-2511-13341:
Zihe Yan and 5 co-authors build a scoring framework for hidden backdoor risk in open-source software supply chains. Modern projects reuse many third-party parts, but weak upkeep and thin review can let stealthy attacks slip in, as the XZ-Util case showed. Judging maintainer behavior with fixed patterns alone misses much of that risk.

The framework models an attack stage by stage and sets a metric for each stage. Language models then judge review activity and privilege changes by meaning, not by hand-made rules. Applied to sixty-six high-priority Debian packages, the study found the current supply chain exposed to several kinds of security risk.
arxiv-2511-13541:
Yue Hou and 4 co-authors propose BaCa, a test-time method for spotting out-of-distribution graphs without retraining. Detectors usually learn only from in-distribution data, never seeing true outliers, so their sense of the boundary stays weak. Graph data also hide several latent factors that shape their structure.

BaCa estimates graphons from test samples alone and mixes them to create diverse boundary-like graphs, avoiding any outside outlier set. Two dynamic dictionaries, kept by priority queues and attention, capture in- and out-distribution patterns and recalibrate the outlier score. Broad tests on real datasets showed clear gains over leading methods, with no fine-tuning of the base model.
arxiv-2511-14641:
Hemant Kumar Sharma models current flow through a tiny transistor made of three quantum dots placed in a triangle on a surface. Electrons inside the dots repel each other and also shake the dots as they pass, and those shakes leak energy into the surface below. Getting all three effects right at once is the challenge.

Sharma treats the electron-phonon coupling exactly through a standard change of variables and handles electron repulsion at the mean-field level. A nonequilibrium Green's function method then yields the spectrum and the tunneling current. The model helps explain how heat and vibration shape transport in molecular-scale devices, a step toward reliable nanoscale electronics.
arxiv-2511-14741:
Jared N. Lakhani widens a statistical model for paired count data so it can handle pairs that move in opposite directions. The bivariate pseudo-Poisson model is prized for cheap fitting when one count is steady and the other is spread out. In its standard forms, though, the rate of the second count grows in a straight line with the first, which forces the two counts to rise together.

Lakhani adds curvature to that rate rule, letting the link bend. The bent form can produce negative correlation between the counts, which the older model could not express at all. The change also lets the model mimic a wider range of joint patterns while keeping its simple structure.
arxiv-2511-14941:
Pau Bosch-Cabot, Alexandra J. Tetarenko, and seven co-authors weigh the jets of two black hole binaries by reading the cavities those jets blew into nearby gas. When a feeding stellar black hole erupts, its jets can plow into surrounding material and store energy there like a calorimeter. The team maps molecular gas around two recent eruptors with the ALMA telescope array.

Around one system, MAXI J1348-630, the gas maps show a clear jet-driven cavity in shape, spectrum, and motion. Around the second system, no such glow appears. The cavity's properties pin down the first jet's power, and the value agrees with independent estimates, which validates the calorimetry approach.
arxiv-2511-15141:
Sunwoo Kim, Geon Lee, and three co-authors present ItemRAG, a retrieval scheme that helps language models recommend products at the level of single items. Model-based recommenders read a shopper's history and pick from a candidate list, and retrieval usually fetches histories of similar shoppers. Those histories are noisy and say little about the candidate items themselves.

ItemRAG instead retrieves information about each item, enriching the descriptions of items in the shopper's history and in the candidate set. Fine-grained item evidence replaces coarse user similarity as the context the model reasons over. The shift targets better picks, especially for new or rarely bought items where user history runs thin.
arxiv-2511-15341:
Wen Shang and three co-authors propose robotic aerial base stations that anchor to tall urban structures instead of hovering. Flying base stations can add wireless capacity where needed, but battery limits restrict hovering to minutes. Robotic versions carry energy neutral grippers that let them perch autonomously. Perching extends service to hours at the same site.

The paper sets out hardware, workflow, and communication needs for the concept. Anchored stations can join the radio access network and boost capacity on demand. That longer endurance removes a fundamental barrier to wider adoption. Urban landforms like towers and rooftops become network infrastructure. The concept paper maps what must be built and tested for sixth generation aerial networks.
arxiv-2511-16141:
Ding Li and four co-authors reveal how electronic quantum shape reshapes phonon dichroism in solids that break key symmetries. Quantum shape describes intrinsic shape traits of electronic states and drives many unusual electromagnetic effects. Through electron phonon coupling, that shape modifies how phonons absorb left versus right circular or linear light. The authors split the two dichroism channels theoretically.

Circular phonon dichroism is dominated by heat magnetic moments, while linear dichroism depends on a heat Drude weight. A sum rule for the heat magnetic moment aids lab detection. A ferromagnetic two dimensional electron gas with Rashba coupling demonstrates the predictions. The work uncovers a quantum geometric origin for common phonon optical effects and suggests measurable signatures.
arxiv-2511-16641:
Run Hou and Andriy H. Nevidomskyy argue that fractional Chern insulator states in twisted molybdenum ditelluride cannot be understood from a single band. Experiments found fractional quantum Hall physics in this moiré material, but most theory used exact diagonalization on one partly filled band, ignoring strong coupling to higher bands.

The authors import a non-perturbative driven similarity renormalization group method from quantum chemistry to include those bands. At one-third filling the many-body gaps shrink a lot compared with the one-band picture. At two-thirds filling, links between bands stabilize the fractional Chern phases at larger twist angles, matching experiment. Examining the orbitals shows the effect comes mainly from dynamic correlations, not from single-particle geometry conditions.
arxiv-2511-16741:
Samuel Frank, James Halverson, Anindita Maiti, and Fabian Ruehle build fermionic neural network field theories, extending the idea that wide neural networks define quantum field theories to networks with Grassmann-valued, anticommuting variables. Bosonic versions were known; fermions need the Grassmann machinery to capture their statistics.

A generalization of the central limit theorem to Grassmann variables yields free theories, realizing the free Dirac spinor at infinite width and a four-fermion interaction at finite width. Yukawa couplings arise by breaking the statistical independence between the fermionic and bosonic output weights. Super-affine transformations of the inputs then realize a superspace formalism, opening a large class of interacting supersymmetric quantum mechanics and field theory models to the neural network construction.
arxiv-2511-16941:
Scott Willenbrock offers a teaching-style survey of unstable particles in quantum field theory, written in honour of Dave Roper's ninetieth birthday. Unstable particles decay after a brief life, so their mass and decay rate cannot be treated like those of stable ones. The survey builds its account from the shape of the propagator, the core object that tracks how a particle moves through a theory.

Willenbrock covers the classic resonance formula, the link between mass and width, and the roles of poles and branch cuts in the maths. He also follows how poles move as inputs change, with side notes on the Roper resonance, a well known excited state of the proton. The piece serves as a guided entry point for students meeting the topic.
arxiv-2511-17141:
Oliver Bölt and 19 co-authors show how ordinary fiber-optic cables can double as a dense seismic sensor network across a research campus. The technique, distributed acoustic sensing, reads vibrations along the fiber itself. The Hamburg WAVE team ran a proto-network over more than 12 kilometers of fiber linking major facilities in Science City Hamburg Bahrenfeld. The facilities include DESY, the European XFEL, and PETRA III, and the campaign ran during May 2021.

The network picked up natural, human-made, and infrastructure vibrations and showed where each couples into the fiber. A special study of doubled fiber loops at the European XFEL examined noise and motion coupling in detail. For campuses whose precision experiments suffer from ground vibration, such sensing offers both a warning system and guidance on where quieting efforts matter most.
arxiv-2511-17241:
Benjamin White and Anastasia Shimorina present a hybrid method for predicting what social media users will do next. Most tools aim at common acts such as likes and reposts, while rare but weighty acts get little study. Their test ground is Bluesky, with millions of conversation threads, twelve kinds of action, and groups of users sorted into twenty-five persona types.

The method blends four parts: a lookup store of past reply patterns, per-persona gradient-boosted models for common acts. A neural model that fuses text and timing for harder cases, and rules for rare acts. By giving rare behaviour its own path instead of letting common acts swamp it, the system aims to forecast the full range of what a user might do.
arxiv-2511-17441:
Shihan Wu and 83 co-authors introduce RoboCOIN, a large open dataset for teaching robots to work with two arms at once. Bimanual manipulation drives human-like dexterity, but datasets for it are scarce because robot hardware varies so widely between platforms. RoboCOIN gathers more than 180,000 demonstrations from 15 distinct robotic platforms, across home, commercial, and industrial settings, covering 421 tasks organized by collaboration action and object.

A layered annotation pyramid labels the data at several levels, from trajectory concepts down through subtasks to frame-level kinematics. A processing pipeline built around a robot trajectory markup language handles quality checks, machine annotation, and unified handling across embodiments. Experiments show training on RoboCOIN improves bimanual manipulation models across many robot bodies. The dataset and code are fully open-sourced for the field.
arxiv-2511-17841:
Ziyue Yang, Feng Liu, Yifei Jin, and Konstantinos Vandikas present RadioGUNet, a neural network for estimating how much a radio signal weakens as it travels across a city map. Accurate pathloss maps help plan wireless networks, but building them from measurements alone is slow.

The network builds on the U-Net design and adds group equivariant layers, which handle rotations and reflections by construction rather than by extra training data. On a public radio map data set, the extended model beats standard U-Net models with a similar size. Code is shared openly, making the method easy to test and reuse.
arxiv-2511-18041:
A. Jimenez-Vargas and D. Ruiz-Casternado study a special class of holomorphic Lipschitz maps on the unit ball of a Banach space. These maps are complex differentiable and stretch distances in a controlled way, with value zero at the origin. Using a compactness notion tied to a chosen operator ideal, they isolate the maps whose image is compact in that relative sense.

They examine the structure of that subclass as an ideal in its own right, using linearization and transposition links with compact linear operators. The work extends operator ideal techniques into nonlinear holomorphic function theory on infinite dimensional balls, a setting where compactness is subtle and useful.
arxiv-2511-18141:
Lucas Amaral, Luben Cabezas, Thiago Ramos, and Gustavo Pereira construct prediction regions for compositional data, outcomes that are proportions summing to one, modeled with Dirichlet regression. Valid prediction sets for such data are not well established, especially given the curved shape of the space of proportions.

They compare three conformal methods: one based on quantile residuals, one approximating highest density regions, and a grid based version of the latter over the simplex. Model runs across cases show the density based approach is robust in coverage, while gridding reduces region size and overcoverage. Applications to sleep stages and plant biomass allocation show practical, coherent results.
arxiv-2511-18241:
Shixun Huang, Eitan Grinspun, and Yue Chang present a neural method for model reduction, shrinking the simulation of deformable objects so it can run in real time. Linear methods are predictable but too stiff for large bends, while free-form neural mappings can be accurate yet behave badly on loads never seen in training. Their formulation builds the decoder from differences of convex functions with an added odd symmetry, bridging the two styles.

Convexity discourages wild, wavy responses when load sizes grow beyond training, helping the model extrapolate in magnitude. The odd part restores a symmetry many physical systems obey, which plain convexity cannot represent. The goal is a compact latent space whose behaviour stays reliable under new load sizes and directions, for use in interactive simulation.
arxiv-2511-18341:
Mohammad Pouranvari maps the phases of a one dimensional model where electrons hop between sites with disordered energies. The site energies are correlated over distance with a power law, and hopping strength also falls as a power law, so two exponents control the whole family of models.

Using large exact studies, Pouranvari combines spectral data and localization checks to chart where states are localized, extended, or critical, finding robust mobility edges and mixed regimes. A scaling analysis extracts critical exponents and transition lines. A guided autoencoder trained on raw eigenstate features matches the same phase map, backing the physics based picture.
arxiv-2511-18441:
Lorenzo Rutayisire, Nicola Capodieci, and Fabio Pellacini present ReCoGS, a tool for recolouring scenes built with Gaussian splatting. A fast method for recreating three-dimensional scenes that can be viewed from new angles in real time. Editing such scenes is an active area, but many tools lean on image diffusion models to invent training views, which brings inconsistency between views, coarse control, and heavy computing costs.

ReCoGS focuses narrowly on recolouring. Its pipeline lets a user select a region of a trained scene precisely and change its colour, and an interactive tool demonstrates the edit live. Code is shared in public. For artists and designers working with captured scenes, the tool offers direct control without rebuilding the scene or waiting on a diffusion pipeline.
arxiv-2511-18541:
Amir Subba, Subhaditya Bhattacharya, and Abhik Sarkar estimate how well a future electron positron collider could detect anomalous couplings between the Higgs boson and gauge bosons that violate CP symmetry. Such couplings would break the symmetry between matter and antimatter. Such couplings are described by six effective operators that modify Higgs interactions.

They study Higgs production with a Z boson at a set collision energy, using polarized beams. Spin related asymmetries are read from Higgs decays to bottom quarks and to W and Z pairs. One decay channel leads sensitivity for two operators, another constrains the rest. Bounds improve with more data but saturate once systematic errors reach a few percent.
arxiv-2511-18841:
Mincheol Jeon and Euinam Huh personalize federated learning by splitting style from content. In federated learning many clients train one shared model with no raw data pooled. One global model fits divergent clients poorly, most when their data skew far apart, and talk costs cap what can be shared.

FedSTAR pulls each client's style factors out of the shared content code. The server then merges class wise prototypes with a transformer attention step that weighs client inputs with care. Clients swap compact prototypes and style vectors in place of full model weights, which cuts traffic. Personal fit survives the merge. Skewed, chat shy fleets are the target.
arxiv-2511-19341:
Thomas Hughes, Michael J. Wilensky, and Philip Bull probe the Hubble tension, the mismatch between measures of how fast the universe expands. Different methods give values that disagree beyond their stated errors. Many groupings of the data have been tried to blame physics or hidden errors.

Their Bayesian jackknife study works through sixteen independent measurements, testing whether they fall into meaningful clusters. After checking the usual early-versus-late split, they try scenarios where certain subsets carry a bias, such as the local distance ladder or microwave background data. Population parameters describe each subset, letting the data itself point to the tension's origin.
arxiv-2511-19441:
Marien-Lorenzo Hanot and Kaibo Hu rewrite the linearized Einstein equations in a form that suits careful computer work. Simulating gravity is hard: gauge choices, constraints, and tensor symmetries all cause trouble. Their new form casts the ADM equations as a wave system built on a tool called the divdiv complex.

That structure makes the system well posed, meaning small changes in inputs cause only small changes in outputs. It also points to schemes that keep the physics intact on a grid. The authors build such schemes for two kinds of grids and prove error bounds under weak assumptions.
arxiv-2511-19541:
Sajjad Taravati argues that shaping dispersion is the master key for space-time metamaterials. These are materials patterned in both space and time. They can steer the frequency, size, momentum, and path of waves all at once. That goes far beyond merely breaking one-way behavior rules.

The link between frequency and wavenumber acts as a blueprint for the whole design. By mapping that link across slow, light-speed, and fast modulation regimes, the article shows how shaped change routes energy among harmonic modes. Effects include beam splitting, one-way flow, uneven frequency shifts, gain, and momentum gaps. The framework is then tied to real wave devices.
arxiv-2511-19741:
Xinran Liu and four co-authors ask whether a learned shortcut for optimal transport still works on new data. Transport plans match one distribution to another at some cost, but full computation scales badly. Sliced methods project the problem to one dimension, where the answer is cheap, and learn a good projection direction.

The open question is transfer: can a slicer trained on one pair of distributions serve unseen pairs when the data shift? The authors study the min-sliced transport plan framework with that question in focus. The answer matters wherever transport is recomputed often on related, evolving data, from shape analysis to image generation.
arxiv-2511-20041:
Petr Molodyk, Jaemoo Choi, David W Romero, Ming-Yu Liu, and Yongxin Chen present MFM-Point, a multi-scale flow matching method for generating point clouds. Direct point-based generators are cheap to train and simple, but they usually trail methods that work through latent features, meshes, or voxels. The authors aim to close that gap without losing the simplicity.

Generation proceeds from coarse to fine, which improves quality and scale at no extra training or inference cost. A structured downsampling and upsampling plan preserves the geometry of unordered point sets and keeps the resolutions aligned. In tests, MFM-Point leads the point-based methods and rivals the best representation-based ones, with strong results on multi-category and high-resolution tasks.
arxiv-2511-20541:
Ranieri, Palmieri, and Biasotti teach networks to find cracks in statues before conservators can. Their 2025 paper applies semantic segmentation to cultural heritage monitoring. Statues and monuments degrade outdoors, developing structural cracks. Manual inspection is slow, subjective, and often hard to access. Pixel-level image labeling can flag fine cracks automatically.

The study compares U-Net models with four different encoders. ResNet-50, ResNet-101, and two ConvNeXt V2 sizes were trained. Training used the OmniCrack30k dataset of crack images. Scores included overlap measures like mIoU, Dice, and Jaccard. ConvNeXt V2 Huge topped every metric on the test set. Bigger backbones and higher input resolutions helped consistently. A second test used unlabeled photos of real cracked monuments. Models generalized despite never training on heritage images. ConvNeXt variants caught hairline cracks best in that trial. Complex textures and lighting did not break them.
arxiv-2511-20641:
Tang, Wang, Zhang, Wei, and Zhang rescue rare labels in multi-label image recognition. Their 2025 paper presents CapNet for long-tailed visual recognition. Real images carry several labels, but common ones dominate training data. Rare tail classes get ignored by biased models. CLIP's design favors single-label matching over multi-label tagging.

CapNet models label correlations from CLIP's own text encoder. A graph network propagates information along those correlations. Learnable soft prompts refine the label embeddings further. A distribution-balanced focal loss reweights training toward rare classes. Test-time ensembling combines predictions for better generalization. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts vision to text cheaply. On VOC-LT, mean average precision reached 93.03 percent. That beat the LMPT baseline by over five points. COCO-LT results hit 76.36 percent, up to ten points ahead. Ablations on NUS-WIDE confirmed each component helps. Head classes kept their accuracy while tails improved.
arxiv-2511-20741:
Futoshi Hamanoue reports in 2025 a feasibility study of Aurora-DD, a method that keeps superconducting qubits from losing their phase. Qubits drift out of phase as they idle, and that drift corrupts quantum computations. Aurora pairs a fixed XY8 pulse sequence, which echoes away slow noise, with one global phase offset. The offset is tuned in advance on a calibrated emulator, not live on the machine.

Across 30 randomised trials at each of four phase settings, the emulator runs cut mean-squared error by 68 to 97 percent against an unprotected baseline. A three-run campaign on IBM's real ibm_fez hardware pointed to roughly 99 percent lower absolute error. Hamanoue stresses those hardware numbers are proof-of-concept only. A side branch adding zero-noise extrapolation proved unstable, sometimes amplifying errors badly, and now sits in an appendix as a warning.
arxiv-2511-20841:
Edmond Tong and colleagues present in 2025 OVAL-Grasp, a system that lets a robot grasp objects by the right part for the job. Grabbing a knife by the blade fails the task even when the grip is firm. Geometry-only methods struggle with appearance-defined parts, blocked views, and unseen objects. OVAL-Grasp needs no training for new objects, working zero-shot from language and vision alone.

Given a photo and a task, a large language model names which parts to grasp and which to avoid. A vision-language model then segments those parts, and builds a heatmap of actionable regions for the gripper. On 20 household objects with three tasks each, it beat two grasping baselines. On the Fetch mobile manipulator it segmented the correct part 95 percent of the time and grasped the right area in 78.3 percent of attempts. Under clutter, part selection succeeded 80 percent of the time.
arxiv-2511-21641:
Michael Ruderman shows control engineers how to tune a feedback controller without any model of the machine, in 2025. Plant models are often unavailable in practice, especially in motion control, yet PI and PID controllers still need principled tuning. His PI-Lead design revives the ultimate sensitivity idea behind the classic Ziegler–Nichols rules, extended with loop-shaping insight.

A three-step procedure sets the integration time constant, the control gain, and the Lead element in turn, using only experimental observations of the output. The design guarantees a sufficient phase margin for the assumed class of type-one stable processes. Ruderman validates the method on a noise-perturbed electro-mechanical actuator with translational motion. The tuning proves robust against feedback noise, because the ultimate oscillations it hunts appear unmistakably at low frequencies where sensor noise cannot mimic them. The result is a practical, simple recipe for engineers who cannot model first.
arxiv-2511-21741:
Conrad D. Hougen, Karl T. Pazdernik, and Alfred O. Hero build a geometric topic model that tracks how research themes drift inside co-author communities, in 2025. Topic models sort document collections into themes, but modern versions built on dense transformer embeddings tend to miss rare niche topics. They also fail to line topics up smoothly across time.

Their method, MSTML, fuses text with co-author network data. Hellinger distances, a way to compare probability distributions, and Ward's linkage build a hierarchical topic tree that holds both local detail and global structure. The experiments show the approach recovers rare-topic structure and visualizes gradual topic drift over the years. A notable lesson emerges: interpretable word-count models, paired with principled geometric alignment, beat embedding models at alignment even though transformers win on coherence. Because novelty lives in niche topics, the authors argue alignment deserves priority when mapping a field's evolution.
arxiv-2511-21841:
Bozorgnia and colleagues argue that searches for very heavy dark matter particles, particles far above a TeV in mass, need a better map of dark matter motion near Earth. The standard model assumes a smooth Maxwellian spread of speeds. The Large Magellanic Cloud, ploughing through the Milky Way's halo, should add a fast tail and bunch incoming particles into one sky patch.

The team introduces new techniques for turning simulated velocities into detector flux, then reworks limits from plastic etch detectors at the Ohya mine and aboard Skylab, which recorded no suitable tracks. Because the fastest particles arrive from a preferred direction, a detector's latitude matters. The Ohya site happened to sit near the latitude that maximizes the flux in their calculation. Bounds shift when the Magellanic boost is included, which matters for future detector design.
arxiv-2511-22241:
Borlakov and Kazakov, theoretical physicists at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, revisit the oldest weak-interaction theory's bad reputation. Fermi's four-fermion theory is non-renormalizable and its scattering amplitude grows with energy, violating unitarity, which is why the Standard Model replaces it with W and Z boson exchange at high energies. The authors ask what the theory itself predicts once its ultraviolet divergences are summed properly, using recurrence relations for divergences licensed by the Bogolyubov-Parasyuk theorem's guarantee that counterterms stay local.

Checked through three loops, the recurrences yield renormalization group equations summing leading logarithms to all orders. Numerically, the outcome splits by operator: the unit operator's amplitude hits a Landau pole. The physically relevant V-A operator, the actual weak current, turns asymptotically free. So radiative corrections tame the growth and restore unitarity. In that regime the amplitude even overlaps with the gauge-boson theory's behavior.
arxiv-2511-22341:
Rosenthal, Schmidt, Graf, and colleagues at TU Munich audit the exams used to grade vision-language models, and find the formatting alone moves the scores. Multiple-choice visual question answering is a standard benchmark, but earlier work showed answers shift with choice order. This study varies three subtler prompt-formatting factors, things like separators and answer markers that change nothing semantically. Across seven multimodal models and five datasets, generating 48 distinct prompt formats for the same questions.

Accuracy is highly sensitive to these cosmetic changes, independently of order effects and of model confidence. Existing debiasing strategies fail to neutralize the formatting biases. The warning is direct: a reported score partly measures the prompt template used, so cross-paper comparisons with different formats are unreliable. The study deliberately builds on the earlier order-bias literature rather than re-litigating it, isolating formatting as a separate, uncontrolled variable in current evaluation practice.
arxiv-2511-22441:
Zhang and colleagues measure how easily artificial intelligence can work out where a social media photo was taken. Their system, GEO-Detective, imitates a human investigator. It picks strategies based on how hard an image looks. It uses tools such as visual reverse search to gather outside clues about landmarks, signs, and building styles. Ordinary users with such tools could expose locations that photo owners never meant to share.

GEO-Detective beat plain large vision-language models overall, especially on images with no obvious geographic features. On country-level guesses it improved accuracy by over 11.1 percent compared with baseline models. It kept a gain of about 5.2 percent at finer scales, while outside clues cut its rate of unknown answers by more than half. The team also tested four defences and found watermarking the most effective, warning that current safeguards are weak against this kind of agent.
arxiv-2511-22741:
Coriasco, Kirilov, de Moraes, and Tokoro determine exactly when a class of partial differential equations on non-compact spaces is globally solvable. The operators come from involutive structures, systems of vector fields closed under Lie brackets, on a product of a non-compact manifold with a torus. Global solvability hinges on the operator's range being closed, deciding whether every compatible right-hand side actually has a solution, in smooth and distributional senses alike.

The authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for that closed range, working in Fréchet-Schwartz spaces and their duals to handle the non-compact geometry. They also prove that a weaker notion of global hypoellipticity, a regularity property of solutions, already forces the range closed for operators on smooth paracompact manifolds. That extends a compact-manifold result to the non-compact setting. It completes a piece of solvability theory for involutive systems.
arxiv-2511-23041:
Nguyen and Rosseel ask whether large language models judge people from their spelling the way humans do. In online writing, a stretched or shortened word, like funnnn instead of fun, quietly signals things about the writer. The team measured those impressions on three scales, formality, carefulness, and the writer's apparent age, for both human raters and several language models.

Overall the models' ratings correlated strongly with humans' ratings, with GPT-4o reaching a correlation of 0.905 on raw scores in the paired setup. But the match broke down on the differences between spelling variants. There, correlations fell to about 0.53 for GPT-4o and nearly zero, 0.043 in the table, for Llama3-8B. Rating distributions also differed, and the size of the penalty depended on the variation type, so models share the broad human bias but not its finer shape.
arxiv-2511-23341:
Allen and colleagues ask how few edges a host hypergraph can have while containing. As a sub-structure, every member of a class of hypergraphs, the universality problem of combinatorics. For graphs the answer for D-degenerate graphs, those whose every part has a low-degree vertex, was known to be near a power of n. And the team generalizes the construction and the counting lower bound to r-uniform hypergraphs.

They prove a universal hypergraph exists whose edge count grows like n raised to the power r minus one-over-D. Multiplied only by powers of logarithms, and that this is best possible apart from those logarithmic factors, which remain the paper's open problem. The result covers every degeneracy D above one, and the authors note the tree-like case D equals one likely follows with minor adjustments. Though whether the extra logarithmic factor is needed there is unclear.
arxiv-2512-00641:
Facial expression recognition often collapses when the people or cameras change between training and deployment. Razieh Ghaedi and co-authors propose GAT-ADA in 2025, a graph-attention network with adversarial domain alignment for cross-domain expression recognition. Severe domain shift is the central obstacle.

The framework pairs a ResNet-50 backbone with a batch-level graph attention network that models relations between samples under shift. Adversarial alignment pushes the model toward features that work in both domains. Robust expression recognition supports accessibility tools and human-computer interaction that must work for new users without retraining. Batch-level graphs let the model borrow strength from similar faces in the same batch. Adversarial alignment is the mechanism that forces domain-blind features.
arxiv-2512-00841:
Du Wenzhang proposes a market-based twist on federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains one model across many devices or sites without pooling their data. For multimedia tasks, the method strains under uneven data across clients and tight communication limits, especially with large models.

Classic averaging methods send full model weights back and forth, and they can diverge when client data differ a lot. The proposed system, KTA v2, trades knowledge in prediction space instead of raw weights. Clients buy and sell predictions in a knowledge market. Trading compact predictions could cut traffic while keeping learning stable.
arxiv-2512-01141:
Akshat Bagade, Maanas Baraya, Chittebbayi Penugonda, and Muhammad Yousuf teach machines to rename variables in a 2025 paper. Developers often inherit code whose variable names are generic or misleading. Teams moving fast leave many functions undocumented, which slows comprehension for everyone who reads the code later.

Poor names raise the risk of subtle bugs. They also make it harder for large language models to reason about code, since names carry much of the meaning. Their neural variable name repair system learns to suggest readable identifiers. Automatic renaming could help teams clean legacy code and help AI coding tools understand it.
arxiv-2512-01941:
A Schrödinger operator describes a quantum particle moving through a potential landscape, and bound states appear as eigenvalues below the spectrum's edge. Jussi Behrndt and three co-authors study in 2025 what happens with complex-valued potentials, in one or two dimensions, when the coupling is weak.

Complex potentials break the usual rules, since energies need no longer be real numbers. The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions on the potential for discrete eigenvalues to exist in this faint-coupling regime. They also examine whether such eigenvalues are unique and how their algebraic multiplicity behaves. The results tidy a corner of spectral theory where intuition from real potentials fails.
arxiv-2512-02241:
Some systems hang between life and death. Bits branch, move, and wipe each other out, and the group as a whole lives or dies. Peter Grassberger's 2025 paper reports fine-grained computer runs of one such class: parity conserving directed percolation. It is the second most weighty class of these life-or-death phase shifts.

What sets this class apart is parity. The count of bits is kept modulo two, so a finite system splits into even and odd camps with unlike fates. Careful runs pin down the class's traits near the tipping point, in one space dimension plus time. Shared classes let one pattern forecast the acts of many unlike systems, so each sharp trait tightens a broad net.
arxiv-2512-02841:
Lechen Zhang and five co-authors test whether one system prompt can steer a language model well in many languages. System prompts condition model behavior at inference time with little cost. Most prior study covers English only, yet real deployments serve the whole world at once.

A single prompt that behaves reliably across languages is the goal. The team measures steerability cross lingually, hunting for languages where steering slips.
