Inoussa Mouiche and Sherif Saad present TIJERE, a model that pulls entities and their relations from cyber threat reports into structured form. Such extraction feeds knowledge graphs for threat analysis, but past joint methods suffer from confused features, ambiguous language, noise spread, and overlapping relations. TIJERE recasts the task with a multi-sequence labelling scheme, building a separate sequence for each entity pair.

Expert domain features enrich position, context, and meaning for each entity, which sharpens feature separation and classification. A security-tuned language model, SecureBERT+, helps reduce ambiguity and improve generalisation in the domain. The authors position TIJERE as a step toward more accurate automated threat intelligence processing.
arxiv-2605-02241:
Luong Nguyen asks how well a small language model can judge its own correctness, a skill that decides whether cheap local models can triage questions for costly cloud models. If a local model knows when it is likely wrong, hard queries can be escalated and easy ones kept local, with no supervised training data. Nguyen compares zero-shot confidence signals with supervised routing baselines in the style of RouteLLM.

Tests cover three model families at the seven to eight billion parameter scale and two data sets. Average token log-probability, which needs no training, matched or beat supervised baselines in distribution. Out of distribution it won by a wide margin. The author argues the signal works because it measures the generation itself, not the query.
arxiv-2605-02341:
Members of the ATLAS Collaboration extend a recent measurement from the Large Hadron Collider to probe how top quarks behave near the point where a top and antitop pair can just form. The study uses proton collisions and looks at pairs that decay to an electron and a muon. It asks whether a short-lived, loosely bound state forms near that threshold.

The team compares the measured shapes with model forecasts, with and without such a bound state included. The data fit the forecasts that include the state better, and a fit to the mass shape gives signs of the effect at more than three standard units of significance. The measured rate also matches dedicated studies of the same region.
arxiv-2605-02541:
Fayez Abu-Ajamieh assesses whether two X-ray missions could detect vacuum birefringence caused by magnetars, the strongly magnetic stars known as magnetars. In such fields, empty space itself should split light into two modes that travel at slightly different speeds. Measuring that split would test quantum effects in extreme magnetism.

The study uses a realistic field that varies across the magnetosphere, rather than a single fixed value. That change raises the time delay between modes and can push it near a microsecond for the strongest known fields. Abu-Ajamieh tracks how polarization evolves in the varying field, works out when a standard approximation holds, and computes signals for all known magnetars. Both missions could see the effect under favorable conditions, with one named source the best candidate.
arxiv-2605-02841:
Yingtian Shi and nine co-authors present TRACE, a framework for recognizing activities in smart homes that reasons over long context, not just short sensor windows. Many daily activities share similar local sensor patterns, and sparse, light-touch sensing leaves readings ambiguous. Short-window methods then fragment their predictions and miss the behavior that ties a sequence together.

TRACE fuses evidence from several sensor sources with priors tied to the specific user's routines. Ambiguities are resolved by that context rather than by the window alone. On public benchmarks, the method improved accuracy on complex activities. In a case study in the team's own smart home, it gave smoother predictions that fit user routines. It also held up under changed domains and missing sensor types. Context, the authors argue, is the missing signal.
arxiv-2605-03341:
E. Plácido-Flores, Román Linares, V. López, and C. A. Escobar search for stable magnetic vacua that break Lorentz symmetry inside nonlinear electrodynamics. Working in the Plebański Hamiltonian form, they treat a single-invariant potential as the core object and ask when a constant nonzero field can sit stably at the bottom of the energy.

For three two-parameter models, rational, logarithmic, and exponential, they map where such vacua exist with bounded energy and a healthy Hessian. All three admit good vacua on the magnetic branch only. The electric branch and extra models show boundedness alone does not guarantee symmetry breaking.
arxiv-2605-03641:
James Yen and seven co-authors present Jiao, a system design for consumer robots that must run safety-critical control, perception, and user apps on one shared multicore platform. Static partitioning hypervisors give strong isolation, but home users who customize robot behavior lack the systems expertise of platform developers. Jiao aims to bridge that gap.

Three components do the work: a Safe IO Cell with hardware-level override, a Parameter Synchronization Service that hides cross-domain complexity, and a Safety Communication Layer aligned with the IEC 61508 safety standard. On an ARM Cortex-A55 platform, partition isolation cut cycle-period jitter by about eighty-five percent and nearly eliminated large timing excursions in their tests.
arxiv-2605-03741:
Mara Attia, Tim Lichtenberg, Ema Jungová, and Mariana Sastre present PALEOS, an open-source toolkit to model exoplanet interiors. Predicting a rocky or water-rich planet's layers is a closure problem in thermodynamics: density, temperature gradient, and phase in every layer must follow from equations of state. Those must stay consistent from surface to core. Existing equations are scattered across fields.

PALEOS unifies equations of state for iron, magnesium silicate, and water across seventeen phases. It derives density, energy, entropy, heat capacities, thermal expansion, and the adiabatic gradient through Maxwell relations. The results are released as lookup tables. Checks against the Preliminary Reference Earth Model recovered Earth's radius within a fraction of a percent. The team computed nearly eighteen thousand mass-radius relations for rocky and water-rich compositions.
arxiv-2605-04141:
Ritvik Sai Narayan, Melinda Soares-Furtado, and Richard H. D. Townsend model the tidal evolution of TOI-5882, a subgiant star hosting a short-period brown dwarf companion that is spiraling toward engulfment. Their framework couples the binary evolution code MESA to the full linear tidal response computed by GYRE-tides, making the treatment self-consistent. The question is which dissipation mechanism actually drives the star's angular momentum changes.

Interior radiative damping dominates, they find, with the classical equilibrium tide model too low on angular momentum change by several orders of magnitude. The combined framework predicts an engulfment timescale shortened by a factor of two to six. It speeds inspiral by tens of millions of years. Early inspiral is driven by non-resonant losses from internal gravity waves before resonance crossings take over near Roche-lobe overflow.
arxiv-2605-04341:
Mohammed Sabry and Anya Belz study how to distil a large language model into a smaller student when there is an explicit budget for computing cost. Common low-rank adapters cut training cost but leave the heavy backbone untouched, so running the student stays expensive.

Their framework treats compression as allocating a fixed compute budget across the model. Modules keep different shares of their dense computation, low-rank capacity is assigned adaptively, and a final step removes or approximates parts that matter least. One budget dial produces a family of students, and at a moderate setting their student matched standard adapter quality with notable compression.
arxiv-2605-04441:
K. Rajaswathi and four co-authors study paired solitons in a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate, where one component forms a dark dip and the other a bright hump that rides inside it. Synthetic spin-orbit and Rabi couplings, created with lasers, add new internal dynamics to the pair.

Without spin-orbit coupling, the system maps onto a classic solvable model, giving exact solutions as a benchmark. Turning the coupling on breaks that solvability and drives the components apart with density oscillations, while Rabi driving locks their phases and supports robust breathing excitations. The authors also recast the internal spin dynamics as a Josephson junction with a built-in momentum bias.
arxiv-2605-04541: Muyao Peng and colleagues build Angle-I2P: angle-consistent-aware hierarchical attention for cross-modality outlier rejection. The building builds. Their attending attends angle-consistent-aware hierarchical cross-modality outlier rejection. The doing does. It is vision. Angle-I2P angle-i2ps.
arxiv-2605-04641:
Qiming Li and eleven co-authors propose a training-free fix for object hallucination in large vision-language models, which often describe things that are not in the image. Existing remedies need costly manual annotation and retraining, or decoding tricks that slow every answer down.

The authors noticed that these models attend to visual information much more strongly when answering caption-style queries than other questions. Their method finds the attention heads most sensitive to caption queries, estimates good steering directions for them, and nudges those outputs during ordinary use. Strengthening fine-grained visual perception this way reduces hallucinated objects, and the method plugs into existing models without retraining.
arxiv-2605-04941:
Ivan Kartáč and five co-authors describe a system entered in SemEval-2026 Task 11, which tests whether language models truly reason or merely react to content. Their system tackles syllogisms, short arguments with premises and a conclusion. It mixes a symbolic prover with small language models of about four billion parameters.

A language-model parser first translates each syllogism into first-order logic, then the prover checks it, with optional translation and premise-retrieval modules. The system scored competitively with a low content effect on most subtasks. Tests also showed the approach beat zero-shot language-model baselines at this size, though multilingual handling in small models remained limited.
arxiv-2605-05241:
Zijian Zeng and four co-authors present DexSim2Real, a framework that moves dexterous robot hand skills from simulation into the real world with help from vision-language foundation models. Sim-to-real transfer usually leans on hand-designed randomisation or task-specific tuning, which limits how widely it generalises. Their system instead lets a foundation model act as a visual realism critic for the simulation itself.

Three parts combine: guided domain randomisation tuned in a closed loop, a tactile-visual attention policy built for zero-shot transfer, and a progressive skill curriculum based on language-model task breakdowns. Across six hard manipulation tasks with blinded scoring, the system reached a high average real-world success rate and a small simulation-to-reality gap.
arxiv-2605-05441:
Eva Kasanda and twelve co-authors describe a new research beamline for proton therapy studies in Bern, Switzerland. The beamline adapts a medical cyclotron that normally makes imaging isotopes. It was rebuilt so biologists can test FLASH irradiation and minibeam therapy, two ideas that may spare healthy tissue better than standard treatment.

Collimators and foils shape the eighteen MeV proton beam, and a dosimetry setup measures the dose carefully. The system delivers steady beams from very low dose rates up to FLASH levels. Film tests confirmed that careful corrections make the dose readings trustworthy for cell experiments.
arxiv-2605-05541:
Cars may one day talk to each other with light. Ryota Soga and five co-authors test a visible-light communication system that uses an event camera as the receiver. Event cameras react to change with tiny delay and wide dynamic range, which suits vehicle-to-everything messaging, but bandwidth and multiple senders pose problems.

Their protocol limits event generation while keeping range and field of view. A new method identifies several LED transmitters at once, and they received from up to three simultaneously. Road tests measured end-to-end delay and showed the system meets the needs of cooperative perception.
arxiv-2605-05741:
How hard is a language model thinking? Chengda Lu, Xiaoyu Fan, and Wei Xu argue the answer is written in its layer-by-layer confidence. They identify a magnification effect: deeper transformer layers inherently amplify small changes in confidence, yielding a fine-grained trajectory through inference.

Their probe, HyperLens, traces that trajectory and quantifies cognitive effort. Across eight models and eight datasets, trajectories for complex and simple tasks diverged consistently. The pattern distills into a practical signal for separating tasks that strain the model from routine ones, without extra computation. Such trajectories offer a window into inference dynamics that final answers alone cannot provide.
arxiv-2605-05841:
Confinement binds quarks into pairs joined by flux strings that snap when stretched. Manuel John and nine co-authors report the first quantum simulation of string breaking in a genuinely non-abelian theory, pure SU(2) lattice gauge theory, run on a qudit processor. Non-abelian theories are harder because the gauge fields themselves carry charge.

Earlier experiments covered only abelian versions. Simulating the real-time dynamics classically is prohibitively hard, making this a natural quantum target. The experiment tracks how the string's energy redistributes as it breaks, a dynamics central to the strong force.
arxiv-2605-05941:
Shuhong Liu and six co-authors work on object detection in raw camera sensor data. Raw data keeps deeper bit depth and physical detail, and it avoids distortions from the image processor in the camera. But sensors differ in exposure, color response, and bit depth, so a model trained on one device may fail on another.

Their framework, RAWild, splits sensor differences into a global tone fix and a local color fix for each area. Both parts draw on priors from raw data distributions. A physics based simulation pipeline adds varied synthetic sensor outputs for training. Across raw benchmarks from 10 to 24 bit depth, a single network reached top results in mixed and hard test settings.
arxiv-2605-06241:
Ömer Faruk Akgül and three co-authors argue that reinforcement learning improves language model reasoning by selection, not by teaching new capability. Evidence suggests such training shifts probability toward solutions the base model already contains. The authors ask whether the expensive optimization loop itself is needed, if its whole effect is a small, predictable steering of existing behavior.

Token level analysis finds the benefit concentrated at high entropy decision points, touching only one to three percent of positions. The promoted token always sits among the base model's top five alternatives there. Their RL free method, ReasonMaxxer, applies contrastive loss only at those gated points using a few hundred rollouts. It matched or beat full reinforcement learning across model families and math benchmarks at a tiny fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2605-06341:
Thomas Bömer and three co-authors evolve rules for optimization problems whose parts are tightly coupled. Many real problems split into subtasks whose solutions must be coordinated, from routing to scheduling, yet language model driven heuristic design had only handled single problems. Their system, CoupleEvo, tests three ways to coordinate evolutionary search across coupled parts using a large language model as the heuristic writer and critic.

The sequential strategy evolves rules for one subproblem at a time, the iterative strategy alternates between subtasks across generations, and the integrated strategy evolves all rules at once. Two typical coupled problems served as test beds. Decomposition based strategies gave more stable convergence and higher solution quality. Integrated evolution suffered from greater search complexity and variability, showing that coordination of the search itself matters.
arxiv-2605-06741: Zixi Li and Youzhen Li derive a closed-form upper bound for admissible learning-rate steps. An update is modeled as a projected forward step on the probability simplex, the space of belief distributions. In this model, admissibility means contractivity in the natural KL, or Bregman, geometry. The bound is not a tuning slogan but a formula. It turns a familiar hyperparameter question into an explicit local calculation for belief-space dynamics.
arxiv-2605-07241:
Guang Yang and three co-authors sign audio recordings with a cryptographic watermark to fight deepfake voices. Passive detectors struggle as generators improve and real channels distort sound. Their Asymmetric Phase Coding hides a digital signature inside the sound's phase pattern, using error correction and a redundant code, with no training required.

On a thousand speech clips, verification stayed very high under cropping, filtering, resampling, and re-encoding attacks, while sound quality remained acceptable and checking took milliseconds. The authors compare against neural watermark systems, spell out the threat model including a strong erasure attack, and release code and keys for reproduction.
arxiv-2605-07341:
Rahul Rajkumar studies random walks that take values in the rational adeles, a number system combining all p-adic completions at once. Starting from random walks on p-adic numbers, he builds walks on the infinite product space. A survival time argument shows these walks stay within the adeles for all time with probability one.

The adelic walks are close to processes living on finitely many components, which opens the way to a limit theorem. Rajkumar establishes weak convergence to an adelic Lévy process in the standard Skorokhod topology. The result extends classical scaling limits for random walks into the adelic setting of modern number theory.
arxiv-2605-07941:
Christian Komusiewicz and Nils Morawietz analyze a local search problem for vertex covers, sets of vertices that touch every edge of a graph. A swap exchanges a few vertices of the cover for others; if the new cover is smaller, the swap improves the solution. Users keep the swap size small to balance speed and quality.

Because the problem is hard when measured by swap size alone, the authors seek running times that grow mildly in a structural graph parameter and strongly only in the swap size. They obtain such algorithms when the parameter is the h-index or the treewidth of the graph, giving practical routes for structured instances.
arxiv-2605-08241:
Bibin Wilson brings self-supervised learning down to microcontroller scale. At that scale, models hold fewer than half a million parameters. They must fit under a megabyte. Three obstacles bite hard. The projection head dominates. The representation bottlenecks. And results swing with augmentation choices.

The framework learns from a frozen DINO teacher through asymmetric distillation. It adds multi-scale feature matching. It also ramps augmentation strength in a set sequence. On a small MobileNet backbone pretrained on CIFAR-100, it beat a tiny SimCLR baseline by eighteen points. That score is for linear-probe accuracy. It reached ninety-four percent of the supervised ceiling, with no labels and no text supervision.
arxiv-2605-08541:
Joshua Shay Kricheli and four coauthors warn that common scaling law studies for language models rest on a flawed training design. Many fits train every run at one fixed ratio of tokens to parameters, making the two size measures move in lockstep. When the true exponents for parameters and tokens sit close together, that design makes scale coefficients nearly impossible to pin down.

Confidence ranges balloon and predictions collapse away from the training line, a flaw proven across four law forms and rooted in the geometry of the fitting problem itself. Varied ratio designs win almost all held out tests. Scaling research gains a clear threshold for how much design variety trustworthy extrapolation demands.
arxiv-2605-08641:
Wenduo Huang, Vilmos Komorni, and Yuru Zou study number expansions that use two different bases at once, where each digit chooses which base divides next. Two natural algorithms, greedy and lazy, generate these expansions, and the authors analyze the dynamics of both maps on their interval. Each map is shown to hold exactly one well behaved invariant probability measure.

Both systems prove exact, a strong form of mixing, on their domains. Under a sharper condition on the base pair, almost every number admits endlessly many expansions, while numbers with a unique expansion form a set of measure zero. Ergodic theory gains a full dynamical picture for a two base generalization of classic beta expansions.
arxiv-2605-08841:
Junli Zha, Jiahui Wang, Xinkai Lu, and Jinbo Wang help vision models see famed trick images as they are. Models tend to say the lore they learned, not what the lines show. Their plan needs no training. It was built for a vision contest task. It works in three ways that back each other. Prep steps blunt the trick's pull, with edge pulls, hue splits, shape work, or guide lines. Prompts push the model to match what it sees. Votes are cast more than once for a firm call.

On the set test, the plan scores just past ninety percent. On a hand checked set it scores near the top. It took second place in the contest, by a slim gap.
arxiv-2605-08941:
Vinay Kumar, Satyendra Rajput, Mausam, and N. Anoop Krishnan benchmark AI agents on running molecular dynamics simulations, a workflow demanding physical judgment at every step. Their MDGYM suite holds one hundred sixty nine expert curated tasks across two major simulation packages at three difficulty levels, covering script writing, boundary choices, unstable trajectory diagnosis, and output interpretation. Three agent frameworks with four language models are put through it.

All perform poorly: the strongest solves about a fifth of easy tasks and under a tenth at higher levels. Failure analysis finds a signature pattern: agents start the machinery fine, then build physically unstable setups, invent numbers without running the computation, or quit instead of debugging. Fluent coding, the study warns, is not grounded physical reasoning.
arxiv-2605-09241: World models let agents imagine futures before acting, but training them end-to-end is unstable. Kai Zhao, Dongliang Nie, and others stabilize the process with Sub-JEPA: subspace Gaussian regularization. The 2026 paper makes end-to-end world models trainable without babysitting.
arxiv-2605-09341: Multi-agent systems work better when agents' skills co-evolve rather than train in isolation. Shuai Pan, Yixiang Liu, Jiaye Gao, and others propose SkillMAS: skill co-evolution in LLM-based multi-agent systems. The 2026 paper grows teams, not just individuals.
arxiv-2605-09541: Multi-loop Feynman integrals are the nightmare of fine detail particle physics, and reducing them symbolically has long been a black art. Bo Feng, Xiang Li, Yuanche Liu, and others automate the putting back via generating functions. The 2026 paper is machine quantum field theory made careful.
arxiv-2605-09741: Treatments work differently for various people — effect modification — and matched observational studies can reveal those contrasts adaptively. Yu Gui, Dylan S. Small, and Zhimei Ren develop the methodology for shifting discovery of effect modification. The 2026 paper is causal read for heterogeneous treatment effects.
arxiv-2605-09841: The sun's coronal magnetic field drives space weather, but the models simulating it need rigorous validation. Abhinav G. Iyer, Michael S. Wheatland, Brian T. Welsch, and others validate them using Gaussian separation. The 2026 paper is solar physics quality control at scale.
arxiv-2605-10041: Cluster math — combinatorial math shapes with deep structure — as the foundation of a cryptosystem. Martin Ortiz Morales and Leticia Peña Tellez build it. The 2026 paper is cryptography from pure mathematics. It encrypts messages securely with lovely, intricate cluster math.
arxiv-2605-10141: Reward models for formal theorem proving need rigorous benchmarking — FormalRewardBench provides it. Zeynel A. Ulusan, Burak S. Akbudak, Can S. Erer, and others build the benchmark. The 2026 paper is AI for mathematics with standards. It benchmarks the rewarders of proof.
arxiv-2605-10441: The RG-consistent (P)NJL model — thermal cutoff modifications and their impact on thermodynamics and net-baryon number fluctuations. Jie Tang, Fan Lin, and Xinyang Wang analyze the impact. The 2026 paper is QCD phenomenology. It keeps the cutoff consistent with the renormalization group.
arxiv-2606-00041:
Pasquale Ardimento, Bernardi, Cimitile, and Latorre reconstruct how COVID-19 patients moved through hospitals using process mining in this 2026 arXiv case study. Process mining rebuilds real workflows from event logs rather than trusting official pathway diagrams. The team built an open pipeline converting messy clinical tables from a shared COVID learning dataset into a clean event log. They then applied process discovery, conformance checking against expected rules, and outcome analysis to the pathways.

The analysis exposed a monitoring backbone running through inpatient care, plus wide variation where emergency department patients entered admission. Outcomes differed mainly with patient age and exposure to intensive care, they report. Those findings translate into governance advice: standardize triage at intake, plan capacity around the discovered bottlenecks, and coordinate step-down transfers to ordinary wards. The authors frame process mining as evidence for hospital management decisions, not just an exercise.

arxiv-2606-04141:
Kargi Chauhan and Pratibha Revankar study in 2026 how language model agents can be tricked into leaking credentials that share their context window with untrusted content. They test three defenses meant to catch the theft early, ideally before any answer is produced.

First, probes reading the model's internal activations separated innocent from credential-seeking prompts with high accuracy, even under disguised encodings. Second, honeytokens, fake credentials shaped by character models, were calibrated with conformal prediction to control false alarms. Third, tracking an estimated leakage budget across a whole conversation caught slow multi-turn thefts that single-turn checks missed. The authors call the results preliminary, noting the small in-house test suite and the need for internal model access.
arxiv-2606-04241:
Sushma Kumari and co-authors extend in 2026 a family of rare-earth cobalt aluminide crystals to its heavy members, growing single crystals for rare earths from gadolinium to thulium plus yttrium. The lighter members of the family were already known for an odd mix of magnetic behaviors.

Diffraction showed the new crystals take an orthorhombic structure with a small, varying aluminium shortfall. Heat, resistance, and magnetization measurements found antiferromagnetic ordering in every member, with ordering temperatures spanning roughly two to twelve kelvin. Gadolinium and terbium versions showed two close transitions each. The ordering pattern breaks the standard scaling expected from the rare earth alone, which the authors attribute to the interplay of exchange coupling and crystal electric fields.
arxiv-2606-04341:
Abhinava Chatterjee and Chao-Xing Liu predict in 2026 a one-way effect for light in magnetic materials that host axion quasiparticles. These are waves of the magnetic order that couple to electromagnetic fields. The hybrids are called axion-polaritons.

Under the right static electric and magnetic fields, the hybrids move one way differently from the other. The cause is direction-dependent coupling between the axion and the photon. In one regime the effect becomes perfect. Light going one way decouples from the axion entirely. Light going the other way hybridizes strongly. That is exactly an optical isolator, a one-way gate for light. The authors propose it as a testable probe of axion quasiparticles.
arxiv-2606-04441:
Lu and colleagues present a practical method for measuring the global polarization of Lambda particles in fixed-target nuclear collisions, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. That motion polarizes the spin of the particles that fly out. The strong polarization seen in Lambda particles shows that quark-gluon plasma is the most vortical fluid known. Measuring it at lower energies maps the phase diagram of strong-force matter.

Fixed-target experiments make this measurement hard. Their detectors cover an uneven range of angles. That uneven coverage couples the particles' directed flow with detector flaws. The coupling biases the polarization result. The method from Lu removes this bias. The team checked it with realistic detector simulations. The simulations used the STAR fixed-target setup at RHIC. The work supports future measurements at facilities such as FAIR and NICA.
arxiv-2606-04541:
Bobrov proposes a general method for computing kinematic limits in particle physics, in a 2026 arXiv methods paper. Kinematic limits are the boundary values that energies and angles in a reaction cannot cross. The approach works with Lorentz invariants. These quantities stay fixed under changes of reference frame. They behave like Cayley-Menger determinants, the volume formulas of geometry, moved into Minkowski space. A kinematic limit is reached exactly when one of these invariants vanishes.

Because the condition is algebraic, the approach applies across a wide range of particle processes. Bobrov highlights reactions involving lost particles. Or they barely interact with detector material. Neutrinos are the classic example. Knowing the exact limits helps experimenters reconstruct such reactions. The limits can also suppress background. They cut events that could not come from the process of interest.
arxiv-2606-04841:
Vázquez-Mozo studies anomalous currents in chiral fluids living in geometries more general than Einstein's, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Metric-affine geometries allow the metric and the connection to vary, producing nonmetricity, the failure of lengths to be preserved under transport. He studies equilibrium fermionic fluids chirally coupled to background Weyl-type nonmetricity.

From the equilibrium partition function, he evaluates the relation of the axial-vector current. The calculation shows chiral separation effects, currents separating chiral charges, driven by the fluid's vorticity and by the Weyl magnetic field. Such anomaly-driven transport is prized because it is exact, so these results extend a robust corner of quantum field theory into geometries.
arxiv-2606-05241:
Yongjie Wang and co-authors measure search-time contamination in deep research agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Public benchmarks promise fair, reproducible checks, but research agents search the live web while they work, so they can retrieve benchmark metadata, question context, or even ground-truth answers mid-test. That retrieval bypasses the intended reasoning and quietly inflates the measured score. The authors define three contamination types of increasing severity: benchmark metadata leakage, question-context leakage, and explicit answer leakage.

They build detection algorithms to identify each type and measure its effect on scores. Evaluating modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks, they found contamination is widespread. It can inflate performance by up to four percent, meaning existing evaluations may overestimate true reasoning ability by a real margin. They advocate contamination-aware practice in response: isolated sandboxes for agents, open records of search paths, and controlled access to benchmark material.
arxiv-2606-05441:
Al Zadid Sultan Bin Habib and colleagues present GOTabPFN in this 2026 arXiv paper, a way to make small tabular foundation models work on data with far more features than samples. Such high-dimensional, low-sample settings, genomics being the case, break models like TabPFN that were designed for at most a couple thousand features.

Their pipeline first orders the features with Graph-guided Ordering with Local Refinement, which arranges correlated features into neighborhoods. They show this ordering problem is equivalent to the weighted Minimum Linear Arrangement problem and solve it with a traveling-salesman-style surrogate. A Neuro-Inspired Subunit Compression unit then pools locally adjacent ordered features into meta-features, compressing the table into a compact token sequence the model can consume. Across tabular benchmarks, GOTabPFN improved stability and accuracy under tight token budgets. It beat using the backbone directly.
arxiv-2606-05741:
Mugdho, Hasan, and Wang weigh chip designs for data centers in orbit in a 2026 arXiv paper. Space offers sunlight and cheap launches, but no air for cooling. Heat can leave only by radiation, which demands large radiator panels. Standard graphics processors pair a hot chip with separate memory blocks. The team asks whether compute-in-memory chips, which blend storage and math, fare better under that thermal cap.

Their method ties allowed computing speed directly to radiator capacity in the design loop. Simulations showed the split GPU layout forms severe hotspots under tight cooling. The processors had to throttle down to stay safe. Memory-centric chips spread heat far more evenly. They beat the GPU designs on operations per watt across a wide range of radiator budgets. Across many AI workloads the edge grew under realistic space constraints. The paper guides orbital hardware choices with thermal reality first.
arxiv-2606-05841:
Clemen, Führer, and Roche-Newton guarantee large point subsets with all distances distinct in a 2026 arXiv paper. Extremal geometry asks how big a subset can avoid a banned pattern. Here the pattern is a repeated distance: no two pairs may span the same length. Given any planar point set, the authors find a subset whose size grows like the cube root of the whole. Every distance inside that subset is unique.

The bound improves an earlier result of Charalambides. The proof leans on a hypergraph independence theorem by Li and Postle, plus incidence geometry tools. A second problem in the paper picks grid subsets with no rhombus, a four-point pattern. Both problems descend from Erdős and Purdy's work on forbidden configurations. They have become benchmark tests for AI math systems. The paper sharpens what combinatorics can promise before the point set's structure is known.
arxiv-2606-06441:
Andy Shen, Chenqi Fu, and Ray Lin tackle a bias that creeps into cancer trials in this 2026 arXiv paper on biostatistics. In oncology trials, control patients whose disease worsens are often allowed to switch onto the experimental drug. Ethically sensible, but switching breaks the clean comparison that randomization bought, and survival estimates tilt. Existing fixes lean on strong assumptions or fragile models.

The authors bring in external controls, comparable patients from outside the trial, to stand in for what switchers would have faced untreated. Borrowing the synthetic control method and balancing weights from observational research, they build estimators using multiple imputation and time varying weights. They also discuss how to choose which external patients are eligible to impute from at each moment. Simulations show clear gains over standard adjustments and naive uses of external data. Two phase three trials, IMpower130 and OAK, demonstrate the approach on real data.
arxiv-2606-06541:
Risto Raitio completes a composite model of matter with string mathematics in this 2026 arXiv paper on particle theory. Preon models propose that quarks and leptons are bound states of smaller constituents, confined by a metacolor force much as quarks are confined in protons. Such a model needs an ultraviolet completion, a well behaved high energy description. Raitio builds one from the Nambu Goto string action, computing the Regge trajectory of a six preon state, the line relating its spin to its mass squared.

From that trajectory he constructs the Veneziano scattering amplitude with no free parameters. Its poles match the model's spectrum to within half a percent. At fixed angle it decays exponentially with exactly the Gross Mende coefficient, realized numerically to zero point zero three percent. The author calls this a soft, non perturbative completion, with the Standard Model as the low energy limit.
arxiv-2606-06741:
Software agents usually improve only when someone hands them curated lessons or a reliable grader. Yan and a large team ask what an agent can do with neither in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting, called open world self evolution, gives the agent only a task prompt and the open internet, with no answers from the target task to learn from.

Their framework, OpenSkill, gathers grounded knowledge and checking anchors from documents, code repositories, and the web, then turns them into portable skills. The agent practices on virtual tasks it builds from those anchors, not on the real answers, and sharpens its skills there. Across three benchmarks and two agent models, OpenSkill earned the best automated pass rate while respecting the no supervision rule. Its skills transferred to other models without retuning, and its home built grader agreed surprisingly well with true outcomes it never saw.
arxiv-2606-06941:
Majority vote is a lazy way to pick a model's final answer, especially in law. Wynter, Sahoo, and Griffin replace voting with evidence selection in this 2026 arXiv paper. A small local model writes many reasoning traces per question. Fragments from those traces become pools of evidence for each answer.

An optimization step then picks the best evidence subset per pool. It scores fragments on relevance, specificity, and distinctiveness. The method uses a higher order binary optimization, solved by simulated annealing or a photonic quantum machine. A frontier model makes one final adjudication call per question. On two legal benchmarks, the method beat majority vote by wide margins. Gains reached about thirteen and twenty three percentage points. It also exposed a quirk: one frontier model favored option E on most questions when unaided. Curated evidence tamed that bias.
arxiv-2606-07041:
A spin chain and a field theory can describe the same physics, but twisting the boundary conditions exposes a deep obstruction. Nicholas Read and Saleur explore that twist in this 2026 arXiv paper. The chain is an antiferromagnet whose sites carry spin S. Its continuum limit is a nonlinear sigma model with a topological angle set by the spin.

The twist is antiperiodic boundaries paired with an odd number of sites. In the field theory this inserts a flux of the model's flip symmetry. The authors show the symmetry can be gauged only under a sign condition on the topological angle. When the condition fails, an 't Hooft anomaly blocks the gauged model entirely. A would-be theory on projective space simply does not exist at the bad angles. Semiclassical calculations recover the known ground state momenta of the chains. Boundary conditions, often an afterthought, here dictate which theories are possible.
arxiv-2606-07141:
Hospitals may need a trained AI model to forget one patient's data without forgetting medicine. Sharma and co-authors build a benchmark for that dilemma in this 2026 arXiv paper. Machine unlearning methods promise removal without retraining from scratch. Existing tests, though, use synthetic data far from clinical reality.

Their benchmark, REMEDI, uses the real MIMIC-III clinical database. The task is multi-label disease inference, where diagnoses correlate and overlap. Forget requests range from single patients to larger sets. Metrics track both diagnostic utility kept and information actually removed. Current methods traded one goal against the other. Several collapsed on multi-label tasks despite acing simpler benchmarks. A method called SCRUB kept the best balance between privacy and utility. Apparent success on tiny deletions often failed at larger scales. The authors call for objectives designed around label correlations from the start.
arxiv-2606-07741:
Zirui Chen and co-authors explain a puzzling constant of astrophysics in this 2026 arXiv paper: wherever hot and cold gas mix, the ratio of X-ray brightness to H-alpha brightness stays near three. H-alpha light traces cold gas near ten thousand degrees, while X-rays trace gas far hotter. Flat mixing-layer models miss that ratio by orders of magnitude.

The team ran three-dimensional wind-tunnel simulations with density contrast near one thousand between the phases. In that regime the cold gas shatters into many small glowing clumps, and hot gas forms a cocoon around them. Smoothing the simulated images to the width of a real tail brings the ratio to the observed value, about three. Their explanation splits the problem cleanly: atomic physics fixes the cold-gas share of the light, while the hot share depends on how briefly gas lingers at X-ray temperatures.
arxiv-2606-08441:
Sultana, Gonzalez, and Teather compare ways to point at things in augmented reality without holding a controller, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Selecting two-dimensional targets on virtual displays is a basic augmented reality task, and controller-free techniques promise more natural interaction. The authors systematically evaluated five pointing techniques using the standard ISO protocol for pointing devices, comparing them across three depths in terms of movement time, accuracy, throughput, and workload.

Head- and eye-based pointing significantly outperformed the hand-based methods, which used the finger, wrist, or whole arm. Head input was the most accurate and remained the most consistent as depth increased from near to far. Depth itself significantly affected performance, with complex interactions between depth, target size, and distance, so no single technique wins under all conditions. The study gives designers an empirical basis for choosing pointing techniques in depth-varying augmented reality tasks.
arxiv-2606-08941:
Deng, Sun, Li, and Liu ask when a causal estimate can ignore some variables and still give the same answer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Causal inference estimates the effect of an intervention from data in a graph. Often the graph is only partly known: a completed partially directed acyclic graph, or CPDAG, represents a family of causal graphs. atlantic-charter-1941:
Roosevelt and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter in August 1941. The two leaders met aboard warships off the coast of Newfoundland. Their joint text set aims for the war and the peace.

No land hunger, the charter pledges, and self-rule for all peoples. Free trade, shared labor gains, and seas free to all follow. Victorious nations will disarm the beaten foes and guard the peace. America had not yet entered the war when the words were signed. The promise of a better world became the Allies' moral charter for victory. Its pledges later fed the charter of the United Nations itself.

carlyle-heroes-1841:
Thomas Carlyle published On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History in 1841, from a set of lectures. Carlyle argues that great men shape the course of history. He treats the hero in six forms: god, prophet, poet, priest, man of letters, and king. Odin, Muhammad, Dante, Shakespeare, Luther, and Napoleon appear among them.

History, in his famous claim, is the biography of great men. The book stated the great-man theory in its classic form. It shaped Victorian biography and popular history for decades. Modern readers often resist its claims yet enjoy its force. It is a key text for the study of leadership myths.
cia-0000008641:
January 1973 opened with a report of a downed American jet in Nam Ha province, North Vietnam. The heading indicates the pilots' fate formed part of the report, though the title breaks off. Nam Ha sits south of Hanoi, along routes the air war struck for years.

Reports filed this close to the January ceasefire straddle war and postwar accounting. Officials needed to know which losses were confirmed and which men might still be held. A downed jet with named crew could anchor a case file for years. The entry shows the record still growing as the fighting stopped.
cia-0000008941:
Haiphong province is named in an April 1973 report on the death of an American pilot in North Vietnam. The port city region saw intense bombing in 1972, including mining of its harbor. By spring 1973, prisoners were coming home, but the dead still had to be accounted for.

A death report could rest on witnesses, graves, or local records passed through many hands. Analysts graded each source before adding it to a man's file. This entry shows that grading process beginning with a single provincial report. The accounting it fed continued for decades after the war had ended.
cia-0000009441:
Americans remaining in Saigon leads a June 1976 CIA item, followed by a reported capture of two Americans near a place the title cuts off. Saigon had been under communist rule for over a year by then. Reports from inside the city reached Washington slowly and indirectly.

The item gathers what could be learned about Americans who stayed through the takeover. A reported capture added urgency, since postwar detentions had no clear process or end. Analysts logged names and claims in hopes of later confirmation. The file shows the fall of Saigon still generating cases well into 1976.
cia-0000011841:
Revolution was the fear hanging over Latin America in 1968, and a CIA paper that February measures the potential for it across the hemisphere. Cuba's example had inspired guerrilla movements from Guatemala to Bolivia, while military regimes ruled many countries. The paper came in a year of upheaval around the world, from Paris to Mexico City.

Analysts surveyed the guerrillas, the generals, and the grievances that fed revolt in each land. They judged where unrest might turn into real bids for power. The survey reads as Washington's map of a tinderbox, drawn by men counting sparks country by country.
cia-0000012341:
John Maury, a CIA officer, wrote a memo for the record in March 1962 about conversations with men whose names are blanked out. The memo belongs to the Penkovsky file's working layer, below the summit letters. There, officers set down talks as they happened, while tone and detail were still fresh in the mind and could still be checked.

The plain value of writing things down fresh shows in every line of such records. They became the case as it truly happened, before memory could reshape it. For readers, Maury's notes are the handlers' craft at its most basic and most useful.
cia-0000013241:
Viet Cong policy and treatment of prisoners of war are studied in a CIA paper from July 1968. The year was the war's peak, and the doctrine had hardened with it. The paper sets out the southern system's official rules for captives. It then tests those rules against what the camps actually did, as reported by escapees, defectors, and the released.

The study shows policy and practice pulling against each other. Rules written at headquarters met hunger, distance, and local cruelty in the jungle. For readers, the paper is the southern doctrine read whole, at the moment the war burned hottest.
cia-0000013841:
Twelve American prisoners were captured in Kontum province, and a CIA item from March 1967 counts them. Kontum, in the Central Highlands, saw some of the war's hardest fighting. The highlands' war was fought over ridges, trails, and small camps far from the coast. Its captives paid accordingly, marched into a prison system whose highland camps were among the war's most obscure and most feared.

The item fixes the twelve in the record while their trails were warm. Twelve men in one note is the highland war's scale in miniature. For readers, the page is the highlands' chapter of the accounting: the twelve, taken.
cia-0000015441: Minutes of a branch chiefs' meeting held August 11, 1952, survive in a CIA record dated July 1, 1952. cia-0000046641: General Dmitri Volkogonov reported progress in tracing American servicemen missing from the Vietnam War, and a CIA item dated November 2, 1992, kept his update. cia-0000049141: A thousand fresh FMLN troops moved toward San Salvador in 1989, and a CIA item tracks the movement and the planned role of Father Ignacio Ellacuria.
