cooper-deerslayer-1841:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Deerslayer in 1841, the last Leatherstocking tale written and the first in the hero's life. Cooper went back to Natty Bumppo's youth on Lake Otsego, the Glimmerglass of the novel, in the 1740s. The book completes the five-volume arc of America's first epic hero.

Young Natty, called Deerslayer, joins his friend Chingachgook to rescue a kidnapped Delaware maiden from the Hurons. Around a floating ark and a settler's lake castle, scalp hunters and soldiers push Natty toward his first killing. He takes a human life reluctantly and earns a new name, Hawkeye. Cooper builds the moral code of the American hero here: merciful, truthful, and deadly only when forced. It is the genesis volume of the Leatherstocking Tales.
emerson-essays-first-series-1841:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Essays: First Series in 1841, with Self-Reliance and The Over-Soul inside. The book is the founding document of American intellectual independence in prose of rare force and fire. Emerson had honed the essays as lectures, and their voice still sounds spoken and urgent on the page.

Self-Reliance commands trust in one's own thought against conformity, consistency, and the crowd's dull pressure in life. The Over-Soul traces one spirit through all souls, the ground of his calm moral optimism in man. History, Compensation, and Circles round out a set that young America took as a charter of selfhood. Lines like trust thyself entered the language and never left common American speech since that day. The book still serves as the doorway into Emerson for most new readers.
europmc-pmc10039041:
Shin and colleagues report a single test that aims to detect several early-stage cancers at once, in a 2023 study. Early detection greatly improves cancer outcomes, yet no one test could screen for many cancer types. The team built a test around exosomes, tiny parcels shed by cells into the blood.

Their method reads chemical patterns on exosomes with a light-based sensor and AI analysis. They report results for six cancer types at early stages. The study points toward blood tests that could screen for many cancers in one draw, though wider trials must come first.
europmc-pmc10168541:
Altammar reviews nanoparticles in a 2023 paper, covering their traits, how they are made, their uses, and the challenges they pose. Nanoparticles are specks of matter thousands of times smaller than a hair's width. At that scale, familiar materials gain new traits that engineers prize, from brighter colors to stronger chemical action.

The review compares green and chemical methods of making the particles. It surveys uses in medicine, industry, and farming. It also weighs risks to human health and to nature. The paper is a broad, plain guide to a vast field.
europmc-pmc10663641:
Hu and co-authors reviewed gamma-delta T cells in 2023, a less common arm of the immune system. Most T cells carry alpha-beta receptors; these carry gamma-delta ones instead. The team's own work has used donor Vdelta2 cells to treat late-stage solid tumours and tuberculosis. The review asks how far that promise can go.

It traces the cells from their find in 1984 to their growth in the thymus gland. Subtypes differ by receptor shape and by the signals they release. Hu shows how each subtype fights tumours and germs in its local setting. Roles span infection, immune disease, blood cancers, and solid tumours. Donor cell therapy for cancer gets a full plan for what comes next.
europmc-pmc11701741:
Tegenfeldt, Kuznetsov, Manni, Berkeley, Zdobnov, and Kriventseva update OrthoDB and BUSCO in this 2025 paper. OrthoDB offers functional and evolutionary notes on orthologous genes, meaning genes in different species that descend from one ancestral gene. It extends experimental knowledge of gene function to newly sequenced genomes. This update expands coverage to 5,827 eukaryotic genomes.

Coding DNA sequences and gene locus coordinates were added to the resource. Access now spans browsing, downloads, a REST interface, and program packages for Python and R. OrthoLoger, the inference tool behind the database, is released as a Conda package and via BioContainers. Its mapper component streamlines annotation of newly sequenced genomes. BUSCO, the companion tool that judges genome completeness from expected genes, is covered in the same update.
europmc-pmc12240541:
McCallum and colleagues explained how two virus variants dodge immunity in 2021. The Delta variant of SARS-CoV-2 had swept to global dominance. Kappa, a close cousin, spread in the same wave. Both carried changes in their spike protein.

Serum from vaccinated people neutralized the variants less well. Several lab antibodies lost their grip on altered spike sites. Delta reshaped one spike region that antibodies target. Binding strength to the human entry receptor stayed near the original for most forms. McCallum gives a structural account of immune escape. It appeared in Science in 2021.
europmc-pmc1240241:
Schlumpf and co-authors tested sunscreen chemicals for hormone effects in 2001. UV screens guard skin against sun damage and cancer. They also enter cosmetics to keep products stable. Traces had been found building up in wildlife and people.

Six common screens were tested in cells and young rats. Five made breast cancer cells grow faster in dishes. That growth could be blocked by an estrogen blocker drug. In rats, one screen raised womb weight with dose. Schlumpf calls for deeper safety checks on these widely used chemicals. One screen, B-MDM, showed no such activity in cells.
europmc-pmc12851941:
Avsec and co-authors presented AlphaGenome, a DNA prediction model, in 2026. Earlier models traded sequence length against prediction detail. Each covered only some types of genomic measurement. AlphaGenome takes one million base pairs as input at once.

It predicts thousands of functional tracks at single-base resolution. Outputs span gene expression, chromatin access, and binding maps. Splice site usage and strength are also predicted. Trained on human and mouse genomes, it won 25 of 26 variant tests. It also reproduced known variant mechanisms near the TAL1 cancer gene. Trained tracks include splice sites and contact maps.
europmc-pmc1440941:
Each chromosome keeps to its own zone in the cell nucleus, or so textbooks said. Branco and Pombo tested that claim in 2006 with a sharp imaging method that keeps fine DNA detail intact. They looked at human blood cells and found zones blend far more than models allowed.

Pairs of chromosomes that blend most also swap parts most often, forming translocations, a type of damage. Busy gene-reading hubs sat in the blended zones. Blocking gene reading changed how chromosomes met. Branco argues that gene activity shapes how chromosomes mingle. That mingling, in turn, affects how stable the genome stays in each cell type.
europmc-pmc1828741:
Conchillo-Solé, Ventura and co-authors launched AGGRESCAN in 2007, a web tool that predicts where a protein is likely to clump. Protein aggregation, where chains stick into deposits, is tied to diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. It also plagues industry, where made proteins pile into useless lumps.

The tool rests on a scale of clumping tendency for natural amino acids, drawn from living-cell experiments, and on the idea that short stretches drive aggregation. It scans a sequence for hot spots, predicts how a mutation would change clumping, and compares proteins or whole sets. Tests recovered known aggregating fragments from disease proteins and forecast mutation effects on deposition. It also separated the habits of folded proteins, unfolded chains, amyloid-forming proteins, and proteins from bacterial inclusion bodies.
europmc-pmc1945041:
Weiner, Kirschner and co-authors proposed in 2007 that crawling cells are organized by traveling waves of their own skeleton protein. Actin filaments push the cell's front edge outward, and many actin regulators were known. How they coordinate into shape and movement was not understood.

The team tracked the Scar/WAVE complex, a key actin assembly trigger, in human neutrophils, fast-moving immune cells. One of its parts, Hem-1, rode in propagating waves that sweep the leading edge. The complex switches actin assembly on, while built actin in turn strips the complex off the membrane. That two-way loop self-generates waves of new actin growth. Such waves show traits of real crawling, including flowing around barriers. Cell motility, they argue, is the collective product of many self-organizing waves.
europmc-pmc2013941:
Sporns, Honey and Kötter mapped hub regions in brain networks in 2007. Cortex regions link through fibre bundles forming a complex network. Hubs are highly connected nodes thought to coordinate information flow. The team analysed cortical networks of the cat and the macaque. They combined connection counts, local pattern measures and centrality, which marks nodes on many shortest paths.

That combined approach reliably identified hub regions in both species. Many hubs were already known as multisensory or multimodal areas, which combine several senses. Hubs split into provincial hubs inside a cluster and connector hubs between clusters. Removing each type from the network had opposite effects on its small-world index, a measure of efficient wiring. The results link a hub's network position to its likely functional role.
europmc-pmc2018741:
Peirce presented PsychoPy in 2007, a free software suite for psychophysics, the study of how people sense and respond to stimuli. Most vision studies present images on computer screens and record responses. Existing tools could be costly or hard to adapt. PsychoPy was written in the Python language using only free libraries. It runs across major operating systems.

Scripts are meant to be easy to read and write, while still allowing full custom control. The package handles stimulus presentation and response collection from many devices. It also fits psychometric functions, curves linking stimulus strength to responses. Users can add support for new stimuli or hardware and share changes back. That open design lets the whole research community improve the system.
europmc-pmc2082641:
Henderson and a large group of co-authors set out in 2007 to define therapeutic misconception in medical research. The term describes patients who join a trial yet fail to see that research differs from treatment. Informed consent depends on grasping that difference. The idea dates to 1982 interviews with psychiatric patients, but no consistent definition had emerged since, blocking measurement of the problem.

Scholars from medicine, law, philosophy and other fields met at the University of North Carolina in 2005. They debated the literature for a year and evaluated draft survey questions. The paper proposes a definition with specific dimensions. It also shows how each dimension can be turned into survey items. That gives researchers a valid scale to measure the misconception and test ways to reduce it.
europmc-pmc2125041: A medical paper on the permanent life of connective tissue outside the organism. The living tissue, kept. This article preserves that cell biology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2125941: A medical paper on the factors concerned in the appearance of nucleated red blood corpuscles. The nucleated reds. This article preserves that hematology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2126341: A medical paper on renal function influenced by proteose intoxication. The poisoned kidney's work. This article preserves that nephrology. It awaits future readers. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128241: A medical paper on production of fatal blackhead in turkeys by feeding embryonated eggs. The turkey killer. This article preserves that veterinary parasitology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2128441: A medical paper on mesenchyme and mesothelium. The embryonic tissues. This article preserves that histology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2128541: A medical paper with an histological study of the central nervous system in experimental botulinus poisoning. The poisoned nerves. This article preserves that neurology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2140341: A biology paper on the nature of the latent period in the photic response of Mya arenaria. The clam's light delay. This article preserves that zoology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2140841: Stomach acid and enzymes should melt living tissue, yet organisms walk through them unharmed, and this paper investigated that resistance. The experiments probed why pepsin and trypsin fail against the living. The protected life, explained. The article preserves that physiology research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2361241:
Simmonds and colleagues reviewed surgery for colorectal cancer that had spread to the liver in 2006. Removing the liver deposits, called resection, might cure some patients, but doctors had no agreed rules for who should get the operation. No randomised trials existed to settle the question.

Of 529 studies found, only 30 met all their quality rules, and most were case series rather than trials. Death within 30 days of surgery was uncommon, with a median rate of 2.8% across studies, and the main serious problem was bile leaking with abscess near the liver. About 30% of patients were alive five years after surgery, and two-thirds of those survivors were free of disease. Such long survival is rare without surgery, the authors noted, but picking the right patients needs more work.
europmc-pmc2409341:
Marcus and colleagues showed in 2008 that one plant wall polymer can hide another from view. Plant cell walls mix several sugar polymers, and researchers map them with antibody probes that glow where a polymer sits. Xyloglucan is the main cross-linking polymer in the walls of many flowering plants, yet probes found it in only a few cell types.

The team raised a new antibody, LM15, tuned to a seven-sugar motif of xyloglucan, and checked it on sugar arrays. In tobacco and pea stems it lit up only scattered cells. Then they stripped out a second polymer, pectic homogalacturonan, a pectin component, with an enzyme. The xyloglucan signal suddenly appeared abundantly across the stems, in distinct patterns per cell type. The authors concluded pectin masks xyloglucan, so published wall maps may need rethinking.
europmc-pmc2475541:
Meletis and colleagues traced the hidden stem cells of the adult spinal cord in 2008. Spinal cord injury usually leaves permanent disability, yet the adult cord holds cells that can grow into nerve tissue in a dish. The team used genetic fate mapping, a labelling trick that marks one cell type and all its descendants permanently.

Nearly all the dish-growing stem cell power sat in ependymal cells, the cells lining the cord's central canal. After injury these cells switched on and multiplied. Most of their offspring became scar-forming glial cells, the support cells that wall off damage. A smaller share became oligodendrocytes, the cells that insulate nerve fibres. The authors proposed steering what ependymal offspring become after injury. That could offer a homegrown alternative to transplanting outside stem cells into patients.
europmc-pmc2515341:
Blais and co-authors tested in 2008 whether culture changes the way people look at faces. Eye-tracking studies since 1965 had suggested everyone scans a face in the same triangle pattern across eyes and mouth. The team recorded where Western Caucasian and East Asian observers looked while they learned and recognised faces of both races.

Western observers followed the classic pattern, scattering fixations over eyes and mouth of faces from both races. East Asian observers instead concentrated on the centre of the face, around the nose. The difference held across learning, recognition, and race-categorising tasks. The authors conclude that extracting information from faces is not a single universal routine, but a strategy shaped by culture.
europmc-pmc2577641:
McCoy and Tansey reviewed in 2008 the double-edged role of TNF, an inflammatory signal, in the brain. TNF rises at injury sites and in diseases from stroke to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, making it an tempting drug target. But TNF comes in two forms, soluble and membrane-bound, and works through two receptors with different preferences, so blanket blocking may do harm.

The review assembles animal and clinical evidence. The soluble form, acting through receptor TNFR1, drives much of the damage in neurodegeneration. The membrane form, favouring TNFR2, supports normal functions including synaptic scaling, the tuning of connection strength, and the birth of new neurons in the hippocampus. The authors argue future therapies should block TNFR1 signalling selectively while sparing TNFR2, rather than shutting TNF down entirely.
europmc-pmc2632741:
Burak and Fiete modelled in 2009 how grid cells in the rat brain could track position accurately enough for dead reckoning, estimating location from movement alone. Grid cells fire at positions forming a regular triangular lattice, and they were hypothesised to integrate velocity signals. Existing models accumulated errors so fast they needed constant sensory resets, casting doubt on the idea.

The authors show that continuous attractor models, where activity forms a stable pattern that shifts with movement, escape this problem. Fed only velocity and heading, both periodic and bounded networks produced regular grid responses and integrated accurately. They quantify how error grows with network size and noise. With realistic variability, the networks integrate over roughly 10 to 100 metres. They hold accuracy for 1 to 10 minutes. The work sets upper bounds on accuracy and proposes discriminating experiments.
europmc-pmc2680341:
Church and colleagues, with the Mouse Genome Sequencing Consortium, reported in 2009 a finished assembly of the mouse genome and what it reveals about rodent-only biology. The mouse is the main stand-in for humans in medical research, so telling shared inheritance from mouse invention matters. The new build was assembled piece by piece from cloned chunks, the most careful kind.

The finished genome exposed a burst of recent copying in mouse DNA. Whole stretches had been duplicated lately in rodent history, expanding certain gene families. The new copies mostly code for proteins of reproduction, matching the fast evolution of breeding traits. Genes that stayed single and barely changed since the common ancestor with humans are the likeliest to have kept their old jobs, the authors argue. Those are also the safest models for human biology.
europmc-pmc2832341:
Matos, Trufelli, de Matos, and da Silva Pinhal reviewed immunohistochemistry in 2010. This lab method uses antibodies to hunt set targets in tissue slices, from single proteins to whole germ types. The method lets pathologists settle diagnoses that standard pink-and-blue staining cannot separate, and it guides prognosis and research as well.

The review walks through both halves of the craft: preparing slides, from fixing tissue through the reaction steps, and then reading and scoring the staining that results. It covers the method's history since the early nineteen forties, its strengths, and its pitfalls in interpretation. The authors close by urging pathologists and clinicians to share one language for results, so patients gain the full benefit.
europmc-pmc2877741:
Hersperger and colleagues reported in 2010 that a rare group of HIV patients who control the virus without drugs have killer T cells that arm themselves unusually fast. These elite controllers keep virus levels near zero for years. The team compared their HIV-specific CD8 T cells, the immune cells that kill infected cells, with cells from patients at other disease stages.

After brief contact with HIV protein pieces, elite controllers' cells rapidly raised perforin, the protein that punches holes in infected cells so they can be destroyed. Cells from patients with high virus levels did this weakly. Other functions, like making several signals at once, did not separate the groups as cleanly. Fast perforin loading looks like a direct weapon behind elite control.
europmc-pmc2913941:
Brancati, Dallapiccola, and Valente reviewed in 2010 Joubert syndrome and its related disorders, a family of congenital conditions united by one brain malformation. On scans the malformed midbrain and hindbrain form a shape called the molar tooth sign, the group's defining hallmark. Incidence is estimated near one in eighty to one hundred thousand births, likely an undercount.

Affected children show low muscle tone, unsteady movement, developmental delay, abnormal eye movements, and disturbed breathing as newborns. Many families add eye, kidney, liver, or extra-finger involvement, sorted into six subgroups. Ten causative genes were known by writing, and every one builds parts of the primary cilium, the cell's antenna, placing the group among the ciliopathies. Inheritance is almost always recessive, so recurrence risk shapes counseling.
europmc-pmc2939541:
Romero-Ortuno and co-authors built a frailty screening tool for older Europeans in a 2010 study based on a large survey of health and ageing. Family doctors need a quick way to spot patients at risk, and no simple measure fitted that setting.

Drawing on thousands of respondents aged fifty and over from twelve countries, they combined five survey items echoing a standard frailty definition. Statistical modelling sorted people into non-frail, pre-frail, and frail classes for each sex. The classes differed across many health and social measures and predicted death risk by the follow-up wave. Two web calculators were released.
europmc-pmc2940741:
Saeed and colleagues studied how Ebola virus gets inside cells in a 2010 laboratory study using live virus and look-alike particles. No vaccine or specific treatment existed then, so the entry step looked like a promising drug target.

In two cell lines, uptake did not depend on the usual clathrin or caveolae routes. Instead the virus triggered gulping of surrounding fluid, a process resembling macropinocytosis, along with local reshaping of the cell skeleton. Blocking key regulators of that gulping, or adding a drug that hinders it, cut entry sharply. The virus then travelled through early and late sorting compartments.
europmc-pmc2970541:
Lyko and co-authors compared DNA methylation, a chemical marking system, in the brains of honey bee queens and workers in a 2010 study. Queens and workers share the same genome yet differ hugely in body, fertility, and behaviour, a split set by larval diet.

Genome-wide maps of the marks in brain tissue showed differing patterns between the castes. The contrast supports the idea that food-triggered marking helps lock in two very different life paths from identical DNA. Because brain marks were the focus, the work also speaks to how environment shapes behaviour through molecular settings in social insects.
europmc-pmc3022541:
Chaitanya, Steven, and Babu reviewed in 2010 how one repair protein breaks apart when brain and nerve cells die. The protein, called PARP-1 in short, normally helps fix damaged DNA after cell stress. When injury is severe, cutting enzymes slice it into pieces of distinct sizes. Each cutting enzyme leaves its own characteristic set of pieces behind.

Those pieces work like fingerprints for the kind of cell death under way. The review sorts which enzymes, including caspases, calpains, and others, cut the protein during stroke, trauma, and slow nerve loss. It also covers what some pieces do after they are cut, and how they bind other proteins. Reading the fingerprints could help doctors tell death pathways apart in damaged tissue.
europmc-pmc3046141:
McGowan and coauthors reported in 2011 that a mother's care in a rat's first week of life leaves marks across a broad stretch of the brain genome. The marks reach far beyond any single gene. Earlier work had tied high licking and grooming care to chemical marks on a single stress gene in the hippocampus. The team scanned a long chromosome region holding that gene, measuring marks, gene activity, and a second chemical tag together.

Adult offspring of high care mothers showed coordinated mark changes over a wide span, with many genes in the region more active. Some genes stayed unchanged, so the response was patterned rather than blanket. A gene family involved in wiring synapses responded most strongly of all. Because cross fostering flips the pattern, the marks reflect care received, not inheritance. The study reframes early care as a genome wide programming event in the brain.
europmc-pmc3052441:
Palafox-Carlos, Ayala-Zavala, and González-Aguilar reviewed in 2011 how dietary fiber changes the fate of antioxidants eaten in fruits and vegetables. Antioxidants may help prevent degenerative disease, but the richest source in food is not always the one that delivers the most to body tissues. Fiber, the indigestible wall material of plants, travels with antioxidants through the gut and can hold onto them.

How much of an antioxidant is freed during digestion, and then absorbed, depends on the food's structure and on chemical links with fiber and other food parts. The review gathers evidence on those interactions and how they play out along the digestive tract. Fiber can delay or reduce release for some compounds while aiding others later in the gut. The authors argue that health advice and food design should count the fiber context, not just the antioxidant totals on a label.
europmc-pmc3070641:
Herberts, Kwa, and Hermsen assessed in 2011 the risks that must be weighed before stem cell therapies reach patients. Stem cells promise treatments for worn out tissues and diseases with few options, and lab made pluripotent cells have raised hopes further. The authors argue that a product's risk depends on many features at once, from cell type and growth rate to delivery route and whether the treatment can be undone.

Known and possible harms include tumors, unwanted immune reactions, and infections carried by the cell product. Cells that renew without limit carry the highest tumor concern, and no patient had yet received them when this was written. Trials with adult connective tissue stem cells have mostly been reassuring, though serious events have occurred. The authors call for risk checks built into development from the start, not added after promising headlines.
europmc-pmc3114741:
Marcus Lechner and colleagues presented a computer program for finding matching genes across species in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Matching genes inherited from a shared ancestor help researchers compare genomes and guess gene function. With genome counts rising fast, older tools needed too much memory for the job.

Their program refines a best-match search method and spreads work across the cores of ordinary computers, cutting memory needs sharply. Tested on more than seven hundred bacterial genomes, it found a small set of proteins present in nearly every one of them. Because it runs on standard hardware, labs can compute fresh matches for their own data instead of waiting for database updates.
europmc-pmc3197541:
Rebecca Wong reviewed programmed cell death in cancer, from its failure to its exploitation, in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research. Healthy cells self-destruct on cue; cancer is in part what happens when cells that should die refuse. The death machinery is intricate, with many pathways and checkpoints where faults can arise.

Defects at any step can help transform a cell, seed spread, or blunt chemotherapy, and a silenced guardian gene is one notorious example found across human cancers. Yet the same machinery is the target of many modern treatments designed to push cancer cells back over the edge. Wong surveys the mechanisms, the carcinogenic faults, and the promise and safety hurdles of death-restoring drugs.
europmc-pmc3221041:
Hélène Botella and colleagues uncovered a zinc arms race between tuberculosis bacteria and human immune cells in this 2011 study in Cell Host and Microbe. Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages, the very cells meant to kill it. Gene-activity surveys of both partners during infection showed a striking pattern of metal-related genes switching on.

Macrophages flooded the bacterial compartment with free zinc within hours of infection, apparently trying to poison the invader. The bacteria answered by switching on pump genes, especially one called ctpC, that expel heavy metals. Mutants lacking that pump kept zinc trapped inside their cells and grew poorly within macrophages. The authors propose that metal poisoning and resistance form another front in the long fight between host and microbe.
europmc-pmc3221341:
Wendy Brouwer and colleagues reviewed why people stop using online healthy-lifestyle programs, in this 2011 systematic review. Internet interventions can tailor feedback and goals to each user, yet their real reach is low and dropout is high. The team asked which design features are linked to greater exposure, meaning how long and how often people actually engage.

They gathered sixty-four studies that measured exposure objectively, through log-ins, visit length, or completion. Programs used a wide mix of techniques, with feedback, interactive elements, and email or phone contact the most common. Only a few features showed consistent links to better exposure: peer or counselor support lengthened visits, while personal contact and website updates brought more log-ins. The authors note that inconsistent exposure measures blocked firmer conclusions.
europmc-pmc3229841:
Marc Ghany and colleagues wrote this 2011 practice guideline on treating genotype 1 chronic hepatitis C, issued by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Hepatitis C genotype 1 was the commonest and hardest-to-treat form of the virus in the United States. The guideline updates recommendations for clinicians managing these patients.

The document was formally approved by the association and endorsed by infectious-disease, gastroenterology, and viral-hepatitis organizations. Its advice rests on a formal review of the world literature published up to June 2011. They also rest on established manuals for judging health practices and writing guidelines. The authors' clinical experience plays a part as well. It offers a data-supported approach meant to make care uniform, at a moment when treatment for this infection was changing quickly.
europmc-pmc3257741:
Marco Vinolo and colleagues reviewed how short-chain fatty acids regulate inflammation in this 2011 article in Nutrients. These fatty acids, mainly acetate, propionate, and butyrate, are the chief products when gut bacteria ferment fiber. Beyond feeding the gut lining, they influence water and electrolyte absorption and, increasingly clearly, the immune system.

The fatty acids act on immune and blood vessel cells in two ways. They switch on dedicated receptors on the cell surface. They also block enzymes that remove chemical tags from histones. Through these routes they shape the signals immune cells release, their ability to migrate to inflamed sites, and their capacity to destroy pathogens. The review gathers the newest findings on isolated cells and on recruitment and activation, and highlights treatment possibilities for inflammatory diseases.
europmc-pmc3271041:
Jorja Warren and colleagues validated a blood test for colorectal cancer based on a methylated DNA marker, in this 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. About half of Americans in the screening age range skip recommended screening, leaving tens of millions untested. A simple blood draw could bring many of them in, catching cancers earlier.

The test looks for methylated Septin 9 DNA in plasma. In samples from cancer patients, healthy controls, and colonoscopy patients, the improved assay caught ninety percent of colorectal cancers while correctly clearing eighty-eight percent of people without the disease. It worked for early-stage cancers and for tumors anywhere in the colon, including hard-to-reach regions. False positives ran at about twelve percent. It also detected a small share of precancerous adenomas. The authors propose offering it to average-risk adults unwilling or unable to have a colonoscopy.
europmc-pmc3312841:
Akbarzadeh, Samiei, and Davaran reviewed tiny magnetic particles and their growing role in medicine, in a 2012 article. These particles, far smaller than a cell, can be guided by magnets outside the body and made visible on scans. The review stresses that good medical uses start with well controlled recipes for making particles that match in size and crystal quality.

Sections cover how the particles are made, how their surfaces are coated so they can carry drugs or attach to chosen targets, and how labs check their properties. The authors also explain the physics of how such small magnets behave, which differs from bulk magnets. Together the pieces frame a toolkit for imaging, drug delivery, and other biomedical tasks.
europmc-pmc3334941:
Tewarie and colleagues built agreed quality rules for eye scans used in multiple sclerosis research, reporting in 2012. The scans, called OCT, measure thinning of the nerve layer at the back of the eye, a window on nerve degeneration in MS. For such scans to serve as trial outcomes across many hospitals, readers must judge scan quality the same way.

Starting from older eye literature rules, three readers agreed only moderately on a training set of scans. Disagreements were dissected, and a new checklist was written around seven checks covering obvious flaws, signal strength, centering, software errors, other eye disease, lighting, and beam placement. Its name, OSCAR-IB, strings the seven initials together. Agreement jumped to a solid level on the training set and held on a fresh set of scans. The authors recommend the checklist for multicenter studies and trials.
europmc-pmc3348041:
Muehlenkamp, Claes, Havertape, and Plener reviewed how common self injury is among teenagers worldwide, in a 2012 article. Two related behaviors are tracked: self injury without suicidal intent, and the broader category of deliberate self harm, which includes acts with any intent. Claims that rates are climbing had outrun solid evidence, and studies used clashing definitions that made countries hard to compare.

Gathering fifty two studies published between 2005 and 2011, the team found the two behaviors reported at similar average rates, around one in six adolescents. Studies that asked a single yes or no question found lower rates than those using detailed behavior checklists. Average rates had not risen over the previous five years, suggesting a plateau rather than an epidemic curve. The authors urge the field to adopt one shared way of asking, so future comparisons mean something.
europmc-pmc3364341:
Yu and co-authors built a large-scale computational system for predicting which drugs interact with which protein targets. Reliable prediction would speed drug discovery, but interactions are many-to-many: one drug can hit several targets, and similar drugs can share targets. The team integrated chemical, genomic, and pharmacological data to feed two machine learning methods.

Models built with random forests and support vector machines agreed closely in testing, reaching specificity above ninety percent across internal and external validations. The authors then applied the validated models across enzymes, ion channels, G-protein-coupled receptors, and nuclear receptors. They mapped the predictions onto disease associations and target networks for follow-up research.
europmc-pmc3372341:
Tellier argued in 2006 that flu spreads through the air in fine aerosols far more than planners admitted. Many guidelines treated large droplets as the main route, so protection against tiny airborne particles was often skipped. Canadian and United States pandemic plans then advised surgical masks, not tight respirators, for routine care.

Reviewing decades of published findings, Tellier found the evidence for aerosol spread extensive and consistent. Reference books by leading experts already described aerosols as a key route. Given the high death rates of bird flu strain H5N1, he urged stronger protection for health workers, including N95 respirators. The paper pressed pandemic planning to take airborne spread seriously.
europmc-pmc3373041:
Ooi, Goh, and Gubler reviewed thirty-five years of dengue control in Singapore in 2006. Dengue is spread by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, and its four virus types mean a person can be infected up to four times. With no vaccine near approval, cutting mosquito numbers was the only prevention available.

Singapore's program, the review argues, worked because it rested on disease and mosquito data rather than habit. Earlier campaigns elsewhere, run as strict top-down drives, succeeded briefly but could not be sustained. The authors trace how Singapore sustained its effort after those earlier drives faded. Their account offers a working model for cities facing dengue's worldwide return.
europmc-pmc3383741:
Cohen and a large team followed African couples in 2012 to test whether bacterial vaginosis raises a woman's chance of passing HIV-1 to her male partner. The condition, where normal vaginal flora is replaced by other bacteria, was already linked to women catching HIV more easily. Nobody had measured the onward risk to partners.

The cohort covered more than two thousand couples in which the woman had HIV-1 and the man did not. Women with bacterial vaginosis passed the virus to partners at a markedly higher rate, with risk more than three times that of women with normal flora. The finding adds partner protection to the reasons for treating the condition. It also points prevention work toward vaginal health.
europmc-pmc3414841:
Nik-Zainal led a team that catalogued every mutation in twenty-one breast cancers in 2012 to read the processes that scarred their genomes. All cancers carry acquired mutations, and their patterns record the damage and repair failures the cells lived through. Math methods pulled apart the overlapping patterns into separate signatures.

Several distinct signatures appeared, some single-letter and some double. Cancers with broken BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes showed a characteristic mix plus a telltale pattern of deletions. The team also found kataegis, storms of local hypermutation clustered near genome rearrangements. A family of enzymes that edit DNA letters is proposed as one culprit. Most signatures still lack an explanation, marking work ahead.
europmc-pmc3418241:
Onomoto and a large team identified in 2012 the cellular meeting place where virus alarms are raised. Sensors such as RIG-I detect viral RNA inside cells and trigger interferon, the body's antiviral messenger. How the sensor actually meets viral RNA was unclear. Using a new antibody, the team watched where RIG-I gathers during infection.

It collects in granules packed with viral RNA, stress-granule markers, and other antiviral proteins, which the team named antiviral stress granules. A flu virus stripped of its alarm-blocking protein formed many granules and much interferon; the intact virus formed few. Blocking granule formation cut interferon and let viruses multiply faster. The granule, they conclude, is where foreign RNA is sensed.
europmc-pmc3461341:
Lutz and Quinn proposed in 2012 that shifting cytokine levels form a common thread tying together muscle loss, obesity, and immune aging. Aging brings frailty: muscle mass, strength, and stamina decline while belly fat grows, and the immune system weakens, raising cancer and death risk. One signal, interleukin-15, is made richly by muscle and fades with age in animal models.

That signal blocks fat deposition and insulin resistance, feeds muscle in some settings, and is required to build and keep natural killer cells, the immune patrol in question. As fat-derived inflammatory signals rise and interleukin-15 falls, all three declines advance together. The review follows the fat and muscle signals that act on killer cells and argues the shared chemistry is a target worth testing.

europmc-pmc4033041: Microbes got a who-holds-it-together study. This 2014 paper finds keystone microbes. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides ecology. Berry's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped microbial ecology. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc4058041: Breast cancer got an MMP-9-drives-spread study. This 2014 paper finds MMP-9 driving spread. The authors reveal the driving. Their work guides oncology. Mehner's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer research.
europmc-pmc4210641: Lungs got an ILC2-allergic-inflammation study. This 2014 paper finds ILC2s start allergic lung inflammation. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides immunology. europmc-pmc4263141: Worms got a parasite-exosome-immune study. This 2014 paper finds worm exosomes modulate immunity. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides parasitology. Buck's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped parasite science. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc4270441: Vision got a DNNs-rival-IT-cortex study. This 2014 paper finds neural nets rival visual cortex. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides neuroscience. Cadieu's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped AI vision. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc4284641: Physics got a hot-carrier-plasmon predictions paper. This 2014 paper predicts hot carriers from plasmons. The authors reveal the predicting. Their work guides physics.
