gao-gaoreports-b-311241: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Carahsoft Technology Corporation; Allied Technology Group. The May 16, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-241: Fishing quota management costs went unrecovered in 2005, and GAO's report says the costs varied and were not recouped as required. The review counts the missing dollars. The fishermen deserved the fair fees. The costs had to be recovered. The fishermen deserved the fair fees.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-341: The Pentagon's ethics guardrails needed tightening in 2005, and GAO's report says procurement integrity safeguards could be stronger. The review names the gaps where contracts could be gamed. The taxpayers deserved honest buying. The safeguards had to be strengthened. The taxpayers deserved honest buying.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-441: Army repair shops lacked a real boss in 2005, and GAO's report says the depots' work went unwatched. The findings demand the supervision. The report warns that the repair depots deserved honest management. The repair depots deserved honest management. The boss had to show up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-141: Military readiness had gaps and risks in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon needed to identify and address the shortfalls. The findings demand the reckoning. The report warns that the fighting force deserved honest assessment. The gaps had to be closed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-341: Unemployment benefit patterns got analyzed in 2006, and GAO's report examines factors associated with benefit receipt. The findings do the analysis. The report warns that the safety net's patterns deserved understanding. The factors had to be known. The safety net's patterns deserved understanding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-541: Puerto Rico's tax-break phaseout shaped its economy in 2006, and GAO's report examines fiscal relations and trends during the transition. The findings do the math. The report warns that the island's economy needed honest accounting. The trends had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-641: Embassy building was progressing in 2006, and GAO's report says State had made progress on new embassies, though operations planning needed work. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the diplomatic fortresses needed running plans too. The planning had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-141: Federal workers' health premiums were finally cooling in 2007, and GAO's report says the growth had slowed, varying by plan. The findings parse the trend. The report offers a breather, not a victory, in the health-cost wars. The slowdown had to last.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-241: Repeat-offender nursing homes kept hurting patients in 2007 — GAO's report says tougher federal enforcement had not deterred the worst actors. The findings name the failure. The report's fury: fines that do not bite are just the cost of doing harm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-441: Freedom-of-information requests were piling up in 2007 — GAO's report says the processing trends showed why improvement plans mattered. The findings track the growing backlog in detail. The report's creed: the public's right to know should not wait in line forever.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-541: The thrift board's expense watch needed keeping in 2007 — GAO's report says due diligence on admin costs should continue and deepen. The findings press for vigilance over the fees. The report's math is simple: small fees times millions of savers equals big stakes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-641: Closing bases without breaking towns took a plan in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon needed a strategy to smooth the shutdowns and talk straight. The findings demand better communication. The report's lesson: the base may close, but the community stays.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-141: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at maritime Security: Federal Efforts Needed to Address Challenges in Preventing and Responding to Terrorist Attacks on Energy Commodity Tankers. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-41: The Government Accountability Office dug into US Postal Service Facilities: Improvements in Data Would Strengthen Maintenance and Alignment of Access to Retail Services in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-541: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at financial Audit: Special Counsel Expenditures for the Six Months Ended September 30, 2007. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-641: The Government Accountability Office dug into department of Energy: Office of Science Has Kept Majority of Projects within Budget and on Schedule, but Funding and Other Challenges May Grow in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-741: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at higher Education: Veteran Students Received Similar Amounts of Title IV Aid As Nonveterans but More Total Aid with GI Benefits. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
guide-to-self-knowledge-the-fundamental-: Guide to Self-Knowledge, 1841. The mind's powers. This book preserves that guide. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
hawthorne-grandfathers-chair-1841:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Whole History of Grandfather's Chair in 1841, a history for children. The book tells New England history, from the Puritans to the Revolution, through one old chair. Hawthorne wrote it for young readers in the days before his fame as a romancer grew.

Grandfather, in a Boston parlor, traces his chair's owners through persecutions, wars, and witch trial years. The chair hears of Endicott, King Philip's War, and the Boston Tea Party in its long life. Children Laurence, Clara, and little Alice question, doubt, and dream over the tales by the fireside. Hawthorne makes dry annals into scenes a child can feel, without hiding the era's harsh deeds. It was a pioneer work of American history written for the young at home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowe-konrad-101:
Konrad Löwe, an Austrian actor, is profiled briefly in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Prossnitz, Moravia, on February 6, 1856, he first took a law course at the University of Vienna. He then went on the stage in 1878. After engagements in several Austrian and German cities, he joined Vienna's Hofburgtheater in 1895.

The entry notes that he played heroic parts with that company. It also records a second career as a writer. Löwe published a volume of poetry, Leben und Lieben, at Leipzig in 1890. He adapted Grabbe's play Herzog Theodor von Gothland for the stage in 1892. The short article shows the encyclopedia's wide net, which took in Jewish performers and artists as well as rabbis and scholars of its day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machim-masahod-:
Masahod Cohen Machim, a Moroccan envoy to England, gets a very short entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He came in 1813 as the envoy of Mulai Sulaiman, emperor of Morocco. That ruler's reign saw Christian slavery abolished in his country. The entry gives no other detail about the mission itself.

The article adds one family note. Machim's son, Meir Cohen Machim, visited England in the same role in 1827. Its sources are two histories of the Jews in Great Britain. The brief notice still matters as a record. It shows a Jewish diplomat carrying messages between Morocco and Britain in the early nineteenth century. Few entries in the encyclopedia are shorter, yet it fixes two dates and a family line that might otherwise be lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martinet-adam-1:
Adam Martinet, a German Catholic Orientalist, is given a brief entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, contributed by Crawford Howell Toy. Martinet was born at Höchstädt, near Bamberg, in January 1800, and the encyclopedia admits that the date of his death was uncertain. He taught as a professor in the lyceum, or secondary school, at Bamberg.

His claim on the encyclopedia's attention rests on one book: "Tif'eret Yisrael," a Hebrew reader published at Bamberg in 1837. The volume offered selections from biblical and newer Hebrew literature, with notes and a glossary to help students. Its modern selections came from writers such as Rapoport, Wessely, and Friedländer. The entry closes by pointing readers to two German biographical reference works for anything further.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metuentes-lit-f:
Metuentes, literally the fearing ones, was a Latin term for Gentiles who drew close to Judaism without full conversion, used in inscriptions and by the poet Juvenal. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs explain the word in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. It matches the Greek phrase for those who worship God in Josephus and the book of Acts.

The article connects the term to Gentiles who kept the Sabbath and avoided forbidden foods, the people Paul met in Antioch, Thyatira, Thessalonica, and Athens. Inscriptions from around the Black Sea record similar worshipers of the Most High God. It ends by pointing readers to the related entries on proselytes and the Hypsistarians, with a short bibliography from Schürer and Bernays.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-millet-10841:
Millet, a grain of sandy soils, appears exactly once in the Bible, and that single mention fills a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and Immanuel Löw, published in 1906. In Arabia and Italy it makes a bread that is excellent when fresh. Ezekiel lists it among the grains, beans, and lentils baked into his symbolic loaf.

The whole question is which plant the Hebrew word doḥan names. Because Ezekiel's list seems meant to cover every bread grain, scholars fought over Indian millet, panicum, and sorghum, comparing the Arabic dukhn and evidence from inscriptions and modern floras. The article recommends simply translating millet, and sorts the neighboring Hebrew grain words into sorghum and panicum as it goes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monatsschrift-f:
The Monatsschrift für die Geschichte und Wissenschaft des Judenthums was the oldest and most important monthly of Jewish scholarship, as Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik record in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Zacharias Frankel founded it at Dresden in 1851, judging that emancipation's political fight was won and that Jews could now turn to the scientific study of their own history and literature.

Frankel edited the first seventeen volumes; Heinrich Graetz followed for nineteen more. Publication lapsed in 1887, then resumed in 1892 under M. Braun and David Kaufmann, and from January 1904 the journal spoke for the Society for the Promotion of the Science of Judaism. Its run of editors is itself a history of the discipline the journal created.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosconi-judah-l:
Judah Leon ben Moses Mosconi was a Bulgarian scholar and Talmudist born at Ocrida in 1328. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Wars in Bulgaria drove him out about 1360, and he traveled across Europe, Asia, and Africa. He studied in Negropont, in Egypt, in Morocco, in Italy, and in France.

Mosconi knew philosophy in Hebrew and Arabic, but his chief work was a supercommentary on Ibn Ezra's commentary on the Pentateuch. He had read some thirty other supercommentaries on his travels and judged most of them worthless. He insisted that commentators must study grammar, a step many had skipped. Persecution left his other treatises unfinished, though he did revise the Yosippon and write a preface for it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-music-synagogal:
Synagogue music began as the musical declaiming of Scripture and prayer, and it never stopped being sung. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen trace it in this Jewish Encyclopedia article. The lessons in Nehemiah were already read with a kind of chant. Over centuries and across many lands, that chant grew into the full melody of the services.

The article argues that the synagogue took its system straight from the Temple. A former Levite singer, Joshua ben Hananiah, described the choristers walking from the Temple orchestra to the synagogue. Instruments there had only accompanied the voices, so losing them changed nothing in the song. What remained was cantillation: a recitation shaped by the words and their accents, more chant than tune.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-natanson-ludwik:
Ludwik Natanson was a Polish doctor and leader of Warsaw Jewry. Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in 1821, he studied medicine at Wilna and Dorpat. He finished his degree in 1847 and settled in Warsaw. He died there on June 6, 1896.

Natanson helped start a Polish medical journal in 1847. He edited it until 1864 and wrote many essays for it. During a cholera outbreak he treated rich families and the poor alike. He served hospitals and gave free care to poor patients. From 1871 he led the Warsaw Jewish community until his death. He helped build its great synagogue, hospital, schools, and loan fund.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nigrin-negrin-s: Simon Nigrin was an author who lived in Jerusalem. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived early in the seventeenth century there. He was a grandnephew of Moses Nigrin, the cabalist. A work on prayer is supposed to be his. Derush al ha-Tefillah explains the important prayers in homiletic form. It was printed at Dyhernfurth in 1732. It is quoted under two other titles as well. They are Me'on Shelomoh and Bet Shim'on Shelomoh.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-obadiah-11641:
Obadiah is a name borne by thirteen men in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch, Schulim Ochser, and others wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jacob Zallel Lauterbach was among those others. The name, as read in the old text, means a worshiper of God. The best known bearer was steward to King Ahab.

When Jezebel hunted the prophets of God, Obadiah hid them. He kept one hundred of them safe in caves. In a time of great hunger he met Elijah. He then brought Ahab word that the hunger would end. Later rabbis said Obadiah came from Edom by birth. They said he won the gift of prophecy for that brave act. They also told how he spent his wealth to feed the hidden men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheimer-sam:
Samuel Oppenheimer was a German banker and court factor. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Heidelberg about the year 1635. He died at Vienna on May 3, 1703. He won the marked favor of Emperor Leopold the First.

Samuel lent the emperor great sums for the Turkish war. Prince Eugene sent him prized Hebrew books from Turkey. Those books formed the core of a famed library. Jews had just been cast out of Vienna at that time. Yet the emperor let Samuel settle there in peace. His whole train of folk came with him to the city. He was let build a great house in its heart. He was named chief factor and court Jew there. He lent funds to the chief general in Hungary too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paderborn-11841:
Paderborn is a town in Westphalia, a province of Prussia. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews are first named there in the year 1606. In that year the diet of the town took a step. It sought to bar any growth in the Jewish count.

The charge was that Jewish loans bore too high a rate. The prince bishop gave the Jews a set of hard rules. They could charge just one small coin per week per thaler. Each year they had to settle in full with debtors. Each bond of debt had to be passed by the town. They could no more lend funds on land at all. They could deal in gold, in gems, and in rings. No claim of theirs could stand past two years in law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porto-oporto-10:
Porto, also called Oporto, is a city in northern Portugal. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In old times it held the largest Jewish group after Lisbon. It was the seat of the chief judge for its region. Its Jews lived in their own quarter, the Juderia.

In 1386 King John the First set apart two streets for them. They were Victoria street and Saint Miguel street. The synagogue stood in Saint Miguel street. Immanuel Aboab records that he saw it himself. Stairs to the old quarter are still called the Synagogue Steps. The entry keeps the memory of that lost community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prefaces-and-de:
Prefaces and dedications in Hebrew books are treated by Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein. Their article appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew word for a preface is hakdamah. A known saying gives the reason authors love them. A book without a preface is like a body without a soul.

The preface grows out of an older form, they say. Rabbis opened talks with a verse called a petihah. That opening stands at the head of many midrashic talks. The first true preface is a letter by Amram Gaon. It opens his prayer-book of the ninth century. Maimonides used a like letter in his Guide. Later authors took up the form in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-primogeniture-t:
Primogeniture is the right and lot of the first-born son. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jewish law splits the first-born in two kinds. One kind deals with the estate a father leaves. The other deals with the buying back of the first-born. Rules for each kind stand apart in the books.

For the estate, the law stands in Deuteronomy. The first-born son is to take a double share. That rule held for a son by any wife. It held even where a man had more than one wife. The article shows how far back the custom runs. It then traces the right through rabbinic law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-punctuation-heb:
Punctuation in Hebrew texts is the subject of an article by Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When the Bible text took its final shape, it held letters alone. No signs marked the vowels of the words. No signs marked where sentences or parts began.

The schools of Palestine fixed that shape in early centuries. The Masorah then took up the task of guarding the text. Reading was passed down by voice and custom alone. Chapters were marked by mere spaces in the scroll. The article traces how vowel points and stops grew. It shows how Jews learned to mark sense in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rain-12541:
Rain mattered deeply in ancient Palestine, where farms needed it. Emil G. Hirsch, Immanuel Benzinger, Wilhelm Bacher, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Unlike Egypt, Palestine did not rely on hard irrigation work. Its crops depended on rain from heaven.

The article gathers Bible verses that link rain to obedience. Full rain comes as a reward for keeping the commandments. Drought comes as a warning when Israel sins. A second part turns to rabbinical teaching on rain's source. Rabbis debated ocean water, clouds, and how drops fall. The entry joins weather, farming, and faith in one topic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reggio-12641:
Reggio is an Italian city on the Strait of Messina. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It is capital of the province of Reggio di Calabria. Jews lived in Calabria as early as 398.

The article describes the city's ghetto, called Strada Giudeca. It stood apart, with entry only through one gate. Jews there worked in silk making and trade. Many belonged to a strong merchants' guild. They could lend money at up to ten percent. Frederick II tolerated them but made them wear a badge. Queen Joanna II later taxed them after false charges faded. In 1492 Spanish exiles greatly enlarged the community. The entry mixes daily work with royal policy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-richardson-sir-:
Sir Benjamin Ward Richardson was an English physician born at Somersby in 1828. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died in London on November 21, 1896. He took his medical degree in 1854.

The article calls him a friend of the Jews. Descent, sympathy, and Bible training tied him to Jewish ideals. His 1888 romance retells the life of Bar Kokba. It shows deep knowledge of second century Jewish history. His last work rested on the life of Maimonides. As a medical author he praised Jewish dietary laws. He defended Jewish practices at every public chance. He often lectured before Jewish literary societies. He was knighted in 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenberg-alber:
Albert Rosenberg was a German physician born at Schloppe, West Prussia, on September 17, 1856. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. Rosenberg earned his medical degree at the University of Berlin in 1880.

His essays deal with diseases of the throat, nose, and voice box. Topics include tuberculosis of the larynx, growths at the base of the tongue, and nosebleeds. He also weighed the value of X rays for throat doctors, a new tool then. Most of his findings went into a manual on the mouth, throat, and larynx, issued in 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-runkel-solomon-: Solomon Zalman Runkel was rabbi of Mayence and afterward of Worms, and he died before 1426. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His Hatan Damim, printed at Prague in 1605, gives a cabalistic commentary on the Pentateuch built on gematria and notarikon, letter-number methods. It also gathers ritual laws for circumcision and weddings. Runkel left the commentary unfinished, and Isaac ha-Kohen completed it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomonsen-mart:
Martin Salomonsen was a Danish physician born in Copenhagen on March 9, 1814. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was the father of the bacteriologist Carl Julius Salomonsen.

Salomonsen took his medical qualification in 1838 and studied physiology afterward. He served the Royal Guards, then became a Copenhagen district physician in 1844. There he pushed hard to reform the statistics of disease in the city. Largely through him, doctors had to report cases weekly from 1850. His study of Copenhagen's epidemics won him an honorary doctorate in 1854. After qualifying, he had taken up the study of physiology with zeal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-reub:
A. Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel ben Reuben of Chartres, a French poet who wrote prayers for synagogue use. His one known work is a reshut, an opening poem in Aramaic. It was recited with the Targum of the hafṭarah for the Feast of Weeks.

The poem has sixty half-lines, all ending in the same rhyme. Samuel signed it with the name Samuel ha-Ketabi. The scholar Gross read that name as a pun. Chartres sounds like the old French word for a charter. The Aramaic word for such a document is ketab. So the poet built his pen name from his home city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwarz-israel-:
Isidore Singer and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Israel Schwarz. He was a German rabbi. Schwarz was born at Hürben, in Bavaria, on March 15, 1830. He died at Cologne on January 4, 1875. His father, Rabbi Joachim Schwarz, educated him. At eighteen he passed the state examination for Bavarian rabbis.

Schwarz became district rabbi of Bayreuth while still a teenager by office. He stayed there until 1856. Cologne then called him to its rabbinate. He backed the Alliance Israélite Universelle with ardor. He founded several local branches of that society. His Tiḳwat Enosh, from 1868, gives his own translation of Job. It adds the sages' sayings on Job and old commentaries. He also translated his brother Joseph's geography of Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shem-13541:
Shem was the son of Noah named first whenever the three brothers appear together. Emil G. Hirsch, Ira Maurice Price, Wilhelm Bacher, and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Genesis lists Shem, Ham, and Japheth in that order. In the table of nations, though, Shem's line comes last.

That placement may reflect the compiler's longer plan for Shem's line. His descendants run far down into later history. Rabbinic writing calls Shem the most important brother. It says he was born circumcised and served as priest and prophet. From him came Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The entry joins the Bible's spare lines with the honor rabbis heaped on this ancestor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siebenberger-is:
Isaac ben David Siebenberger was a Russian Hebraist who died at Warsaw in 1879. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He devoted himself chiefly to apocryphal literature in translation. His versions appeared in both Hebrew and Judeo-German.

Siebenberger translated the Book of Tobit into Hebrew in 1839. Judith followed in 1840, and Baruch in 1841. His Maccabees translation came out at Warsaw in 1843. Each translation carried his commentaries and introductions along. He also published an elementary Hebrew course for learners. That book outlined Hebrew grammar with tales and fables. His great Hebrew-German dictionary ran from 1846 to 1862. It covered all words of the Bible and Mishnah. The entry honors a translator who opened hidden books to common readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-jean-henr:
Jean Henri Simon was a Belgian engraver and soldier born at Brussels in 1752. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He learned engraving from his father Jacob Simon. Before age fifteen he was engraver to Prince Charles of Lorraine. In Paris he later served the Duke of Orleans and the king.

When war came, Simon commanded a company under General Dumouriez. He was wounded at Anderlecht and at Boucar and rose to lieutenant-colonel. Accused of treason, he proved himself innocent. He later taught engraving and served the empress Josephine. His gem engravings were so fine that some were sold as real antiques.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spalato-spalatr:
Spalato, or Spalatro, was a commercial port of Dalmatia. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The city had been noted since Roman empire days. Its earliest Jewish residents came from Servia and Rumania. Many years passed before a true community formed there.

After the expulsion from Spain, exiles settled there in numbers. Spalato then held the chief Jewish community in Dalmatia. Its Jews traded with Africa, Turkey, Venice, and Ancona. Local trade and finance lay almost wholly in their hands. The community kept an ancient and beautiful synagogue. By 1905 its Jews had scattered and it was in decline.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sutro-theodore-:
Theodore Sutro was an American lawyer born in Prussia in 1845. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Aix-la-Chapelle on March 14. His family emigrated to America when he was five. He graduated from Harvard in 1871.

Sutro took his law degree at Columbia in 1874. He entered the New York bar that same year. Tax law became his known specialty over time. He served as New York's tax commissioner from 1885 to 1898. In 1887 he rescued the failing Sutro Tunnel Company. His new Comstock Tunnel Company took over its stock. He wrote often on taxes, corporations, and mining law. The entry links a legal career to a family venture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tannenbaum-abne:
Abner Tannenbaum was a Yiddish and Hebrew journalist born in 1848. Joseph Jacobs and Laura Landau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Schirwind, East Prussia, on March 1. He studied at Kamenetz-Podolsk and at Kishinev. Odessa's university honored his history and geography studies.

Tannenbaum first chose a commercial career in drugs. He managed a wholesale drug business for years. In 1887 he emigrated to New York. There he gave himself fully to journalism. He translated Jules Verne novels into Yiddish. His science and history pieces filled American Yiddish papers. He wrote them for Russian immigrants hungry to learn. In 1905 he published a history of Jews in America. A geography of American industry followed the same year. The entry honors a popularizer for a new immigrant public.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teruel-14341:
Teruel, a city of Aragon in Spain, once held a prominent Jewish community. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its Jews enjoyed set privileges in the Middle Ages. In the fourteenth century they paid a yearly tax of 300 sueldos.

Many worked in trade and in wool-weaving. In the attacks of 1391, many were killed. Others took Christianity to save their lives. A local rule made papers legal only with the communal secretary's seal. Breaking that rule cost a fine of twenty gold gulden. The entry also names noted wool dealers and scholars. Isaac ben Sheshet's responsa supply much of the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tombs-14441:
Burial customs of the ancient Hebrews are traced in this article. Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Hebrews buried their dead from the earliest times. Cremation, practiced by Moabites and Edomites, struck prophets as sinful. It served only as an added punishment for criminals.

The oldest burials were pits or heaps of stones. Achan and a conquered king rest under stone heaps in Joshua. Absalom's body went into a forest pit. Families often buried their dead on their own land. Samuel and Joab were both buried near home. Later rules pushed graves outside the towns. Rabbinic law set them fifty ells from settlement. Lepers were kept apart even in death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tull-edmund-145: Edmund Tull was a Hungarian artist born at Szekesfejervar in 1870. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was educated at Budapest, Milan, and Paris. In Paris he studied under J. P. Laurens and B. Constant. His first work showed the Cathedral of Notre Dame. It drew attention at the Budapest exposition of 1896. His etchings are prized in London and Vienna. Peasant Mowing and The Island of Capri hang in Budapest's art museum. Archduchess Isabella owned his painting The Smithy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-van-oven-joshua:
Joshua Van Oven was an English surgeon and community worker. He was born in England in 1766 and died at Liverpool in 1838. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Abraham Van Oven. Joshua trained under Sir William Blizard and gained his license in 1784.

In London, Van Oven built a large practice among Jewish patients. He helped found the Jews' Free School and served as its president. He also gave weekly talks to the pupils. His biggest project was the Jews' Hospital in Mile End. Bad business deals later forced him to move to Liverpool.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wine-14941:
Wine holds a place of honor in the Scriptures. Emil G. Hirsch, Judah David Eisenstein, and the Executive Committee wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The vine ranks above all other forest trees. Wine cheers God and man, says the Book of Judges. It revives the faint in the wilderness.

Israel itself is pictured as a vine from Egypt. A blessed wife is like a fruitful vine. Peace means resting under one's vine and fig tree. Plenty of wine signals broad prosperity. Wine libations formed part of the Temple sacrifices. Singing usually accompanied the drinking of wine. The entry follows wine through law, poetry, and daily life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-xerxes-15041:
Xerxes was a king of Persia who ruled from 485 to 465 BCE. Emil G. Hirsch and Eduard Meyer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of King Darius of Persia. His name takes many forms in the old tongues. The entry gives the Persian, Babylonian, and Greek forms.

In the Hebrew text his name is spelled in a set way. He is named in the Book of Ezra at one point. A charge by the Samaritans against the Jews is tied to him. He is the king in the tale of the Book of Esther. The Book of Daniel names him as a father as well. There he is the father of Darius of the Medes. The short entry links one king to three books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zabludowski-jeh:
Jehiel Michael Zabludowski (1803-1869) was a Russian scholar of Hebrew tale lore. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Byelostok, he died in that same town. He gave his life to the study of the Haggadah most of all.

He wrote notes on that lore for more than one journal. His notes ran in Ha-Maggid, Ha-Meliz, and Ha-Karmel in turn. He wrote two books on the theme of his life. One is a guide to the true sense of tale texts. Its name is Mishan Mayim, or Support of Water in tongue. The second book came out three years after his death. It gives notes on hard parts of the Midrash Rabbot. The entry rests on a Hebrew press note and a book list.
king-henry-viii-pg1541:
This edition of Shakespeare's Henry the Eighth prints the full cast and scene plan. The dukes of Norfolk and Suffolk head the English lords. Cardinal Wolsey and his servant Cromwell follow, with Campeius, the pope's legate. Archbishop Cranmer, Bishop Gardiner, and Queen Katherine hold the church and court sides.

The contents move through a hall at Blackfriars, where Katherine's divorce is tried. Kimbolton, where she dies, and a palace yard and gallery fill later acts. The plan shows the play's pattern: one great figure falls in almost every act. Buckingham, Katherine, and Wolsey each get a farewell of famous dignity. The christening of Elizabeth closes the action on a note of prophecy.
lafontaine-fables-wright-1841:
Jean de La Fontaine published his Fables in France in books that appeared from 1668 onward. Elizur Wright turned them into English verse in 1841, and his version became a classic in its own right. The tales are short poems, most of them about animals who talk and scheme like people.

Foxes, wolves, ants, and grasshoppers act out pride, greed, folly, and wit. Each fable ends with a pointed moral, often sly rather than preachy. La Fontaine drew on Aesop and older sources but made the verse light, shrewd, and musical. French children still learn these poems by heart, and Wright's rhymes carry much of their charm into English.
love-s-labour-s-lost-pg2241:
In Love's Labour's Lost, Shakespeare builds a comedy almost wholly on words. Four young men of Navarre vow three years of study without women. Four ladies of France arrive the same day and wreck the vow. What follows is a war of puns, sonnets, and set speeches.

Berowne, the wittiest lord, protests the oath even as he signs it. The ladies answer every flourish with cooler, sharper wit. Pages, constables, and a curate keep the low comedy bubbling. The play's talk is its action, and its action is talk. A death reported in the last scene sends the lovers to wait a year.
massachusetts-body-of-liberties-1641:
Massachusetts Bay Colony adopted the Body of Liberties in 1641, its first full code of laws. Minister Nathaniel Ward did much of the drafting, drawing on the Bible and English legal practice. The code lists about one hundred liberties, duties, and rules for colonial life.

Its clauses protect life, property, and fair trials, and they limit cruel punishments. Other parts cover women, children, servants, strangers, and even cruelty toward animals. Some rules feel harsh today, since the colony tied law closely to Scripture. Even so, the code stands as an early American attempt to write rights down.
michelet-proces-des-templiers-vol-1-1841:
Jules Michelet, the great French historian, edited the trial records of the Knights Templar for the Royal Press at Paris in 1841. This first volume covers the case against the order, which France crushed between 1307 and 1314. The text is in French, drawn from the old court papers.

Readers get the questions put to the knights, their sworn answers, and the pope's own documents on the affair. Under torture and fear, many men confessed to charges they later took back. Michelet's edition let readers judge the famous case from the raw record for the first time.
michelet-proces-des-templiers-vol-2-1841:
Jules Michelet's edition of the Templar trials closes with this second volume, printed at Paris in 1841. It picks up where the first volume left off in the court record of 1307 to 1314. The French text prints the rest of the case against the Knights Templar.

More hearings follow, with further sworn statements from knights, servants, and churchmen. The papers show the trial grinding on toward the order's end and the death of its last master. Read with volume one, it gives the fullest old record of the Templars' fall. The two volumes together print the core of the surviving trial record.
miller-old-red-sandstone-1841:
Hugh Miller was a Scottish stonemason who taught himself geology in the quarries of Cromarty. His Old Red Sandstone, published in 1841, grew from letters written for a local paper. It made him famous almost at once.

Miller describes the strange fossil fishes locked in red rock layers near his home. He writes of their scales, fins, and armor with a poet's eye. At the time, such finds raised hard questions about the age of the earth. The book became a classic of popular geology for its clear prose and wonder. Stone by stone, he reads a vanished sea full of strange life.
nennius-history-britons-giles-1841:
The History of the Britons is a Welsh Latin work tied to the name Nennius and dated to the ninth century. J. A. Giles translated it into English in 1841. It mixes chronicle, genealogy, and marvel, and it holds a famous place in the Arthur story.

Nennius lists twelve battles that Arthur fought against the Saxons, naming places few can now find. That list is the earliest sign of a historical Arthur, centuries before the romances. Around it sit older British traditions and wonders of the land. Scholars still debate how much of it is history and how much is hope.
openalex-w1560020441:
Henry Heberle, Rosane Minghim, and three co-authors built this tool. Their paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics in 2015. Set comparisons fill many workflows in biological science. Venn diagrams display such comparisons in a familiar way. Existing tools for building them were limited, they note.

Their web tool, InteractiVenn, handles up to six sets. Users can merge sets while keeping the diagram's shape. The tool lists the elements inside any subset. Sets can be saved, reloaded, and exported as images. The team tested it on two biological datasets. It is freely available online for any research field.
openalex-w2077680141:
Qiu-Yue Zhong, Bizu Gelaye, Alan Zaslavsky and colleagues tested a short anxiety questionnaire in pregnant women. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Anxiety disorders in pregnancy harm mother and baby. Early detection leads to earlier treatment. A brief, valid screening tool was needed.

The GAD-7 asks seven questions about anxiety symptoms. The team studied pregnant women in Peru. They compared questionnaire scores with clinical diagnoses. A good cut-off score balanced detection and false alarms. The tool performed well in this group. It is short enough for busy prenatal clinics. Screening could bring anxious mothers to care sooner. The study supports wider use in pregnancy care.
openalex-w2117103941:
E. Abbas, Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE team measured particles made by light in lead collisions. Their paper appeared in 2013. In near-miss collisions, lead nuclei do not touch. Their strong electric fields act like beams of light. Those photons can create charmonium particles when they strike a nucleus.

Charmonium was picked out through its decay into leptons. Events with almost no other activity were selected. Two production patterns were measured one by one. One pattern matched models with moderate nuclear shadowing. Electron pair production from two photons also matched theory. The results probe how gluons are spread inside nuclei. Shadowing cuts gluon numbers at small scales.
openalex-w2124312641:
Rahel Wampfler, Felista Mwingira, Sarah Javati, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2013. They compared ways to detect gametocytes, the stage of malaria parasites that mosquitoes pick up from human blood. Finding them well matters because their numbers show how likely a person is to pass malaria on.

The team tested field and lab methods in a survey of children in Papua New Guinea. They used RNA-based tests for two kinds of malaria parasite and for gametocyte markers. RNA testing found far more infections than DNA testing did. About two in five positive children carried gametocytes for each parasite kind, a share DNA methods would have badly understated.
openalex-w2127627541:
João Calixto wrote this review alone for the Brazilian Journal of Medical and Biological Research in 2000. He surveys herbal medicines, covering whether they work, whether they are safe, and how their quality should be controlled. He also covers marketing and the rules that govern these products in different countries.

Calixto stresses that data are too thin for most plants to guarantee quality, effect, or safety. The belief that herbal drugs have no side effects is false, though harms occur less often than with synthetic drugs. He compares regulatory models, from prescription drugs to dietary supplements. He urges shared standards and farm-grown plants over wild harvests for uniform quality.
openalex-w2143036141:
Michel Kulbicki, Valeriano Parravicini, David Bellwood, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2013. They set out to draw the world's reef fish regions with numbers rather than opinion. Reef fishes are the most varied group of sea fishes, and their ranges are fairly well known, yet global region maps stayed rough.

The team built on one hundred sixty-nine species checklists spread across all tropical oceans. They ran the data through four different classifications, allowing for shaky species names and uneven list quality. All four approaches delivered converging results for the regional divisions. The work gives evolution and conservation studies a shared, measured map of reef fish homelands.
openalex-w2158718341:
András Hoffer, András Gelencsér, and Pascal Guyon led this 2006 study in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics. They studied humic-like matter, the brown stuff in smoke from burning plants. Such smoke specks scatter and soak up sunlight, so how they handle light shapes climate math.

The samples came from Amazon air in a 2002 smoke study. The team pulled the matter out, made fresh specks, and tested them. At green light the matter soaked up little. Toward UV light it soaked up far more. At the shortest wavelength tested, it supplied up to half of all the light the smoke soaked up. Across the full sun spectrum, its share was smaller but still hard to ignore.
openalex-w2292507041:
Lars Söderström, Anders Hagborg, Matt von Konrat, and colleagues published this checklist in PhytoKeys in 2016. They present the first worldwide list of accepted hornwort and liverwort species. Such a working list is a step toward the long-standing goal of an online flora of all known plants.

The checklist holds over seven thousand four hundred species in nearly four hundred genera and ninety-two families. It merges names, classification, and geography into one central dataset for the two plant groups. Before this effort, scattered records blocked global study of these plants' richness and conservation. Built since 2008 by a community of specialists seeking consensus, the list exposes where knowledge of this flora still has gaps.
openalex-w2388080941:
Rodrigo Quiroga and Marcos Villarreal published this methods paper in PLoS ONE in 2016. They present Vinardo, a new scoring function for the popular AutoDock Vina docking program. Docking software predicts how drug candidates grip their target proteins, and the scoring step decides which predicted poses and molecules look best.

The usual way to train scorers, fitting them to measured binding strengths, turns out to dock poorly. Instead, the authors combined scoring, shape refinement, and re-docking trials on carefully curated datasets. The result is a simpler function tuned directly for docking performance. Tests show it improves all three jobs a scorer must do: ranking poses, placing molecules correctly, and screening libraries for hits. It is a drop-in refinement of a tool thousands of labs already use.
openalex-w2607075141:
Ángel Cruz-Roa, Hannah L. Gilmore, and Ajay N. Basavanhally, with colleagues, published this 2017 study in Scientific Reports. It uses deep learning to find invasive breast cancer in digitized microscope slides. Pathologists normally mark a tumor's extent by eye, a slow task that varies between readers. Computer help must also survive slides from different labs, stains, and scanners.

The authors trained a convolutional network to label cancerous regions across whole-slide images. They tested it on slide collections gathered from different sources. Performance measures in the paper show the system detecting tumor extent accurately and reproducibly. Such consistency matters because tumor extent drives staging and treatment decisions. The work points toward computer tools that back up pathologists rather than replace them. Reliable automation could cut the tedious parts of slide reading while keeping experts in charge.
openalex-w2766814241:
Esperanza Huerta Lwanga, Jorge Mendoza-Vega, and Víctor Manuel Kú-Quej, with colleagues, traced plastic through a farm food chain in Scientific Reports in 2017. Their field sites were traditional Mayan home gardens in southeast Mexico, where waste handling is poor. Plastic pollution is global, but its movement into land animals eaten by people had not been examined. The team sampled soil, earthworm casts, and chickens.

Microplastic counts climbed at each step: lowest in soil, higher in earthworm casts, highest in chicken feces. Chicken gizzards, which people eat, held microplastic particles and many larger plastic fragments. Crops, another eaten part, held macroplastic too, though no microplastic was found there. The data give the first field evidence that plastic debris moves along a terrestrial food chain. That path leads directly to the human dinner table in these communities.
openalex-w2800469141:
Sailesh Samanta, Dilip Kumar Pal, and Babita Palsamanta mapped flood susceptibility in Papua New Guinea in Applied Water Science in 2018. Floods are among the country's most devastating disasters, amid quakes, volcanoes, and landslides. The study area is the Markham river valley in Morobe province. The team tested whether satellite data, mapping software, and a statistical model could flag flood-prone land.

They built a database of one hundred forty-three past flood locations. Ten factors fed the model, from elevation and slope to soil drainage and distance from the main river. Seventy percent of sites trained the model; the rest could test it. Resulting scores sorted the valley from least to most flood prone. The map gives planners a practical tool for siting homes and infrastructure. It also shows a cheap method transferable to other data-poor, flood-hit regions.
openalex-w2809286541:
Mehdi Adjeroud, Mohsen Kayal, and Claudie Iborra-Cantonnet lead this study of coral recovery at Moorea, in French Polynesia. The metadata record leaves authors and year blank; the sample itself names them. Coral reefs face repeated disturbances, from storms to bleaching, at a quickening pace. Whether assemblages can bounce back between hits is a live question.

Using long-term yearly data, the team tracked the reef slope through decades of disturbance. Since the 1990s, large events repeatedly crashed coral cover and abundance there. Yet by 2014, four years after one extreme decline, juvenile and adult colonies matched or beat pre-disturbance levels. No shift to seaweed dominance occurred. Recovery happened despite constantly low larval recruitment, implying new corals survived unusually well. Species composition still shifted, as species differ in fragility and rebound speed. The authors call Moorea a new benchmark for reef resilience.
openalex-w2824297141:
The ALICE Collaboration reported charged particle counts from proton-lead collisions in Physical Review Letters in 2013. Betty Abelev heads the long author list. At the Large Hadron Collider, lead-lead collisions had shown fast particles strongly suppressed. Physicists needed a control experiment to tell whether that effect begins in the incoming nuclei themselves.

Using the ALICE detector, the team measured how many charged particles emerge at each momentum. The runs took place at 5.02 tera-electronvolts per nucleon pair, during a short 2012 run. The resulting nuclear factor compares proton-lead output against plain proton collisions. Deviations would expose cold nuclear effects like parton shadowing or gluon saturation. Such effects must be subtracted before claiming hot, dense matter in lead-lead runs. The measurement became a reference point for heavy-ion physics at the LHC.
openalex-w3094535741:
Amanda McQuade, You Jung Kang, Jonathan Hasselmann, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It examines microglia, the brain's immune cells, that lack the gene TREM2, in human models of Alzheimer's disease. Variants in TREM2 raise Alzheimer's risk about as much as the best-known risk gene does.

Microglia clear dead cells and protein clumps, signal with immune messengers, and also nourish neurons and shape synapses. Using stem-cell-grown human microglia and chimeric mouse models, the team removed TREM2 and watched the response. Gene activity and cell function both fell short in the knockout cells. The deficits help explain how a single immune gene can tilt the brain toward Alzheimer's, and where treatments might intervene.
openalex-w3110082941:
Richard Orlandi, Todd Kingdom, Timothy Smith, and colleagues issued this consensus statement in the International Forum of Allergy and Rhinology. It is the 2021 update of the international statement on rhinosinusitis, long-term inflammation of the nose and sinuses. Five years had passed since the first version.

Care for this common condition advanced quickly in that span. The update adds more than forty new topics, with fresh weight on diagnostic flow charts, quality measures, cost-effectiveness, and new therapies. A structured method was used to grade the evidence behind each point. Specialists worldwide contributed, making the document a shared reference for how rhinosinusitis should be diagnosed and treated today.
openalex-w3178377341:
Hendrikje Jorissen, Pierre Galand, Isabelle Bonnard, and colleagues studied how coral larvae choose where to settle. Reef corals begin life as free-swimming larvae that must attach to a surface to grow. Crustose coralline algae, hard pink algae that coat rocks, are known to attract settling larvae. Whether larvae respond to chemicals or microbes from these algae was unclear.

The team offered one common coral species six kinds of these algae from three habitats. All six triggered settlement, but only one species drew larvae onto its own surface. That alga carried a distinct mix of bacteria and chemicals, including two lipid groups flagged as likely cues. The results suggest larvae read microbial and chemical signs when picking a home.
openalex-w3181754241: Gianfranco Parati, George Stergiou, Grzegorz Bilo, and colleagues wrote this 2021 position paper for a working group of the European Society of Hypertension. It covers how to measure blood pressure at home. It also covers why the readings matter in care and how to use them in practice. The preserved sample holds only the title page and author list, with no readable body text or recommendations.
openalex-w4210665241:
Bo Meng, Adam Abdullahi, Isabella Ferreira, and colleagues studied how the Omicron variant enters human cells, in Nature in 2022. Earlier variants used a surface protein called TMPRSS2 to help cut their spike and fuse with cells. That fusion can merge many cells into large clumps linked to disease. Omicron carries over thirty spike mutations, so its entry route was in doubt.

The team found that Omicron's spike forms such clumps far less well than Delta's. Its spike is cut less efficiently at a key site. As a result, Omicron shifts away from cells rich in TMPRSS2 toward other entry paths. The change may help explain why Omicron's pattern of illness differed from earlier variants.
openalex-w4293030541:
Agustín Aibar-Almazán, Ana Voltes-Martínez, Yolanda Castellote-Caballero, and colleagues review the current state of osteoporosis care, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2022. Osteoporosis has been called the silent disease of this century. It weakens bones until they break easily, mainly in postmenopausal women and older adults. At its root, bone removal outpaces bone building.

The review covers how the disease is diagnosed, including bone density scans and dual X-ray methods. Drug treatments slow bone loss, while newer options include cell therapies and bioactive gels that aim to rebuild bone. Lifestyle measures matter too: exercise, diet, and quitting smoking or heavy drinking. The authors present the field's basis and its newest strategies in one overview.
openalex-w7156154641:
Ryohei Oishi, of Hokkaido University, led a 2026 physics study of the piezomagnetic effect in TbPt6Al3, a rare-earth compound in the new class of magnets called altermagnets. The piezomagnetic effect means a material gains magnetization when squeezed. The team measured single crystals under one-direction stress while varying temperature and magnetic field.

Below the magnetic ordering temperature, magnetization grew in a straight line with stress, showing the effect clearly, though a predicted nonlinear form did not appear. The measured coefficient at very low temperature was more than a hundred times larger than in other altermagnets and related magnets. The authors attribute the strength to the strong spin-orbit coupling of terbium's electrons, linking a rare effect to a specific atomic cause.

Shinya Kimura, of Meiji Pharmaceutical University in Japan, published an English-language review in 2026 on supramolecular gels for pharmaceutical use and on how such gels form. These soft materials arise when small gelator molecules self-assemble through noncovalent interactions, and their structures can be precisely designed, including stimulus-responsive behavior. The review summarizes the author's studies in two directions.

First, sugar-coupled gelators were built as drug carriers targeting the small intestine. One gel broke down under a specific enzyme and released its model drug cargo as it degraded, proving the concept of enzyme-responsive delivery. Second, high-speed atomic force microscopy watched gel fibers grow in repeated bursts of elongation and pause, leading to a block-stacking model of how the fibers assemble.
openalex-w7206164141:
Vera Lucia de Oliveira Jordao argues that school management and teaching coordination sit at the center of good education today. Writing in English in a 2026 Brazilian journal, she reviews national and international research plus official Brazilian documents. Rapid social, cultural, and technical change, she notes, has widened what principals and coordinators must do, from leadership and planning to guiding how teaching happens.

Jordao ties quality to shared work: democratic management, ongoing teacher training, careful use of digital tools, inclusive teaching, and close ties between school and community. Her findings stress teamwork among staff, respect for education professionals, and planning done with participation rather than by decree. When managers and coordinators act together, she concludes, schools become fairer, more inventive, and more focused on learning.
openalex-w7206214741:
Alcebiades Pereira da Silva Neto and three colleagues study PMZITO, a program run by the military police of Para, Brazil, that works with children and teenagers. Rather than waiting for crime, the program teaches citizenship through educational, cultural, sports, and social activities. The authors combined published research, documents, and fieldwork, using a questionnaire answered by military police officers.

Officers reported that the program strengthens preventive policing and brings police and community closer together. It also promotes values tied to citizenship and human rights and helps build a culture of peace. Challenges remain: more training for officers, more institutional respect for prevention work, and room to expand. The authors present PMZITO as a social prevention policy that makes public safety more humane and participatory.
openalex-w7212185641:
Anderson de Oliveira Morais Borges and Ismael Santos Araujo review the place of social psychology in Brazil's welfare plans. The field has grown fast in this work in the past years. Its promise is care that is more human and more apt to change lives. The pair read ten past studies from 2015 to 2025. They asked what the field adds to the fight on want and unfair gaps.

Psychologists in this work, they find, stand as a bridge. They link lone lives to the plans that serve them. They build trust, hear with care, and honor the range of lives in a town. Blocks still stand in their way, in rules and in ethics. But the field, they conclude, can act as a force for change. That force holds when the work stays bound to fair shares and just ends for all.
openalex-w7213194141:
Eva Luciana de Moura Guimaraes tells of a school scheme in Concordia, Santa Catarina, called Leads of Lore. The scheme ran with young kids, in the first five years of school. It joins two roots. One is a famed school in Portugal where kids steer their own path. The next is a mind scheme by a Brazil shrink, built to train heart skills in kids, staff, and homes alike.

The aim was two-fold: skill in sums and words, and growth of the self. Kids were to stand as leads of their own lore, not as cups to fill. The plan ties the I, the you, and the we: a child learns who she is, meets the next child as a peer, and joins a group that learns as one. Such schemes bet that heart growth and book growth rise as one, each the prop of the next.
openalex-w7213229541:
Sarah Larissa Gomes Flores leads a team that sums up a tree clan of the far north of South America: Sextonia. One kind, Sextonia rubra, is Brazil's lone home-born tree of the clan. It was long filed with kin clans, till a new kind forced a fresh sort. The tree is cut hard for its wood. Yet its sap and bark lore stayed thin on the page till now.

The bark, the team finds, is rich in a set of ring-shaped fats. Two of them mark the tree like a stamp. Sap tests show fight in them: they curb rot, kill mold and the young of pests, and guard cells from rust-like harm. One such use is held by a grant of sole rights. A cut tree with drug seeds in its bark, the team holds, is worth more standing than felled.
openalex-w7213778641:
Aline Juliana Oja Persicheto, as hyphenated in the sample, asks what recent research says about children's literature in science teaching. Her single-author 2026 theoretical study maps articles in the CAPES journals portal from 2015 to 2025. It concerns the early years of elementary school in Brazil.

Scientific literacy in childhood must respect how young children take up ideas, she argues. Discussion of children's books in science lessons does appear in recent work, though still timidly. Studies focus mostly on classroom practice and on building method tools for teachers. Joining stories with natural science, Persicheto concludes, can support scientific literacy when the link is planned as real teaching, not decoration.
openalex-w7214076441:
Juciara Rodrigues Duarte da Cruz and Soane Santos Silva study data-based learning management at a state school in Bahia. Their 2026 qualitative, documentary study reads performance reports from the Plurall platform for final-year high school pupils. The school's 2025 national basic education index result is the reference point.

Platform data can reveal learning difficulties, guide interventions, and support teaching decisions, they find. Indicators alone do not translate the complexity of learning, they warn. Real test conditions and each student's singularity escape the dashboard. Data-based management can be a strong teaching resource, the authors conclude, only when indicators are treated as material for analysis rather than as verdicts on pupils.
openalex-w7214680241:
Jeferson Vitorino dos Santos, Natan André de Jesus, and Gelson Leonardo Rech ask, in a 2026 article, when a researcher is born. Their material is unusual: a letter Santos wrote to his course coordinators in June 2026, in his first months of a master's degree, before the article existed. Reading that letter beside thinkers such as Paulo Freire, they trace what changes as someone learns to research.

Becoming a researcher, the analysis finds, is not a straight road from doubt to certainty. Doubt itself widens: first aimed at one's own preparation, it later reaches claims, readings, and choices once taken for granted. Not-knowing is not eliminated but learned, bounded, and turned into material for intellectual work. What marks the researcher, they conclude, is growing responsibility for questions, interpretations, and the limits of what one claims to know.
openalex-w7216280741:
Alcino Antonio Duarte Neto and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva wrote a 2026 article on technologies, citizenship, and education in Brazilian schools. The digital shift has changed how people teach, learn, talk, and take part in social life, opening teaching chances and new risks at once. Their library study reads studies and normative documents through three lenses: digital citizenship, technology-mediated teaching practice, and the risks of digital culture.

Digital technologies can favor shared learning, autonomy, creativity, joining in, and media competence, they find, when tied to teaching goals and guided by the teacher. Risks include privacy and data protection failures, cyberbullying, misinformation, undue exposure, unequal access, and misuse of tools. Bringing technology in well requires ongoing teacher formation, school safety and inclusion policies, and education aimed at critical, ethical, and responsible digital life, the authors conclude.
openalex-w7221112641:
Charles Eduardo Freitas de Souza, Bryan Johnnes Alves Silva, and Manoel Joaquim Ramos Neto reviewed studies from 2021 to 2026 on training judo and Brazilian jiu-jitsu together at the elite level. The two grappling arts share roots but compete under different rules, and the authors ask what each can lend the other.

Judo stresses grips, off-balancing, and throws, while jiu-jitsu favors positional control, transitions, and submissions on the ground. Both demand strength, power, muscular endurance, grip, and fast recovery, in different mixes. Joint training could widen an athlete's repertoire and adaptability, provided coaches respect each sport's rules and manage fatigue. Notably, the reviewed studies did not prove that combined programs improve competitive results.
plos-pbio-0020141:
Vanina Guernier, Michael E. Hochberg, and Jean-François Guégan mapped human diseases worldwide in PLOS Biology in 2004. They asked what drives the pattern of where diseases occur. Their answer gives ecology a lead role: climate, hosts, and vectors shape the map more than wealth or health systems alone.

The authors compared disease richness across countries with a wide set of factors. Warm, wet places with rich wildlife tended to hold more kinds of human disease. That pattern warns that changes in climate and land use may shift disease maps in coming years. The paper frames health as part of ecology, a view that has only grown since in the study of emerging infections.
plos-pbio-0020341:
Delphine Fagegaltier and Bruce S. Baker studied gene balance in fruit flies in PLOS Biology in 2004. Male flies have one X chromosome, females two. Dosage compensation boosts the male X so both sexes get equal gene output. A protein complex lands on the male X to do the boosting.

The team found certain sites on the X can call the complex in on their own, even when moved elsewhere. Those sites act as entry points from which the complex spreads. Knowing them explains how a whole chromosome gets singled out for special treatment. The fly system is the clearest case of chromosome-wide gene control, a puzzle with echoes in human X-linked disease.
plos-pone-0000041:
José Malpica, Soledad Sacristán, Aurora Fraile, and co-authors studied germs that do not commit to one host in a 2006 paper. Multi-host pathogens infect several species, moving among them. That flexibility makes them hard to control, since curing one host leaves the others as refuges. The team examined association and host selectivity in such pathogens.

Selectivity asks whether a pathogen uses its hosts evenly or favors some over others, and association asks which hosts it links together. The answers shape how diseases jump between wildlife, livestock, and people. Knowing a pathogen's host preferences helps predict where it will strike next and where control efforts will pay off most.
plos-pone-0000141:
Maki Yoshihama, Hung D. Nguyen, and Naoya Kenmochi published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies introns, the stretches of DNA that are cut out of a gene's message before a protein is made. The focus is the genes for ribosomal proteins, the parts of the cell's protein factories, which are unusually rich in introns.

The authors trace how these introns have been gained, lost, and moved over evolution. Because ribosomal protein genes are ancient and shared across life, their intron history offers a window on how genomes change. The work helps settle how dynamic introns really are across long spans of time.
plos-pone-0000241:
Hong Sjölinder and Ann-Beth Jonsson published this infection imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Meningococcal sepsis is a fast, often fatal blood infection. The authors use imaging to follow disease dynamics, how the infection develops and spreads in the body over time.

Sepsis kills by speed, so a clear picture of its timeline is clinically valuable. The approach turns a disease that unfolds in hidden stages into one that can be watched step by step. Watching the disease unfold in images shows which organs are hit and when. The work supports faster recognition and better-targeted treatment of meningococcal disease, where hours decide outcomes.
plos-pone-0000341:
Masaki Nishida and Matthew P. Walker published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Daytime naps are known to help consolidate motor memory, locking in a practiced skill. The authors connect that benefit to sleep spindles, brief bursts of brain activity during sleep. They show the spindles act in regionally specific parts of the brain.

A nap is not uniform rest; specific rhythms in specific regions do the memory work. The study links spindle activity to the size of the learning gain after waking. The finding refines advice on naps and practice, and informs research on sleep-based rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0000441:
Carlos S. Moreno and colleagues tested a hard question about ovarian cancer treatment, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein p53, when working, can arrest the cell cycle, halting division. Chemotherapy often relies on cells dividing to kill them. The team gathered evidence that p53-mediated arrest can actually inhibit chemotherapeutic treatment of ovarian carcinomas.

The idea is uncomfortable: a protective protein might shelter tumor cells from the drugs meant to kill them, by putting them into a resting state. If so, a tumor's p53 status could predict whether a drug will help or underperform. The study warns that more cell-cycle arrest is not always better in cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0000541:
Kany-Kany Angelique Luabeya and colleagues ran a randomized controlled trial of supplements for South African children, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. The trial tested zinc or multiple micronutrient supplementation to reduce diarrhea and respiratory disease, two leading causes of child illness and death in poor regions.

Randomized trials are the gold standard because they separate the supplement's effect from luck and background differences. Zinc had strong prior evidence for diarrhea, while multi-micronutrient mixes were cheaper to deliver. A head-to-head trial in the children most affected tells programs which investment actually buys health.
plos-pone-0000641:
Shuxian Jiang, Yigong Fu, John Williams and colleagues described the cannabinoid system inside mouse embryonic stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. What decides whether a stem cell renews itself or becomes a specialized cell is a core question in biology. The team looked at two receptors, CB1 and CB2, and the cannabinoid signals that bind them.

They report where these receptors are expressed and what they do as stem cells form embryoid bodies and turn toward blood cell lines. Cannabinoids are best known from cannabis and from adult tissues. Finding their machinery at work in early embryos opens a new angle on how cell fate is steered.
plos-pone-0000741:
Mohammed Bakkali studied short bits of DNA that some bacteria go out of their way to take in. Many bacteria can absorb DNA from their surroundings and add it to their own genome. That uptake has real medical and money stakes, since it can spread drug resistance genes. Two bacterial families, Pasteurellaceae and Neisseriaceae, prefer DNA that carries certain short sequences.

Those favored sequences appear far more often in the bacteria's own genomes than chance would explain. Bakkali asks how such short sequences build up, move, and persist over time. One idea is self-recognition: by favoring their own sequence marks, bacteria trade genes mostly with kin. The study maps the pattern and weighs what could keep it in place.
plos-pone-0000841:
John P.A. Ioannidis, Nikolaos A. Patsopoulos and Evangelos Evangelou asked why pooled gene studies so often disagree with each other. A meta-analysis pools the results of many studies into one sum, and checks how much the parts differ. Such pooling was used more and more on genome-wide association studies. There, teams hunt the same gene effects and try to copy each other's finds.

The team's subject is heterogeneity: real gaps between study results. Some gaps are noise. Others are signs that groups, designs, or biases truly differ. Gene hunters who know how much gap to expect will not cheer too soon, or drop a true find too fast. The study is a guide to reading pooled claims with care.
plos-pone-0000941:
Biju Parekkadan, Daan van Poll, Kazuhiro Suganuma and colleagues tested whether molecules from stem cells can rescue a failing liver, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fulminant hepatic failure is sudden, severe liver collapse. Calming the immune system may offer a way out that avoids needing donor liver cells.

Mesenchymal stem cells, taken from bone marrow, are known to temper immune responses. The team asked whether the molecules these cells release, rather than the cells themselves, could reverse the failure. A cell free treatment would be easier to store, dose and approve. The study is an early step toward that idea, tested in a severe disease model.
plos-pone-0001041:
S. Hoyt Peckham, David Maldonado Diaz, Andreas Walli and colleagues documented turtle bycatch in small scale Pacific fisheries, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Industrial fishing bycatch, animals caught by accident, is known to harm seabirds, mammals and turtles. The impact of small scale coastal fisheries had been largely overlooked.

The team show that such fisheries jeopardize endangered Pacific loggerhead turtles. Small boats working close to shore can meet turtles where they feed and breed. Counting that harm changes the conservation ledger: protecting turtles means working with local fishers, not just fleets. The paper pairs the finding with the scale of coastal fishing worldwide.
plos-pone-0001141:
Northeast India is the only land bridge between the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. It may also have been a corridor for early human migrations into East Asia. B. Mohan Reddy and co-authors present genetic evidence on that route in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their focus is the Austro-Asiatic speaking tribes of the region.

The Austro-Asiatic language family is considered among the oldest in this part of Asia. The authors argue that these tribes supply a genetic link between South and Southeast Asia that had been missing. Their data bear on how the first peopling of East Asia unfolded.
plos-pone-0001241:
In some animals, RNA from mitochondria, the cell's power plants, turns up outside them, positioned in the egg at the spot that seeds germ cells. Youichirou Ninomiya and Shizuko Ichinose checked whether mammals do the same, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The phenomenon had been reported in several non-mammal groups but not in mammals.

The authors examined the expression and distribution of mitochondrial ribosomal RNA in the mouse oocyte and zygote. Whether the RNA localizes to a germ cell determinant in mammals bears on how universal that mechanism is. Their study brings the mammal case into an otherwise broader story.
plos-pone-0001341:
Two groups of tiny cyanobacteria, Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus, carry out much of the ocean's photosynthesis. Christophe Six and colleagues studied how they divide the ocean's light environment between them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Phytoplankton cells are entrained in the water column and so are often exposed to rapid changes in irradiance within the upper mixed layer.

The authors report that light variability illuminates niche-partitioning among marine picocyanobacteria: the groups specialize on different light regimes. Who wins where determines how much carbon the ocean fixes. Their work links a physical variable, flickering light, to global primary production.
plos-pone-0001441:
Farba Karam and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a blood test for hidden TB in people with HIV. Finding and treating hidden TB in this group can cut illness and death. The team tested a home built blood test that reads a key immune signal. They asked if the test stays sound as HIV gets worse.

They report the test kept its power to spot hidden TB in HIV patients. But its readings did shift with how far HIV had gone. That caveat matters for how results are read in clinics. The work supports use of the test, with care, in places where both ills are common.
plos-pone-0001541:
Phillipa Hay and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on eating disorder acts in South Australia. Proof on whether such ills are rising had been mixed. The team used two matched community surveys ten years apart. Both asked the same questions on eating acts in the general public.

They found that eating disorder acts had in fact risen over that span. A matched design makes the trend claim much firmer than loose reports. A real rise urges more funds for early care and school based guards. It also prompts work on what drove the rise in that decade.
plos-pone-0001641:
Arnaud Muller, Elise Glattard, Omar Taleb, and their co-authors measured morphine made by the body itself in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Morphine is best known as the main active drug in opium from poppies. Yet it also turns up in animal tissues and cell types, including the mammalian brain. Its making pathway had already been traced in a human nerve cell line.

The team studied a human cell line called SH-SY5Y and the cerebellum of mice to pin down where this in-house morphine occurs. The full text gives the detection methods and the amounts found. It also covers what the pattern suggests about why nerve cells would make a pain drug of their own. The work adds to the view that morphine-like signals form part of the brain's own chemistry, not just plant medicine.
plos-pone-0001741:
Vikram Paruchuri, Anil Prasad, Kevin McHugh, and their co-authors studied a calcium-binding protein in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. S100A7 is a small protein first noted in psoriatic skin lesions and later in squamous tumors of skin, lung, and breast. Its expression tracks with high-grade HER-positive tumors and a high risk of progression.

The team reports that lowering S100A7 inhibits signaling from epidermal growth factor in breast cancer cells. It also blocks the formation of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. The full text gives the cell experiments and pathway readouts. Bone is where breast cancer often spreads, so a protein linking tumor signals to bone-eating cells is a target worth attention.
plos-pone-0001841:
Jordi Moya-Laraño, Dejan Vinković, Eva De Mas, and their co-authors modeled spider body evolution with pendulum physics in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Animals were thought to gain from pendulum mechanics as they hang and swing, trading height for speed. Convincing evidence was lacking.

The team shows the shape evolution of spiders is predicted by pendulum mechanics. Leg and body proportions match what good swinging needs. The full text gives the model and the species data. A law of physics that predicts anatomy across species is a rare result. It explains why hanging spiders evolved their marked long legged build.
plos-pone-0001941:
Nita Bharti and co-authors modeled how measles spreads along coasts in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Models help map how epidemics move through space and time, and what control steps might do. A leading model for spread between places, the gravity model, weighs both distance and the size of towns.

The team asked whether the mix of land and sea at coasts warps that spread in ways plain models miss. Coastal areas bunch people in lines and ports rather than even spreads. If models ignore that shape, they may misjudge where measles goes next. Better maps of spread help aim vaccines where they count most.
plos-pone-0002041:
Karine Bagramyan and co-authors built a test that spots botulinum toxin at vanishing levels, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Botulinum neurotoxin is among the most potent poisons known, a threat in spoiled food and a feared bioterror agent. A fast, cheap, and highly sensitive test for the active toxin in foods or blood was badly wanted.

As the title states, their method detects toxin type A at attomolar levels. That is a billionth of a billionth of a mole per liter, even in complex samples. Such sensitivity could flag tainted food early and let doctors track the toxin in patients.
