More hidden rules hurt the scoring institution, especially in tightly connected networks. False approvals fell in sparser networks when people copied each other. The results complicate the simple call for full transparency: what people learn from peers can matter as much as official explanations. Designers must weigh openness against the gaming it invites through social channels.
plos-pone-0346341:
Seda Kutluer, Milena Pavlova, and Wim Groot study ruinous medical bills in old age. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. They used a 2017 survey on health, aging, and retirement in Europe. It covered more than thirteen thousand older people in eleven EU states. All lived with long-term diseases such as diabetes or heart disease.

Having one illness did not drive the worst bills. Having several at once did. The pattern held at every spending line the team tested. Risk ran highest in Poland, Italy, Greece, and the Czech Republic. Spain sat at the low end. The authors urge policy makers to focus on people juggling many chronic conditions at once.
plos-pone-0346441:
Rui-jun Yang and colleagues tested respiratory samples in one eastern city. The city is Quzhou. Sampling ran across nine months in 2023 and 2024. Twenty eight hundred samples were tested in all. Thirteen common germs were checked per sample. Cases mixed clinic flu like illness and severe ward cases. Results were split by age, place, and season.

About fifty nine percent of samples tested positive. Flu led the germ list. A pneumonia bacterium ranked second. Adenovirus ranked third. A quarter of positive cases held two germs or more. Young children tested positive most often. Older adults tested positive least often. Multi germ watching should replace flu only checks.
plos-pone-0347541:
Jaba Rani Sarker, John Rolfe, and Jayanath Ananda ask coastal Bangladeshi rice farmers what a climate-proof seed is worth to them, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Rising seas push salt water into paddies, yet salt-tolerant rice varieties that already exist remain little planted, a puzzle this study probes with a choice experiment.

Farmers fell into three segments with different willingness to pay, shaped by age, savings, and land size. The findings show adoption is not one decision but several, depending on a household's resources and risks. Extension programs that treat all smallholders alike will keep missing; pricing and support tailored to each segment stand a better chance of getting tolerant seed into salty ground.
plos-pone-0347641:
Alexander D Clark, Jingmai K O'Connor, and co-authors described a new fossil bird from the early Cretaceous period whose ornamental tail feathers stretched to twice its body length. The bird belongs to the enantiornithines, the dominant bird group of that era, many of which sported a single pair of ribbon-like tail feathers ending in small vaned tips. Their 2026 description names the species Plumadraco bankoorum and examines its exceptionally preserved plumage.

The tail feathers end in proportionally small racket-shaped tips, and their fine preservation reveals structural variety not seen in relatives. Such ornaments likely served in courtship display, as in some living birds. The authors caution that untangling sexual selection from survival pressures in extinct birds is hard with so little soft tissue evidence, and they frame the feathers as a product of both.
plos-pone-0347741:
Ransmond Berchie and colleagues tackle a subtle trap in diabetes drug trials, in this 2026 PLOS ONE statistics paper. Drugs called SGLT-2 inhibitors, now central to diabetes and heart care, cause an early dip in a kidney measure called eGFR. Trialists naturally ask whether patients with bigger dips fare differently in the long run, but that dip is itself caused by the drug, which biases simple comparisons.

The authors use a method that sorts patients by the dip they would have had on either treatment, using a correlation model to handle what cannot be observed. Their framework shows how to ask the question without fooling oneself. It matters because misreading the early dip could scare doctors off drugs that protect kidneys over time.
plos-pone-0347941:
Chi Le Phuong leads a team of eight asking Vietnamese health students whether deliberately infecting volunteers can ever be right, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human challenge studies infect healthy volunteers on purpose to speed vaccine and treatment science, and they are being proposed for lower income countries. Students at Ho Chi Minh City's medical university answered a survey after engagement sessions, and joined discussion groups and interviews, as part of a project running since 2020.

Familiarity with the idea was moderate, and support was real but cautious. Deliberate infection made these studies less acceptable to students than ordinary trials or observational research. Those open to joining cited altruism, social value, and national benefit, especially against diseases endemic at home. The context presses hard: the country has no rules for such studies and limited intensive care depth. The authors say local voices, not imported enthusiasm, should set the terms.
plos-pone-0348241:
Hui Wu and co-workers design a decision method for picking drone sensor mixes to watch for landslides and other hazards along highways. Different terrain needs different eyes, and budgets rule out carrying everything. Their 2026 study ranks single sensors by performance at varied flying heights, then scores every pairing for four kinds of highway country, from flat farmland to mountains and city edges.

The best mix shifted with height and terrain in sensible ways. Color plus heat cameras won at low heights in several settings, while laser and radar joined in the mountains and at altitude. A one-size fleet would waste money and miss hazards; matching sensors to place and height sharpens watchfulness for road crews.
plos-pone-0348441:
Li Qi and Lanlan Zhao asked how folk seek help from a bot, set next to help from peers. They mined thirty thousand turns of talk from two stores. One held chats with AI. One held posts from a big help board. Word tools then scored each line for soft words, hedges, and tone.

With the bot, the soft shell fell away. Hedges and please-and-thanks near died out. Nor did folk beg as meek guests. They spoke like a boss who gives clear tasks. The team says bots cut the social cost of the ask. The flip side is less drill in the hard art of state a vague need well.
plos-pone-0349041:
Pierre Chauvin and colleagues confronted a blind spot in French medicine: the country's universalist rules bar collecting race or ethnicity data, which hides who bears the heaviest cancers. At one Paris university hospital, they worked around the ban with an anonymous survey using birthplace. The survey covered seven hundred and eighty women with breast cancer. They paired it with years of fieldwork among African women in the region.

The aggressive triple-negative form of the disease proved at least three times as common in women born in Sub-Saharan Africa as in women born in France. Those women also arrived with more advanced disease. Interviews surfaced reasons: low awareness, different beliefs about causes, shame and secrecy, traditional healing first, and a hard-to-navigate system. The authors call this cancer a telling example of how official blindness can cost health.
plos-pone-0349141:
Amon Exavery and a large team studied whether community support programmes help Tanzanian children living with HIV keep the virus fully suppressed. They followed more than twenty-six thousand orphaned and vulnerable children on treatment between twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-three, each with at least two virus measurements. The programmes combined household economic help, links to teen clubs, and health insurance.

Among children whose virus started undetectable, about one in eight saw it rebound, but those receiving programme support were roughly a quarter less likely to rebound than similar children without it. Among children starting with detectable virus, about seven in ten reached full suppression. The authors credit steady, practical support around families, not medicine alone, with helping children stick to demanding daily treatment.
plos-pone-0349341:
Tim Faverjon, Jean-Philippe Cointet, and Pedro Ramaciotti ran a controlled experiment on how recommendation algorithms quietly learn users' politics. Working from real sharing data for nearly forty thousand users of the platform X, they trained a recommender on synthetic versions of the data where each step could be inspected. Their 2026 study asks whether basic recommendation logic alone manufactures an ideological map of users.

It does: elementary principles trained on what people share arranged users along a left-right line inside the system, independently of age or gender. The team then edited those internal positions and watched the offered content shift in leaning, diversity, and relevance. The authors argue the political geometry is an emergent byproduct of ordinary recommendation, with consequences for segregated information diets.
plos-pone-0349441:
Christina Ruan and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One scoping review of what helps and hinders Americans with sickle cell disease in actually using health care. Despite severe pain and organ damage, many patients seem to be avoiding the system. The reviewers screened hundreds of articles and kept seventy that described barriers, facilitators, or patterns of care use in the United States.

The commonest barriers were social and interpersonal, including strained relations with providers, followed by economic and institutional obstacles. Technology, education, patient autonomy, and trusting provider relationships helped people engage. Individualized pain plans and quality improvement programs reduced avoidance in several studies. The authors call for multi-level interventions and for health systems to rebuild trust with this underserved patient group.
plos-pone-0349641:
Elene Asanidze and co-authors surveyed doctors in Tbilisi, Georgia, about stress, mood, and working life, comparing them with professionals outside medicine. Doctors everywhere face long hours and emotional strain, but Georgian data were scarce. Their 2026 anonymous survey gathered three hundred ninety physicians across specialties plus two hundred forty non-medical workers, using standard screening scales for stress and depression alongside questions on sleep, satisfaction, and outlook.

Physicians reported clearly higher stress and more moderate-to-severe depression than the comparison group in initial analyses. Stress eased as years of experience grew, suggesting younger doctors carry the heaviest load. The team also examined differences by specialty, gender, and experience across well-being measures. They present the findings as a baseline for supporting physician mental health in Georgia, where the topic has been little studied.
plos-pone-0349941:
Yunjie Liu and colleagues created RAGER, a free software platform that analyzes two kinds of gene data together. One kind shows which genes are switched on in a sample, and the other shows which stretches of DNA are open and ready to be used. Studying both at once can reveal how gene control goes wrong, but the tools were hard for non-specialists.

RAGER chains the popular analysis tools into one automated workflow, so a researcher can run the whole job with far less coding. The authors show it working on two published datasets, finding patterns in gene activity and DNA openness together. It runs on the Snakemake system and is shared openly for anyone to download.
plos-pone-0350141:
Xianli Ge and colleagues measured what happened after China tied bulk buying of generic drugs to a quality pass mark. Under the policy, listed generics must prove they match the original drug, and winners gain huge state orders at lower prices. Monthly counts of passed generics were tracked around the 2018 policy start, split by listed and unlisted drugs.

After 2018, passed generics grew by close to three extra drugs per month. Gains showed up both for listed drugs and for drugs outside the lists, which hints at spillover pressure across the industry. An earlier 2016 step showed no clear effect. Linking market access to proof of sameness, the data suggest, moves makers to certify quality.
plos-pone-0350241:
Lu Han and colleagues froze four soft soils in the laboratory to guide a subway dig that must pass beneath a working station in China. The builders plan to freeze the ground solid, excavate inside the ice wall, and let it thaw after, so the frozen soil's strength and heat behavior decide the safety margins. Samples of silty clay, mucky soil, residual soil, and weathered rock were tested from mild frost down to deep cold.

Cold made every soil conduct heat better, most sharply in the weathered rock and least in the mucky soil. Frost heave, thaw settlement, and shear strength under pressure were measured alongside, showing how temperature and squeezing together steer behavior. Numbers like these feed directly into freeze-pipe spacing and timing: freeze too little and the wall leaks, too long and the thaw sinks the street.
plos-pone-0350641:
Abdullah Hasan and colleagues interviewed twenty adults with type two diabetes at a major hospital in northern Jordan about daily self care. Diabetes is common and rising in Jordan, yet daily lived barriers were poorly mapped. Deep interviews covered food culture, faith, feelings, drug routines, and clinic gaps, sorted with careful theme methods and member checks.

Six themes emerged: cultural pressure around food, trouble sticking to drug routines, religious and cultural shaping of habits, emotional burden, gaps in health services, and coping tactics that work. Faith and family can hinder or help, often at once. Care plans that fit Jordanian culture and community life, the authors argue, will beat generic advice.
plos-pone-0350741:
Cintia Ronchi Lemos and seven colleagues gather what is known about the downsides of clear orthodontic aligners, in this 2026 PLOS ONE systematic review. Aligners are popular because they are nearly invisible and removable, but their harms are less advertised than their comfort. The team searched seven databases and grey literature, keeping thirty-four studies that reported side effects.

Pain was the most common complaint, peaking within a day and fading within a week. Roots of moved teeth shortened slightly on average. Reports also covered plaque, white spots on enamel, speech changes, bad breath, and jaw symptoms, though the evidence there was patchier. Patients weighing aligners deserve this fuller picture alongside the cosmetic appeal.
plos-pone-0350841:
Long Zheng and colleagues searched for genes that respond to capsaicin, the hot compound in chillies, in a common form of breast cancer in 2026. Capsaicin can slow these cancer cells, but its downstream targets were murky.

Starting from a public data set of treated cells, the team screened changed genes, mapped their networks, and confirmed two standouts in lab tests. Both genes ran high in breast tumors and linked to metabolic and immune features of the tumor surroundings. Survival data added clinical weight. The pair gives researchers concrete leads for how a food compound perturbs cancer cells.
plos-pone-0350941:
Sijing Wang and colleagues tested a sound based way to spot muscle fatigue while people use a passive leg exoskeleton. Sensors listen to tiny muscle vibrations during repeated squat lifts of a ten kilogram load. Five leg muscles were recorded, and features from timing, tone, and pattern fed learning models judged by leaving one person out at a time.

A voting rule across muscles worked best, sorting tired from fresh states with accuracy above ninety percent and spotting fatigue within about a second and a half. Model scores also tracked how hard people felt the work was. Wearable makers could use such live fatigue reads to tune help and warn before form breaks down.
plos-pone-0351141:
Practicing piano with two hands demands split-second timing, and tired hands lose precision. Xiaoyu Meng and colleagues built a simulated practice gym, PianoGym, that plans rhythm exercises while respecting fatigue limits, in this 2026 PLOS One computer science paper.

The catch is that feedback arrives only after each exercise ends. Their controller watches timing errors and two fatigue signals, then picks the next drill from a set library. A slow safety layer tracks long-run fatigue while a fast guard screens each candidate drill against a fatigue estimate. A planning controller then searches only among drills the guard allows, aiming for safe, steady progress.
plos-pone-0351241:
Begona Tapia-Alzuguren and colleagues looked at why blood levels of sertraline, a common mood drug, vary so much between patients. Genes that break the drug down differ by person, and other drugs can speed or slow those pathways. Records covered seven hospital patients with gene data and sixteen drug level checks in routine care.

Before drug clashes were counted, level patterns matched gene based groups for one pathway best, called CYP2B6 in lab shorthand. After counting other drugs, patterns for that pathway grew clearer, and a second pathway also showed useful links. A third pathway showed no steady link. Even in seven patients, the message is plain: genes alone do not set dose, the full drug list matters.
plos-pone-0351541:
Katrina Himpson, Thomas Le Berre, and Edward Hodges follow rescued sea turtles after release into the Indian Ocean. Their 2026 study fits satellite tags to rehabilitated olive ridley, green, and hawksbill turtles. Tracking of wild turtles is common, but released patients are rarely followed. The team wanted survival, movement, and behaviour after rehabilitation. Comparisons with wild turtles of the same species and life stages anchored the interpretation.

The released turtles did well. They survived for extended periods and behaved like their wild counterparts. Species and age shaped their routes. Monsoon currents pushed hard on open-ocean travellers. Turtles actively swam against drift to hold position, or rode the currents along shelves and ridges. Juveniles and olive ridleys, both scarce in the tracking literature, feature prominently here. The results validate rehabilitation twice over: the animals genuinely return to wild life, and their tags teach science what healthy turtles do.
plos-pone-0351641:
Naufal Nordin, Woi Pui Juan, and Nurul Umira Samsudin tested how well young children join what they see with how their hands move. That joining skill supports writing and class work. About one hundred and fifty children, near ten years old on average, at three city schools in Kuala Lumpur took a standard drawing test and had their pencil grips classed from photos.

Test scores tracked teacher judged mastery in Malay, English, science, and maths, with the strongest links in science and maths. Age adjusted scores kept clear links only for science and maths. Older children tended to score higher on raw marks. Grip type played a smaller role than the joining skill itself, which schools can screen early.
plos-pone-0351741:
Ongoing stomach pain and fullness without visible disease, called functional dyspepsia, may involve quiet immune activity in the small intestine. Imteaz Mahbub, Bimal Chandra Shil, and Sadeed Araf Reza counted allergy-linked white cells in gut lining samples in Dhaka, Bangladesh, for this 2026 PLOS One study.

Forty-six patients with the condition were compared with forty similar people whose stomach checks looked normal. Biopsies came from the same stretch of intestine and cells were counted under a microscope. Counts ran clearly higher in the patients than in the comparison group. The authors link the finding to low-grade immune activation and suggest it may guide future treatment choices.
plos-pone-0351841:
Molino, Martí-Fis, and Rodriguez-López built a method to reconstruct storm rainfall curves from daily records in a 2026 study. City drainage design needs rain intensity for many storm lengths, but tropical towns often keep only daily totals. Eight rain stations near Havana supplied fifteen years of daily data, plus one detailed recorder for fine timing.

Daily totals were split into shorter bursts using the detailed record's patterns, then fitted to standard storm curves for return times up to a thousand years. One regional model merged all stations. Engineers in data-poor regions can thus design drains and culverts with defensible numbers instead of guesses.
plos-pone-0351941:
Some children are born with a doubled drainage tube on one kidney, and both branches can go wrong at once. Huazhang Liu and colleagues report a robot-assisted operation, in PLOS One in 2026, that joins one branch to the other and also rebuilds the bladder connection in a single surgery.

Twelve children treated between 2021 and 2024 were reviewed. Most came in with urine infections; others leaked urine or had belly pain. Surgery took about three hours and hospital stays about five days. Two children had infections afterward that cleared with simple care. At later checks, swelling had shrunk, no leakage or backflow remained, and kidney function had improved.
plos-pone-0352141:
XuYan Liu and colleagues survey in 2026 how nurses who reshape their own jobs may also act in new and inventive ways at work. Their study drew on questionnaires from nurses in large hospitals in southwest China. Statistical modelling tested whether feeling safe in a team and feeling backed by the workplace linked the two.

Reshaping one's job was linked with more inventive behaviour. Both team safety and felt support carried part of that link on their own, and together they formed a chain as well. The authors suggest managers can help by letting nurses adjust their work, building trust inside teams, and making support easier to feel.
plos-pone-0352341:
Rameshwor Parajuli, Wilna Oldewage-Theron, and Surya Niraula reviewed studies on junk snacks and sugary drinks among children and teenagers in Nepal. Diets there are shifting fast, and the country now faces underweight and stunting alongside rising overweight. Their review gathered work from city, fringe, and rural areas to see how snack habits line up with body weight.

Snacking on unhealthy foods was highest in cities and was tied to higher odds of overweight and obesity. Fringe areas sat in the middle, and rural children snacked least, though marketing and easier access are pushing rural intake up. Most children still had normal weight, yet the reviewers warn Nepal faces both problems at once and needs action on each.
plos-pone-0353241:
Surve and colleagues set out a study plan in 2026 for improving how babies and toddlers are fed in a tribal area of India. In Palghar District, many young children grow too slowly, and frontline health workers are the main source of feeding advice for mothers. Gaps in worker knowledge and local barriers still hold back good feeding habits.

Over two years, the team will first measure what workers and mothers know and do, then train workers and counsel mothers, then measure again. About four hundred sixty mother and baby pairs will take part through local child care centers. Readers get a careful plan for testing whether training changes feeding in daily life.
plos-pone-0353841:
Andrew D Meyer led a team of eight authors on this 2026 protocol for a pilot trial of bleeding after children's tonsil surgery. Up to one child in twenty returns to emergency care bleeding, and most are taken back to the operating room. Earlier case reports suggest a mist of tranexamic acid, a clot-protecting drug, might calm the bleeding instead.

Children in the pilot will receive three misted doses of the drug or salt water, and the team will measure feasibility, drug levels, and side effects. The pilot prepares a larger trial of the TEAPOT approach.
plos-pone-0353941:
Niina Mäenpää and five colleagues report what happened when a Finnish hospital adopted a gene test that predicts whether early breast cancer needs chemotherapy, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. One hundred and twenty-nine patients with hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative tumours were tested over two years. The assay reads the tumour's gene activity and estimates both recurrence risk and likely chemotherapy benefit.

Testing changed recommendations for most patients: nearly three quarters were spared chemotherapy they would otherwise have been offered. The hospital saved part of the cost through avoided treatment, and the wider economy saved much more by keeping working-age patients at work. The authors stress that smooth testing routines and clinician training made the difference.
plos-pone-0354141:
Alex Junior Aparecido Silvestrini and three colleagues draw the chromosome map of lentils and their wild cousins with glowing DNA probes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The genus Lens holds the cultivated lentil plus six wild relatives, each with shuffled chromosomes that confuse breeding and genome assembly alike. The team designed short DNA probes from gene order comparisons, painted them onto dividing cells in two colors, and read the patterns chromosome by chromosome.

Each chromosome in six species produced a distinct two color signature, turning identification from guesswork into direct observation. The patterns confirmed that the published genome assemblies had assigned their pieces to the right chromosomes, and they verified the rearrangements that gene comparisons had predicted. Close relatives proved highly similar in sequence despite their structural shuffling. A precise karyotype gives lentil breeders a reliable map for moving traits from wild species into the crop.
plos-pone-0354241:
Sung Pyo Park and four colleagues follow newly diagnosed glaucoma patients in South Korea for ten years, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study of national insurance records. The disease, in its open-angle form, slowly steals vision and is managed mainly with daily eye drops. Nearly sixteen hundred patients diagnosed in 2010 were tracked through a decade of prescriptions and operations.

One class of drops dominated first-year treatment, given alone to about two fifths of patients. Over ten years the average number of drops and active ingredients per patient climbed steadily, as single drugs stopped being enough. About three patients in a hundred eventually needed surgery. The numbers give doctors a realistic script for counselling the newly diagnosed.
plos-pone-0354341:
Alexandra Guttentag and five colleagues measure how well Americans understand the costs of their own healthcare, in this 2026 nationally representative survey of more than two thousand adults. Patients are asked to shop and plan around prices they often cannot see. The twelve-question survey probed knowledge of drug prices, insurance terms, and strategies for planning or disputing costs.

Knowledge was patchy. Most people knew drug prices vary between pharmacies, and over half knew how to contest a hospital bill, but only a third understood hospital chargemasters, the master price lists behind bills. Terms like deductible were easier to explain than formulary. Knowing an emergency visit's cost in advance was the hardest planning task. Adults with stronger cost literacy tended to be older and more confident managing their care. The authors see room for education targeted at bills and insurance.
plos-pone-0354741:
M David Diggs and co-authors run in 2026 a small exploratory study on whether short bursts of hard cycling help teenagers with attention disorder learn new language words. Older teens with no Portuguese took one online lesson, with three half minute sprints placed before the lesson, after it, or not at all. Learning was checked that day and a week later through recall, recognition, and sentence making.

No difference reached statistical strength, yet patterns hinted that exercise before the lesson helped word memory, while exercise after hurt sentence making and recognition. With fewer than thirty participants, the authors stress the pattern is a lead for larger, wider studies, not a firm rule.
plos-pone-0354841:
Cemaliye Karadayı Numan, Yalın Kılıç, and Hülya Şenol published this 2026 survey study of teachers in North Cyprus. Just over three hundred secondary teachers rated their own school's values-centered culture, how fairly the school actually treats staff, and their own willingness to go beyond the job description for the school.

Careful statistical path analysis showed fairness carrying part of the culture effect: value-centered cultures strengthened citizenship behavior partly by making teachers feel justly treated. Numan argues school leaders should build values and fairness together, since each feeds teachers' extra effort.
plos-pone-0355041:
Amanuale Zayede and three colleagues published this 2026 study of cleaners employed by the University of Gondar in northwest Ethiopia. Cleaners work amid dirty waste daily, and they may quietly carry gut bacteria that resist key antibiotics. The team compared stool samples and surveys from hospital janitors and campus janitors who work outside the hospital.

Resistant bacteria turned up often in both groups, with different risk patterns in each. Recent urinary infections mattered for hospital janitors, while older age and buying antibiotics without a prescription mattered for the others. Zayede argues cleaners belong in national resistance monitoring and deserve stronger hygiene training.
plos-pone-0355341:
Michal Ordak, a single author, published this 2026 analysis of how anti-vaccine posts on Facebook misuse numbers. Working with nearly six hundred Polish-language posts, Ordak built a coding scheme of ten kinds of faulty statistical reasoning and checked how often each kind appeared and which kinds traveled together.

Treating correlation as proof of cause was the most common error, followed by ignoring base rates. Certain mistakes paired up in steady patterns, especially skipping denominators alongside gut-feeling reasoning. Ordak argues that health messages should name and correct these specific errors, since vague appeals to trust science do little against a confident but flawed chart.
plos-pone-0355741:
Longxue Wei and seven others take stock of the visible diversity in old maize varieties in this 2026 study. Landraces, varieties shaped by farmers over generations, hold genetic raw material that modern breeding needs, but their traits are seldom measured in a planned way. The team grew one hundred nineteen landraces and scored nine yield and flower-structure traits, applying diversity indices, clustering, and regression techniques to find the patterns and the most telling measures.

Variation was wide on every trait. The team distilled the nine measures to four main components, and a composite score singled out ten top landraces for breeding attention. The collection sorted into three groups with distinct flower shapes, grain traits, and field performance. Four traits, mostly describing the tassel's branching, proved most telling for choosing. The authors offer the framework as an efficient way to mine landrace collections for elite material.
plos-pone-0355841:
Theresa Barberi, Rahila Khuroo, and Alan Friedman report in 2026 on a new line of lab mice. The mice were built to help test immune treatments for human cancers. Those treatments target a growth signal protein found on many tumours. Normal mice reject the human form of that protein. So the team made mice that carry a short human version. Their bodies accept it as their own.

The mice stayed tolerant even after the gene was switched off in adults. They also accepted mouse tumours carrying the same marker. Blood cells carried the marker strongly. Levels were lower in the liver, lung, kidney, and brain. A known antibody still binds the short form. The line offers a safer test bed for such treatments.
plos-pone-0355941:
Miaomiao Li and colleagues set out a plan, published in 2026, for comparing non-drug treatments for cannabis use disorder. No medicine is approved for this condition, so counseling-style therapies and brain-based approaches carry the treatment load, yet they have rarely been compared directly with each other. The planned review aims to rank them in a single framework.

Following their protocol, the team will search major medical databases for randomized trials. They will combine the results in a network meta-analysis, which lets treatments be ranked even when they were never tested head-to-head. They will judge success mainly by verified abstinence and days of use, alongside how many patients stay in treatment and what harms appear. Final results are scheduled for late 2026, and the ranking should help clinics choose treatments on evidence rather than habit.
plos-pone-0356141:
Marie Beermann and colleagues asked whether surgeons can judge a fibroid treatment's success in the operating room. Could ultrasound do the job instead of waiting for an MRI? Their 2026 prospective study treated seventeen women with microwave ablation, a heat procedure for uterine fibroids. Fibroid volume was measured before treatment with both methods. The burned volume was read by ultrasound right after. MRI checks followed within a week and at six months.

Ultrasound and MRI agreed closely on ablated volume, close enough for live guidance. But the sobering secondary finding was regrowth. Nearly half the treated fibroids showed living, blood-fed tissue again by six months. That was despite technically successful ablation. The study supports ultrasound for immediate steering. It also warns that a clean first result does not guarantee a lasting one.
plos-pone-0356241:
Filippo Cendron and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE giving the first look at microRNAs in dolphin milk. These tiny RNA molecules fine-tune gene activity, and milk carries them in quantity in land mammals, but no marine mammal's milk had ever been profiled. The team searched the bottlenose dolphin genome for microRNA families, compared dozens of whale and dolphin genomes, and sequenced the small RNAs in pooled milk samples.

They cataloged several hundred high-confidence microRNA precursors across many conserved families, with a few losses along the dolphin lineage, including nine families missing from all cetaceans. In the milk itself, just four families dominated, accounting for over seventy percent of all microRNA reads, and those same families headline land mammals' milk too. The work is framed as an exploratory first map, suggesting evolution kept milk's regulatory recipe stable as mammals returned to the sea.
plos-pone-0356741:
Muhammad Jawad Asghar and a plant breeding team compare several statistical models for picking lentil varieties that yield well in many places, not just one lucky site. Weather swings make variety performance jump between sites and years, and each stability model sees that jumping differently. The team grew a set of lentil lines across four contrasting environments in blocked plots and scored them with four established approaches.

All models agreed that variety-by-place interaction was real and strong. Older regression sorting, mixed-model prediction, and a combined yield-stability index each highlighted somewhat different winners, with the combined index best at naming broadly reliable lines. Asghar and colleagues advise breeders to consult several models together rather than betting a release decision on any single one.
plos-pone-0357041:
Jooyoung Cheon and Eun Young Choi examined how people in South Korea actually feel in their last month of life. They used family exit interviews from a national aging study. The study covered deaths between 2006 and 2020. Their 2026 analysis included 1,731 adults who died in hospital. It tallied eleven symptoms reported by relatives. It then asked which circumstances predicted each symptom.

The average decedent carried nearly five symptoms. Loss of appetite led, followed by severe fatigue and depression. Each affected more than half. Long illness, dependence on others for daily tasks, and pain in the final year predicted almost every symptom. Yet barely one decedent in twenty had received hospice care. In a country where hospital death is the norm, the authors call the palliative gap critical.
plos-pone-0358241: Vakili and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on software that stages sleep from brain waves. Their system reads a single channel of EEG, the signal of brain activity. It joins multi-scale time encoding with layered sequence learning in one model that stays aware of context. Accurate staging from one channel could make sleep studies cheaper and easier to run at home.
plos-pone-0358341:
Angela Hibbs and three colleagues studied new postgraduate students at a UK university, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Students starting taught postgraduate courses arrive with expectations formed by marketing, prior study, and hope. When reality differs, satisfaction and success can suffer. The team explored those pre-arrival expectations in depth.

Hibbs's study maps what incoming postgraduates expect from teaching, support, and campus life. Universities can compare that map with what they actually provide, and close the worst gaps. The work looks beyond the undergraduate experience, since postgraduates are often older, working, or returning after years away. Honest recruitment and better induction both start from knowing what students think they signed up for.
plos-pone-0358441: Bohorquez Santiago and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper on adding copper to a bone-like coating. The coating is synthetic hydroxyapatite, the mineral that hardens bone, laid down as a thin film. Their method uses a laser method aided by plasma to add the copper. Copper can fight bacteria, so coated implants might resist infection while bone grows onto them.
plos-pone-0358641:
Yusuf Demirtaş and Saime Şahinöz wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about medical education in Türkiye. It studies medical students in their final year in Hatay and Ordu, two provinces marked by disaster in recent years. The topic is disaster preparedness perceptions, how ready the students feel for disasters, and the factors tied to those views.

Doctors are front-line responders after earthquakes and floods, so their felt readiness matters for real response. Comparing two provinces and the factors behind perceptions helps faculties see where training falls short. Medical schools in disaster-prone regions are the audience for evidence about their own students' confidence.
plos-pone-0358741:
Courtney Bir and four colleagues analyze American attitudes toward pandemic rules in a 2026 PLOS ONE article, using survey data from January 2021. COVID-19 controls asked people to give up ordinary freedoms for a shared benefit, and resistance was loud. The authors probed how beliefs about society's duties and personal rights lined up with actually following spread reducing behaviors.

Agreement that healthcare is a human right, that society must protect the elderly, and seat belt wearing all went with a higher likelihood of taking part in protective behaviors. Having someone at high risk in the household also raised participation. Belief that gun ownership is a right pulled the other way, lowering participation across behaviors. The pattern maps a values divide that future public health campaigns will still have to cross.
plos-pone-0358841: Saarela and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on adults in acute hospital care who carry more than one lung infection at once. A multiplex PCR test can name many viruses and bacteria from a single sample. The team used it to find how often such mixed infections occur. Mixed infections can change treatment, since a drug for one germ may miss the other.
plos-pone-0359341:
Meltem Ozagir, Sergen Devran, Orkun Akkoc, Bülent Bayraktar, and Ilker Yucesir wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on exercise training. It studies blood flow restriction training, a method that uses a cuff to partly limit blood flow in a limb during light exercise. The authors test arterial blood flow changes at different compression levels.

The work is a cross-sectional experimental study of a practical version of this training method. Knowing how each cuff pressure changes artery flow helps set safe, effective levels for athletes and patients in rehab. Trainers and physiotherapists need exactly this dose information before using restricted-flow training widely.
plos-pone-0359441: Choukair and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on teens with long-term illness in Germany. As these teens move from child care to adult medicine, the team measured strain from physical and mental symptoms. They also looked at how well each teen's family functions. The study draws out what this means for support during the handover. A rough transition can leave young patients lost between two systems.
plos-pone-0359641:
Yecai Guo, Meiyu Liang, and Tianyue Jiang published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents a speech enhancement method, software that cleans noisy recordings so voices come through clearly. The method integrates a channel attention mechanism of the squeeze-and-excitation kind, which teaches the network which sound channels matter, with an improved CGAN, a generative model.

Cleaner speech helps hearing aids, phone calls, and voice recognition in noisy places. Attention mechanisms let the model focus on speech-like parts of a signal instead of treating all noise alike. Audio engineers and researchers in speech technology are the readers comparing this design against other enhancement methods.
pmc-13194341:
Kristin Riedel is first author on a 2026 rat and human tissue study of how estrogen shapes blood vessel tone. Women's vessels relax more through beta receptors, a class of adrenaline response proteins, than men's. But the role of estrogen receptors in keeping that pattern was unclear. Arteries from rats were tested after blocking estrogen receptors or giving cross-sex hormones.

Blocking estrogen receptors made vessels squeeze harder and relax less, in both large and small arteries. Two beta receptor types also showed about half the gene activity, while a third did not change. Estrogen given to males shifted their vessels toward the female pattern. Testosterone in females did nothing. Human arteries likewise showed higher levels of those receptors in women, suggesting a shared mechanism.
pmc-13195441:
Reham M Hashim leads a 2026 randomized trial on numbing the airway for awake intubation in bariatric surgery patients. Placing a breathing tube while awake is safest when a difficult airway is expected, common in obesity, but patients need good numbing. The trial compared ultrasound-guided airway nerve blocks against topical lidocaine spray, using a video laryngoscope.

Eighty obese patients were split evenly between the two methods, with light sedation for both. The nerve block group had less coughing and gagging, more first-attempt successes, and shorter intubation times. Comfort was better, with lower pain scores and no recall, and heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen dips were fewer. Blocks, the authors conclude, beat spray here.
pmc-13196741:
Yan Jin and colleagues describe a 2026 light-based computer for hard choice problems. Their machine uses tiny pulses of light called Kerr solitons, which circle inside small glass rings. The goal is to solve logic puzzles that grow too large for normal computers.

Each soliton acts like a switch that can settle in one of two states. Links between switches can be set freely through an electronic feedback loop. The team ran more than ten thousand trials on over one hundred random logic puzzles. The machine matched or beat standard software solvers in their tests. It used very little power per pulse and took about a millionth of a second per feedback step.
pmc-13201941:
Plant flavonoids are being refined into cancer drug options, and a 2026 virtual study led by Precious A Akinnusi asks how small chemical changes affect their grip on a breast cancer target. The research article models methylated flavonoids binding to HER2, a receptor that drives an aggressive breast cancer subtype.

Docking scores ranked eupatolitin, rhamnetin, and three other flavonoids as the best forecast binders. Comparing parent compounds with modified versions showed that adding methoxy groups at two specific positions strengthened forecast binding in every case, while changes elsewhere did not help. Simulations backed complex stability, and the authors frame the pattern as a design rule needing lab confirmation.
pmc-13205541:
Cancer immunotherapy can bleach patches of skin, and a 2026 report led by Thomas Breakell presents treating that side effect with a targeted cream. The article presents three patients with melanoma who developed facial vitiligo during or after immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and received topical ruxolitinib.

Repigmentation and quality of life were measured with clinical photographs, a semi-automatic assessment tool, and surveys. The authors report marked facial repigmentation alongside improved quality of life for the treated patients during follow-up. No side effects were observed in this small series, and the team proposes the cream as supportive care for a distressing, visible complication of treatment.
pmc-13209141:
A published study of new intensive care nurses draws constructive criticism in a 2026 letter by Xu Liu. Writing to the editor, Liu and Li Ning comment on a qualitative study of stress coping and resilience in newly licensed ICU nurses. They praise its challenge-adaptation-growth framework before raising methodological points.

The letter notes an apparent contradiction: one section describes a strong trust relationship between researchers and participants as fellow ICU staff, while another states no prior relationships existed. It also asks whether member checking was used, what transcription style was chosen, and flags nurses being called patients once in the results. Future research directions close the letter.
pmc-13212041:
Why adults lose permanent teeth in Baghdad is counted tooth by tooth in a 2026 study by Falah Hasan Jumaah at Mustansiriyah University's dental teaching hospital. The prospective cross-sectional study recorded every extraction in the oral surgery clinics between October 2024 and May 2025, along with each patient's age, sex, and health background.

In total, 1,096 patients lost 1,408 teeth during the study window. Dental caries overwhelmed every other cause, accounting for the vast majority of extractions, while gum disease explained only a small share in this population. Age mattered for gum-disease extractions but not for caries, and patients with systemic disease were less likely to lose teeth to decay.
pmc-13236741:
Ghani and Ferrer develop a quick test for unwanted microbes in wine. Wine is made when yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol, a craft thousands of years old. The wrong microbes spoil that process, so catching them early is crucial for makers who cannot wait days for lab cultures to grow.

Their method joins two tools. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification copies a microbe's DNA at one steady temperature, with no cycling machine. A lateral flow dipstick, like a home test strip, then shows the result by eye. Together they promise fast, cheap checks in the winery itself, so a bad batch can be caught before spoilage takes hold.
pmc-13237141:
Mayer and colleagues test how explaining success and failure shapes what people come to believe about their own new abilities. Healthy people usually credit success to themselves and blame failure on outside forces. People with depression or low self-esteem often reverse that pattern, and learn about themselves in a harsher, biased way.

The study asks whether those habits of explanation actively build new self-beliefs, not just colour old ones. Volunteers formed beliefs about a fresh ability while their attributions were tracked. Showing cause and effect here matters for therapy: if blaming oneself for failure writes new, durable self-doubt, then retraining explanations could protect self-esteem.
pmc-13241441:
Mohd Aji's team in Malaysia modeled whether citrus-born D-limonene can green up shale fracking fluids. Low surface tension between fluid and trapped gas aids yield but standard surfactants pollute. Atom-level modeling tracked methane, water, and limonene across mild and reservoir-like extremes. Free-energy math anchored the tension figures.

Heat slashed surface tension sharply in mild conditions, far less under deep pressure. Pressure itself barely mattered across the tested range. More limonene always lowered tension, though hot squeezed systems needed higher doses. The team frames limonene as a workable, if dose-hungry, green additive.
pmc-13242441:
Nanor Karageozian wrote a conceptual review on how time itself is treated in refugee studies. The article appeared in the Journal of International Humanitarian Action in 2026. Migration research has lately paid more attention to timing, waiting, and speed, but refugee studies has rarely made time its central concept. Karageozian surveys social theory on time and checks how selected refugee research uses, or misses, those ideas.

The review sorts time into timing, sequence, rhythm, speed, duration, and the pull of past, present, and future. Each dimension plays out at personal, community, and policy levels in forced displacement, from asylum waiting rooms to camp routines. Karageozian argues the levels intertwine and should not be studied in isolation. The paper closes by urging balance between movement and stuckness, and between refugee agency and the structures around it. It gives researchers a shared vocabulary for temporality.
pmc-13243441:
Qingdong Yang, Zhongfu Li, and Xinhua Wen built a material that makes light behave as if the material were racing along, though nothing moves. Their paper appeared in Light: Science and Applications in 2026. In a real flowing liquid, light traveling with the flow is delayed differently from light fighting upstream, but the effect is tiny because flows are slow. Their metamaterial, a lattice of metal structures and gyromagnetic parts, engineers the same coupling artificially.

The measured response was enormous: an effective velocity of three-tenths the speed of light, the first demonstration of its kind. The effect is purely one-directional in character, which is exactly what device designers crave. Such non-reciprocity underlies components that pass light one way and block it the other, including gyrators and isolators that work regardless of polarization. The authors present the design rules, rooted in symmetry, that made the giant response possible.
pmc-13244341:
Feng Xu, a hospital pharmacist in China, wrote a personal essay on rediscovering the human side of a job being squeezed by policy and software. The piece appeared in Palliative and Supportive Care in 2026. National bulk purchasing has crashed drug prices so far that colleagues joke pharmacies have become worthless, while mandatory barcode scanning adds clerical load. AI agents now review prescriptions, counsel patients around the clock, and digest research faster than any human.

Against that backdrop Xu traces a personal shift from technical focus toward pharmaceutical humanistic care. The essay argues that what software cannot supply is presence: reading a dying patient's fears, weighing dignity alongside dosage, and staying answerable as a person. Technical excellence remains the floor of the profession, not its ceiling. The piece is a quiet manifesto for pharmacists to defend the relational core of their work.
pmc-13244841:
Vanessa Zwaans and colleagues describe a salvage heart operation for a prosthetic valve infection that had eaten into the aortic root. Their case report appeared in the Journal of Cardiothoracic Surgery in 2026. A seventy-one-year-old man returned eight weeks after an aortic valve replacement with a vegetation and a leaking, partly torn-out prosthesis. A standard risk score put his chance of dying in a redo operation at about one in two.

Surgeons found a ring of infection with an abscess tunneling into the left atrium and destroying its roof. They cut away all infected tissue up to the fibrous skeleton between the valves, rebuilt the sacrificed structures with biological tissue and a custom-made component, and replaced the aortic valve. The modified approach spared his mitral valve, which the standard operation would have sacrificed. He survived. The case argues radical cleaning need not always mean maximal replacement.
pmc-13244941:
Emmanuel Uwambajimana and colleagues examined why babies born too early die in two rural Rwandan hospitals with rates triple the national average. Their retrospective study appeared in Maternal Health, Neonatology and Perinatology in 2026. Records of every preterm baby admitted to the Kiziguro and Ngarama units from 2020 through 2024 were mined for what predicted death.

Roughly a fifth of the preterm deaths clustered at Kiziguro. The strongest predictors were the earliest gestational ages and newborn sepsis, which roughly tripled the odds of death. Infections in the mother, too little kangaroo mother care, and inadequate breathing support also raised risk. Overall mortality ended near national figures once case mix was considered, but the drivers are plainly fixable. The authors prescribe staff training, better infection control, reliable breathing support, and serious promotion of skin-to-skin care. Their message: in these wards, deaths follow resources and routines more than fate.
pmc-13245641:
Widhani and colleagues tested how well three artificial intelligence chatbots answer patient questions about lupus, in this 2026 JMIR Formative Research study. Lupus is a complex, flaring disease, and patients often search online for answers. The team posed twenty-two frequently asked questions, written in Indonesian, to ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

Five clinical immunologists, blinded to which bot wrote what, graded the answers for accuracy, and the researchers also scored readability. Gemini earned the best accuracy marks, though all three bots were judged satisfactory overall and the gaps between them were small. Every bot wrote at a hard reading level, which the authors flag as a real barrier for patients.
pmc-13246941:
Alakmeh, El-Hajj, and Nordquist evaluated a hands-on training course in neck-spine surgery in this 2026 Acta Neurochirurgica study. Cervical spine operations are high-risk, and practicing on cadavers offers a realistic but safe classroom. Twenty-four surgeons and trainees completed a three-day course in Sweden covering front and back approaches to the neck, with supervised practice on anatomical specimens. Answered questionnaires before, after, and six months later.

Every respondent said the course met expectations. Six months on, most participants reported operating more independently, especially in the standard front-of-neck fusion operation and in laminectomy. Participants valued the cadaver practice itself far above any other element. The authors present such courses as a valuable bridge between training and independent operating.
pmc-13247141:
Garvetto and co-authors explored a crop disease after dark in this 2026 Plant Direct study, asking what clubroot does at night. Clubroot, caused by Plasmodiophora brassicae, swells the roots of cabbage-family plants into tumor-like galls, hijacking the plant's metabolism and hormones. Because plant energy and defense run on a day-night clock, the team sequenced gene activity in infected Arabidopsis roots during the night at two infection stages.

Night changes were stronger in younger, mid-stage infections than in late ones. Some disrupted processes appeared only at night, and RNA modification stood out as the most clearly boosted night process. Infection also warped the rhythm of the plant's central circadian clock parts. The authors read this as the pathogen manipulating defense and metabolism around the clock.
pmc-13247641:
Park and Kim report the newest Visible Korean anatomy dataset in this 2026 Journal of Korean Medical Science article. The long-running project freezes cadavers and mills them into serial slices, photographing each surface to build a digital body that can be dissected endlessly on screen. Their 2024 female cadaver dataset, shot with a larger medium-format sensor, was compared slice by slice with the 2023 dataset.

Pixel size shrank from five hundredths of a millimeter to three, nearly tripling pixel density. Fine structures such as brain nuclei, fiber bundles, vessel walls, and facial ligaments became clearly traceable across planes. Real pathology, an enlarged heart, atherosclerosis, and a uterine tumor, showed plainly too. With twelve cadavers now accumulated, the authors claim the images rival physical dissection and suit clinical anatomy research.
pmc-13249541:
Kőmüves and a Hungarian team asked whether body chemistry colors a baby bird's feathers, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Collared flycatcher nestlings grow two wing markings, one dark with melanin and one pale stripe with porphyrin pigment. The researchers measured oxidative stress in nestlings' blood, weighing damaging byproducts against antioxidant defenses, and photographed wing feathers with a spectrometer.

Stress rose as the breeding season wore on and in crowded broods, especially for females. Chicks with the worst balance, high damage and low defense, showed shifted ultraviolet color in their dark feathers, hinting at more of one melanin type. Neither stress measure repeated reliably within nests, suggesting diet and chance shape them strongly.
pmc-13249741:
Kristóf Kádár and co-authors use a lab-grown cell model to study tooth enamel in this 2026 paper. Enamel hardens only if calcium crosses a layer of cells called ameloblasts, but the route calcium takes, and which side of the cell does what, was unclear.

The team grew rat-derived enamel cells as a flat sheet and tested calcium entry from each side. Two entry routes split the work: one worked mainly on the inner side, the other mainly on the outer side. Acid on the inner side reduced calcium entry, while acid on the outer side did not. The setup offers a working model for how enamel matures.
pmc-13250341:
Abdisalam Ismail Hassan led this 2026 case report of a rare surgical emergency. A 23-year-old man arrived with belly pain, vomiting, swelling, and no bowel movements, and he had never had surgery before, which made a blockage unusual.

Scans showed swollen small bowel loops, an inflamed appendix, and twisting deep in the belly. At emergency surgery, the appendix had looped around a bowel segment like a knot, blocking it, and was itself inflamed. Surgeons freed the bowel and removed the appendix, and the man recovered fully. The authors urge doctors to suspect this rare knot in young patients with unexplained blockage.
pmc-13250641:
Wu and co-authors map how baicalein, a plant flavonoid, acts inside non-small cell lung cancer. Their 2026 Translational Oncology study combines single-cell sequencing, tissue-location mapping, bulk gene data, and machine learning. Lung cancer of this type remains a leading cause of cancer death, and baicalein's exact targets were unclear.

Single-cell data resolved twenty-one cell populations in tumors and pointed to a core set of baicalein-linked genes. Machine learning narrowed the signal to a ten-gene signature that separated tumor from normal tissue with high accuracy. All ten genes ran higher in tumor areas on tissue maps, and docking tests suggested baicalein binds several of their proteins tightly. In dish tests, the compound slowed cancer cell growth in a dose-dependent way.
pmc-13251341:
Antonio Gallardo-Pizarro and colleagues track infections after CAR T-cell therapy in this 2026 study. The treatment retools a patient's own immune cells to fight cancer, but its two big side effects, a fever storm and brain toxicity, are treated with immune-damping drugs that invite infection.

Among 152 treatments from 2020 to 2023, about three in four brought on those side effects. Infections were proven in about a quarter of those episodes, split between bacterial, viral, and fungal kinds. Risk climbed steeply when several damping drugs were combined. Fever and a common inflammation marker proved unreliable at spotting infection, so the team urges sharper early checks.
pmc-13252741:
Arshad Khanani and colleagues report the COOL-2 trial in this 2026 eye study. Injections into the eye are the most common office procedure for retina specialists, yet numbing them usually means a numbing injection of its own, so the team tested freezing instead.

Eighty patients who needed repeated injections were assigned to four cooling settings, mixing two temperatures with different contact times. The winning setting, the colder temperature held for ten seconds, gave the lowest pain scores, clearly beating a fifteen-second hold. Pain also eased slightly with each visit. A mild, short-lived surface scratching appeared in about a third of eyes at one setting. The authors call cooling workable, with care.
pmc-13252841:
Maria Londono-Mendez and colleagues compare efficient and inefficient grazing heifers across seasons in this 2026 animal study from western Canada. Feed efficiency measured indoors may not hold on pasture, where summer heat and deep winter cold stress cattle differently.

Forty-one heifers were classed by how much feed they needed for their growth, then tracked on pasture from about 14 months of age. Rumen temperature was logged every ten minutes, and blood samples were taken every few weeks. Efficient heifers showed calmer stress and inflammation markers in summer, while inefficient ones carried more of a fat hormone in winter. Growth itself did not differ between groups in either season.
pmc-13253941:
Yosri Fahim, Ibrahim Hasani, and Samer Kabba review tiny particles in cancer care in a 2026 paper. Standard cancer drugs often harm healthy tissue and face resistance. Nanoparticles, extremely small carriers, can deliver drugs to tumors, release them on cue, and combine diagnosis with treatment in one platform.

The review covers how particles are made, measured, and aimed at tumors, plus many carrier types from fat-based to metal. Some products, like Doxil and Abraxane, already help patients. Yet uneven tumor uptake, long-term safety, and factory and approval hurdles keep many designs from clinics, the authors warn.
pmc-13254741:
Aziz Lamghari and colleagues report tuberculosis found through a scrotal abscess in a 2026 case report. A 36-year-old man had two months of growing left scrotal pain with fever. Drainage and standard antibiotics did not help, so a second operation cleaned the area again.

Tests on the pus found acid-fast bacilli, and culture and PCR confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Tissue samples showed granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis, the cheese-like dead tissue typical of TB. The infection sat in the epididymis, a sperm duct. The authors urge TB testing for chronic scrotal abscess in endemic regions.
pmc-13255941:
Arifa Zahir and co-authors screen for Parkinson disease from voice recordings in a 2026 diagnostic study. Parkinson often weakens the voice early, making speech a cheap screening signal. The team recorded 203 people, 121 with Parkinson and 82 healthy controls, and fed three kinds of sound spectrograms into parallel neural networks.

The three-view model reached a mean accuracy of about eighty-seven percent. Adding a feature based on how well speech recognition software agreed with the recordings lifted accuracy to about ninety-seven percent and cut missed cases sharply. The authors say the method suits structured screening settings, while wider real-world testing is still needed.
pmc-13256541:
İnce-Palamutoğlu, Palamutoğlu, and Baş tested how three yogurt styles weather a mock digestive tract. Yogurts made with probiotic starter cultures, standard cultures, or a probiotic sachet stirred in were run through a dynamic in vitro system copying mouth, stomach, and small gut. Nanopore gene reads tracked which microbes survived each phase.

The sachet yogurts started with richer, more even communities than either starter yogurt. Digestion squeezed every sample toward a core ruled by Firmicutes, yet the sachet yogurts' post-digestion mix stayed clearly distinct from the others. The authors conclude sachet use yields a hardier, more diverse product that better withstands digestive stress.
pmc-13260541:
Humaira Yasmin and co-authors present a 2026 numerical study of heat transfer in a special fluid flowing between two rotating disks. The fluid is a Casson hybrid nanofluid, a liquid with non-standard flow behavior carrying two kinds of nanoparticles, moving through a porous material of varying resistance. The model includes electrical Joule heating, friction heating, and time-varying heat generation and absorption. Equations were solved with a semi-analytic method and checked against standard numerical solutions.

Velocity and temperature profiles shifted in clear patterns as parameters changed. Axial velocity rose with the lower disk's stretching parameter, Reynolds number, and suction, but fell as the upper disk stretched more. Temperature profiles rose with the Eckert number, heat source parameter, and suction. The two solution methods agreed closely, with percentage errors near zero. The authors link the results to cooling rotating surfaces, reactor design, and filtration.
pmc-13260941:
Rosa Lisset Salazar Herrán leads a 2026 study of postpartum depression in mothers in a kangaroo mother care program in southern Colombia. Kangaroo care involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact for fragile newborns, and mothers in such programs face added emotional demands. The study surveyed 140 mothers using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and a structured survey covering social, obstetric, and mood factors, to find the rate of depression and its linked factors.

The rate of postpartum depression was 23.5 percent of the mothers surveyed. No clear differences appeared across social factors. Higher rates were linked to vaginal delivery, previous live births, having three or more children, domestic abuse during pregnancy, and lacking support for infant care. A mother's irritation at infant crying was the strongest signal, with an odds ratio of 3.64, the strongest link found. Family support during infant care protected mothers, with an odds ratio of 0.19 for those mothers.
pmc-13261041:
Yoshiyasu Aizawa and Takumi Matsumoto present a 2026 case report of persistent ST-segment elevation mimicking a heart attack. ST elevation on an electrocardiogram usually signals acute myocardial infarction and prompts urgent invasive checks. Their patient was a 95-year-old woman admitted with COVID-19-associated pneumonia and aspiration pneumonia. Her admission tracing showed ST elevation with T-wave inversion in the lateral chest leads, a pattern that looks like an ST-elevation heart attack.

She had no chest pain, no rise in cardiac biomarkers, and normal heart pumping function without regional wall motion problems. Record review showed the same tracing pattern had been present consistently for more than a decade. The authors attribute it to chronic localized heart muscle remodeling, possibly from unrecognized scarring not visible on routine imaging. The case stresses integrating symptoms, biomarkers, and old tracings before assuming a blocked artery.
pmc-13262641:
Pushpam Kumar argues in a 2026 commentary that putting a money value on drug resistance can drive action. Antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to drugs, harms human and animal health together, the focus of the One Health approach. Kumar says clear cost figures remove haze from policy choices and make the case for spending on control.

The piece cites projections of up to one trillion dollars a year in extra health costs by 2050 if resistance grows unchecked. It also cites a global plan costed at about 46 billion dollars a year, with an estimated return of seven to thirteen dollars per dollar spent by 2050. Many side costs, such as harm to animal health and farming, were left out of those sums.
pmc-13262841:
Alfonso C Hernandez-Romieu leads a comparison of two disease watch systems in Puerto Rico in a 2026 journal article. A sentinel system tests patients systematically at set sites, while the island-wide passive system relies on routine reports. The team compared trends for dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and COVID-19 from 2012 to 2023, checking whether the sentinel system matched and led the larger one.

Sentinel trends matched island-wide trends for every disease studied. The sentinel system reported rises up to three weeks earlier for epidemic dengue, eight weeks for Zika, and two weeks for early COVID-19. Chikungunya rises appeared at about the same time in both systems. Agreement was weaker for dengue outside epidemics. The authors back sentinel systems as early warning tools.
pmc-13263641:
Lilian Marques de Freitas and co-authors report a 2026 journal article mapping drug-processing gene variants in Indigenous peoples of the Brazilian Amazon. The CYP gene family makes enzymes that break down most medicines, so variants change how people respond to drugs. These populations are rarely included in genetic studies. The team sequenced the protein-coding DNA of 64 people from twelve ethnic groups.

They found 506 variants across 63 CYP genes. Most were predicted to modify protein function mildly, but 21 had high predicted impact. Eleven variants appear entirely new, absent from public databases. Their distribution differed from global reference populations. The authors offer the data as a foundation for fairer, better-matched precision medicine in the region.
pmc-13263941:
Samy A. Azer and co-authors argue in a 2026 editorial that research philosophy decides whether a study on AI in medical education is sound. They note that papers are most often rejected for design problems: mismatched aims, methods, and conclusions, weak questions, and unvalidated tools. In their experience, these flaws usually trace back to an unexamined research stance.

They urge authors to spell out their assumptions about reality, knowledge, method, and values. Authors should also name their paradigm, be it positivism, interpretivism, critical theory, or pragmatism, in the methods or an appendix. Doing so, they argue, improves a study's logic, transparency, and chances of surviving peer review, especially in fast-moving fields like AI in health education.
pmc-13264441:
Zhi-Ping Zhang wrote a 2026 case report on a burst blood vessel swelling that was first read as a harmless cyst. The vessel was the splenic artery, which feeds the spleen, and its rupture can kill if missed. A plain CT scan, done without dye, caused the error.

The patient was a 49-year-old man with high blood pressure and sudden pain in the upper left belly. The first scan suggested a pancreatic cyst, a fluid sac near the pancreas. He then collapsed as blood leaked in two stages. A dye scan showed the burst swelling, over five centimetres wide. Emergency surgery removed his spleen and saved him. Zhang urges a low bar for dye scans in such pain.
pmc-13264541:
Gretchen Holtgrefe and Patricia A Wight published a 2026 study using optical genome mapping, a way to picture long DNA stretches, on a new mutant mouse line. The mice carry a reporter gene tied to a brain myelin gene. Mutant mice were small, with odd paws and faces, and every carrier showed the traits.

The mapping showed the added gene sat where chromosomes 1 and 2 had swapped parts in an uneven trade. Chunks of DNA were lost from both chromosomes, removing dozens of genes in all. Exact break points were confirmed by targeted sequencing. The authors note the lost region matches a human condition, 1q24 deletion syndrome, so the mice may model it in future work.
pmc-13264641:
Shritesh Bhoyar and Anil Pethe wrote a 2026 review of nanotechnology creams and devices for psoriasis, a long-term immune skin disease that affects more than 40 million people. Normal creams cross the thickened skin poorly, and strong body-wide drugs carry cost and safety limits. Tiny carriers promise better entry and slower release.

The review covers lipid carriers, polymer systems, microneedles, nanoemulsions, nanosponges, and nanofibers. Studies report better skin scores, more drug kept in the skin, and good tolerance for nano forms of three common drugs. Yet hurdles remain: making batches the same each time, scaling up production, meeting quality rules, and cost. The authors map what must be solved before these products reach wide clinical and market use.
pmc-13267041:
TingLan Ma and colleagues report a 2026 survey study on mistreatment of doctors in training. Mistreatment in residency is linked to burnout and people leaving medicine. The team surveyed trainees at three large United States teaching sites, asking about program openness, belonging, mistreatment, burnout, and support.

Of 675 eligible trainees, 266 replied. Both an open program climate and a personal sense of belonging guarded against reported mistreatment. Mistreatment was strongly tied to burnout, while belonging was tied to lower burnout even after support was counted. Openness helped most for trainees who felt they belonged least. The authors urge programs to build both openness and belonging as core supports.
pmc-13268141:
Louisa-Jane Burton and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for studying hospital green spaces in stroke recovery. Hospital stays after stroke are a key recovery window, yet patients often stay inactive and low in mood. Gardens and green areas might offer activity, company, and a lift, but their role after stroke is little studied. The planned study covers three hospital sites with different kinds of green space.

Data will mix site documents and maps, ten days of watching how spaces are used in two seasons, and interviews. About 45 patients and visitors and 30 staff will share their experiences. Stroke survivors and carers in three other places will help refine the resulting theory. The protocol paper sets out the plan; findings will follow. The team aims at practical design advice for stroke units.
pmc-13268641:
Jasper Garay and colleagues publish a 2026 plan for co-designing a virtual reality wellbeing app with an Aboriginal community in Sydney. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples face deep wellbeing gaps rooted in colonization. Their own frameworks center culture as a source of strength and healing. The study partners with an Aboriginal community-run group and Aboriginal-led creative studios.

The three-phase plan uses Indigenous research methods and community action research. About 35 staff and community members per phase will join yarning circles, a group talk method grounded in culture. The last phase adds a survey on cultural fit, acceptability, and feasibility. The finished app will run inside the partner's existing community programs. The authors hope it widens access to wellbeing support that fits the culture it serves.
pmc-13269841:
Shengsheng Liu, Yuanyuan Zhang, Xiaogui Zhao, and Bangtao Yao published a case report in 2026 about eye disease from syphilis in a patient also living with HIV. Syphilis is rising worldwide, yet this pairing of eye conditions is extremely uncommon. One eye showed a rare placoid inflammation of the retina, while the other showed optic nerve disease.

Eye syphilis can be the first sign of the infection, and the retinal condition can lead to blindness if missed. The authors report that their treatment protocol brought complete resolution of both eye problems. They advise screening for sexually transmitted infections when such eye disease appears. The case is presented as a guide for spotting and treating this rare combination.
pmc-13269941:
John Cowgill and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on the structure of a human brain receptor that calms nerve activity. This receptor, built from alpha5 and beta3 parts, sits in the hippocampus, a memory center, and is a target of anesthetics and seizure drugs. Its exact assembly and opening steps were poorly understood.

Using frozen microscope imaging and electrical recordings, the team found most receptors assemble with two alpha and three beta parts. A minority used one alpha and four beta parts. In the resting state, a gate and a zinc lock blocked ion flow. When the natural signal bound, the lock released and the gate opened. Two drugs bound without changing the open shape.
pmc-13271141:
Tien Zubaidah wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a study mapping the symptom and needs journey of cervical cancer patients around the time of surgery. That study followed patients over time with interviews, moving beyond clinical measures to their fears, struggles, and hopes at a vulnerable stage of care.

First, the study justifies its 14 participants by claiming information saturation, but never states when saturation was reached or how it was judged. Second, using Maslow's hierarchy of needs may force linked themes, such as shame, lost self-worth, and wanting yet drowning in information, into a strict order. Other frameworks centred on relationships and meaning might fit better.
pmc-13271241:
Arindam Debbarma and Bryan E. Dowd wrote a 2026 review of dynamic copay health plans, a new design in United States employer insurance. In these plans, the fixed amount a patient pays varies by provider and service. It is shown before care, often in an app. It uses price data that new transparency rules and artificial intelligence tools make available.

Using UnitedHealthcare's Surest plan as an example, the authors trace plan design from broad networks to narrow, tiered networks and reference pricing. They weigh likely gains in predicting out-of-pocket costs against limits: low insurance literacy, little truly shoppable care, and steering effects that fade. They propose layering dynamic copays onto reference pricing and tiered networks.
pmc-13271441:
Natsuhiro Takahashi is lead author of a 2026 journal article on how high gravity affects osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. Bone loss in astronauts shows the skeleton senses gravity changes, and stronger-than-normal gravity, made with a centrifuge, offers a way to test how bone-eating cells respond to mechanical force.
