Baby-Friendly hospital programs start breastfeeding well, but gains fade without community backing. Türkiye layered on family medicine and neonatal intensive care versions, then Baby-Friendly and Golden Baby-Friendly Province programs spanning pregnancy through infancy.

Activities sort into six themes, from one-to-one help for vulnerable mothers to sports-based outreach and public visual messaging. National and world breastfeeding weeks act as yearly campaign surges inside the year-round system. The authors describe provinces shifting from facility teaching toward community ownership and multisector teamwork. They present the model as transferable experience for other countries trying to sustain breastfeeding beyond discharge day.
pmc-13292541:
Franck Yvan Deugoue Djientcheu and co-authors record a 2026 comparison of heart rate variability in Cameroonian handball players, asking what training and gender each do to cardiac autonomic control. Sedentary men, male players, and female players each rested through ten-minute heart recordings. Standard variability measures such as SDNN, RMSSD, and pNN50 were computed alongside frequency-domain powers.

Male players unexpectedly showed higher resting heart rates than the women, 68.75 against 60.38 beats in the reported averages. Sedentary men scored far below male players on every time-domain measure, tying practice to richer variability. Between the sexes, very-low-frequency power ran higher in men, while low- and high-frequency components ran higher in women. Effect sizes for gender were small, and the authors decline a firm verdict on how gender steers the sympathetic-parasympathetic balance.
pmc-13292641:
Pavel Morozov and a large team shine a 2026 exotic light on lipofuscin, the pigment granules whose glow doctors use to judge retinal aging and macular degeneration risk. Standard glow readings have limited bite in the clinic, so the team built a lifetime imaging scope around a nanowire photon detector sensitive far beyond normal sensors. Pigment clumps from 100 human donor eyes, aged 50 to 75, were imaged before and after lab photo-oxidation.

The setup resolved decay components and spectra at each spot across 500 to 1,000 nanometers. Oxidation shifted the emission toward blue, mimicking disease-like change. Fitting a three-exponential model showed the mean fluorescence lifetime rose significantly after oxidation. The authors argue these lifetime signatures read out the pigment's oxidative state directly, opening a route to earlier, sharper diagnosis of retinal disease.
pmc-13292841:
Koki Kawada and colleagues examine pain after knee surgery in a 2026 study of torn meniscus roots. The operation studied pulls the torn medial meniscus root back into place, and the team asked which pre-surgery traits predict lasting pain.

Records covered 508 knees, mostly in women, with an average age the authors report near the mid-sixties. Pain scores were taken before surgery and at final follow-up, plus X-ray and scan measures. Greater outward shift of the meniscus before surgery linked to worse pain later, even after other factors were counted. No patient in follow-up needed bone realignment or joint replacement surgery.
pmc-13292941:
Linnea Ögren and colleagues present, in 2026, a light-based method to map where proteins sit on DNA inside living yeast cells. Finding those bound sites in untouched cells is hard, since most tools favor open DNA regions or need cell breakage.

Ultraviolet light marks bound spots by forming small DNA lesions, which later read as changes during sequencing, a method the team calls Deam-seq. Comparing treated cells with naked DNA gave sharp maps that matched known control sites and older footprint tests. Bound proteins mostly shielded DNA from light harm. The work offers a genome-wide way to study gene control in its natural setting.
pmc-13293441:
Yousif M. Elmosaad leads a 2026 survey in Al Ahsa, Saudi Arabia, on how stigma around mental illness affects whether people seek help. Most people with mental illness get no treatment, and shame is a major reason care is delayed or avoided.

A total of 1085 adults aged 18 and older answered a structured questionnaire on stigma and help-seeking. Stigma was present in 23.1% of respondents, a share the authors report, and 61.0% said stigma might stop them seeking help. People with stigma were clearly more likely to avoid help. Adults aged 30 to 41 were more willing to seek help than other age groups.
pmc-13293641:
Tomohiro Baba reports a 2026 surgical case of suspected Kounis syndrome, an allergic heart event, during lung surgery after a platelet transfusion. A 70-year-old man with low platelets from liver disease had keyhole surgery to remove his right lower lung lobe.

Three minutes after the platelet transfusion ended, his heart raced, blood pressure fell, and his face and arms flushed. Standard pressure drugs failed, so allergy drugs and adrenaline were given for suspected anaphylaxis. Heart tracings showed strain signs from the start of the collapse, yet heart damage markers stayed normal. He stabilized on adrenaline, surgery finished, and tracing changes cleared by the next day.
pmc-13293941:
Giulia Sapuppo and colleagues study survival by disease site in a 2026 retrospective series of radioiodine-refractory thyroid cancer. Such advanced cancers resist standard iodine treatment and often need kinase inhibitor drugs. The team reviewed 43 treated patients and split them by whether spread at drug start was mainly in neck structures or mainly distant.

Median age at diagnosis was 63.3 years, and just over half were women. Papillary tumors were most common. Counter to simple expectation, patients whose disease centered in the neck fared worse on disease-specific survival than those with distant spread. Site alone may therefore help forecast outcome and guide intensity of care.
pmc-13294141:
Songlin Sun and coauthors propose a 2026 scheme of spatial immune types for stomach and colon cancers. Checkpoint drugs change care mainly for the small MSI-H group. Most MSS tumors resist from the start. Cell counts miss the layout, so the authors sort tumors by how cell groups are placed.

Four types are named. One is a stromal wall that shuts immune cells out. One is a myeloid zone that calms attack by fuel use. One is an inflamed zone with mature lymph hubs. One is a thin watch zone at the tumor edge, lost as tumors evolve. Gut germs differ by organ and tilt the mix.
pmc-13294241: Pablo Lastra-Prados and coauthors issued a 2026 correction notice for their study of decay in teeth next to implant-supported prostheses. Only author details were wrong: one coauthor name had been printed with a doubled segment, and the university affiliation for four authors named the wrong institution. The notice gives the corrected name and affiliation and offers an apology. No data, methods, or findings change, and the authors state that the scientific conclusions stand. The original article has been updated to match.
pmc-13294341:
Alon Korngreen argues for reference-grade neuron models in a 2026 perspective. Detailed computer neurons now guide brain research, yet squeezing varied biology and measurement error into one parameter set hides which claims data truly support. Korngreen borrows habits from analytical chemistry: traceable standards, explicit uncertainty budgets, and ensemble forecasts instead of single answers.

Big reconstructions from projects like Blue Brain and Allen Institute efforts show both promise and risk, since scale alone can look like proof. Voltage recordings reduced to one best fit lose the spread that honest models should carry forward. A reference culture would label modeling choices plainly and keep circuit claims tied to evidence.
pmc-13294441:
Taner Dandinoğlu writes a 2026 letter about missed bone harm in a tough prolactinoma case report by Konindala and coauthors. The original case showed a large prolactin tumor resisting hormone drugs and repeated local plus body-wide treatments, ending with full pituitary failure on replacement therapy. Bone checks were never mentioned, and the letter argues that gap matters, above all in men.

High prolactin, low sex hormones, and long pituitary disruption all thin bone quietly. Older men start with weaker skeletons, so fractures of spine or hip can steal independence. Density scans and fracture history should join routine care for such patients, the letter urges.
pmc-13295141:
Vlad Alexandru Ionescu and colleagues untangle confusion in an older man in a 2026 case report. The 67-year-old, a long-term heavy drinker, arrived after a week of confused thinking. Many rival explanations were possible, from liver failure to stroke, kidney damage, or alcohol effects.

Blood tests showed severe excess calcium, kidney injury, mild anaemia, and raised protein, while ammonia stayed normal and brain scans found no stroke. Protein studies revealed a single abnormal antibody type pointing to multiple myeloma, a bone marrow cancer. Fluids plus steroid treatment cleared his thinking quickly, confirming high calcium as the driver and showing how a hidden cancer can first appear as confusion.
pmc-13295941:
Francesco Ferrara and colleagues trace, in 2026, the rise and fall of antibody treatments for COVID-19. Early products given outside hospital cut admissions during earlier waves, while other antibodies calmed severe inflammation in admitted patients.

Once the Omicron variant spread, many spike-targeting antibodies lost their grip as the virus changed, and their use was curtailed. Newer versions aimed at steadier targets also struggled against continued drift, though host-directed antibodies kept working since they ignore the spike. The authors favour broadly acting antibodies, smarter delivery and live virus tracking for future outbreaks.
pmc-13296041:
Richard M Jacques and a large consortium analyse, in 2026, emergency care demand across 21 English hospitals using routine NHS data. Same-day ambulatory care can treat many urgent conditions without admission, but its share of the workload had not been mapped.

Over one year, such conditions made up nearly a third of emergency attendances and two-fifths of emergency admissions, with wide gaps between hospitals. Older patients were more likely to present with these conditions, while deprived areas showed lower rates. Half of these admissions lasted under two days. The authors say much demand could shift to same-day or community care.
pmc-13296241:
Qian Li and colleagues study, in 2026, whether blood mineral balance predicts dangerous clots after childbirth in a Chinese cohort of 25,792 women. They follow clot events in the six weeks after delivery and relate them to calcium, potassium and magnesium measured around birth.

A low calcium-to-potassium ratio stood out as an independent risk marker, with risk climbing below a clear threshold. Part of the link ran through lower haemoglobin and higher clot-breakdown markers. Magnesium showed a curved pattern, safest in the middle. The authors suggest watching mineral balance and anaemia could help cut clot burden after birth.
pmc-13296541:
Simone Carvalho dos Santos Cunha and co-authors review, in 2026, forty dogs treated with radiation for malignant nose tumours at a Brazilian clinic. Surgery is rarely possible for these cancers, which cause bleeding, discharge and facial swelling, so radiation is the main option.

Most dogs arrived with advanced disease. Tumours shrank or held steady in most cases and symptoms eased for most dogs, while side effects hit skin, mouth lining and eyes but stayed manageable. Dogs with later-stage tumours lived shorter lives. The authors say radiation brings real benefit and back earlier diagnosis.
pmc-13297341:
Rosanna Squitti and co-authors study, in 2026, copper-zinc imbalance in bowel cancer, focusing on the loose, active fraction of copper rather than the total. Blood metals, sex hormones and tumour proteins were measured in 152 patients and 140 healthy controls, split by sex.

Patients carried more copper, less zinc and a sharply higher active-copper ratio. That ratio tracked with tumour size and stage, more with size in women and spread in men, and with tissue shifts marking cells loosening their epithelial character. The authors propose the ratio as an informative marker needing validation.
pmc-13297841:
MoonHyeok Choi and his team put a fat-blocking drug to work for joint pain in a 2026 chart review. The drug cuts how the gut takes in fat; past work found it may also cool joint swelling in model studies. From Korean big-data stores, the team pulled 935 patients. All had sore joints from uric acid and had been put on the drug for six months or more.

On any day they took the drug, part of their uric acid was gone from the blood in one clean sweep. Flare-ups of joint pain grew less common. The drug's known belly side effects showed up, but they were mild and could be borne. No new health worry came to light. The team read the find as a case for tests that pit the drug head-on with care as usual.
pmc-13298341:
Thousands of BRCA1 changes sit in limbo as variants of uncertain significance, and Gabriella C Torretto with colleagues built a domain-specific way to judge them in a 2026 study. Uncertain variants cluster in the gene's RING and BRCT regions, and they stall decisions about screening and prevention for carriers.

The team trained a computational classifier just for the BRCT domain, then checked twenty-two variants spanning its score range with laboratory functional assays and structural modeling. The combined evidence supported sorting these variants toward harmful or harmless. The authors argue that tailoring prediction tools to individual protein domains beats one-size-fits-all scoring for interpreting missense changes.
pmc-13302141:
A mother's microbes shift with pregnancy, and when they slip out of balance, trouble can follow, Lucia Maria Procopciuc and colleagues review in a 2026 survey of the maternal microbiome. Vaginal, gut, and oral communities each change across the trimesters, answering hormones, metabolism, and immune tuning. Lactobacillus dominance in the vagina stands as the healthy benchmark in their account.

Vaginal imbalance is tied to womb infection and early birth, gut shifts to gestational diabetes and preeclampsia, and mouth disease to harm through body-wide inflammation. Whether the placenta hosts its own microbiome stays contested. The authors look ahead to microbe-based tests and treatments for mother and baby, built on firmer mechanism work.
pmc-13302241:
Pain sits between general anxiety and fear of the dentist, Edanur Maraş and colleagues suggest in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Two hundred fifty-three adults awaiting root canal treatment completed dental anxiety and fear scales plus state and trait anxiety inventories, and rated their current pain. Mediation analysis tested whether pain carries part of the anxiety effect.

Every psychological measure correlated with the others. The pattern fit a partial mediating role for preoperative pain: anxious temperaments fed dental anxiety partly through the pain already felt. Patients needing work on front teeth, whether first treatment or retreatment, arrived more anxious than those with back-tooth problems. Bigger, adjusted studies should test the pathway, the authors say.
pmc-13304341:
Sonja Dakić leads a 2026 study of gene variants and bleeding risk in heart patients on ticagrelor plus aspirin. The drug pairing prevents clots after heart attacks but raises bleeding, and inherited differences in drug breakdown may add risk.

A total of 105 Serbian patients treated after artery procedures or medically were genotyped for three variants and followed for six months. About one patient in eight bled, mostly minor events. Age of 75 years or more and weak kidney function predicted bleeding far more strongly than any gene variant tested. Gene effects stayed mixed and weak in adjusted models.
pmc-13306341:
Pedro Augusto Vieira de Freitas extracted cellulose from rice straw with greener steps in a 2026 study. Hot pressurised water and peroxide bleaching replaced harsher chemical routes to isolate fibres from this abundant farm waste.

Fibres reached 86% purity and 67% crystallinity in reported checks before acid cutting turned them into microcrystalline cellulose. Fast high-shear mixing at 12,000 rpm sped breakdown, shrank particles to about 10 µm and lifted crystallinity to 70 to 72 percent in the trials. Added to biodegradable PHBV films, the product was tested as a reinforcing filler. The filler was then checked for strength gain inside the printed film.
pmc-13306441:
Francesca Di Rocco summed up review work on athlete life paths and mental health in a 2026 big review. Five data banks were searched for 2015 to 2025, and 52 papers met the rules for the final set.

Health of mind came out as a mix of signs, sport strain, self view and wider life facts across a sport life. Risk ran high at harm, drop from teams and end of sport, while school plus sport and firm plans gave guard. Shame and thin help still block care, and the team backs web based help as one fix.
pmc-13307341:
Muhammad Sadam Zeb and colleagues present a 2026 case report and literature review on systemic mastocytosis that showed up only as a large liver and spleen, with no skin signs at all. Their patient, a man aged 50 years, had weakness, tiredness, and a swollen belly that grew over months.

Tests showed a very high white cell count and low red cells, and early marrow findings pointed toward chronic myeloid leukemia. That idea fell away when gene tests were normal and a KIT change known as D816V was found instead. Care with cladribine and then hydroxyurea brought clear gains within eight weeks.
pmc-13307441:
Xianghong Liu, Yang Peng, and Jing Zhu track in 2026 how checks before marriage and folic acid use link to neural tube defects in Guangxi, China, from 2009 to 2023. A free check up policy began in 2010, a year after a national folic acid plan started across the country.

Rates of checks, supplement use, steady use, and public knowledge all rose over the period, while defect rates fell in a clear trend. Higher check rates and higher supplement rates each tracked with fewer defects in their models. The authors urge lasting support for both steps, and they offer the Guangxi mix of services as a model for other regions.
pmc-13307541:
Elizaveta Kozlova and co-authors unveil in 2026 a new handheld tool that gauges how fast a plant leaf takes in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. Most lab gas analysers cost a lot, weigh a lot, and need steady air flow, which limits wide field use for stress checks.

Their tool instead traps air near the leaf and tracks gas change with simple infrared sensors, with no moving parts at all. Side by side tests with a shop bought analyser, under both watered and dry soil, gave readings that matched well. Small size and low cost suit the tool for broad crop screening and quick stress checks in farms and field research.
pmc-13309741:
Yamen Barakat and co-authors study sound-wave pretreatment for spray-dried infant food powder in a 2026 article. The test food mixed cereal and milk for babies and toddlers, and its sugar-rich feed sticks badly during drying, cutting powder yield. Sound waves shake the liquid feed and may loosen it before drying.

Pretreatment length, dryer heat, and feed rate were varied in a full grid design. Sound treatment thinned the feed and improved spraying, lifting powder recovery from about 12 percent to over 30 percent across the tested runs. Powder also dissolved better, and fat stayed better wrapped inside particles. The authors name settings that gave fine, free-flowing powder with proteins preserved.
pmc-13310641:
Ali Ibrahim and co-authors report blood infection by a rare cholera relative in a 2026 case article. Vibrio albensis sits in the non-epidemic cholera group and almost never infects humans, so its behavior and treatment rest on scattered reports. Repeated fever as the leading pattern makes the case stand out.

The adult patient had a healthy immune system and no water exposure or seafood intake, the usual routes for this germ family. Targeted antibiotics brought full recovery. A full review of documented human infections with this strain accompanies the case. The authors urge clinicians to weigh rare germs when fever patterns defy standard explanations and to keep reporting such cases.
pmc-13310741:
Yao Liu led a 2026 mouse study that used sound based imaging to watch blood flow in the brain during seizures. Temporal lobe epilepsy is common and often resists drugs, yet blood flow shifts during attacks are poorly mapped. The team triggered brief seizures in mice and tracked flow across the whole brain in real time.

Most of 12 key brain areas showed flow that rose first and then fell during attacks. One thalamus area changed earlier than the rest, which hints at an early role. Links between brain areas also shifted in clear ways. Maps like these may help explain how seizures spread and harm tissue.
pmc-13310941:
Alexander Ochoa and co-authors search ancient Medici bones for malaria parasite DNA in a 2026 study. Grand Duke Francesco I and Cardinal Giovanni de Medici, who lived in the 16th century, were tested for six malaria species. Gene capture methods can pull tiny parasite traces from old bone.

Fragments of the deadliest malaria species were found in both men, with far more in the cardinal. The cardinal strain carried two new changes and forms a fresh branch tied to strains from Europe, Taiwan, and the Caribbean. A second, milder species also appeared in the duke. Old DNA can reveal past strain spread.
pmc-13311141:
Lois Gordils-Valentin and colleagues probe a protein that boosts plasmid sharing and germ killing in a 2026 study. Germs pass resistance genes through a secretion bridge on the RP4 plasmid, which can also kill rival germs. A little known gene called trbM strengthens both acts, so its structure and key parts were mapped.

Computer models likened the protein to known surface stickers on other sharing systems. Cousin proteins from three other plasmids restored sharing in strains lacking the gene, and most also restored killing. One key domain kept working when moved to a new frame. Blocking such proteins may slow resistance spread.
pmc-13311241:
Robert Thomas Brady and co-authors report a 2026 case linking a pituitary tumor with Schöpf-Schulz-Passarge syndrome, a very rare skin and tooth condition. The man had many sweat-gland cysts on both eyelids.

He also showed thick skin on palms and soles, missing teeth, and nail changes that fit the syndrome. Blood tests found high prolactin, and scans showed a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor. High prolactin had not been reported with this syndrome before, though it has been noted with multiple eyelid cysts. The authors discuss what the hormone link might mean for skin health.
pmc-13311641:
Anthony C Dowell and co-authors analyze their 2026 New Zealand record study on how the pandemic scrambled the usual seasonal pattern of respiratory illness in primary care. Automated text mining did the sorting.

The software processed over ten million visits from 2018 to 2023, of which 15.1 percent were respiratory. Yearly shares sat near 14 percent before the pandemic, then peaked at 25.2 percent in 2022 in this dataset. Border closures and the late arrival of the virus broke the winter rhythm, and patterns since differ by illness group. Variance has shrunk, but the old seasonal shape has not fully returned.
pmc-13311941:
Jiao Li and co-authors review heart attacks not caused by artery plaque in hypereosinophilic syndrome in a 2026 article. In this disorder, eosinophil counts stay abnormally high and damage many organs, the heart among them.

Heart involvement is frequent in the syndrome and worsens its outlook. Recent proof ties the syndrome directly to heart attacks driven by clots, inflammation, and vessel spasm rather than plaque rupture. Diagnosis and treatment therefore differ sharply from standard heart attack care. The review gathers what is known on rates, mechanisms, diagnostic rules, and targeted therapy, and names research gaps for this distinct condition.
pmc-13312241:
Bushra Alhothli and colleagues report a 2026 review of how a rapid molecular diarrhea panel was actually used in acute care at their hospital. The panel tests stool for 20 to 30 bacterial, viral, and parasitic targets within hours, replacing slower culture methods after its introduction in October 2023. Guidelines urge reserving it for severe or persistent illness.

The retrospective review found that 62 percent of panel orders did not follow clinical guidelines. Orders that broke the guidelines were significantly less likely to find any target and less likely to change how the patient was managed. The authors argue that tightening when the panel gets ordered is a clear diagnostic stewardship opportunity, cutting cost and low-value testing without losing the panel's real benefits for the right patients.
pmc-13312441:
Mustafa Mahmoud Aboulsaad and colleagues report a 2026 study of how squeezing a semiconductor into atom-thin sheets changes the way its lattice vibrates. Quantum confinement is known to reshape electronic behavior in two-dimensional halide perovskites. What it does to their phonons, the quanta of lattice vibration, alongside structure and light emission was an open question.

The team made cesium lead bromide nanoplatelets with exact thicknesses from two to five atomic layers and confirmed the control with structural checks, light emission measures, and computer calculations. Polarized Raman spectroscopy showed steady, systematic shifts in low-frequency vibration signals as thickness grew. Calculations traced the pattern to in-plane lead-bromine bending motions changing more than out-of-plane ones, and iodine-based platelets behaved alike. The authors propose Raman ratios as a gentle, non-destructive thickness gauge for such materials.
pmc-13312541:
Yuichi Kato and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, a cyanobacterium reprogrammed to make the amino acid glutamine from sunlight and carbon dioxide. Glutamine feeds growing cells and fills culture media, but industry makes it by fermentation that needs added sugar, so a photosynthetic route could cut both cost and carbon.

Working with Picosynechococcus sp. PCC 7002, the team imported a glutamate dehydrogenase from Corynebacterium glutamicum and a glutamine synthase from baker's yeast, which raised the glutamine the cells released. Metabolite readings showed citrate draining away, so they added enzymes to refill it and tried lactate feeding and glycogen removal as well. After tuning light and carbon dioxide, the engineered strain produced 170.76 milligrams of glutamine per liter of culture in the best run, proving the photosynthetic concept.
pmc-13312841:
Wan-Jung Lu and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how chronic inflammation helps cancers begin, grow, and resist treatment, and how small-molecule drugs might cut that support away. Inflammation is meant to be a short, tuned defense. When it never switches off, signals such as NF-kB, the JAK-STAT pathway, inflammasomes, reactive oxygen species, and cytokine webs build a tumor-friendly neighborhood.

The review maps these molecular pathways inside the tumor microenvironment, where immune, stromal, and cancer cells trade signals that feed nearly every hallmark of malignancy. Its special focus is the medicinal chemistry of the last five years: campaigns to design inflammation-targeting small molecules against this axis. The authors argue that joining systems-level biology with precision chemistry is the most promising path to a new class of anti-inflammatory cancer drugs.
pmc-13315041:
Erica A. L. Lecchi and a large team review lab models for rare diseases of the cornea and eye surface, in a 2026 journal article. These rare eye diseases are hard to treat: they are scarce, varied, and short on therapy options, so model systems carry the research load.

The review maps the full bench. Dish models run from plain and engineered cells to mixed cell cultures and new 3D organoids. Animal routes run from surgery-made states to gene-edited strains that copy the human disease. Each platform is weighed for strengths, limits, and how well it predicts human response, as the authors set out. Their joined view aims to help labs pick and pair models wisely, so scarce research funds on rare eye disease yield drugs that translate.
pmc-13315441:
Faradiba and co-authors share a field dataset in 2026 on sunlight and surface heat across common city materials in Jakarta, Indonesia. Surface type shapes how hot a city gets, yet measured data from tropical megacities remain scarce, so the team logged incoming and outgoing radiation plus surface temperature in the field.

Readings came every five minutes over runs of 30 to 120 minutes for fifteen surface types, with surface reflectivity also recorded. Materials differed clearly in how much radiation they bounced back and how much heat they could store. The data can feed heat-island studies, cooler material design, and city climate models.
pmc-13315641:
Tairan Chen and colleagues studied in 2026 why barred chickens differ in feather color tint, with yellow-barred and white-barred forms both showing the classic striped pattern. Feather color affects market value, yet the genes behind tint differences inside barred feathers were not clear.

Genome scans and selection tests on 47 birds pointed to several candidate regions and genes, including BRINP2, SLC22A4, SLC22A5, and ACTN1. Feather follicle gene activity differed widely, with 739 changed genes and names such as SLC45A2, BCO2, and EDAR standing out. The changed genes clustered around skin growth, surface layer formation, and keratin building.
pmc-13316741:
Liya Cai and Shuping Li present DSPE-ViT in a 2026 computer vision paper, a light transformer model built to spot tiny, crowded objects in drone photos. Fixed position codes in standard models waste computing power and blur dense clusters of small targets.

Their design prunes useless position dimensions with learned gates and adds density-aware local position signals where targets pack tight. A small-object feature pyramid and a refined box loss sharpen the output further. On a public drone benchmark the model reached 43.2 percent average precision with only about 6.0 million parameters, and it transferred well to sea rescue imagery. The balance of speed and accuracy suits live drone work.
pmc-13317441:
Tzu-Yang Hung and co-authors survey, in a 2026 narrative article, the anesthetic pair tiletamine and zolazepam in dog and cat practice, a workhorse for restraint, induction, and short operations. One drug blocks a key brain receptor while the other calms through a second system, giving fast sleep.

Doses in real clinics often run below label levels, especially into veins, where titration rules. Cats clear the drugs differently from dogs, so recovery varies widely by species. The pair suits healthy animals with a wide safety margin, yet must be avoided with head injury, raised brain pressure, pregnancy, or major organ disease. Mixing with sedatives and pain drugs is common, sometimes stretching recovery. Careful monitoring ties the guidance together.
pmc-13317541:
Panwad Uthiyo and Yuwares Chantem review ten years of cases in a 2026 Thai hospital study on isolated third nerve palsy, where one eye's movement nerve fails alone. A drooping pupil is traditionally read as a danger sign for aneurysm, and they test how far that rule holds.

Of 51 patients kept from records spanning 2015 to 2025, small-vessel ischemia was blamed in 82.4 percent of cases. Nine patients hid structural causes, six of them aneurysms. Pupil involvement appeared in two thirds of structural cases versus a quarter of ischemic ones. It multiplied adjusted odds eightfold, yet its hit rate stayed modest and a spared pupil missed real lesions. Vascular imaging found answers in a quarter of those scanned, backing wider use.
pmc-13317941:
Elsa Martín-De Arribas and colleagues test, in a 2026 methods study, how much the choice of statistical method bends microbiome findings on chemotherapy harm in colorectal cancer. Gut microbes may predict who suffers worst, but each analysis tool tells a different story.

They built one combined toxicity score from symptoms and treatment changes, then ran six popular differential abundance methods under varied data cleaning and correction rules. Overlap in flagged microbes was slim, though effect-size rankings agreed moderately. One method, ANCOM-BC, behaved most steadily across settings. A core set of microbes still recurred, split between low and severe toxicity groups, and an outside dataset echoed the method patterns. Biomarker claims, they warn, must name their method.
pmc-13318641:
Jiedong Kou and co-workers report a 2026 pig study of nerve repair. The target is a cut recurrent laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery. A direct join is often under too much tension. Their method borrows voice fibres from the nearby vagus nerve. Nerve monitoring guides the choice of fibres.

Eighteen cut nerves from nine pigs entered the comparison. Nine nerves got the selective vagus join and nine a direct join. Voice fibres sat mostly in one strand on the outer vagus. Both repairs restored electrical responses within two hours. Responses passed half of starting strength after the joins. Handling the vagus caused no meaningful blood pressure or oxygen change. Long-term voice recovery remains unproven, the authors note.
pmc-13318741:
Wang Meiping, Shamim Akhter, and Mengqiu Tan offer a 2026 integrative review of psychological flourishing across the whole lifespan. Flourishing means positive functioning, not just the absence of mental illness. It spans emotional, thinking, social, and meaning dimensions. No single account yet ties its course from childhood to old age.

The review draws on four major frameworks. They include Seligman's PERMA model and Keyes's well-known mental health continuum, plus VanderWeele's framework and self-determination theory. Each life stage is examined for its own challenges and openings. Long-term and one-time studies are combined with intervention research. The authors sort shared drivers of flourishing from stage-specific ones. Implications follow for research, clinical work, education policy, and public health.
pmc-13318941:
Ying Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 randomised trial comparing two nerve block routes for pain after single-port lung surgery. Both routes used long-acting liposomal bupivacaine. One group received a paravertebral block guided by ultrasound. The other received direct intercostal blocks placed during surgery. Sixty patients were split evenly.

Pain scores were the main outcome over 72 hours, at rest and when coughing. No significant differences appeared at 6, 24, 48, or 72 hours between groups. Opioid use, rescue painkillers, recovery milestones, and side effects also matched. Chest pain scores at one, three, and six months did not differ either. Pain stayed low in both groups throughout. The authors note the trial cannot prove the techniques equal.
pmc-13319641:
Gildas Boris Hedible and co-authors weigh the added worth of finger oxygen sensors in child care visits in a 2026 study across four West African lands. Standard child care rules on their own often miss very low blood oxygen, a strong sign a young child may die. The AIRE project added routine sensor checks to those visits in Burkina Faso, Guinea, Mali, and Niger.

Of 514901 visits logged from June 2021 to December 2022, about three in four children qualified for a sensor check. Adding the sensor found extra severe cases that rules alone had missed, lifting the count by just under five percent in most lands. Guinea gained far less. The gain shows sensors earn their place in front line care.
pmc-13320341:
Renyu Chen and co-authors review lab grown tumor models for pancreas cancer in a 2026 article on organoid craft. This cancer kills often because it is found late and resists most drug care, helped by a dense scar setting and wide variety inside each tumor. Mini tumors grown from patient tissue keep that variety and allow drug tests, yet plain cultures lack set surroundings and vary too much.

Three craft upgrades are mapped in turn, covering built gels and printing for steady builds, joint cultures and flow chips for lifelike settings, and smart imaging plus sensors for close watch. Design rules for each path are weighed next to blocks in scale, standards, and clinic handoff that still stall wide use.
pmc-13320441:
Sakshi Chauhan and co-authors study a variant DNA spool protein in blood cell growth in a 2026 mouse cell study. The variant spool is laid down on active genes all through the cell cycle and is vital for early embryos, yet its role later in life was murky. Genes for it were cut out in young blood cells as they grew into eater cells in dishes.

Cells without the variant copied DNA badly, took heavy DNA harm, and died in large numbers. Those that lived switched on alarm genes all through their growth and kept a broadly normal spool layout across the genome. Mature eater cells still formed, so the variant is key for growth of young blood cells but not a must for their final form.
pmc-13321041:
Nesrin Ocal, Baran Balcan, and Yüksel Peker review the overlap between scarred lung disease and sleep apnoea in a 2026 narrative review. Interstitial lung diseases stiffen the lungs, impair gas exchange, and carry heavy illness burden. Sleep apnoea, where breathing pauses in sleep, proves very common in these patients, even without obesity.

Stiff mechanics, low lung volumes, weak diaphragm action, and severe night time oxygen drops shape a distinct apnoea pattern that standard screening can miss. Night oxygen swings, broken sleep, and stress responses may worsen the lung picture, though causal proof stays largely observational. Airway pressure therapy plus oxygen can ease symptoms and night oxygen, while effects on disease course stay unproven.
pmc-13321141:
Repnik and co-authors audit the questionnaires used to measure psychological resilience in this 2026 review. Resilience, adapting well under serious stress, has been defined in conflicting ways for decades. Dozens of scales claim to measure it. The authors ask what those scales actually ask about, using a preregistered rating study.

Four raters sorted the items of 83 resilience scales into process, trait, and environment categories. Across all scales, traits took just over half of the items, while process content took just under a third. Weighting by how often scales are cited flipped the picture, with process items nearing three fifths. Agreement between raters was substantial. Repnik recommends that researchers choose scales by content, so studies measure the same thing.
pmc-13321441:
Bo Ye and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their 2020 study of nanoparticle delivery for tumour heat therapy. The original work, in Journal of Nanobiotechnology, used neutrophil immune cells to carry nanoparticles in stages toward tumours for photothermal treatment. The correction concerns one figure in that article.

In Figure 9, the stained lung tissue image was wrong and has now been replaced in the original publication. For openness, both the old incorrect and the correct versions are shown. The figure presents stained sections of main organs at day 15 after different treatments, with a scale bar of 100 micrometres. No other part of the article is changed by the notice.
pmc-13322841:
Tingting Liu and colleagues report a broken chemotherapy port catheter in a 33-year-old man with lung cancer, in a 2026 case report. The patient had severe obesity, with a body mass index recorded as 42.1 in the report, and felt repeated pain around the port pocket.

Imaging showed the catheter had failed inside the port itself, rather than breaking free and travelling in a vein. A team from several specialties removed the device promptly, avoiding the risk of a loose fragment reaching the heart or lungs. The authors suggest that very high body weight may add mechanical strain on implanted ports, so such patients need closer checks for device damage.
pmc-13324441:
Ilham Zarguan and co-authors review the long effort to drug Hsp90, a protein chaperone, in a 2026 article. Early natural products showed that blocking Hsp90 can break down many client proteins at once and expose how cells control protein quality.

Later work mapped the chaperone cycle, its partner proteins, and disease-linked assemblies called the epichaperome. Cells also fight back through heat-shock responses and other stress pathways, which limited early drugs. Newer classes aim at single parts or forms of Hsp90, and pimitespib won approval for stubborn gastrointestinal stromal tumors. The authors argue that matching drugs to clear client dependence or biomarkers gives the best results.
pmc-13324841:
Eva J.E. de Bock and colleagues test whether a lifetime of menstrual cycles tracks with adenomyosis severity in a 2026 exploratory study. The tissue injury and repair idea holds that repeated contractions at each period slowly damage the womb lining border.

Ultrasound scans and menstrual histories covered 119 premenopausal participants at Amsterdam University Medical Centre. Exposure counts adjusted for pregnancy, breastfeeding, and hormone use that pauses periods. The median age was 27 years, and 87 percent had used the contraceptive pill before. After accounting for vaginal births and womb surgery, greater total menstrual exposure linked to more severe adenomyosis on imaging. The modest link supports the injury idea without proving cause.
pmc-13325341:
Watcharapong Wararam and co-authors 3D-print ceramic-polymer scaffolds that clean dye and antibiotic waste from water in a 2026 study. Textile dyes and drugs such as tetracycline threaten water safety worldwide.

The scaffold mixes silica from bagasse ash with barium or strontium titanate particles in a printed porous frame. Three actions team up: soaking up pollutants, light-driven breakdown, and vibration-driven breakdown. Adsorption alone removed over 60 percent of methylene blue dye in the tests. Adding ultraviolet light and ultrasound pushed total removal past 88 percent for the dye and 85 percent for tetracycline. Using farm waste silica keeps the design cheap and green.
pmc-13327541:
Willamina M MacDonald, Ethan P Gillespie, and Michael G Jonz show how serotonin drives salt-balance cell growth in young zebrafish in a 2026 study. Freshwater fish larvae use skin cells called ionocytes to hold their internal salt steady, and those cells multiply under ionic stress. The signal behind that growth was poorly known.

Staining showed the cells carry serotonin 2A receptors alongside known ionocyte markers. Acidic water or added serotonin raised cell counts, and a receptor blocker, ketanserin, erased both effects, while draining serotonin stores with tetrabenazine also cut the response. Receptor activity raised a growth-linked signal inside the cells, tying a familiar brain chemical to body salt control in fish.
pmc-13328041:
Alexander Bertuccioli and co-authors review B vitamin intake and cancer risk in a 2026 structured narrative review. Vitamins B2, B6, B12, and folate feed one-carbon metabolism, DNA building, and methylation, yet study findings on cancer have clashed. The team searched PubMed through September 2025, favoring meta-analyses and adding supplement trials where useful.

Riboflavin and vitamin B6 intake generally went with lower colorectal cancer risk across several pooled analyses, including dose-response work. Vitamin B12 links swung by cancer site and may reflect diet and starting nutrition rather than the vitamin itself, while folate results mixed protection with possible harm signals. Careful reading of study quality shapes every conclusion, the authors stress.
pmc-13328341:
Luiza Aymée and co-authors grade genetic markers for naming pathogenic Leptospira in a 2026 study. Growing the bacteria or sequencing whole genomes is often impractical, so single-gene sequencing carries diagnosis, yet primer pairs were adopted without full checks. Ten primer pairs across seven gene regions were tested in computer simulations against five pathogenic species.

Five markers amplified well in theory, but only three, secY outer, redesigned flaB, and lipL32, gave family trees matching core-genome trees. Distance-gap analysis left secY outer and the redesigned flaB able to split both species and strains, with proposed identity cutoffs of 96 and 95 percent for database matching. Standard cutoffs could end years of inconsistent naming.
pmc-13328641:
Vinitha Mingi and colleagues report in 2026 on poor eyesight among garment workers in Hyderabad, India, and its effect on work. Clinics were set up inside five factories. In total, 1,361 workers aged 18 or older had distance and near vision checked, along with corrected vision.

About 87 percent of those checked were women, and about one quarter were aged 40 or older. Distance vision problems affected 6.9 percent of workers, based on the figures reported for the group. Among older workers without distance problems, over half had near vision problems. Both kinds of poor vision linked to worse self-rated work output. The authors suggest regular eye checks at work could help.
pmc-13329341: A 2026 correction by Tatsuo Tsukamoto and co-authors fixes Table 1 in a case report. The report covered a very elderly patient with fast-moving kidney inflammation from microscopic polyangiitis. The notice states that the table heading and example text were shown wrongly. It then gives the corrected admission lab table, with urine and blood values. No wider case narrative is included in the notice. It serves only as a record fix for that table.
pmc-13330541:
Changqing Yin and colleagues test an antimalarial drug against drug-resistant leukaemia in a 2026 study. Chronic myeloid leukaemia is driven by the BCR-ABL fusion protein, and imatinib blocks it, yet resistance is common. The team studied primaquine diphosphate in resistant cells, patient blasts, and a mouse graft model.

Low doses pushed resistant cells toward maturity, while high doses triggered cell death in the reported results. The drug blocked the Wnt and beta-catenin pathway and sped breakdown of normal and mutant BCR-ABL proteins. Colony growth of patient blasts fell, and tumour growth in mice was curbed. The authors propose primaquine as a repurposed candidate worth further study.
pmc-13332441:
Michael A Quail and colleagues reviewed children's heart stress scans in a 2026 retrospective study, asking whether the stress drug regadenoson can be dosed by response rather than by weight alone. Fixed weight-based dosing may give some children far more drug than they need to widen the coronary arteries.

Across 31 scans from 2015 to 2025 in patients with known or suspected coronary disease, the drug was given in small steps until heart rate rose at least 20 percent. All 29 successful studies hit the target, at a median dose of 3.2 mcg/kg against the standard 8 mcg/kg, a cut of about 60 percent, and every scan produced diagnostic-quality images. Stress-related flow defects appeared in 7 of 29 studies, no major side effects occurred, and the authors call for prospective checks with measured blood flow.
pmc-13333141:
Haowei Tai and co-authors developed an image-based way to measure how much damage a dose of histotripsy has done, in a 2026 rat study. Histotripsy uses focused ultrasound pulses to tear tumor tissue apart mechanically, but clinics give one fixed pulse count even though tumors differ in toughness.

Twenty rats with liver tumors received 20, 50, 100, or 200 pulses per spot, spanning light to excessive treatment. Comparing ultrasound images before and after, the team extracted texture features and matched them against tissue damage measured under the microscope. The area covered by nuclear debris tracked closely with two texture measures, with R² values of 0.9 and 0.8, and a random forest model predicted the delivered dose with an R² of 0.9. The authors propose live image feedback so clinicians can tune dosing to each tumor.
pmc-13333341:
Allini Mafra and co-authors chart how age shapes breast cancer outlook in Luxembourg in a 2026 registry study. It sets a baseline just before the national screening program widened in July 2024 from ages 50 to 69 to ages 45 to 74. Age influences tumor type, treatment, and survival, but country-level detail was missing.

The retrospective cohort covered 3,003 women diagnosed with invasive breast cancer from 2013 to 2018, split into four age bands. Women under 40 had the most triple-negative tumors at 24 percent and the most chemotherapy at 78 percent. Five-year survival peaked in the 40 to 49 group at 95.3 percent and the 50 to 69 group at 92.3 percent. It sat at 91.0 percent under 40 and dropped to 65.4 percent at 70 and over, partly because other causes of death compete at that age. Screen-found cancers survived best at 95.8 percent, while advanced stage and triple-negative type carried the worst outlook.
pmc-13333741:
Nomvuselelo Nomzamo Mbatha, Nomakhosi Mpofana, and Dumile Gumede authored a 2026 narrative review of healthcare workers' views on delivering HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in Sub-Saharan Africa. Worker readiness matters greatly as long-acting injectable PrEP, especially cabotegravir, begins to roll out.

Five databases were searched for studies from 2020 to 2025, and five primary studies met the criteria, all covering oral PrEP in Uganda, South Africa, Kenya, and Zimbabwe. Workers' awareness and knowledge varied widely and often reflected prior exposure to pilot projects. Themes covered attitudes, training gaps, and practical delivery concerns. Lessons from oral PrEP programs can prepare clinics for injectable rollout, where dosing visits and cold-chain demands differ.
pmc-13336441: A 2026 correction notice repairs a figure in the Advanced Science article by Guanyun Wang and co-authors on hydroxyapatite scaffolds functionalized with MgAlEu layered double hydroxide nanosheets for bone regeneration. The notice supplies no new experiments. It explains that Figure 2b originally showed the wrong Alizarin Red S staining image, taken from the HL16 group instead of HL8. It republishes the corrected figure using data from the original experiments. The authors state that results and conclusions are unchanged.
pmc-13336641:
Yanli Wang and co-authors report a 2026 tea genetics study linking cold hardiness with leaf quality in one shared regulator. They scored cold tolerance and measured 12 quality-related compounds across 108 tea accessions from across China over two years. Genome-wide mapping pointed to a hub gene named CCR1.

Plant tests showed CCR1 boosts both cold tolerance and catechins, the compounds behind much of tea quality. One letter change in the gene strengthened both traits. Added catechins also eased cold damage by clearing harmful oxygen byproducts. CCR1 works with partner proteins to switch on catechin and cold-response genes. Breeders could use it to raise teas that taste better and survive cold snaps.
pmc-13336841:
Ruimin Ren and colleagues boost the magnetic losses of ultralight wave absorbers in a 2026 materials study. Materials that soak up electromagnetic waves need magnetic loss, but light versions usually lose too little. Using hollow magnetite particles with hollow shares from 0 to 54.1% in set steps, they tested what drives the loss.

Loss depended mainly on surface atom spin, not the bulk inside. The most hollow particles gained about 20% in the loss measure over 2–18 GHz compared with solid ones and kept a much wider useful band at a thickness of 2.0 mm in the reported tests. Their density was only 48.9% of the solid sample value in the comparison. Surface-spin control points to lighter radar and shielding materials.
pmc-13337441:
Hailong Jiao and colleagues rank exercise types for protecting thinking in older adults in a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis. Exercise is a cheap, low-risk way to slow cognitive decline, but which kind works best was unsettled. Six databases were searched through December 31, 2025, starting from 3,816 records.

Eighteen randomized trials with 1,316 older adults survived screening, including people with mild cognitive impairment. Pooled results showed several exercise types improved cognitive scores. The best choice depended on the test used. Multi-modal training led on one global scale, while other types topped different measures in the ranking analysis. The authors call for matching exercise plans to the thinking skills most at risk.
pmc-13337641:
Cheng Zhang and co-authors test adding light therapy to laser treatment for genital warts after cervical cancer surgery in a 2026 retrospective study. Condyloma acuminatum, caused by HPV, often persists or returns in these patients and drags down quality of life. Of 148 patients, 81 received carbon dioxide laser alone and 67 received laser plus photodynamic therapy.

At 6 months the combined group reported a symptom relief rate of 94.03% against 77.78% for laser alone in the outcome tally. Recurrence also ran lower with combined therapy, reaching 11.94% versus 34.57% at 6 months in the follow-up counts. Quality-of-life and sexual function scores improved more in the combined group across several domains. The authors support the add-on for this hard-to-treat overlap of conditions.
pmc-13337841:
Alicia Zou leads a 2026 interview study on how adults with hearing loss find help online. Barriers and aids to reaching information and services were explored to guide a new consumer website called Hear4Health. A behavior framework shaped how findings were read.

Thirteen people took part, including consumers and organization representatives, through focus groups and interviews. Nine themes fell under seven framework areas, from knowledge to social influence. Poor awareness, weak information, distrust of the hearing industry, and stigma blocked access. Peer support and lived experience helped people move forward. Results will guide website design that centers what consumers actually need.
pmc-13338241:
Janina Billian and colleagues study a crisis ward move in Basel, Switzerland, in a 2026 observational study. The unit left a general medical site for a specialist psychiatric site on May 26, 2023. Patient mix, outcomes, satisfaction, and clinician views were compared across the move.

Cases numbered 625 before the move and 686 after, each over twelve months as reported. Age and gender held steady, while mood disorder share fell at the new site. Outcomes, forced admissions, and transfers stayed comparable. Patient satisfaction dropped from a mean of 5.2 to 4.6 in the reported scores, and outside clinicians strongly preferred the old general hospital setting.
pmc-13338941: Frontiers Production Office issued a 2026 correction. It concerns a study of mushroom sugars and gut injury from chemotherapy drugs. Only contact and credit details were wrong. The lead contact email is now correct. A missing affiliation is restored. Numbering of affiliations is fixed. Copyright and citation author lists now match the author list. All findings stand unchanged.
pmc-13341441:
Traditional Chinese exercises for stroke recovery are ranked in a 2026 network meta-analysis by Runze Wang's team. Tai Chi, Baduanjin, Wuqinxi, and Yijinjing are widely used add-on therapies, yet trials rarely compare them directly, so the team searched seven databases through January 2026.

Trials involved adults at any stage after ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke. Main outcomes were arm and leg motor scores, with balance and daily living measures secondary. A Bayesian network approach combined direct and indirect evidence into rankings. Such comparisons help therapists pick among gentle exercise systems that blend movement, balance, and breathing practice.
pmc-13341841:
A blood ratio flags fluid around the heart in young heart attack patients, in a 2026 study by Hang Yu's team. The project enrolled 1,974 patients under 45 admitted in Xi'an between January 2018 and October 2025, grouping them by whether echocardiography found pericardial effusion.

Effusion occurred in 7.1% of patients. The log-transformed NT-proBNP-to-albumin ratio independently predicted it (adjusted OR 3.23), as did plateletcrit (OR 1.87), alongside attack type, pumping function, kidney function, and cholesterol. Adding both markers to a clinical model improved reclassification. The ratio blends heart strain with inflammation and nutrition in one cheap number.
pmc-13342241:
Godspower N. Okeke and co-authors review leishmaniasis in 2026, a set of neglected tropical diseases spread by sandfly bites. The review covers how the parasites cause skin, mucosal, and visceral illness, how the host immune response decides the course, and how immune-based treatments are changing.

Protective immunity rests on Th1 responses, while Th2 skewing and IL-10 dominance let the disease advance. Standard drugs face resistance, kidney harm, relapse, and safety limits, and no licensed human vaccine exists. The authors weigh cytokine therapy, immune triggers, therapeutic vaccines, and mucosal delivery, arguing that pairing immune treatment with drugs offers the best path to lasting cure and fewer relapses.
pmc-13345941:
Xinyue Li, Hui Zhang, Wenxin Dong, and Tongyan Han link mothers' early preeclampsia to feeding trouble in very preterm babies in a 2026 matched study. Eighty-seven infants born before 32 weeks to mothers with early-onset disease were paired by gestational age with 87 born to mothers with normal blood pressure.

Feeding intolerance struck 77.0 percent of exposed infants against 41.4 percent of controls, and reaching full feeds took 13.0 days against 9.5 days. Adjusted models kept early preeclampsia as an independent risk factor, with lower birth weight adding risk of its own. Nurses and doctors, the authors urge, should watch feeding in these infants with extra care and support nutrition early.
pmc-13346341:
Irvine-Brown and colleagues surveyed occupational therapy educators in 2026 on how they understand and teach critical thinking. The skill is prized in therapy education, yet its meaning and best teaching routes vary widely. Educators worldwide answered a survey in English, Spanish, or Portuguese with scored items and open questions, and the team compared language groups while building themes from the written replies.

Views spread along a spectrum. At one end sat concrete, clinic-focused ideas centered on reasoning, evidence use, and decisions. At the other, abstract and socially minded ideas stressing reflection on knowledge, power structures, and action for change. English replies leaned clinical, while Spanish and Portuguese replies leaned social and reflective. Teaching mirrored the split and was uneven across programs. Instead of chasing one shared definition, the authors urge programs to name their stance and teach from it openly.
pmc-13346641:
Urška Puh, Nina Čelofiga, and Judith E Deutsch compare balance games for people living after a stroke, in a repeated measures study published in 2026. Twenty-six adults in the chronic phase played 12 games, half on a custom rehabilitation system and half on a Nintendo Wii balance setup. Pacing was set by the game or by the player.

Noncustom game-paced play produced more weight shifts, larger movement, and higher felt effort, while custom game-paced play gave a stronger sense of control and flow. Enjoyment did not differ clearly between systems. The authors suggest choosing games by goal, since drive for effort and drive for adherence point in different directions.
pmc-13347941:
Allegra G. Hawkins and colleagues present a data portal for single-cell gene activity in childhood tumours, in a resource report from 2026. The Single-Cell Pediatric Cancer Atlas holds evenly processed data for over 700 samples across 55 cancer types, drawn from funded projects and community gifts. Cleaned counts, cell maps, and type labels come ready to download.

Files come as lab-ready objects with raw and scaled counts plus copy-number guesses and summary sheets, and some samples add bulk, spatial, or surface-protein data in the same pack. An open workflow built on alevin-fry handles all processing the same way, and guides online help new users start, widening access to rare tumour data.
pmc-13348241:
Bohao Peng and colleagues highlight a self-repairing skin for lithium batteries. Their commentary was issued in 2026. The skin is built from a zirconium fluoride additive. Normal skins crack as lithium swells. Shrinking cracks them too. Cracks invite spiky growth on the metal. The discussed approach works differently. Voltage frees ions from additive grains. Those ions rebuild a double-layer skin. Rebuilding happens at the anode during running.

Calculations credit the rebuilt layer with fast lithium passage. It beats common skin parts on that measure. Lithium fluoride is one such part. A wide energy gap helps too. Chemical calm helps as well. Both block stray electron flow. Repair framed as built-in beats repair patched later. Safer high-energy metal batteries may follow.
pmc-13349941:
Jing Yi Lee and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on reading circulating tumour DNA during treatment of gastrointestinal stromal tumours. Most of these tumours grow because of faulty KIT or PDGFRA switches, and the drug imatinib transformed their care.

Resistance usually appears within two to three years as new KIT changes emerge, and later drugs are given in sequence without fresh molecular checks. Blood-borne tumour DNA could track those changes over time, but when samples are taken may decide what they show. The authors argue that timing of blood draws is central to using the test wisely when choosing and switching targeted drugs.
pmc-13350041:
Xiaojun Wang and co-authors compared pain relief options for needle access to implanted chest ports in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Ports let patients receive long-term infusions under the skin, but each needle entry through the skin hurts, and easing that pain matters for people facing many sessions.

Seven randomised trials covering nine approaches and 942 patients were combined, letting options compete even without direct trials. Cold therapy and skin stimulation ranked among the methods beating dummy treatment and usual care. Evidence strength for each comparison was graded. A clear ranking helps nurses pick a simple, drug-free method that genuinely dulls the sting.
pmc-13350341:
Guillaume Tcheutchoua Soh and colleagues described abdominal wall hernia care at a second-level hospital in Senegal in a 2026 study. It covered six months of surgery. Hernia repairs made up 34.2 percent of the centre's 199 operations. The burden is heavy where guidelines written elsewhere are hard to apply.

Groin hernias dominated, at three quarters of repairs. One in five operations was an emergency. Mesh was used in just over half of cases. Spinal anaesthesia was the norm for groin repair. Local data like this can seed home-grown guidelines. Borrowed ones often ignore local funding and staffing realities.
pmc-13351941:
Masaya Aoki leads a 2026 study of immune cells in lung tissue far from the tumour in people treated for non-small cell lung cancer. Immunity is usually judged inside the tumour or nearby nodes, yet distant lung tissue may show host traits too. Forty patients who had curative lobe removal gave paired near and distant tissue samples.

Staining counted DC-SIGN-positive cells and CD169-positive macrophages with a hotspot method. Both cell types were more abundant near the tumour than far from it. Counts were linked to clinical traits, smoking history, and time without recurrence. Findings suggest distant lung immunity carries signals about later outcomes that deserve wider testing.
pmc-13352041:
Lindsay D. Butcher leads a 2026 mouse and cell study of how the APE1 protein guards gut lining DNA from a toxin-making Escherichia coli strain. APE1 helps cells handle oxidative stress and repair harm. Mice with lowered or gut-specific loss of APE1 were infected with the genotoxic NC101 strain, and colon cells with reduced APE1 were tested in dishes.

Loss of APE1 in gut cells raised baseline DNA damage, marked by gammaH2AX signals. Germ-free conditions softened that damage, pointing to microbes as a driver. Tests compared the toxin strain, a strain lacking the toxin genes, and the pure colibactin toxin. Findings show APE1 limits oxidative DNA harm during infection by toxin-making gut bacteria.
pmc-13352941:
Anton Yu. Bykov leads a 2026 ultrafast study of hot-electron transfer from gold nanostars into a carbon nitride photocatalyst. Plasmonic hybrids can boost light-driven chemistry, but the carrier dance at the interface is hard to watch. Gold nanostars were joined to poly(heptazine imide), and pump-probe spectroscopy tracked charge motion on ultrafast scales.

Electrons moved from gold into the nitride with an efficiency of about 40 percent, among the highest reported for metal-semiconductor pairs, with a standard error of 12 percent. The spiky star shape helps by relaxing momentum rules that normally block transfer. Strong coupling also reshaped how hot carriers cool down. Findings give designers concrete guidance for sharper solar chemistry materials.
pmc-13354041:
Mariana Teles, Erin Clabough, and Taylor Byron describe remaking a large neuroscience course around active learning in 2026. Big lecture courses limit engagement with hard material, so the redesign mixed recorded lectures online with small-group sessions held in person each week. Student views were captured in 547 open comments from 232 students across two semesters.

An open-source language model, BART, sorted comments into researcher-set themes without training labels. The active format clearly improved felt learning and engagement in comment data. Standard Likert scales, though, missed those gains entirely. A practical framework is offered so other teachers can redesign large courses and judge impact with accessible AI tools.
pmc-13356641:
Clara Fauveau and co-authors studied in 2026 the cancer cells that survive chemotherapy in a dormant, drug-tolerant state and seed relapse. Using 3D lung cancer spheroids given long chemotherapy, they created such persister cells and read their gene activity one cell at a time. They then compared the pattern with human datasets of leftover disease after treatment.

A core persistence signature emerged, and it was enriched in patient samples of minimal residual disease, backing the model. The signature hinted that oncolytic viruses, which infect and kill cancer cells, could strike persisters. Tests in spheroids and patient organoids confirmed that weakness, opening a path to clear leftover disease.
pmc-13356741:
Xu Cheng and co-authors tested a plant stem extract in 2026 for treating E. coli diarrhea in broiler chickens, a costly farm disease usually fought with antibiotics. One hundred eighty young broilers were split into six groups: healthy, infected, antibiotic-treated, and three extract dose groups. The team tracked growth, diarrhea, gut shape, immune and antioxidant signs, and gut microbes.

The extract improved growth, eased diarrhea, and healed gut lining, while raising antioxidant enzymes and calming gut inflammation genes. It also restored gut microbe balance. Computer analysis flagged five core targets, chiefly tied to inflammation and immunity, and the main plant compound bound them stably. The authors propose the extract as an antibiotic alternative.
pmc-13358541:
Chuan Qin and co-authors ask an overlooked question about breast cancer in a 2026 study. Some patients have no cancer left after drug treatment and surgery, a result called a complete response. Yet a share of them still do poorly later. The team asked whether the part of the breast where the tumor sat helps explain that risk.

They studied 293 women treated at one Chinese hospital from 2005 to 2024, all of whom reached a complete response. They compared women whose cancer later progressed with those who stayed well. Sorting out such fine risk signs could help doctors decide who needs extra treatment or closer checks even after a perfect first result.
pmc-13358641:
Abubakar and co-authors report a 2026 study on how rice plants cope with drought. A stretch of chromosome 7 in rice helps plants avoid drying out, and it holds a cluster of genes for aquaporins, channels that move water through roots. The team tested one gene, OsPIP2;1, to see if it drives the effect.

They compared rice lines that differ only near this gene, and plants with the gene knocked down. New tools measured how easily water flows through roots. Lines with the helpful gene version moved water differently, backing the idea that root water flow is the trait's engine. Breeding for such genes could yield rice that holds up better in dry seasons.
pmc-13358741:
Jinxiang Yu and co-authors present a 2026 study on idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a disease that scars the lungs. The damage centers on air sac cells called type II cells, which can stall in a half-repaired state. The team asked which genes, linked to stress around anesthesia and surgery, mark that harmful shift.

They joined single-cell and whole-tissue gene data from patient and healthy lungs, then used machine learning to rank candidate genes. One gene, IGFBP2, stood out in the stressed cell states. Naming such markers could help doctors track the disease and may point to new drug targets for a condition with few options.
pmc-13358841:
Zhiwei Fan and co-authors review a surprising link between exercise, gut microbes, and lung disease in a 2026 paper. COPD, a chronic lung disease, is now seen as a whole-body disorder tied to an unbalanced gut. Exercise helps these patients, and part of the gain may flow through the gut: activity reshapes gut microbes and the chemicals they release.

Those chemicals, including short-chain fatty acids and bile acid products, travel in the blood and can calm or stir lung inflammation. The review joins the scattered evidence into one picture of this gut-lung axis. It also marks what is still guesswork, pointing to trials that could prove the chain.
pmc-13359741:
Hadar Goldvaser and co-authors pool trials of a new breast cancer drug type in a 2026 review. The most common advanced breast cancer feeds on estrogen, and hormone therapy is its backbone. Over time, some tumors change their estrogen receptor so standard drugs fail. New oral degraders both block and destroy that receptor. The team compared them with standard hormone therapy.

Across eight trials with 4,230 patients, the degraders lengthened life and slowed the cancer, but only in tumors carrying a specific receptor gene change called an ESR1 mutation. Patients without the change gained little. The results make a strong case for testing every tumor for that mutation.
pmc-13360241:
Yihui Feng and co-authors present a 2026 computer system that checks newborn babies' ears from plain photos. Bent or misshapen ears can be fixed without surgery, but only in a short early window. Judgment by eye alone can miss that window, and there was no fair way to track gains from treatment. Their deep learning system was built to fill both gaps.

The system screens ears as normal or deformed and can sort six kinds of ear deformity. A score for how severe the bend is lets doctors follow change before and after treatment. The team wrapped the system in a simple web tool for clinic staff. Quick, even-handed checks could help more babies get treated in time.
pmc-13361641:
Suppanut Komjakraphan and co-authors grew killer immune cells from patient stem cells in a 2026 study. Engineered T cells have shown promise in blood cancers, but cells from heavily treated patients are often worn out and scarce. Natural killer cells attack cancer by nature and have a friendly safety record, making them an appealing stand-in. The team drew stem cells mobilized from patients with blood cancers.

Over a 28-day, two-step process, the stem cells became natural killer cells and multiplied about 290-fold. The grown cells carried a young, immature marker pattern distinct from blood-borne killer cells. The team compared their cancer-fighting potential with standard killer cells from blood. A reliable way to grow fresh killer cells from a patient's own stem cells could widen cell therapy options.
pmc-13363241:
Shuncheng Xiang and a large team report a 2026 study on a core-shell emulsion additive that tunes how fresh cement mortar flows. Builders need mortar that holds shape yet spreads well, a balance called rheology. The team made the emulsion by radical polymerization and dosed mortar from zero to ten percent, then measured yield stress, stiffness recovery, and flow under shear, plus the set cement's inner structure.

The additive kept the mortar's basic flow type but shifted its traits with dose. Around four percent gave the best blend of standing stability and working flow, while a ten percent dose made yield stress jump many-fold. Microscopy showed the emulsion coats cement grains as a film, slowing water entry and filling pores, with no new chemistry formed.

Yuexing Wang and colleagues present a 2026 study that designs a new herbicide-resistance allele for wheat on the computer before it exists in nature.
