pmc-13375541:
Shahzad Ahmad and co-authors read blood small stuff and brain health in a 2026 study. The group held 1,082 mid-life adults in Rotterdam with no mind loss. A total of 991 blood compounds were set next to thought tests and brain scans.

Gene, habit, ill, drug, and gut germ shares of each compound's spread were also weighed. A score of compounds tied to scans, and 14 tied to thought in two more old-age groups. One group was then tracked for new mind loss. Blood marks that flag brain risk in mid-life could open a long lead for care.
pmc-13379441:
Stephanie Leeds and colleagues wrote a 2026 practical review for children's doctors on the underuse of epinephrine for severe allergic reactions in babies and toddlers. Epinephrine, given by injection device, is the recommended first treatment for anaphylaxis, which can worsen fast and cause death. Yet it is often given late or not at all.

Barriers include trouble spotting the reaction in very young children, doubt about when to act, prescriptions never filled, devices not carried, and fear of calling emergency services. Antihistamines are often used first by mistake. The review urges doctors to train caregivers to spot warning signs, use the device correctly, and keep it at hand at home, school, and childcare.
pmc-13379541:
Wenjing Zhou and co-authors report a 2026 study on a blood test that may warn of lung cancer returning after surgery. They measured tumour cells circulating in the blood that carry a folate receptor, a surface feature the test detects. Return of the disease after surgery is a major problem, and reliable warning markers are scarce.

The study included 171 patients with early to locally advanced lung cancer who had surgery between 2018 and 2021. Blood was taken around the time of surgery. Patients whose test stayed positive after surgery were more likely to see their disease progress within three years. The marker could help flag patients who need closer follow-up.
pmc-13380741:
Carma L Bylund and colleagues present a 2026 trial of training for children's doctors in how to recommend the HPV vaccine, which prevents several cancers. A clear recommendation from a clinician strongly raises uptake, but recommendations are not always given well. The study tested a structured conversation method called C-LEAR.

Thirty clinics and 58 clinicians were assigned by chance to one of three groups. Two groups used the method, one discussing all adolescent vaccines together and one focused on HPV benefits. The third group had training delayed until after the trial. Training lasted one hour online and included role play. Clinicians were then assessed in simulated and real visits, and by survey, to see whether the training changed their behaviour.
pmc-13380841:
Longmei Guo and a large team published a 2026 computer simulation study comparing two shapes of self-tying orthodontic brackets and their effect on the inner lip. Braces can press and rub the lip, causing discomfort. The team built detailed models of teeth, brackets, and lip tissue to compare round and square bracket designs.

Each model was tested in five tooth positions, with a two-stage simulation covering bracket fitting and tooth sliding. Stress on the lip concentrated at the clip groove of the round bracket and at the sharp edge of the square one. Across all conditions the round bracket produced lower peak stress on the lip. The result favours rounder designs for comfort.
pmc-13384441:
Gao and colleagues design a pricing mechanism for data marketplaces that learns what buyers value before naming a price, in 2026 theoretical economics research. Their mechanism, Maximum Auction-to-Posted Price, works in two stages: run auctions to estimate the distribution of bidder valuations, then set the price from that distribution. The authors prove the design is individually rational and incentive-compatible, meaning truthful bidding is every bidder's best strategy, while the seller balances revenue against price discrimination between buyers.

The theory recasts optimization as an estimation problem, showing regret, the revenue lost versus perfect knowledge, is governed by how well the valuation curve is estimated. With bid data folded in, regret shrinks as bids accumulate, and a version adjusting prices across dataset sales achieves no-regret learning. Simulations and bidding data from the FCC AWS-3 spectrum auction validated the mechanism's behavior. Gao offers the design for platforms selling datasets.
pmc-13389441:
Ahmad Alminnawi leads a 2026 methods study on the thin bony endplate that caps each vertebra. That plate passes load and nutrients toward the spinal disc, and the size and linking of its tiny pores shape both strength and transport.

The team built a partly automated modelling workflow from micro-CT scans of six to eight endplates from four cattle. Each plate was split into a central zone and two edge zones, and pore shape and connection were tied to zone-level strength and flow values drawn from earlier work. Spine researchers gain a repeatable way to link pore structure to predicted performance, useful for studying disc failure and for testing implant designs before animal or human trials.
pmc-13390341:
Diego Martin-Gonzalez and co-authors engineer, in 2026, a soil bacterium to secrete an enzyme that breaks down a common biodegradable plastic. The plastic, PBAT, is used in packaging, but its aromatic rings resist water attack and slow natural breakdown.

The team gave Paracoccus denitrificans a new plasmid carrying a cutinase gene from a Fusarium fungus, fused to a secretion signal so the enzyme leaves the cell. The altered bacterium already has a flexible metabolism and can store a natural polymer. Biotechnology readers gain a working secretion system in a robust host, a step toward microbes that both attack durable plastics and convert the products into useful materials.
pmc-13390841:
Dang Vinh and Phan Thi Yen test, in 2026, a phone app that screens school students for colour vision deficiency and adds tailored study and career advice. Colour blindness can quietly affect learning and career choice, yet paper tests are slow, hard to standardise, and rarely linked to guidance.

The cross-sectional study covered 527 high school students in Danang, Viet Nam. The Android app combines a digital version of the Ishihara plate test with artificial intelligence assisted counselling. School health staff in low-resource settings gain a combined screen-and-advise tool, with validation data on whether phone screening matches the standard it aims to replace.
pmc-13392641:
Akaraphutiporn and colleagues offer a 2026 radiographic study of medial patellar luxation, a condition where the kneecap slips inward, common in small-breed dogs. Using X-rays of 69 stifle joints from 46 dogs, they compared healthy joints with grade II and grade III luxation. They measured the kneecap and the thigh bone in detail, then calculated ratios describing how well the two parts fit together.

Kneecap size itself did not differ between groups, so the bone alone does not explain the condition. The groove that cradles the kneecap told a different story: grade III joints had a significantly shallower trochlear groove and a wider sulcus angle, signs of progressive flattening. The ratio of kneecap height to groove depth stood out as the most useful measure of mismatch. For surgeons, the message is to plan around the thigh bone's shape rather than the kneecap's size.
pmc-13393741:
Tung-Hu Tsai traces how remdesivir travelled from failed Ebola candidate to the first fully approved COVID-19 antiviral, arguing the journey was powered as much by law as by science. Emergency clearance landed on the first of May 2020, roughly ninety-five days after the drug was formally identified against the new coronavirus, and full approval followed that October. Unusually, the pivotal trial was designed and run not by the maker but by a United States government institute.

Tsai arranges the statutes into a life-cycle frame. The institute's legal authority produced the trial evidence in fourteen weeks. A defence research agency's flexible contracting funded at-risk manufacturing before approval. A biodefence law answered the market failure of a hospital-only drug. Production powers shored up home supply. Sustaining that legal machinery, the author concludes, is the soundest pandemic investment.
pmc-13394041:
Rintaro Yoshizumi and twelve colleagues tested whether heat shock protein 72, a stress-response chaperone, protects against atherosclerosis when its levels are raised by combined heat and mild electrical stimulation. Artery disease advances through oxidative stress and macrophage-driven inflammation, and earlier work tied this protein to metabolic abnormalities in diabetes. Mice lacking the apolipoprotein E gene, bred prone to plaques, were fed a high-fat diet with or without the stimulation, in both normal and protein-deleted lines.

Stimulation shrank lesions and their dead cores only in mice that could make the protein; without it the benefit vanished. Treated plaques carried less oxidative damage marker and fewer macrophages. In cultured macrophages the treatment raised the protein, suppressed inflammatory signals, blocked a stress kinase, and nudged macrophages from the inflammatory M1 state toward the reparative M2 state. The authors conclude protection runs through the protein, not blood sugar.
pmc-13394341:
Sophie Hu and Nathalie Auger write a 2026 letter that questions a study of pelvic floor symptoms after childbirth. The study they discuss followed women from a trial of two midwives versus one during labour. It found that second-degree tears, which reach the muscle between vagina and anus, showed no link to symptoms one year later. Hu and Auger worry that the trial itself shaped that result.

Because midwives in both groups tried to prevent severe tears, tears may have been fewer and milder than usual. Trial volunteers can also differ from other mothers, and many women did not reply. The letter urges care when trial data stand in for everyday births.
pmc-13395241:
Senyu Yang and colleagues chart, in 2026, slow brain waves across sleep and waking in 106 adults. Slow waves were long tied to deep sleep alone. Fresh proof shows like waves in waking and dream sleep too. Brain recordings from epilepsy patients let the team measure wave rate, slope, shape, and spread across regions in each state.

Wave features shifted with state in ways that fit rising and falling sleep pressure. Shape with many peaks changed the most between states. The features were sharp enough to sort waking, deep sleep, and dream sleep by wave data alone. The authors back the view that stray slow waves are sleep intrusions. Their values set norms for future work.
pmc-13395841:
Aurelio Amorim Reis and co-authors probe, in 2026, how a gum germ stirs immune alarms in fast-moving gum disease. Gum cells from healthy donors and from patients with grade C disease were dosed with extracts of the germ. The team read alarm genes, calming genes, and chemical tags on two key genes. The germ is a known driver of severe gum loss.

Patient cells ran hot on one sensor gene yet low on a calming gene. A master alarm gene woke after dosing in healthy cells but stayed flat in patient cells. Tag patterns on that gene also shifted only in healthy cells. The authors read a blunted, skewed local defence. That skew may feed lasting tissue loss.
pmc-13396041:
Piotr Paweł Chmielewski and colleagues review how worn-out cells that have stopped dividing drive the slow inflammation of aging, in a 2026 article. Such senescent cells are useful in the short term, helping embryos form, wounds heal, and tumors stay suppressed.

Trouble starts when these cells linger and build up in older tissue, leaking signals that inflame their surroundings, scar tissue, and weaken stem cells. Lab evidence links them to heart, metabolic, joint, lung, and brain disease. The review weighs treatments that clear these cells or mute their signals, called senotherapeutics, and sorts which ideas have solid backing and which still need proof in people.
pmc-13396341:

Knowing the likely target organ in advance could guide scans and early treatment for a cancer whose spread is its main killer.
pmc-13396441:

pmc-13396641:

She had poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and had just started a stronger glucose-lowering regimen when she grew sleepy, tired, and slurred her speech.

Oddly, her blood sugar read 4.1 millimoles per liter, above the usual low threshold, and her symptoms lingered even after glucose was given. pmc-13398141:

In the second study, the researchers separated her backgrounds. pmc-13399841:
Liu and co-authors describe, in 2026, a modified single-bundle ACL reconstruction that uses only the semitendinosus tendon, sparing the gracilis that standard hamstring harvests sacrifice. The native anterior cruciate ligament is roughly 30 millimeters long and 10 millimeters wide, and its loss destabilizes the knee and invites osteoarthritis. Their quadrupled semitendinosus graft is fixed on the tibia with two knotless anchors and on the femur with suspensory fixation.

Folded four times, the single tendon reaches a graft diameter usually between 7 and 9 millimeters, adequate for reconstruction without taking the second tendon. Preserving the gracilis better maintains the muscle function it serves, including knee flexion support. The femoral tunnel entry is placed through the anteromedial approach, its midpoint 6 millimeters from the posterior edge of the lateral femoral condyle. The authors present the technique, documented on video, as functional reconstruction with minimal disturbance to the knee's original anatomy.
pmc-13400141:

The pattern out-predicted established brain signatures for pain intensity and generalized to a different pain type, electrical stimulation. The authors present the model as a bridge between experimental and clinical pain measurement.
pmc-13400241:

pmc-13400741:
Shulang Lin and colleagues present, in 2026, a microscopy advance that sharpens chemical imaging of living cells without labels. Their framework, PHYSIQ, exploits the detection physics to record two perfectly aligned image channels at once, carrying the same signal but independent noise. That pairing trains a self-supervised restoration method with no ground truth needed. Signal quality rose by roughly twelve decibels while true chemical contrast held. The gain enables video-rate volumetric imaging and tracking of fat droplets moving inside live cells in three dimensions.
pmc-13401141:
Mao Yifan and co-authors test, in 2026, whether quercetin, a common plant flavonoid, can rescue placental cells struggling under low oxygen, a lab model of preeclampsia. Oxygen-starved trophoblast cells grew and invaded more slowly. They closed wounds more slowly too, died more and showed ramped-up autophagy, with a key growth pathway switched down. Quercetin reversed those changes. It restored growth and movement while calming the self-eating process through reactivating the pathway. Adding a pathway blocker erased quercetins benefits, supporting the proposed mechanism.
pmc-13401341:

pmc-13401541:
Francis Zamora and colleagues published a 2026 cell study of how docosahexaenoic acid, an omega-3 fat known as DHA, protects Schwann cells from damage by palmitic acid, a saturated fat. Schwann cells insulate peripheral nerves, and fat overload in diabetes and obesity is tied to neuropathic pain.

The team tracked recycling flow using LC3-II and p62 markers, stress signalling, calcium balance, and the lipid-carrying protein FABP5. Adding DHA alongside the harmful fat modulated those pathways, and the study maps how lipid handling, stress responses, and autophagy connect in this nerve cell injury model.
pmc-13401641:

The main results were survival measured from the second-line point, both overall and without progression, estimated with Kaplan-Meier curves. First-line systemic therapy is standard in this cancer. pmc-13402041:

A pituitary scan then showed a small tumor, confirmed after surgery as one making ACTH, the hormone that drives cortisol release. The full answer took 1.5 years from first presentation, likely because hormone output rose and fell in cycles.
pmc-13402441:

Partner violence was reported by 28.3 percent of women in the survey violence subsample.

After adjustment for home wealth, schooling, residence, and mother age, violence alone showed no clear link to any of the three outcomes. Household wealth stood out instead as the strong protective factor across every measure. The authors argue policy should fuse violence prevention into mother and child health work while attacking poverty itself.
pmc-13402741:

pmc-13402941:

A single framework tying origin, niche, and state changes together has been missing.

The review first maps where the states come from and how identity is maintained, then shows how specialized states run drainage, immune surveillance, and tolerance in health. Disease chapters follow the same cells reprogrammed in lymphatic disorders, inflammation and autoimmunity, cancer, cardiometabolic disease, and brain dysfunction. The authors close on translational openings, proposing precision lymphatic medicine aimed at these cell states.
pmc-13403041:
Mahin Nematollahi and Ahmad Ali Eslami build and validate a questionnaire that measures treatment adherence in dialysis patients through the lens of Social Cognitive Theory. Starting from 57 candidate items shaped by literature and experts, they tested the tool in 181 patients in Isfahan, Iran.

The final instrument sorts 30 items into six domains. Self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and social support cover the belief side. Communication skills, disease acceptance, and self-regulation cover the action side. Content validity scores ran high, internal consistency reached a Cronbach alpha of 0.88, and factor analysis confirmed the six-part structure explaining 57.33 percent of variance, with acceptable fit in confirmatory testing. Self-regulation tied most strongly to actual adherence behavior. The authors offer the culturally adapted scale for planning behavior-change support.
pmc-13403641:
Jakeline Barbara Alves and Rosângela Aparecida Pimenta checked a digital teaching game in 2026 that trains health workers to spot sepsis in children. Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can kill fast without quick care. Expert nurses and doctors judged the game in two rounds.

Eleven judges reviewed the first version screen by screen, and every suggestion they made was taken in. Nine judges then scored the revised game. Their agreement hit 100 percent, with a validity index near 0.99 on the scale used. The cleared game can now serve as a teaching tool for a high-stakes topic.
pmc-13403741:
Peilin Wang and many co-authors reviewed in 2026 how tropical crops cope with harsh and shifting growing conditions. Sugarcane, banana, cassava, rubber, and oil palm feed much of the world, yet face heat, drought, poor soils, and pests that often strike together. The review pulls gene-level work across scales into one view.

Gene traits underlie each crop's complex makeup, and shuffled gene blocks drive key survival traits. Farming and breeding have reshaped those genomes for yield, sometimes at a cost to toughness. The authors urge wider use of wild relatives, gene editing, and mixed tree-crop farms to breed hardier tropical harvests.
pmc-13404441:
Pierrick Martinez and a broad team warned in 2026 that natural supplements in cancer care can help or harm, based on dose and setting. Shoppers tend to see such products as safe by default. The review covers ten common agents, from vitamin C and vitamin D to melatonin and selenium.

Each agent can swing between shielding cells and stressing them, much like a coin with two faces. What matters is dose, route, body uptake, and the tumor's own chemistry state. Four checks guide safer use in their frame. One check asks whether cancer-fighting action beats the shield effect. Framing supplements as context-bound tools, not sure goods, is the core shift.
pmc-13404841:
Ritah F Mutagonda and colleagues lay out a 2026 protocol following African children who live with both sickle cell disease and malaria risk. Malaria can trigger painful crises, severe anaemia and death in these children. How often infection strikes each month, country by country, is still poorly measured.

The one-year study will enrol 2,808 children aged 6 months to 17 years at consortium clinics in seven countries. Staff will test for malaria at monthly visits and at extra sick visits over 12 months. Records will cover family background, gene type, past illness and symptoms. Results should inform guidance on preventive malaria medicine for children with sickle cell disease.
pmc-13405641:
Fabiana Bononi do Carmo and colleagues describe a fungal infection that spread through a child's body to the eye socket, in a 2026 case report. Sporotrichosis usually stays in skin and nearby tissue after contact with the Sporothrix fungus. Spread to organs is rare and harder to recognise.

The adolescent was followed for twelve months with a back lesion and lymph channel involvement that later reached the left orbit bone. Culture of deep tissue grew Sporothrix, confirming disseminated disease. Oral itraconazole ran for twelve months as treatment. Skin and bone lesions had fully cleared by month five, and the patient left follow-up after a year in good shape.
pmc-13405741:
Felicia Kneifel and co-authors study patchy blood flow in donor livers kept on a perfusion machine, in a 2026 German series. Machine perfusion at body temperature helps use more donor organs, yet uneven flow can starve parts of the liver. How often this happens and what it costs patients was unclear.

Records cover transplants at Münster between 2019 and 2024 where a CT scan followed within thirty days. Of 91 patients, twenty-seven showed focal under-perfusion on imaging, a rate of 29.7 percent in the reported figures. Heavier grafts were the only independent predictor, and weight tracked with the size of the pale area. Survival was unaffected, but complications and intensive care stays rose.
pmc-13407041:
Vincenzo Crisci and colleagues review, in 2026, the kinds of drawing and copying mistakes made by people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Copying shapes taps spatial skill, planning, attention, and meaning, so the pattern of errors might help tell one condition from another.

Following standard review methods, the team searched three databases for work from 1990 to January 2026 and kept 25 studies using standard tasks with qualitative error scoring. Spatial mistakes and simplified drawings appeared most often across disorders, while repeated elements, rotations, and drawing squeezed against a model were rarer. Alzheimer's disease leaned toward spatial disorganisation, omissions, and conceptual faults. Shared scoring systems, the authors say, would make studies easier to compare.
pmc-13407941:
Aruni S. Areti and co-authors quantify, in 2026, the extra danger carried by patients who arrive for leg trauma surgery already colonised by MRSA, the drug-resistant staphylococcus. Colonisation is a known hazard in planned joint replacement but under-studied in trauma. The team therefore used a large research network covering twenty years. They matched 1,868 colonised patients one-to-one with non-colonised controls.

After matching, colonised patients faced significantly higher odds of wound splitting, pneumonia, sepsis, kidney failure, blood transfusion, deep vein clots, and lung clots, with sepsis odds nearly quadrupled. Surgical site infection rates, surprisingly, did not differ significantly after matching. The authors propose preoperative screening as a risk-stratification tool, with decolonisation or tailored prophylaxis where feasible to blunt the systemic complications.
pmc-13408441:
Anastasia Theodoropoulou, Anita Nasrallah, and a large team investigate in 2026 a Golgi protein whose job is keeping the cell's sorting station stocked with its own enzymes. The protein, GOLPH3, loads resident enzymes into return vesicles as Golgi compartments mature. What controls GOLPH3 itself, and what happens to a whole animal without it, were open questions.

Mice lacking the protein showed disturbed sugar tagging of proteins and fats, growth failure, and poor bone mineralisation, with some embryos not surviving. At the molecular level, two opposing fatty attachments flip how the protein sits on the membrane, and only one orientation exposes the surface that grips enzyme tails for the return trip. The work ties a lipid-based switch to vertebrate development itself.
pmc-13409041:
Samantha J. Goldenstein and co-authors check whether saliva can track the hormones estradiol and progesterone across the menstrual cycle as blood tests do. Saliva sampling is non-invasive and easy to repeat daily. Their 2026 study enrolled physically active women and followed one or two cycles each.

Participants gave saliva daily at home and blood five times across two cycles, with ovulation confirmed by home tests and blood progesterone. Salivary hormone patterns followed the expected cycle shape. Saliva and blood values correlated strongly for progesterone and for the estradiol-to-progesterone ratio, but not for estradiol alone. In cycles without confirmed ovulation, no associations appeared. Agreement in absolute values was poor, so the authors conclude saliva cannot replace blood measurements, though it may reflect the biologically active hormone fraction more closely and suits pattern tracking.
pmc-13410741:
Farah Chouchene and co-authors present in 2026 three Tunisian siblings whose shared inherited condition affected each child's teeth quite differently. Ectodermal dysplasia disturbs skin, hair, and teeth, and missing or odd-shaped teeth form its main dental burden. Same family, same condition, yet the picture varied a lot.

The children were missing between two and eight teeth, with peg-shaped teeth and deep-rooted molars in the mix. Jaw measures showed uneven growth of the tooth-bearing bones, and the teenager felt real social distress. Care ranged from resin reshaping to a removable partial denture for the youngest, with braces referral and two years of growth checks. Tailored, gentle care restored function and looks.
pmc-13411141:
Bakare and co-authors investigate, in 2026, why childhood vaccine card records disagree with what caregivers say actually happened in Kiyawa, a rural district of Jigawa State, Nigeria, where only 32.9 percent of toddlers were fully immunized in the 2024 national survey. Their mixed-methods study, run from September 2022 to July 2023, examined records for 4258 children under five from 3232 women, then interviewed health workers and held community focus groups.

Caregivers judged 441 cards inaccurate, 10.4 percent of those examined in the survey. The main causes were cards filled in for vaccines never given, sometimes because stock ran out after the card was completed, lost or misplaced cards, and card stock-outs when vaccine was given. Any maternal education, versus none, was among the factors associated with inaccuracy in adjusted models. The authors caution that incentive schemes rewarding paperwork over actual vaccination worsen the data, and propose vaccine bracelets and text-message reminders as immediate fixes.
pmc-13414441:
Inês Amaro and co-authors review in 2026 the tangled link between obesity and tooth decay, two chronic conditions that stalk the same populations. Both share sugar-heavy diets, weak oral hygiene habits, and social disadvantage, which alone could manufacture an association. Their state-of-the-art synthesis also weighs saliva changes in obesity and the inflammatory and microbial threads that might bind the diseases biologically rather than merely socially.

Evidence supports shared roots, the authors conclude, not a direct causal arrow from body weight to cavities. Saliva in obesity does look more cavity-friendly, and inflammation markers plus mouth microbe shifts offer plausible bridges. Cross-sectional studies dominate the field, so they press for long-term work tracking both conditions together with standardized saliva measures across ages.
pmc-13414541:
Rhys-Jones and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how an ileal pouch adapts after surgery that removes the colon and builds a storage pouch from the small intestine's last stretch. The pouch must take over water absorption, storage, and controlled emptying in a new microbial setting, and early inflammation of its lining is common. The team searched the literature and weighed which adaptations help and which may feed pouchitis, the pouch's signature inflammation.

Useful changes include stronger water and salt recovery and the ability to stretch, while severe flattening of the absorptive fingers and altered bile acid handling may stir inflammation. Whether keeping small-intestine traits helps is unclear, and barrier leakiness and fuel use by lining cells remain poorly mapped. Knowledge of the ideal pouch microbe mix is thin, and current pouchitis treatments often disappoint. The authors call for studies joining structure, microbes, and diet to design targeted therapies.
pmc-13415741:
Alaa Bella and colleagues describe two Sudanese siblings with mucopolysaccharidosis, a rare inherited storage disorder, in a 2026 case series. An eighteen-year-old man and his thirteen-year-old half-sister showed progressive joint deformities plus problems across many body systems. Enzymes that should break down complex sugars called glycosaminoglycans are missing in this condition, so material builds up in tissues.

Coarse facial features, skeletal changes, and organ dysfunction form the classic pattern the authors used for clinical recognition. Enzyme and genetic testing are scarce in resource limited settings, which delays diagnosis there. Early suspicion still improves supportive care and genetic counseling for families, the authors argue.
pmc-13416441:
Benjamin R. Duewell and co-authors show how one lipid kinase throttles another to keep a key membrane lipid in balance, in 2026. The lipid PI(4,5)P2, though scarce, controls cell intake, movement, and channel activity, and its overproduction can feed cancer growth signals. PIP5K makes most of it; PIP4K was the suspected regulator under study.

PIP4K binds PIP5K and breaks up pairs of PIP5K molecules that form at the membrane. Without those pairs, PIP5K activity drops. That direct disruption gives cells a simple dial for lipid production. The model clarifies healthy control and what may go wrong in disease states tied to this pathway.
pmc-13417641:
Jonquil Pinto and colleagues follow acupuncture patients over time to see how health behaviour change unfolds, in a 2026 study based on interviews and recorded visits. Nine patient and practitioner pairs took part. The patients were mostly women aged 23 to 55. Three women practitioners gave the care.

Patients at distinct stages of readiness needed distinct kinds of help. Those swamped by symptoms and stress first needed calm and control. Those more ready needed help to stay on track. Trust in the practitioner and clear reasons for advice built a cycle that made change feel doable. Feeling better after care also pushed patients to act.
pmc-13418241:
Iddon and colleagues describe a 2026 chemistry method for reading the unit order in lab-made chains called REMO. These chains pair with matching partners through hydrogen bonds, much like DNA strands, and can guide the copying of new chains. Until now there was no direct way to check a chain's exact sequence.

The method cuts the chain backbone in two steps. Methyl iodide first tags nitrogen atoms along the backbone while leaving side chains untouched. Methylamine then cuts at those tagged sites, and each cut yields three fragments that a mass-based tool can read. The team showed the cuts work on chains of varied length and side chains. They also used the method to test how faithfully a mixed-sequence template was copied, a key step toward molecules that copy themselves.
pmc-13418441:
Robert J Oldham and a large team show that blocking certain antibody receptors can strengthen checkpoint immunotherapy, in a 2026 study. Checkpoint antibodies free T cells to attack tumours, yet many patients resist them. Receptors called Fc gamma receptors can blunt antibody action by engaging the drug's tail region in unhelpful ways.

Two tailored blockers were matched to two checkpoint drugs. One boosted regulatory T cell removal and reprogrammed tumour immune cells, raising killer T cell activity. The other shielded drug coated T cells from being eaten by macrophages. Both routes overcame resistance in animal and human cell models. Human trials of the selective blocker are under way.
pmc-13418741:
Yichen Zhang and colleagues probe the spin pattern inside very thin films of ruthenium dioxide, a material at the center of debate over a new kind of magnetism. Bulk samples show no clear magnetic order, yet strain from a surface below might change the picture in films just 2 nanometers thick. The team grew such films under strong stretch from their base layer.

Light-based tools that can read electron spin, backed by computer calculations, mapped the energy states of the film. The maps showed two spin textures living side by side, one that flips under mirror reflection and one that stays the same. Careful symmetry checks ruled out plain nonmagnetic causes for the pattern. The result points to a strain-born spin order that relaxed or thick material does not show, opening fresh ground for oxide electronics research.
pmc-13418941:
Shreya Ramachandran and colleagues present a near-silent MRI method for filming body processes as they happen, such as contrast dye uptake. Standard dynamic scans are loud, which hurts success with newborns, young children, and other sound-sensitive patients. Their method sweeps the scan path in smooth arcs that rotate step by step, keeping coverage even while the picture updates fast.

Tests on phantoms and in living subjects held image quality steady across a range of speeds. The arc path raised noise slightly over the quietest standard, by 0.3 to 14.2 decibels across settings tested, yet stayed far below normal sequences. Those standard scans ran louder by 20 to 35 decibels in the same comparisons. Quieter dynamic scans could widen who can be imaged without sedation.
pmc-13419241:
Tian Tan and colleagues compare three close cousin constructions in Mandarin Chinese that pair a verb with a word for downward motion. The three forms look alike and share ground in grammar and meaning, which makes them hard to separate by feel alone. The team used a counting method that measures how strongly certain verbs are drawn to each form.

Counts of real usage showed which verb types cling to which construction and how far side meanings stretch from the core one. Each form carries its own center of meaning, with the others shading off in set directions. Maps of pull strength make those shades visible rather than guessed. Language teachers and grammar writers can use the maps to explain a contrast that textbooks often leave fuzzy.
pmc-13419341:
Ryan B Choi and Rohan Khera trace how artificial intelligence is changing the electrocardiogram from a simple diagnostic tracing into a digital biomarker. The heart tracing has anchored cardiac care for a century, read by eye for known patterns. Machine learning now mines the same lines for risks and traits no human reader can see.

The review covers deep learning methods, the use of tracing images, and small wearable devices that could spread the tools worldwide. Gains in reach come with open problems in openness of the models, in which traits they pick up, and in slow uptake at real clinics. The authors sort what is proven from what is promised. Clinicians get a map of where AI heart readings already help and where caution still rules.
pmc-13419441:
Aditi Ramakrishnan and colleagues argue that sexually transmitted infection care and antibiotic stewardship, long run as separate fields, should plan together. The trigger is doxy PEP, a dose of doxycycline taken after sex to prevent infection, which raises worries about breeding resistant germs. Gonorrhea resistant to that drug family already appears more often among users in trial data.

The authors lay out shared tools, from joint clinics to combined data systems, for guiding both the preventive drug and the tests around it. Resistance checks in related bacteria and in the gut are part of the plan. Working together could protect a useful prevention tool from losing power early. The piece gives program leaders concrete forms that the partnership could take.
pmc-13419641:
Dobihal and colleagues report a 2026 study of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium behind many drug-resistant hospital infections. One strain, ST258, dominates worldwide for unclear reasons. The team traced a control system in the bacterium, called CrrAB, and found it switches on a gene for a protein they named CfmP, which alters the bacterium's hair-like fimbriae.

Using protein analysis, the team showed CfmP adds an oxygen-based change to a single building block in a fimbria protein, a chemical edit not described before in this context. Without CfmP, the bacterium lost the virulence that the control system normally drives, which marks the edit as essential to causing disease.  Blocking CfmP could blunt this pathogen without killing it outright.
pmc-13420141:
Nicola J Reavley and colleagues assess 25 years of Beyond Blue, Australia's national mental health awareness effort, against population survey data. Campaigns to lift public understanding of mental illness have run for decades in many countries, with effects that are hard to prove. Beyond Blue paired awareness drives with carer support, early help, primary care reform, and research funding from the start.

National surveys of literacy, stigma, and service use show broad gains across the period. Mid-2000s analysis found that states with heavier campaign exposure showed better recognition of depression and sounder beliefs about treatment. Early national data had shown half the public blaming weakness of character for depression, a view that has faded. The paper weighs how much of the shift one program can fairly claim.
pmc-13420341:
AlQahtani, Pacheco, and AlBadran described in 2026 a technique for repairing a torn posterior labrum with the patient seated upright. The labrum is the cartilage rim that deepens the shoulder socket. Most surgeons use a side-lying setup for this repair, and the seated pose is said to hide the rim's lower back part. Posterior shoulder instability is uncommon but causes real pain and lost function, above all in contact and overhead athletes.

AlQahtani sets out a repeatable method. A back-side viewing portal exposes the hidden lower rim. Front and back portals swap between viewing and working roles. A controlled forward push on the arm bone opens the view. Anchors fix the rim from bottom to top, restoring its shape and the joint capsule's tension. The note keeps the comfort and access gains of the seated position while following standard repair principles, the authors say.
pmc-13420841: Sumiyama introduces himself in this 2026 message as the new editor-in-chief of DEN Open, the Japan Gastroenterological Endoscopy Society's open-access journal. He thanks his predecessor, the founding editor, and the society leaders who appointed him. He pledges careful peer review that respects authors' time. Above all he champions case reports, arguing that rare clinical experiences, however small the study, can teach lessons that directly help future patients. He especially invites younger colleagues worldwide to submit their work.
pmc-13422941:
Zhang and colleagues, writing for the CHOPARD committee in 2026, examine whether antiphospholipid antibodies in the blood predict bad pregnancy outcomes. The women studied have lupus, an autoimmune disease that mainly strikes women of childbearing age. These antibodies are known risk factors in the general population.

The single-center Chinese cohort covered 441 pregnancies in 410 patients, and about one in six patients carried the antibodies. Adverse outcomes, defined as fetal death, early severe pre-eclampsia, or early severe placental failure, struck nearly twice as often in antibody-positive pregnancies. Not all antibody types mattered equally. The IgG forms of two antibodies and the lupus anticoagulant each raised risk, while the IgM forms did not. The highest-risk pattern combined the lupus anticoagulant with at least one IgG antibody, which roughly quadrupled the odds of an adverse outcome.
pmc-13423141:
Joanne Welsh and four co-authors publish a protocol for a scoping review of maternity care for autistic women and birthing people in the United Kingdom. Services there face growing scrutiny for missing diverse needs, and autistic patients can meet extra barriers through communication differences, rigid routines, and low staff awareness.

The review will search several major databases for work published between January 2000 and July 2026, then screen reference lists for more. Extracted material will cover study setting, focus, and findings. The team plans to map the literature by domain, covering both patients' experiences and the difficulties professionals face in giving good care. Their aim is a clear picture of where provision falls short.
pmc-13423941:
Sharma and co-authors set out in 2026 to establish normal values for a handheld device that tests feeling in hands and feet. Doctors need such values when judging nerve damage from diabetes. Their study population was healthy adults in India.

The team tested 345 adults aged 18 to 93 who had no diabetes or nerve disease, measuring vibration, warmth, and cold thresholds on both sides of the body. Thresholds were consistently higher at the foot than at the hand, meaning the feet felt less. Vibration and warmth thresholds rose with age, while cold thresholds changed little. Women were generally more sensitive than men. Height, weight, and body mass index had no meaningful effect, so the authors present age- and sex-based reference values.
pmc-13424741:
Milad Faraji, Maedeh Faraji, and Nasrin Kazemipour catalogue the ways scientists induce diabetes in laboratory animals, since the disease's mix of hormone, metabolic, and immune faults cannot be reproduced in a dish. Their review sorts the toolbox into five families and gives mechanisms, typical doses, and timing for each.

Chemical agents such as streptozotocin and alloxan dominate practice for their simplicity and low cost. Diets and hormones model the overfed route to type 2 disease, while viruses and immune triggers mimic autoimmune attack. Surgery removes part of the pancreas directly. Bred strains, from NOD mice to GK rats, develop disease on their own. Comparative tables weigh fidelity against convenience for both major diabetes types.
pmc-13425541:
Jing Huang and colleagues built a leaner computer program for outlining organs and tumours in medical scans, a task called segmentation. Most such programs use two halves, a reader and a rebuilder, but theirs drops the rebuilder to save computing power.

Called R3Net, the program instead refines its picture in loops, reusing the same stages and blending features from several scales. The team tested it on heart MRI scans, belly CT scans, and thyroid ultrasound images. It matched the accuracy of standard two-half models while using fewer settings and less computation. Huang argues that careful refinement inside the reader half alone can carry the whole segmentation task.
pmc-13426941:
Abejirinde and colleagues built in 2026 a standard way to classify remote patient monitoring programs, so very different services can be compared fairly. Monitoring at home expanded fast during the pandemic, but with no shared labels, judging which programs work, and for whom, is guesswork. The team reviewed real programs across several countries and health conditions.

Eighty-seven articles supplied the raw material, worked over with clinicians, managers, researchers, and patient partners. Twelve common features, from program size and data flow to alert handling and equity aims, were grouped into four domains. Two domains, integration and equity, are goals every program should chase. The other two run on scales where neither end is automatically better. Crossing the four gives sixteen program types, offered as a guide for design and investment.
pmc-13427341:
Trouilloud and Dubois wrote in 2026 an insight piece on new tools for watching the earliest heart take shape inside living mouse embryos. The heart is the first organ to work in an embryo. Errors in its forming cause many birth defects, yet its tissue movements had never been measured continuously at cell detail. The piece discusses work by Raiola, Torres, and colleagues in Spain.

Their computer pipeline stitches many live-imaging datasets into one continuous model of the forming heart tube. It tracks how patches of tissue deform as the flat cell sheet folds into a tube, and it predicts rearrangements at the level of single cells, deeper than earlier methods reached. The analysis shows the deformation follows strongly compartmentalized patterns. Trouilloud and Dubois present the approach as a step toward virtual models of development.
pmc-13427441:
Michihide Maeda and coauthors tested preoperative predictors of extra therapy after surgery for stage IB cervical cancer in a 2026 retrospective study of 191 patients. Radical hysterectomy is standard at this stage, yet many patients then need adjuvant treatment, exposing them to dual-modality burdens. Candidate predictors were tumor size on MRI scans and blood levels of squamous cell carcinoma antigen measured before surgery.

Receiver operating analysis set cutoff values for each marker, with a focused look at stage IB1 to IB2 cases. Knowing likely adjuvant need before surgery helps counseling about combined treatment and fertility or recovery trade-offs.
pmc-13427641:
Spura, Elgabarty, and Kühne speed up a gold standard simulation method so it can treat electron correlation and quantum nuclei. Path integral dynamics smears each atom into a ring of copies to capture quantum jiggle, but pricing the best electron math on every copy is slow. Their 2026 method prices a cheap approximation on the ring. The expensive coupled cluster correction runs only on the ring's center. Two tricks stack on top, all three layers needed to make the math feasible.

They aim the method at a proton shared between water and formaldehyde, a lopsided hydrogen bond. Quantum nuclei widened the bond length spread and pulled the proton back from its classical lean toward formaldehyde. The chance of finding it nearer formaldehyde fell from four fifths to three fifths of the time. Magnetic shielding readouts showed electron correlation and nuclear quantum effects pulling with like strength, sometimes in opposite directions.
pmc-13427741:
Santos and Keane proposed in 2026 a honesty standard for health studies that use federated learning. Federated learning trains artificial intelligence across institutions without pooling raw data, and it is sold as privacy-preserving. The authors argue that most health papers using the label are in fact single-site simulations. They borrow the self-driving car scale, which grades automation from level 0 to level 5, to grade real federation.

Their six levels run from no federation at all to fully self-running systems that keep learning across separate institutions. Middle levels cover pure maths simulations and real but limited multi-site training. They propose that every study state its level in one sentence inside its abstract. The authors compare the scheme to reporting rules already used for clinical trials and prediction models in medicine.
pmc-13427941:
Yalikun and colleagues published a 2026 study on kidney injury after brain vessel surgery. Dye used during neuroendovascular surgery can strain the kidneys afterward. The team reviewed 2,412 patients treated under general anesthesia over a decade. They compared injury rates across five kinds of brain vessel problems.

Overall, fewer than two in a hundred patients developed kidney injury. Rates jumped to about one in ten for bleeding aneurysm and neck artery cases. By contrast, unruptured aneurysm cases sat near half a percent overall. Diabetes and kidneys already under strain added risk on their own. The authors call for prevention plans tailored to each procedure type. Kidney checks after surgery deserve extra weight in high-risk groups.
pmc-13428341:
Christina M. Campagna and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, how a helper protein finds its place inside cilia, the hair-like sensors on cells. The protein, RIC-8, assists a class of signaling proteins and gathers in one special zone near the cilium's base. Faults in proteins of that zone cause a family of diseases called ciliopathies. Work ran in both roundworms and human cells, letting the team cross-check findings.

In worms, RIC-8 settled into its zone as larvae developed, guided by a short protein motif and by the transport trains that move cargo along cilia. It also tuned how a smell-sensing neuron answered chemical cues. In human cells, both RIC-8 versions proved necessary to build cilia at all. Cell biologists gain a map of how a conserved signaling helper is delivered and what it does on arrival.
pmc-13431541:
Mariam M AlEissa and a large team measured antibody responses to the COVID virus in a Saudi cohort in 2026. They asked what sets severe cases apart from the most grave ones. The group study spanned several centers and 406 people, sorted into five bands from healthy controls to patients in intensive care.

Two antibody types rose with illness level across most bands, yet the severe and intensive care bands showed no clear gap between them. A stand-in test of how well antibodies block the virus from latching onto cells showed no split across bands at all. Older age and extra health faults tracked with worse illness, while sex did not. The authors say antibody counts show exposure and immune stir, yet counts alone cannot explain the slide into grave illness.
pmc-13431641:
Samuel A Miller, William B O'Dell, and Flora Meilleur charted in 2026 how rising X-ray dose warps fine detail of a fiber-cut enzyme. The team drew thirty-six models of the same enzyme from one crystal, each from data soaked with more dose than the last. Such work ranks as the best way to catch crystal harm from X-rays.

Radiation harm comes in two kinds: a broad fade that shows early, and spot harm at set sites that stays hidden until model building. Spot harm can cut key bonds or strip parts from amino acids, which tempts readers to mistake scars for real traits of the enzyme. At the active site, dose-linked shifts in charge clouds grew plain across the series. The authors urge tight dose limits in cold crystal work on this enzyme class.
pmc-13431841:
Hasan and collaborators used whole-genome optical mapping on one family. The method images very long DNA strands to spot large changes. In this family, myotonic dystrophy type 1 passed from father to children. A separate Parkinson's disease ran alongside it. The family's pattern was odd, with shifts in how hard it hit and repeat changes from parents to children.

The young-onset proband carried a 10-fold expansion of the disease repeat, with heavy methylation. Her healthy father passed a 1.8-fold shrunk version to a younger sibling. Ill aunts showed wide genome-wide copy number changes. These included loss of a chromosome 19 segment linked to Parkinson's disease, plus losses on chromosomes 16, 17, and 22. The proband also carried large breaks touching six suspect genes and deep global hypomethylation. The authors suggest genome shakiness passed down the family helps explain its varied pictures.
pmc-13433941:
Ming Li and co-authors taught a deep net in 2026 to name single molecules. It reads the faint current dips they make in a pore. Such reads could one day spell proteins and sugars letter by letter. Kin molecules make near-twin dips, which blurs the call. Stock nets miss the fine time grain and train too flat to catch weak tells.

Their frame sharpens dips with a sliding spread gauge, mines weak tells with a time-weave net, and reweighs hard cases as training runs. Test piles span sugar kinds, root drugs, DNA bits, and bile kin, at mixed hard grades. The frame beat top rivals by wide steps on each pile and carried its skill to fresh piles. The authors pitch it as a broad tool for pore reads.
pmc-13434041:
Bob Meeusen and co-authors swept the genome in 2026 to map what a clan of protein tag removers needs to work. They found a charge feeder that wakes two of the three kin forms. These removers burn metal hearts to strip tags and steer cell signals. Whole-genome cut screens plus fine letter edits built the map.

The feeder grips the two forms through its head tail and lends electrons from a held blood pigment to their metal hearts. Both forms run rust-shy, so the feed keeps them live. The third kin form wants no such feed. Cell tests tie the wake path to how cells meet DNA harm. The authors hint that cell rust state talks to picked removers through this gate.
pmc-13434241:
Jonah Kember and colleagues track how the hippocampus, a brain area key for memory, changes shape and job from age 5 to 21. Brain scans from 471 young people were mapped one person at a time. The team split the long brain area into front and back systems.

With age the back system shrank in area by 39.4 percent yet worked more on its own. Its border with the front part grew sharper over time. Links from the back system to mid parietal areas grew with age and with better memory scores. The pattern helps explain why memory for places gets stronger as children grow.
pmc-13434441:
Feng and colleagues examine SETD2, a gene tuning protein that marks DNA for reading, in the gut lining and its microbes. Loss of balance between host and gut microbes is a hallmark of inflammatory bowel disease. Their 2026 study deletes SETD2 only in mouse gut lining cells. It then profiles gene activity, chromatin openness, fecal microbes, and small molecules to trace how the deletion stirs colitis, colon inflammation.

Without SETD2, the gut lining overproduced Reg3 lectins, proteins that kill bacteria, and the microbe mix skewed: helpful resident species thinned while waste products built up. When the team transplanted fecal microbes from healthy like donors into the knockout mice, the worsened colitis eased markedly. Host gene tuning thus guards the gut's microbial balance, the authors conclude. Restoring that balance can offset the damage when the guard fails, a fresh angle for bowel disease therapy.
pmc-13434741:
Cheng and co-authors monitored a 34.9 meter deep subway station excavation in Tianjin's soft soil, built top-down, to map how digging deforms the retaining walls, ground, and neighboring buildings over time. They contrasted the top-down sequence with conventional bottom-up excavation using field instruments and numerical simulations of both approaches.

Top-down digging produced much smaller horizontal wall displacement than bottom-up excavation, and the depth of peak displacement migrated downward more slowly as digging advanced. Soil heave beneath the pit lifted the diaphragm wall by up to 20 millimeters, creating differential movement over 10 millimeters between wall and columns inside the excavation. That heave worsened uneven settlement of adjacent buildings, lifting far-side foundations while near sides settled downward. The ratio of peak surface settlement to peak wall movement ranged from 0.4 to 2.0 once uplift was counted.
pmc-13436341:
Jordi Corral and coauthors find a Klebsiella pump twin that shapes drug response and virulence in 2026. Klebsiella pneumoniae haunts hospitals with lung, blood, and urine infections. The pump, SxtPR, was first found in a cousin germ where it drove resistance and disease.

The Klebsiella version plays a like dual role, the team reports. Pumps of this family push drugs out of the cell, which blunts antibiotic action. A pump that also aids virulence makes a tempting drug target. Blocking it could both resensitize germs and disarm them. Follow up work can test pump blockers in infection models.
pmc-13437241:
Alvin Kwon and colleagues used a large United States kidney cohort to test whether phosphate balance tracks with stubborn high blood pressure. In chronic kidney disease, phosphate builds up and harms vessels, while blood pressure that resists three or more drugs is common and deadly. Their 2026 analysis drew on the CRIC study and kept 3,752 adults with full pressure data.

Patients in the top quarter for blood phosphate had higher odds of resistant pressure than those in the bottom quarter. A urine measure of phosphate showed a similar link, and a combined burden index, built by multiplying phosphate by parathyroid hormone, showed the strongest tie, with odds more than doubled. The links held after other factors were weighed in adjusted models. The authors stop short of claiming cause, and they propose trials to test whether easing phosphate load can soften pressure that drugs alone fail to control.
pmc-13439641:
Muhammad Asim, Essa Abdulla Abuhelaiqa, and Hassan Ali Al Malki describe how Qatar kept living kidney donors returning for lifelong checks, reporting in 2026. Donors face slightly higher long-term risks of high blood pressure, diabetes, and kidney failure, so follow-up matters. Many countries struggle to keep donors in view. Qatar's national program, run from Hamad Medical Corporation since January 2017, requires kidney clinic visits at one and six months, then yearly, with standard tests each time.

The register held 349 donors, 233 of whom gave after the program began. Early visit rates stayed near complete, and yearly attendance held above ninety percent from 2020 onward even as donor numbers quadrupled. Phone visits carried the service through the pandemic years. The authors credit coordinator outreach, redesigned routines, donor teaching, and steady quality checks for the durable record.
pmc-13439841:
Areni Altun and colleagues listen to migrant mothers in Australia describe hunting for mental health support around birth, reporting in 2026. Migrant women face higher rates of distress in pregnancy and after birth, layered with cultural and system barriers. Online focus groups and interviews gathered accounts from women of Chinese, Arabic, and Indian language backgrounds who had given birth in Australia. Conversations ran with interpreter help and were read for shared patterns.

Three themes emerged from the accounts. Services felt fragmented and hard to navigate, with support that often missed cultural expectations. Stigma, traditional beliefs, and broken family networks shaped whether women spoke up or sought help. Digital platforms offered connection and guidance, yet language gaps and uneven digital skills limited their reach. The authors call for care pathways built around migrant women's real circumstances, online and off.
pmc-13440441:
Lucy Beggs and colleagues review methods for judging the cost-effectiveness of whole cancer treatment sequences, writing for health technology assessment audiences in 2026. Cancer patients often move through several lines of therapy, so judging one drug alone can mislead. Pathway models add decision points to compare sequences and the best entry point for a new option. The team searched for methodological papers and past reviews, then gathered best-practice advice on model structure and evidence gathering.

Nine structure papers and five evidence papers qualified. Patient-level models fed by data spanning multiple treatment lines earned the strongest backing. A flexible multi-state network method was the best-rated way to gather evidence, though sparse data often forces separate analyses per line. The authors warn that thin data can erase the gains pathway models promise, and they call for methods built for data-poor settings.
pmc-13440741:
Yousif and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 60-year-old farmer in a low-resource setting. His single brain lesion looked like a tuberculoma or a glioblastoma on scans, but it proved to be a parasite cyst. He presented with one week of seizures and worsening weakness on his left side, and he had previously been treated for tuberculosis in the lungs.

MRI showed a ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe. Surgeons removed it completely through a skull opening, and tissue testing revealed a cysticercus larva, the tapeworm stage that causes neurocysticercosis, surrounded by inflammation. He then received two weeks of the antiparasitic drug albendazole plus seizure medicines. Follow-up imaging showed the lesion gone, and he recovered fully and stayed seizure-free. The authors urge keeping parasites in mind for such lesions.
pmc-13441341:
Zahl-Olsen and co-authors independently tested the Individual Problems and Strengths scale, a therapy-monitoring questionnaire inside the Systemic Therapy Inventory of Change, using records from 841 Norwegian therapy clients. Routine outcome systems only help if their constructs hold up, so the team applied a stepwise confirmatory factor analysis designed specifically for validity testing.

The original eight-factor version of the scale received satisfactory support for its construct validity in their analysis of the client data. Its scale reliability, however, earned only poor to mixed support across the eight factors examined. Every alternative factor structure, whether proposed earlier or recently, failed to find support in their stepwise testing procedure. The authors conclude the developers should go back to the future: refine the original eight-factor model and abandon the rival versions that accumulated around it over the years.
pmc-13441841:
Patrick Louie G Lipio and colleagues dissect rice mutants that trade main root length for a thicket of side roots, reporting in 2026. Roots buy water and nutrients at a real carbon price, so shape matters for crop efficiency. The teg1 mutant grows stunted seminal and crown roots with sleepy root tips, yet sprouts denser and longer large lateral roots, the branching kind. Crossing it with our1, a mutant that stretches every root type, set up a test of carbon budgeting.

The double mutant poured growth into large laterals while main roots stayed short, and total root length matched the wild type. Radioactive carbon tracing showed fresh carbon streaming preferentially into those elongating laterals. Root-to-shoot weight balance stayed normal despite the reshuffle. The authors present the gene pair as a genetic lever for building root systems that spend carbon where foraging pays best.
pmc-13442741:
Bhanu Ramachandran and colleagues report a 58-year-old man whose body formed clots in many places at once in a 2026 case paper. He had no past illness, yet scans found lung clots, large loose clots in two heart chambers, and artery clots that starved his left leg. His heart pumped weakly, with an output share of 20 percent on scan, and his rhythm ran in flutter.

Clot-cause tests, from immune clot states to broad panels, came back clear. Surgeons first pulled clots from his leg, then built a bypass that clotted again, and at last cut the leg below the knee. Gene tests later found a faulty titin gene, which explained his weak heart muscle. He left on a blood thinner, and rhythm care later held his heart in steady beat.
pmc-13443541:
Zhujun Zhang and colleagues build an air-stable surface electrene for ammonia making in a 2026 paper. Electrenes float a sheet of loose electrons at their surface, a gift for reactions that need electron gifts. Most such materials die on contact with air or damp, which has capped their use.

Their oxygen-doped BaSiN2 kept its active skin in open air, with a work function near 1.5 eV that marks easy electron gifts. Surface electrons switch nitrogen gas on, and hydrogen steps then renew the active skin in a loop. With ruthenium loaded on top, the catalyst made ammonia at 43 mmol per gram per hour at 300 degrees and mild pressure. Air steadiness beat top rival catalysts in their tests.
pmc-13444141:
Hejia Henry Wang and colleagues test a mutant KRAS peptide vaccine with twin immune drugs in metastatic colon cancer in a 2026 trial. These tumors, stable under standard gene checks, shrug off brake-freeing drugs alone. KRAS faults, found in about 40 percent of such cancers, can mint targets that vaccines teach T cells to hunt.

Thirteen pretreated patients took the pooled vaccine, which covers six KRAS faults, plus nivolumab and ipilimumab. Both prime aims, safety and immune spark within 17 weeks, were met in the run. Vaccine-linked harms stayed grade 1 or 2 in all cases. Tumor-hunting T cells rose in 8 of 12 checked patients on direct tests, and in all 12 after lab growth. The team backs wider trials of the pairing.
pmc-13444641:
Mi-Kyung Park and colleagues examine a protein from Acanthamoeba, a tiny free-living amoeba, as a possible new cause of airway allergy, in a 2026 study. The protein, called profilin, belongs to a family known for cross-reactions between pollens and plant foods. Earlier mouse work had linked it to inflamed airways, but its role in people was unclear.

Skin prick tests covered 176 patients with allergic airway disease, alongside a standard panel of common airborne triggers. Thirteen patients reacted to the amoeba protein, and most of those also reacted to tree, grass, or weed pollen. Blood tests and cell studies showed a mixed response tied to both allergy and inflammation, which supports adding the protein to allergy testing.
pmc-13444741:
Mengdie Zhao and colleagues build a chart-based tool that estimates survival for patients with cancer spread to the brain who receive radiation treatment, published in 2026. Doctors lack a shared way to judge how long such patients may live, yet that judgment shapes care choices. The group set out to build a score from facts that clinics already record.

Records came from 298 patients treated between January 2020 and December 2021. Six factors carried the score: sex, the type of the first cancer, a standard grade for brain spread, tumor control, and two kinds of drug treatment given around radiation. Split at a set score, low-risk and high-risk groups lived for clearly different spans, and checks showed fair accuracy for one, two, and three year estimates.
pmc-13446041:
Shutong Liu and colleagues test five food-grade gums as additives for flour from germinated indica rice, hunting for one that slows staling and one that firms the gel, in a 2026 study. Germination lifts the grain's nutrition, yet the flour turns stale fast and its structure wobbles. Each gum brings a distinct chemistry to the mix.

Soybean hull gum gave the weakest setback on cooling, the sign of the strongest brake on short-term staling. Carrageenan gave the hardest gel and the most ordered, linked framework. Tests of water movement, crystal form, and heat behavior showed the first gum spreading water and breaking starch order, while the second wove the network tighter. The pair split the honors, guiding gum choice by product goal.
pmc-13447341:
Hermisson and colleagues present a 2026 expert statement on home care for severely ill ME/CFS patients, a long-term condition marked by exhaustion. Its defining feature is post-exertional malaise: even minor physical, mental, or sensory effort can trigger a crash in symptoms. Family members give most of the care and often lack support. 

The guide structures daily care so it prevents overexertion and keeps the patient's condition stable. Measures were gathered from what patients and family caregivers found effective in practice, then sorted and refined by professionals.  They also name gaps in knowledge and services. The statement gives concrete direction for a group whose needs are often misunderstood.
pmc-13448041:
Chen presents a 2026 commentary, written as a letter, on hip positioning during single-position lateral spinal fusion surgery. The commented study measured how hip configurations in the side-lying position change lumbar curve and pelvic angles, aiming to guide positioning for fusion outcomes. Chen praises the systematic X-ray evaluation but raises a confounder the field must settle.

Muscle relaxation from general anesthesia may itself explain much of the lumbar curve reduction seen, since awake positioning differs from anesthetized positioning. Prior studies have shown anesthesia relaxes the paraspinal muscles that hold the curve. If the drug, not the hip angle, drives the change, positioning advice built on these measurements could mislead surgical teams. The letter models useful peer critique: it names one variable that could overturn the conclusion and asks for it to be controlled.
pmc-13448841:
Heng Jiang and colleagues build in 2026 a flexible camera modeled on the compound eye of the fruit fly, aimed at mixed-reality headsets that must follow moving scenes. The fly's vision pairs panoramic eyes with head muscles for tracking in dim light and neural circuits for fast processing. The team's device copies all three levels in artificial form.

Plastic optical fibers and curved microlens arrays give real-time panoramic imaging, while two tethers mimic head muscles to sweep the view across 270 degrees and hold weak signals in sight. A learning algorithm plays the neural role, rebuilding interactive mixed-reality scenes at up to 7,000 frames per second. The authors frame the camera as a step toward bioinspired wearables that keep wide, continuous track of their surroundings.
pmc-13450241:
Ruiqin Peng and colleagues review in 2026 manganese oxide catalysts for lithium-oxygen batteries, a chemistry whose energy density could dwarf today's lithium-ion cells. The promise stalls on sluggish reactions, side products, and insulating lithium peroxide crusting the cathode until the battery chokes. Manganese oxides appeal as rescuers because they are abundant, cheap, and structurally varied, coming in tunnel, layered, and spinel forms with adjustable oxidation states that host oxygen reactions and lithium traffic.

The review organizes recent engineering moves: reshaping pores, tuning surface sites, punching in defects, doping with foreign atoms, and building composites. Each lever shifts the catalyst's electronic structure and steers whether lithium peroxide forms as films or particles and how cleanly it decomposes on recharge, which decides polarization losses and cycle life. The authors close with the field's remaining obstacles and design guidelines meant to carry these catalysts toward practical cells.
pmc-13452241:
Rengeerli Sa and co-authors feed in 2026 a creatine-building compound to Tibetan sheep and track meat quality through the gut-muscle path. The trial held 120 young male sheep in four groups for ninety days, with the compound at three doses over a base diet. Gut germ reads, muscle molecule scans, and meat tests were tied together.

The top dose shifted set gut germ groups and raised two useful gut acids. Muscle fat-path molecules moved, and meat in that group showed stronger antioxidant power, a redder tone, and a tenderer bite. Links among gut germs, muscle molecules, and meat traits backed the gut-muscle story. The authors back the compound as a feed plus for plateau sheep.
pmc-13453441:
Pascal Gottmann and nine co-authors ask why Göttingen minipigs resist fatty liver disease that plagues people and other pig breeds. Their 2026 study compares liver gene activity in these minipigs with that of humans, mice, and pig breeds prone to the disease. The disease, shortened to MASLD, builds fat in the liver and ties to diabetes and scarring.

The minipig liver switched 692 genes in a pattern no other group shared, touching fuel use and signal paths. Eleven gene switches, three liver made hormones, and six other secreted proteins stood out as the strongest candidates. A network analysis put two switches, HMBOX1 and PATZ1, at the hub, steering about 41 percent of the changed genes. The team offers these genes and proteins as leads for drugs that could copy the minipig's protection.
pmc-13454441:
Joonggon Kim and five colleagues present, in 2026, an image-based method to grade gray mold damage in stored kiwifruit without cutting the fruit open. The mold, Botrytis cinerea, shortens shelf life for the golden Haegeum variety. The team sorted infected fruit into four levels, from no marks to heavy fungal growth and tissue collapse.

Fruit softened as damage rose, and breathing rates climbed with each level. A ripening gas appeared at level three and spiked at level four. Their learning system focused on the lesion area rather than the whole photo. Three network designs each reached about 90 percent accuracy in sorting the levels. Heat maps confirmed the models looked at the mold itself, not the background. The authors offer the setup as a fair, explainable grader for packing sheds.
pmc-13458741:
Yu Jiang, Juan Yang and Shanshan Yang published this 2026 study testing whether three blood markers together spot sepsis in newborns better than any one alone. Neonatal sepsis is a leading cause of newborn death, yet its early signs are vague. The markers, interleukin-6, procalcitonin and serum amyloid A, all rise with infection. The authors measured them at admission in babies in a neonatal intensive care unit, before antibiotics began.

The study enrolled 140 newborns: 60 with confirmed sepsis, 40 with suspected sepsis and 40 without infection. All three markers ran much higher in confirmed sepsis, and higher still in severe cases. Individually, the markers scored between 0.908 and 0.932 on the standard accuracy curve measure. Combined, the panel reached 0.985, catching 93.3 percent of cases while correctly clearing 92.5 percent of non-cases in this sample. The authors propose the trio as a fast support to blood culture for early diagnosis and severity grading.
pmc-13459341:
Dawei Wang and co-authors mapped the scale and drivers of urinary stone disease in eastern China using health records for nearly a million people. Their 2026 prospective cohort study drew on the Yinzhou electronic records system covering 966,481 participants followed between 2009 and 2022. The team estimated how incidence changed year by year and which lifestyle and metabolic factors raised risk, calculating how many cases might be prevented by removing each factor from the population.

Stone incidence climbed steadily, rising 5.3 to 6.8 percent per year from the mid-2010s to 2021, and roughly one in ten Chinese adults is affected overall. Smoking, drinking, high body mass index, diabetes, abnormal blood lipids, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease all raised risk, while regular exercise protected against stones. The prevention math was striking: weekly exercise carried the largest population benefit, needing only about twenty-one people active to avert one case in the reported measure.
pmc-13459841:
Qingting Bu, Jin Yang, Hua Cheng, Zhenyu Pan, and Tao Zhang measured in 2026 how unevenly the tuberculosis burden falls across countries. Drawing on Global Burden of Disease 2021 data for 204 countries and territories, they tracked disability-adjusted life years from 1990 to 2021. Two statistical lenses were used: a slope index capturing absolute inequality linked to social development, and a Gini index capturing relative spread.

Absolute inequality fell by more than half across the three decades, which sounds like progress. Relative inequality nevertheless crept upward, with the Gini index rising slightly over the same period. Regional gaps stayed wide, and both measures dipped then climbed with age. The authors urge research into the drivers behind these stubborn disparities.
pmc-13459941:
Priscila Machado and co-authors surveyed Australian adults on what they actually know about ultra processed foods, the industrial formulations now blamed for much diet related disease. Public debate uses the term constantly, but nobody had mapped lay understanding nationally. Their 2026 study questioned 1,086 adults aged twenty to sixty four in mid 2024 with free listing tasks. It also used image identification of products among twenty foods, knowledge scoring, and sorting tasks that reveal which attributes people attach to the ultra processed label.

Respondents described what came to mind for the term and attempted to classify real products, generating a functional knowledge score for each participant. Models then linked identification accuracy and knowledge scores to traits such as age and education. The sorting tasks exposed the attributes Australians associate with ultra processing, from packaging and additives to health halos. Mapping this folk understanding is prerequisite to food policy the public can use.
pmc-13460241:
Kim and co-authors explain how systems genetics can illuminate early-onset colorectal cancer in this 2026 paper. Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in the United States. Cases before age 50 have been rising for decades. The reasons mix genes and environment. Systems genetics treats genes as a network, combining gene activity patterns, protein interactions, and drug-gene links.

The paper does three things: it reviews recent systems genetics studies of this cancer, walks readers through a step-by-step protocol for running such analyses, and discusses current limits. Those limits include findings that may not generalize across populations and results that depend heavily on context. The authors hope the guide encourages cancer researchers to adopt network methods when hunting for diagnostic markers and candidate drugs.
pmc-13461841:
Jun Suzuki and colleagues lay out, in a 2026 guide, a standard two-port robotic method for removing one lung segment. Two chest openings keep the robot's strengths while limiting cuts between the ribs. Segment removal demands exact knowledge of small airways and vessels, plus a reliable segment border. Errors in naming an airway threaten safety, above all in complex cases.

Steps run from planning with a 3D model of the patient's anatomy, through port placement fitted to the treated side, to teamwork between console and bedside staff. A dye given into a vein lights up under special imaging to draw the border. Airway identity is double-checked when anatomy is tricky. Two videos show the sequence adapted to a right lower segment and a left upper segment. Results from hospital cases, covering operating time, blood loss, and tumor removal, frame the method as workable and safe.
pmc-13461941:
Zhi Wang and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a gene signature tied to a chemical tag process called lactylation. It predicts survival in lung adenocarcinoma, the common lung cancer type. Lactylation has been linked to tumor growth and immune control, yet its sorting value was unclear. The team combined single-cell and bulk data. One cohort served to build the model, and two outside cohorts checked it.

The signature held 15 genes and split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with different survival in all three cohorts. The model ranked patients accurately at home and moderately well outside. High-risk tumors showed sugar burning, low-oxygen responses, and growth signaling, plus an immune setting. Lab tests singled out one gene, TUBA1C, as a lead candidate. The authors present the signature as a checked tool for survival prediction, not yet a guide for drug choice.
pmc-13462041:
