Juebin Gu, Yufei Dong, Mulin Liu, and Lin Lin test, in a 2026 hospital study, whether a fast gene-based blood test adds value for spotting bloodstream infection. Blood culture, the standard test, is slow, so early treatment choices are made blind. The gene test, droplet digital PCR, hunts pathogen DNA directly in blood. The team built a prediction model from routine signs in one patient group, then checked the added test in a second group.

The routine group held 814 patients. Age and one inflammation marker were the only signs tied to a positive culture, and the model sorted cases modestly. In the second group of 336 patients, adding the gene test lifted sorting accuracy, though not firmly by one strict test. Re-sorting measures improved clearly. The authors present the gene test as a helper for early risk sorting, not a stand-in for culture.
pmc-13462241:
Saartak Allena and colleagues benchmarked quantum machine learning methods for sorting breast cancer cases using clinical and gene data. Quantum models promise new pattern-finding power but must squeeze rich data onto very few simulated quantum bits.

The dataset held 2,509 patients, cut down from 63 features to at most 12 summary components for the quantum runs. The best quantum model, a quantum nearest-neighbour method, reached about 75 percent accuracy with an AUC of 0.8148 on held-out checks. Classical methods using all 63 features reached about 94 percent accuracy, well ahead of every quantum model. Shrinking the data hurt both families, Allena notes, so no quantum advantage appears at this scale yet.
pmc-13462441:
Xiang Bai and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that an enzyme gene called PRSS1 helps stomach cancer invade and spread. Public gene data flagged PRSS1 as a hub gene in stomach tumors. The team confirmed higher levels in tumor tissue, cancer cell lines, and patient blood. Those levels ran highest in advanced disease and tracked vessel invasion, stage, and lymph node spread.

Silencing PRSS1 in cancer cells slowed movement and invasion in dish tests and cut spread inside the belly in mice. Protein checks showed the silencing reversed a shape-shifting program that lets lining cells loosen and wander, called epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Two cutting enzymes fell, while a sticking protein rose. A growth signaling route, MAPK/ERK, also quieted. The authors conclude PRSS1, easy to measure in blood, may serve as a marker of aggressive stomach cancer and a target worth testing.
pmc-13462841:
Selvi Helina and colleagues map, in a 2026 field study, a virus crippling chili pepper production in Lampung Province, Indonesia. The virus, pepper yellow leaf curl virus, is spread by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci and curls and yellows leaves. Surveys with lab confirmation covered the seven chili districts of the province. Symptoms ranged from curling and yellow mosaic to shrunken leaves and stunted plants, varying by farm setting.

Infection proved widespread. Disease incidence hit 91 percent in Tanggamus and 85 percent in West Lampung, with severity nearing four fifths in both. Gene tests confirmed the virus, and its sequences matched known Indonesian strains closely while forming one tight family group, apart from foreign viruses. That sameness fits rapid regional spread by the whitefly. The authors warn the virus threatens further spread to other growing centers. They urge combined control: suppressing the whitefly, planting resistant varieties, and developing mild-strain protection.
pmc-13463641:
François Ritter leads a team that projects a sharp fall in the carbon stored by European forests. These forests soak up carbon and help slow climate change, yet harvests, fires, storms, and beetle outbreaks now kill trees faster than regrowth replaces them. The group joined country reports with satellite maps of damage and tree mass.

Their model, run at eighteen-kilometer detail from 2010 to 2030, sees the EU-27 forest carbon sink drop by about thirty-nine percent. The 2030 sink would land about twenty-seven percent below the level tied to EU climate goals. Planting three billion trees alone cannot close the gap, the team finds. Pairing planting with a deep cut in harvests could still meet the target.
pmc-13463941:
Piotr Olejnik and three co-authors review how chronic kidney disease clouds thinking, stage by stage. More than a tenth of adults worldwide live with kidney disease, and memory and focus problems can appear at any stage. The review ties clinic records to the molecular paths behind the decline.

Small vessel damage, a leaky brain barrier, uremic toxins, and body-wide inflammation all feed the harm. Early stages lean on vessel and focus troubles, while late stages add toxin and dialysis swings to the mix. Transplant drugs bring their own risks after surgery. Sorting the pattern by stage, the authors argue, can sharpen both study design and day-to-day care.
pmc-13464241:
Nagao and colleagues reported in 2026 a drainage catheter that went in easily but refused to come out. After catheter ablation for a rhythm problem, a 66-year-old woman developed cardiac tamponade. Tamponade is dangerous fluid pressure around the heart. Doctors drained the fluid through a needle below the breastbone. A thin pigtail catheter was left in place and seemed correctly positioned.

Two days later, the catheter resisted removal with marked force. Scans revealed the problem. The tube had slipped through the transverse pericardial sinus, a natural passage behind the aorta. It had re-entered the heart sac from the other side. Draining the fluid collapsed the passage around its sharply bent course like a trap. The team refilled the sac with saline to reopen the passage. They eased the catheter out timed with the heart's relaxation phase. Smooth insertion, they warn, proves nothing about placement.
pmc-13464341:
Ruan and co-authors built in 2026 a scoring chart, called a nomogram, to estimate whether a small lung nodule is cancerous before surgery. The chart drew on 1,419 patients whose nodules of three centimeters or less were removed and examined between 2012 and 2025. Ordinary clinical details were combined with precise measurements from thin-slice CT scans. A held-out group of 425 patients checked the chart.

Four of every five removed nodules proved malignant. Seven factors fed the final score, and suspicious scan features dominated. They multiplied the odds of cancer roughly sixfold and more. Nodules wider than two centimeters roughly quadrupled the odds. Women faced higher odds than men. Patients found without symptoms had lower odds, a reminder that incidental nodules differ from symptomatic ones. The chart discriminated well, scoring about 81 percent on the accuracy curve in training and about 78 percent in validation. Predicted risks matched observed outcomes closely.
pmc-13465141:
Rašeta and colleagues present a 2026 study validating pasteurization for wide chicken sausages, where standard temperature endpoints may overshoot and waste energy. In thick products, the center keeps cooking after heating stops, a cooling inertia that adds lethal effect on microbes. The team profiled temperatures across three commercial pasteurization runs of ninety-millimeter chicken sausages in plastic casings.

When active heating stopped at a lower core limit, the cooling phase more than tripled the accumulated lethality before the product cooled, reaching a high final value on the study's integrated scale. In other words, the process was safer than the thermometer at switch-off suggested. Counting cooling inertia honestly could let producers cut heating time and energy while keeping the same safety margin, and it separates later quality loss, from enzymes or oxidation, from microbial risk.
pmc-13465441:
Wysokinski and colleagues tracked sulphur through the life of pea plants in a two-year field study reported in 2026. Sulphur is a key nutrient for legumes. It supports the root nodules that capture nitrogen and the storage proteins in seeds. The team measured sulphur content, uptake, and several efficiency indices at six growth stages. Roots and shoots were analyzed separately, with seeds added at full ripeness.

The values moved in clear phases. Sulphur content and uptake rose early, between the four-leaf stage and stem elongation. Content then eased downward toward pod filling while uptake and the harvest index kept climbing. The nitrogen-to-sulphur ratio stayed in a healthy band throughout. By full maturity, none of the measures changed further. Both the study year and growth stage shaped the numbers, while the cultivar rarely did. The authors conclude the fertilizer dose kept plants adequately supplied all season.
pmc-13466241:
Melike Dönmez Tekin and co-authors review outcomes for patients whose head and neck cancer returned or spread and who received cetuximab-based treatment, in a 2026 single-center study. Fifty-seven patients treated at a Turkish university hospital between 2012 and 2025 form the group. Cetuximab regimens still matter here even as immune therapies spread.

Records supplied age, stage, lab values, and scan results for each patient. The team estimated time without disease worsening and overall survival, then tested which traits lined up with longer or shorter survival. Such prognostic sorting can help doctors judge who gains most from this older drug backbone and who should move to other options sooner.
pmc-13466641:
Lyu and a clinical team built a simple prediction model in 2026 for which mothers with sepsis will crash into septic shock. Existing warning scores perform poorly here. The study reviewed 139 women treated at one referral center over nearly a decade. Four factors measured at diagnosis fed the model. Records were split so the model faced patients it had not learned from.

The four predictors were surgery during pregnancy, a clotting time, a bacterial infection marker, and blood oxygen level. Together they sorted future shock cases well. The accuracy score reached 0.87 in both the learning and test groups, where 1.0 is perfect. Higher scores tracked with worse outcomes for mothers and babies. Lung infections were the commonest source, at about 45 percent of cases. Gram-negative bacteria caused most infections, and shock struck postpartum cases far more often, about 43 percent against 19 percent.
pmc-13466941:
Hongtao Sun and a large team engineer tiny spheres with a gradient of crosslinking from core to shell to block tumor blood vessels in liver cancer treatment, in a 2026 study. Blocking spheres face a trade-off: stiff ones resist crushing but cannot squeeze deep into vessels, while soft ones drift after placement. Their design grades the internal bonding to get strength and flexibility together.

Bench models of vessel networks showed the new spheres traveled distally and stayed put better than uniform or standard core-shell versions. Pig kidney tests confirmed the behavior in a living system. Human trials in liver cancer then verified that the spheres blocked vessels effectively and safely, tying mechanical design to clinical reach.
pmc-13467041:
Daniel Blaschke, a physicist, derives a far faster way to compute the limiting speeds of line defects gliding through crystals, in a 2026 methods paper. Dislocation theory predicts that elastic energy blows up at certain speeds that depend on crystal shape, splitting slow, middling, and faster-than-sound glide regimes. Those thresholds feed models of how materials hold up under extreme strain rates.

One awkward case, edge dislocations in crystals with mirror symmetry but certain stubborn elastic constants, had resisted every fast method. The new derivation handles exactly that case about a hundred times faster than the previous approach. Strength modelers who screen many crystal orientations gain the most from the shortcut.
pmc-13467541:
Andrés Baeza-Morales and co-authors test in 2026 a red pigment from a salt-loving microbe against several cancer cell models, including drug-resistant lung cancer. The pigment, bacterioruberin, comes from the archaeon Haloferax mediterranei and had barely been studied in solid tumors. The team exposed lung, breast, and melanoma cell lines to a pigment-rich extract and measured survival, growth, oxidative stress, and cell death.

The extract killed cancer cells and slowed their growth across the models. Treated cells showed more reactive oxygen species, a sign the pigment pushes cells toward oxidative damage, plus changes typical of apoptosis, the orderly form of cell death. Importantly, growth inhibition held up in lung cancer cells that resist standard drugs by pumping them out through the P-glycoprotein system. That reach into resistant cells is what makes the pigment worth further study.
pmc-13467641:
Hongyu Chen, Bowen Ke, and Ruotian Jiang review in 2026 whether classic psychedelics could help treat chronic pain. They frame chronic pain as a disorder of a maladapted central nervous system. In their account, pain signals traveling upward hold it in place, and so do the rigid expectations the brain brings to them. Standard painkillers rarely undo that rigidity, which is where psychedelics, known for loosening mental patterns, might fit.

The review gathers the research on what these drugs bind to in the brain, how they may change pain circuits, and what early clinical studies in pain patients show. It also confronts weak points in the field: psychedelic trials are hard to blind, and patient expectations can inflate results. The authors call for new validation strategies and argue that brain plasticity and subjective experience may each carry part of the benefit.
pmc-13467741:
Wei Li and five colleagues published this 2026 greenhouse study on whether silicon and nitrogen fertilisation can help rice defend itself against invasive apple snails, voracious grazers of paddy fields. Silicon can harden defences, while excess nitrogen from polluted water might soften them. The team grew rice seedlings under two silicon levels and three nitrogen levels, measured leaf chemistry and toughness, and let snails feed to gauge the protection.

Silicon made rice grow larger at low and high nitrogen, raised sulfur at every level, and lifted tannins and the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio at the middle level. For defence, silicon increased flavonoid content and the force needed to fracture leaves under all nitrogen regimes, and the snails grew less on silicon-fed plants. Nitrogen modified several effects but never erased the silicon benefit. The authors propose silicon amendment as a crop protection strategy amid eutrophication and invasion.
pmc-13467841:
Ma and co-authors teach machines to classify gout from routine clinical data. Their 2026 retrospective study draws 7,383 adults from a Jiangxi hospital's records between 2020 and 2026, labelling gout by the international classification framework and comparing against a mixed hospital population. Because a single uric acid value does not capture the disease, the models integrate inflammatory, metabolic, kidney, blood, demographic, and lifestyle variables.

After imputation of missing values and statistical feature selection, four algorithms were trained and tested on a hold-out split. Random forest performed best overall, reaching a discrimination score of about 0.90 in training while keeping sensitivity above 96 percent, and it stayed ahead in the test set. Calibration and decision-curve analyses accompanied the accuracy metrics. The authors present routine-variable models as a practical aid for flagging gout in ordinary clinical settings.
pmc-13468041:
Farhat Abbas and colleagues introduce a 2026 special issue on the three great families of plant pigments: anthocyanins, carotenoids, and betalains. These compounds paint flowers and fruits, help plants cope with stress, and shape ties with pollinators and enemies. They also carry nutritional, medicinal, and industrial value for people. The editors frame a collection of twelve original research and review articles gathered for the issue.

The collected works span the full arc from how pigment molecules are built and genetically regulated, through how plants use them to adapt, to applications in agriculture and industry. The editors note that the regulatory networks behind pigment production are intricate and fast-moving, leaving practical uses still open. Their introduction serves as a guide to the issue and an argument that pigment biology now connects molecular genetics to ecology and commerce in one continuous story.
pmc-13468341:
Mingming Chen and colleagues traced the evolution of ammonium transporter genes across green plants and mapped their activity in oilseed rape. These transporters pull ammonium, a key nitrogen feed, into plant cells, shaping how well crops use nitrogen.

The team catalogued 368 transporter genes from 35 species, split almost evenly between the AMT1 and AMT2 families. Small local duplications drove family growth across plant history, while whole-genome doubling dominated in the Brassica triangle group. Most rape transporters responded to hormones and low nitrogen, with tissue-specific patterns across the plant. Four genes stood out as breeding candidates, Chen reports, two of them linked to plant height and yield differences.
pmc-13468841:
Valdemar Farre and colleagues draft in 2026 a planning framework for beyond-5G and 6G networks that scatter antennas across a city instead of concentrating them in cell towers. Their four-layer scheme jointly places spread-out antenna arrays and passive reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, reflective panels that steer radio waves around corners. A digital twin loop inside an open radio access network runs multi-agent reinforcement learning and fractional math to tune active and passive beamforming in real time.

Monte Carlo simulations of a dense city setting reported a 45 percent increase in spectral efficiency. They also found a 30 percent cut in uplink interference, and 84 percent fewer coverage holes than legacy 5G layouts. Non-line-of-sight coverage grew by 40 percent without the capital cost of new towers. Operators facing 6G build-out bills get a blueprint claiming software and surfaces can stand in for concrete and steel.
pmc-13468941:
O’Keefe and colleagues wrote a methods communication in 2026 on reporting artificial intelligence use in horizon scanning. Horizon scanning means watching for emerging health technologies and trends to guide policy. The authors reviewed current guidelines, policies, and stakeholder statements on AI use in research and publishing.

From 139 collected data points, they consolidated a minimal set of 46 reporting items in six categories. The items aim to make AI use in scanning transparent, reliable, and responsible. They cover how AI tools are chosen, used, and checked across the research cycle. The authors present the set as an interim standard filling an immediate gap. They note the items still need validation with users before becoming a firm framework. They urge scanning teams to keep embedding AI openly while standards mature.
pmc-13469041:
Dingzhi Liu and co-authors reanalyze public single-cell data in 2026 to find the signaling conversations that help liver cancer suppress its immune attackers. Hepatocellular carcinoma is among the deadliest cancers, and its microenvironment is crowded with regulatory T cells that brake immunity and exhausted T cells that have given up. The team pulled single-cell RNA sequencing data from a public repository and processed it with standard clustering and cell annotation workflows.

Their reanalysis highlights a candidate axis between the signal MIF and the receptor PTGDR as an immunoregulatory program tied to those dysfunctional T-cell states. Mapping which cells send and receive such signals matters because immunotherapy for liver cancer works in only a minority of patients. A named sender-receiver axis gives drug developers a specific conversation to interrupt, and the study shows public data, carefully re-mined, can still yield fresh targets.
pmc-13469341:
Zhang and colleagues identify a new switch for bacterial virulence in this 2026 plant pathology study. The bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola causes bacterial leaf streak of rice and depends on a type III secretion system, a needle-like structure that injects proteins into plant cells. A control chain called HrpG-HrpX turns this system on, but what sits above it in this bacterium was unclear.

Deleting the gene for a regulator named GpaR made the bacteria far less damaging to rice and weakened their effect on a test plant. Levels of hrpG, hrpX, and related secretion genes dropped sharply without GpaR. Binding tests showed GpaR attaches directly to the start regions of both genes and switches them on, and restoring either gene largely brought back virulence.
pmc-13470341:
Harikrishna and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on computer stress modeling in dentistry. Finite element analysis splits a tooth or implant into tiny blocks for math testing. It predicts where biting forces pile up inside oral structures. The review traces the method from engineering roots into dental labs.

The authors survey uses across implants, braces, root work, and crowns. Modeling guides implant shapes and tool designs before patient testing begins. It also maps stress in enamel, dentin, jawbone, and gum ligaments. No bench test matches its three-dimensional detail, the authors argue. Weak material data and loose modeling habits still limit trust, they warn. The search reached back to 1969 across five major databases. Nine dental specialties fall within the review's wide survey scope.
pmc-13472241:
Wu and colleagues present a 2026 meta-analysis, a study that pools results from earlier research, on exercise capacity in children who have received a heart transplant. Young recipients often tire easily, yet the size of the fitness gap and its causes were unclear. The authors gathered studies comparing recipients with healthy children of the same age on peak oxygen uptake.

Seven studies covered 90 recipients and 118 controls. Recipients scored lower on peak oxygen uptake. The gap was 9.5 milliliters per kilogram each minute in the pooled results, a clear deficit. Their peak heart rate was about 30 beats per minute lower and blood pumped per minute was also reduced, while blood pressure matched controls. The deficit did not shrink with age or with time since transplant, and the authors link it mainly to the transplanted heart losing its normal nerve supply.
pmc-13472541:
Ozturk and Oner asked in 2026 whether nurses who guard patient rights well also give more patient led care. Patient led care puts each person's values and picks at the core of each choice. The team polled 397 nurses at public, school, and trust hospitals across Türkiye in the cold months. Two set forms scored their rights guard acts and their skill at patient led care, split by part.

Each rights part tracked close with each care skill part, in strong links across the board. All five rights parts stood on their own as marks of top tier care skill. The two tightest links were care for patient values and picks, and the rule of help first, harm none. Nurses taught in patient rights scored higher on care skill than peers with no such class. The authors urge rights teach in school and in ward drills.
pmc-13473341:
Makhambetov and colleagues built in 2026 a rapid DNA test distinguishing two moth pests of Kazakh apple orchards. Field surveys in southern and southeastern Kazakhstan collected specimens, identified by form and by a mitochondrial gene barcode. The team then designed a multiplex quantitative PCR test, which detects both species' DNA in one run.

Codling moth made up about eighty-three percent of collected specimens. The barcode reliably separated the two species. The new test showed high specificity, with no false positives from non-target species. It detected the target DNA with full success down to five picograms per reaction, a tiny amount. The authors present the assay as a fast, sensitive tool for plant-health monitoring in orchards. Quicker species identification helps growers time control measures and meet phytosanitary rules for fruit trade.
pmc-13473841:
Zhang and a large team in China tested in 2026 a fresh peptide, NAP2, as a brake on Alzheimer's disease in mice. The peptide blocks a dock called NgR1, which catches Nogo-A, a myelin protein that halts nerve growth. That catch fires a path named ROCK, tied to cell harm. The team gave the peptide for three months to mice bred to grow the disease's brain marks, then ran maze tests and brain checks.

Treated mice learned and recalled far better than their plain kin. Their brains held fewer amyloid plaques, the sticky clumps of the disease, and less of the worst clump form. Spines on brain cells, the buds that hold links, grew back in count. Tau, the twin mark protein, bore less of its harm linked tags. The peptide also saved cell power plants from clump harm, and its grip on the ROCK path was plain to see.
pmc-13473941:
Vedelago and colleagues present a 2026 viewpoint on moving three-dimensional printing in radiotherapy from local craft to global standard. Printed items already serve clinics as body molds that hold patients still, surface pads that boost skin dose, test phantoms, and proton therapy parts. 

The question the authors press is whether a printed device made in one hospital can be trusted in another. Without shared standards for printers, materials, and quality checks, a bolus or phantom carries local assumptions that may not travel. The stakes are dosimetric: a small density error in a printed part becomes a dose error in a patient. The piece argues for common validation protocols now, while the field is young, rather than after inconsistent practices harden into habit across hundreds of centers.
pmc-13474841:
Veerle Van Oeckel and co-authors evaluate a co-design process in 2026 that tackled sitting time at school among teens in Flanders, Belgium. Twelve pupils and three teachers helped build the program across ten pupil sessions and five teacher sessions. The program then ran for six weeks in the school. Feedback came from forms, group talks, and surveys with pupils and teachers.

Pupils liked being involved, yet fitting sessions inside lessons strained time and focus. Teachers wanted a lighter role that still let them feel heard. Both groups gave views on what helped or blocked rollout. Future co-design work can borrow these lessons on pacing and roles.
pmc-13475341:
Alireza Maboudi argues in 2026 that artificial intelligence in drug work misses the craft that turns a molecule into a medicine. Discovery tools excel at finding molecules that bind targets and pass early property screens. Yet most failures strike later, when a molecule must dissolve, stay stable, and reach the body in a usable form. Formulation science decides those traits, and most pipelines barely model it.

The essay grants that learning tools already help in narrow formulation tasks. Its charge is about framing: success is claimed at the molecule stage, long before a product exists. Case points show how solubility and delivery faults sink strong binders. Builders are urged to wire formulation into models from the start.
pmc-13477141:
Laura Maitoza and coauthors report in 2026 on using whole blood for babies having heart surgery with a heart-lung machine. The study covers infants under two months old treated at one center between 2019 and 2023. Whole blood filled the bypass circuit and met early transfusion needs, instead of separate blood parts given one by one.

Ninety-five infants were included in the review of their charts. Babies given whole blood were exposed to fewer donors, a median of three compared with five, and needed fewer separate blood parts during surgery. Hospital stay, breathing support time, and later transfusion needs did not differ clearly, so the authors call for more research on whether the approach improves recovery.
pmc-13477641:
Marcus Hunter and Luis R. Martinez published a 2026 review on cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, a dangerous flare that can follow HIV treatment. The fungus Cryptococcus causes meningitis that still drives a large share of AIDS deaths. Up to a quarter of survivors develop the syndrome after starting HIV drug treatment, when the returning immune system meets leftover fungus in the brain.

The review builds a timeline of immune change. Before treatment, skewed helper T cell responses and weak defenses let fungal antigen build up. During recovery, surging T cells, uneven control, and guiding signals draw killer cells into the brain, where the response can turn harmful. The authors discuss new mouse models, compare a related fungal species, and survey immune-focused treatments and vaccines now being tested.
pmc-13478341:
Vijaykumar and colleagues developed a double-layer seed coating for oilseed crops in 2026, wrapping seeds in plant-based polymers that carry a fungicide, a helpful fungus, and crop-matched fertilizer bacteria. Layers keep the chemical and living inputs apart so each releases in turn. The coating was tested in lab, greenhouse, and field work on groundnut, with lab and greenhouse checks also run on sesame and soybean.

Coated seeds kept the highest germination after storage, between 78.8 and 86.7 percent, losing only 5 to 8 percent while untreated seeds fell far more. Seedling deaths ran 60 to 75 percent lower than in untreated seeds across the crops tested in the assays. In groundnut fields, coated seed emerged 20 to 27 percent better, cut stem rot by about 80 percent, and yielded 21.1 quintals per hectare against 12.9 for untreated seed.
pmc-13479241:
Francesc Franquesa-Garcia and the DIADEMA investigators published a 2026 multicenter study using artificial intelligence to measure fluid in diabetic macular edema, a swelling that threatens vision in diabetes. Eyes received a dexamethasone implant, a slow-release steroid placed inside the eye. Baseline eye scans were quantified by validated software that measures fluid pockets in nanoliters.

The real-world Spanish database held 101 previously untreated eyes. More fluid inside the retina at baseline predicted larger letter gains by month twelve yet worse final vision, a pattern suggesting severe disease that improves but cannot fully recover. Fluid under the retina predicted worse final vision more cleanly. Shrinking intraretinal fluid by 100 nanoliters at three months tracked with about one and a half extra letters gained. The authors propose objective fluid volumes as counseling tools.
pmc-13479441:
Hafize Gökben Ulutaş and coauthors published a 2026 study of how lingering corneal infiltrates after viral eye infection change the cornea's physical behavior. Subepithelial infiltrates, cloudy spots under the surface, can persist after adenoviral epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and blur vision. Patients kept for at least six months after the acute episode were compared with healthy controls.

The study covered 23 affected eyes from twelve patients and 32 control eyes. Affected eyes saw worse, showed steeper corneal curvature readings, more optical distortion, and higher corneal cloudiness values, mainly in front and central zones. An air-puff device that films corneal bending found one movement measure, the first applanation length, significantly shorter in affected eyes. The authors conclude the infiltrates leave measurable mechanical fingerprints, not just optical ones.
pmc-13479541:
Xue Han and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial on timing a single dose of dexmedetomidine to blunt the pain sensitivity caused by the anesthetic remifentanil. That opioid can paradoxically leave patients more sensitive to pain after thyroid surgery. One hundred eighteen patients were assigned to receive the calming drug before anesthesia, at skin closure, or to a control group.

Pain thresholds measured on the forearm thirty minutes after surgery were higher in both drug groups than in controls. Only the skin-closure group showed less pain sensitivity around the wound at twenty-four hours. Resting pain scores, rescue medication use, recovery quality scores, circulation stability, and side effects were also tracked. The result favors giving the dose late in surgery for lasting protection.
pmc-13479641:
Linda van der Spek and colleagues published a 2025 review of what helps or hinders paying parents and expectant parents to quit smoking. Cash rewards after proven quitting are among the best-value tools for helping people stop smoking, yet programs struggle to launch and survive. Nine data banks plus gray reports were searched through August 2024.

From 1,100 unique records, thirty-seven met the rules for writing up how programs were run. Two screeners worked alone at first and settled clashes by talking them through. The barriers and helpers found span design choices like reward size and proof method, staff views on paying for health habits, and parents' own feelings about fairness and stigma. The review aims to help new programs copy what worked rather than hitting the same walls again.
pmc-13479741:
Sheng Luan and coauthors published a 2026 software paper with visPedigree, an R package that brings animal and plant breeding pedigree work into one tool. Breeders juggle pedigree cleaning, analysis, and drawing across split tools, which makes routine work harder in groups with huge full-sibling families and uneven record depth. The package is built around a new tidy data object.

Tools cover pedigree cleanup and error checks, tracing ancestors around any chosen animal, inbreeding and part-inbreeding math, and diversity counts based on founders and ancestors. Working group size and kinship tables come built in, along with diversity gauges borrowed from ecology. A time check tracks how complete pedigrees are across generations. Drawing scales up for the full-sib-heavy subsets common in fish and shellfish breeding programs.
pmc-13480741:
Benoliel and co-authors compare one-sided and two-sided jaw muscle pain in 2026, asking whether the two patterns are really the same disorder. They recruited clinic patients meeting standard criteria for masticatory myofascial pain, meaning chronic aching in the chewing muscles, over a two-year period. Demographic and clinical details were recorded, and the groups were compared statistically, with promising variables carried into a regression model.

Tenderness refused to respect the pain map, since patients hurt on one side were tender on both, and two-sided patients could be tender on just one side. Three features did separate the groups, each significantly tied to one-sided pain: waking from sleep because of pain, nausea, and pain being the patient's main complaint. Age, sex, and other background traits matched between groups, and the authors say the split, especially its possible link to headache, deserves testing in a larger cohort.
pmc-13481641:
Maria Carmela Saturno and co-authors report a 2026 case of two germs attacking the retina at once in a woman with a sound immune system. The 52-year-old had repeat flare-ups of toxoplasma eye infection, a parasite-driven disease, and the latest flare in her left eye shrugged off standard antiparasitic drugs. Surgeons sampled the eye jelly for gene tests.

Tests found both the parasite and Epstein-Barr virus in the sample. Care mixed injections into the eye of a drug that calms immune cell growth plus a standard antibiotic, body-wide antiparasitic drugs, and an antiviral for eight weeks. Sight held steady, retinal shape settled, and repeat gene tests faded to clear for both germs. No flare returned in follow-up. Stubborn eye cases deserve coinfection checks even when immunity looks normal.
pmc-13482341:
Tian, Zheng, and Foijer ask in 2026 whether the chromosome chaos inside triple-negative breast cancer cells reshapes nearby immune cells to the tumor's advantage. Chromosomal instability, frequent chromosome sorting errors during division, marks this aggressive cancer type, which lacks the usual hormone drug targets. The team forced instability in a standard cancer cell line using reversine, a drug that blocks a division checkpoint protein, then grew the cells with human macrophages.

The scrambled cells steadily raised their output of three macrophage-attracting signals, CCL2, CCL5, and IL-6, after treatment. In shared dishes the treated cancer cells pushed macrophages toward the M2-like state, the wound-healing mode that suppresses immunity and helps tumors, with only a modest rise in fighter-type markers. Contact was not required, since shared fluid alone did the same, and the reprogrammed macrophages ate more cancer cells yet released migration-speeding factors.
pmc-13482541:
Simona Bo and co-authors report a 2026 trial testing whether diet style beats plain weight loss for fatty liver tied to metabolic strain. The six-month trial split 173 patients with the liver condition plus excess weight into three arms: Mediterranean fare, low-carb high-protein fare, and standard advice. Of those enrolled, 148 finished, and liver fat was read by a scan-based stiffness tool.

Liver fat fell inside the low-carb and standard arms, with no clear edge between arms. Every arm lost weight, trimmed waist measures, improved metabolic readings, and cut ultra-processed food intake. Path modelling found diet label itself carried no direct effect on liver fat change. Drops in body mass index and in ultra-processed food intake each predicted liver fat gains on their own. Coaching that patients can stick with may beat strict diet branding.
pmc-13482641:
Yadav and colleagues race four optimization algorithms in 2026 at one unglamorous but vital job, fitting the circuit model that battery managers use to predict a lithium-ion cell's voltage. They parameterized a two-resistor-capacitor equivalent circuit for a commercial cell across charge levels from 10 to 100 percent, judging fit error, speed, and whether the fitted values stayed physically sensible. Trust-region and BFGS methods led the pack.

Trust-region fitting erred by 0.922 millivolts on average and BFGS by 0.971 millivolts, while Levenberg-Marquardt trailed at 2.441 millivolts in mean error under the same tests. In validation drives the leaders held voltage errors under 0.022 volts and 0.065 volts respectively, while the Gauss-Newton method often failed to converge at all in this study. Speed reversed the ranking, with Levenberg-Marquardt fastest at 0.244 seconds of compute, BFGS next at 0.383 seconds, and trust-region slowest at 0.655 seconds overall.
pmc-13483141:
Emre Vuraloglu presents a 2026 qualitative study of how a leading chatbot reasons through borderline thyroid cases. Subclinical hypothyroidism, where the gland signal hormone runs high while the main hormone stays normal, splits guidelines and doctors alike. Five scripted cases spanning the grey zone went to ChatGPT, and replies were coded with a structured frame plus reflective theme work.

Seven themes surfaced, from guideline grounding and personal tailoring to trial treatment, risk sorting, and shared choice. Themes folded into three stances: a cautious guideline-led stance, a proactive risk-led stance, and a balanced stance built on shared choice with the patient. No patient data fed the exercise, so the stances map the model's habits rather than real-world safety. The coding frame gives later, larger studies a way to grade chatbot reasoning in grey zones.
pmc-13483541:
Tetsuya Uchino and co-authors compare two ways of guiding an obturator nerve block in a 2026 randomized trial. Eighty patients having bladder tumor surgery through the urethra received the block either with ultrasound guidance or with nerve stimulation, using an approach between the thigh muscles. A mix of numbing medicine and contrast dye was injected, then X-ray imaging showed how far the fluid traveled.

Contrast reached the obturator canal in 90 percent of ultrasound-guided cases and 75 percent of stimulation-guided cases, a gap that did not reach statistical significance. Volumes used were similar in both groups. The authors note that muscle anatomy around the nerve's rear branch could limit spread, and they suggest the side-lying surgical position may help fluid move upward.
pmc-13483641:
Po-Yuan Chen describes a modified ankle operation for tendons that repeatedly slip out of place beside the outer ankle bone. Published in 2026, the retrospective series reviews patients treated between 2005 and 2025 whose soft-tissue restraints were too damaged for standard repair alone. The technique shifts a shaped piece of fibula bone backward and adds a flap of its outer covering for support.

Eleven patients had complete follow-up averaging over five years. Foot and ankle scores, pain ratings, general health scores, and activity levels all improved significantly after surgery. Every patient returned to daily activities, and those who had played sports resumed them, with no repeat dislocations. One complication is detailed in the full report. For severe restraint damage, the bone-plus-covering approach offers durable stability.
pmc-13483741:
Kentaro Yamane leads a 2026 prospective study of a water-soluble bone sealing material used during open heart surgery. Ninety adults having chest-opening heart operations at three United States centers received the product, called Ostene, to stop bleeding from cut breastbone. Surgeons recorded bleeding area, severity, amount used, time to stop bleeding, and any return of bleeding.

Control succeeded during surgery in 87 of 89 patients assessed for effectiveness. Roughly one quarter experienced a later rebleed in the operating room, on average about four hours after the first stop, and nearly all were settled by reapplying the same material. No patient bled from bone in the first day after surgery. Adverse events were few and judged unrelated to the product, supporting its role as an alternative to traditional bone wax.
pmc-13483941:
Samot and co-authors tracked gum health over time in French patients with Parkinson's disease, whose tremor and stiffness can make brushing hard. Their 2026 study examined 40 patients at a first visit and again about seven months later, recording plaque, gum pockets, and the amounts of several mouth bacteria. The group expected decline, so stability itself would be informative.

Clinical measures barely moved between visits, and several trended slightly better rather than worse. The share of deep gum pockets fell from 20 percent to 3 percent, though that change missed statistical significance in this small group. One harmful bacterium, Treponema denticola, dropped sharply, with loads down about 93 percent after adjustment for follow-up time. Hygiene habits in the group were good at the start. Samot says bigger studies must confirm whether supported care explains the steadiness.
pmc-13486041:
Mojtaba Moradi tests whether a common amino acid can shield human sperm from heat damage during laboratory preparation for fertility treatment. Published in 2026, the experiment splits semen from 30 men with normal counts into plain and proline-supplemented portions. Each portion then sits at cool, body, or fever-level heat for three or twenty-four hours.

Heat exposure clearly damaged movement, survival, and chemical balance in unprotected samples. Adding L-proline at a set dose preserved movement and survival under heat and strengthened antioxidant defenses, raising protective enzymes and overall capacity while adjusting damage markers. Shape of the sperm did not benefit measurably. Clinics that must hold samples through long procedures or warm transport gain a cheap candidate protectant worth clinical testing.
pmc-13487341:
Jie Qiu charts how a toddler's middle ear absorbs sound energy differently from a six-year-old's, to sharpen childhood ear diagnostics. Published in 2026, the cross-sectional study measures wideband absorbance in 579 normal-hearing children covering 1,158 ears across five age groups and sixteen frequencies. Testing runs at ambient pressure and at each ear's peak pressure point.

Sex and ear side made no meaningful difference to the patterns. Age changed everything, since infants under six months showed a double-peaked M-shaped curve while children aged three to six showed a single hump near 1600 hertz. A learning model sorted age moderately well, leaning hardest on low-to-mid frequency readings. Maturation steadily rebuilds the middle ear's mechanics, so adult-shaped reference curves would misread healthy infants.
pmc-13487941:
Anne Morice and colleagues look beyond the jaw in cherubism, a rare childhood bone disease caused by changes in the SH3BP2 gene, in a 2026 clinical study. The disease usually enlarges the jaw, where bone is replaced by fibrous tissue. After one severe case also showed low bone mass elsewhere, the team assessed ten more patients for growth, bone density, and blood markers of bone turnover and inflammation.

Height and weight were normal across the group. Markers showing bone breakdown and formation ran high, and higher values tracked with more severe jaw disease. The authors argue that checks beyond the face should become routine, so the full course of this rare condition is better understood.
pmc-13490441:
Mekcha and team replaced natural pasture hay with Napier grass hay in dairy cow diets and measured milk and methane together. Smallholder farmers need feeds that raise yield without raising climate cost per liter. Their 2026 experiment rotated five crossbred cows through five diets, from all pasture hay to all Napier hay. The Latin square design let every cow try every diet, with concentrate added per liter of milk.

Milk yield climbed from about eleven liters daily on pasture hay to about sixteen liters on full Napier hay across the rotations. The richer Napier diets also raised protein intake, nutrient intake overall, and feed efficiency in the cows measured. Estimated methane per kilogram of milk fell from about twenty-seven grams to about twenty-one grams as Napier share rose. Mekcha calls full replacement a practical climate-smart strategy for smallholders.
pmc-13491641:
Anjali Gupta and seven co-authors present a 2026 fidelity study of Water First, a school program that promotes tap water drinking to prevent childhood overweight. An earlier trial in eighteen elementary schools found the program raised water intake, and this analysis asked how faithfully schools delivered it. Observers checked promotional materials, water stations, and drinking vessels twice weekly during the program.

Fidelity scored highest in cafeterias and lower at hallway stations and in classrooms, while fewer than half of home activities came back completed. Stronger classroom fidelity linked to less fruit juice drinking, and stronger hallway fidelity linked to less soda and milk intake. Cafeteria fidelity was tied to a small drop in body mass index scores. Home activity completion showed no link to outcomes.
pmc-13491741:
Yan-mei Cheng and five colleagues review in 2026 the long-term fate of sixty-seven patients with Marfan syndrome treated at one cardiac surgery center between 2000 and 2022. The inherited condition weakens connective tissue and threatens the aorta, the main artery leaving the heart. The team searched records for clinical features that predicted death during a median follow-up of about four and a half years.

Survival fell from roughly three quarters of patients at one year to under half by fifteen years. A left ventricle stretched to sixty-five millimeters or more before surgery more than doubled the risk of death. Needing emergency breathing support also marked high risk, while having surgery was linked to lower mortality even after careful time-based adjustment. The authors propose ventricle size as an extra warning sign beyond aorta diameter.
pmc-13491841:
Shota Torii and seven co-authors report in 2026 a medication interaction that quietly overdosed a dialysis patient's blood thinner during cancer treatment. The sixty-four-year-old Japanese man had kidney cancer with tumor growing into the large vein returning blood to the heart, so doctors started warfarin to guard against clot spread. His clotting ratio sat safely in range before cancer drugs began.

Nine days after starting lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab, his clotting ratio jumped well above target even though the warfarin dose never changed, and he felt no symptoms. Small dose adjustments and close monitoring brought values back into range by day eighty without cutting the cancer drug. Because dialysis clears neither medicine, the authors warn that these patients need the same interaction vigilance as everyone else, with weekly checks early on.
pmc-13492641:
Martin V Pusic and Olle ten Cate reflect in 2026 on how artificial intelligence rewrites what it means to be a competent clinician. Medical training was built for an age of cognitive scarcity, when finding and digesting evidence took scarce hours, so education arrived in periodic curated doses. Modern AI flips the problem into cognitive abundance, with instant syntheses, adaptive learning paths, and continuous feedback on tap.

Using a three-layer model of competence spanning textbook knowledge, context-specific judgment, and personal style, the authors argue that clinicians are shifting from knowledge keepers to orchestrators of distributed thinking. Long-term memory will hold fewer raw facts and more skill at finding, choosing, and validating information. Training systems, they urge, must now teach AI literacy, hybrid reasoning, and ethical stewardship as core professional virtues.
pmc-13493741:
Zeno Fratton and eight colleagues follow in 2026 the real-world performance of bimekizumab, a psoriasis drug that blocks two inflammatory signals at once, across three referral centers in northern Italy. Charts for 126 adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis tracked skin clearance, safety, and how long patients stayed on the drug for up to two years.

Complete clearance arrived fast and held: about sixty-two percent fully clear at week sixteen, eighty percent at one year, and seventy-seven percent at two years. Palm and sole involvement predicted weaker early clearance, and nail disease plus acid-reducing medicines also dragged on week sixteen results. Two-year retention reached seventy-two percent overall, but patients new to biologics stayed on at ninety-two percent against sixty-four for the previously treated. Yeast infections and eczema-like rashes led the side effect list.
pmc-13494041:
Nagasawa and co-authors look for bacteria that can defend rice against Burkholderia glumae, the germ behind bacterial panicle blight, a disease that rots seedlings and grain. Instead of testing microbes, their 2026 team collected bacteria from rice seedlings that stayed healthy despite exposure. They used an in-planta screening method that lets the plant itself reveal its protectors. Three isolates were then tested alone and together in two soils.

Two isolates proved to be close matches to Paenibacillus hunanensis, and a third was Sphingomonas aquatilis. In the first soil, seed treatment with the isolates suppressed the disease, but in the second soil the single strains failed. That failure is a reminder that soil chemistry can make or break biocontrol. The three-strain mixture, however, protected rice in the stubborn soil too. The authors present the screening strategy and cocktail as a route to disease control with less pesticide.
pmc-13495441:
Claudio Bertiola-Flores leads a team reviewing, in a 2026 article, peer tutoring inside clinical simulation for health sciences students. Both methods push active, safe, team learning, yet their joint gains had never been summed. The team searched three databases for trials and near-trials from 2020 to 2025.

Eleven studies with 860 students and 107 tutors qualified, mostly in low- to mid-complexity simulation rooms. Gains showed in hands-on skills and in softer ones: confidence, communication, drive, and reflection. Students reported high satisfaction and less anxiety, in rooms that felt safe to fail in. Tutors, close in age and stage to learners, gave feedback and set a trusting tone. The authors call the pairing cheap and sound, while flagging small samples and short follow-up, and they urge formal tutor training under faculty watch.
pmc-13498741:
Bhavna Singla and co-authors review in 2026 computer systems that use live, updating hospital data to predict sepsis early. Sepsis is a dangerous body-wide response to infection, and late recognition delays treatment. Artificial intelligence tools promise earlier warnings, yet their quality and readiness for ward use remain unclear, prompting a structured search of three major databases for studies from 2015 to mid-2025.

Eight studies met the rules, covering intensive care, emergency departments, and multi-hospital systems, with patient counts from several hundred to over half a million. Model types ranged from boosted decision methods to deep neural networks, and accuracy was generally moderate to high, with several tools warning hours before onset. Most studies carried moderate bias risk from backward-looking designs and varied sepsis definitions, so the authors call for forward testing in real workflows.
pmc-13499041:
Sunghyun Jun, Colleen Marie Arrasmith, and Volha Liaudanskaya draw together in 2026 what is known about chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a brain degeneration linked to repeated head impacts. Connecting years of knocks to later disease has lacked a single clear mechanism. Their synthesis spans population studies, brain tissue work, and clinical reports to build one chain from exposure to decline.

Initial injury sets off energy failure in brain cells, inflammation, and damage to nerve fibres across several cell types. Over time those processes promote misfolded proteins, including tau, which gathers in a distinctive pattern around small blood vessels deep in the brain's folds. Symptoms vary widely and current scans and fluid tests lack precision, while no single lab model captures the full course, leaving detection during life as a central research need.
pmc-13499341:
Shi and colleagues report a 2026 study of how tomato plants defend themselves against a fungus gnat, Bradysia impatiens, whose larvae chew roots, stems, and leaves and cut yields. The team combined two profiling methods, gene activity and small-molecule chemistry, on leaves one week after larvae were introduced to the soil.

Feeding triggered wide gene reprogramming: nearly three thousand genes changed activity. The changed genes clustered in defense pathways, including MAPK signaling, hormone signals, pathogen-interaction routes, and the building of phenylpropanoid compounds, a class of plant defense chemicals. Chemistry profiles shifted alongside the genes. Because larvae also damaged stems and roots, the leaf response mixes direct chewing defense with whole-plant alarm signals. The mapped response gives breeders candidate genes and chemicals for tomatoes that resist this pest with less insecticide.
pmc-13500441:
Arefayne Mesfen Dessye explores in 2026 what he calls the Ethiopian paradox, where a nation famous for distance-running dominance also loses many elite runners early to burnout and injury. His mixed-methods study compared 60 retired elite Ethiopian endurance runners in two equal groups. One group's careers lasted at least ten years and the other's ended within seven, blending training log analysis and psychological surveys with in-depth interviews.

Durable runners showed steadier training loads, stronger coping with adversity, and lower maladaptive perfectionism, each difference statistically significant in the reported comparisons. Interviews distilled three separating themes, covering coaching that granted guided autonomy, an athletic identity integrated with the rest of life, and community support acting as a buffer. Combining the strands produced a three-pillar durability profile offered to coaches as a framework for building long careers rather than burning bright and short.
pmc-13500841:
Longfei Dang leads a four-author team proposing a 2026 imaging algorithm for borehole radar, a tool lowered into drill holes to picture rock formations underground. Existing logging methods force a trade-off: they see a few metres in fine detail or reach far with blur. The new time-frequency joint algorithm uses the direct wave, the signal that travels straight from transmitter to receiver, as a stable reference for normalizing amplitude and synchronizing timing, which suppresses source jitter.

Wavelet and Fourier filtering clean out-of-band noise, and adaptive amplification that grows with time compensates for signal spreading and absorption in rock. In experiments the method stretched the detection range to about 8.5 to 10 metres, well beyond the under-3-metre reach of conventional high-resolution logging. Spatial resolution at the same time improved to the centimetre level, roughly 5 to 10 centimetres. The authors flag that wider geological testing is still needed.
pmc-13501841:
Jinrui Xing leads an eight-author team with a 2026 study of the gut-brain axis in adolescent mice made depressed by chronic unpredictable mild stress. Stressed mice lost interest in sugar water, gave up sooner in a swim test, and moved less in an open field, the standard behavioural signature. The team sequenced gut microbes from intestinal contents and measured brain-linked chemicals in the gut lining by mass spectrometry, then correlated microbes, chemicals, and behaviour.

Microbe variety fell in the stressed group, and community structure shifted modestly but clearly. In the colon lining, the whole serotonin pathway sagged: serotonin itself, its precursor, its breakdown product, and kynurenine all dropped, while phenylethylamine and norepinephrine rose. One bacterium, Lactobacillus acidophilus, tracked with both happier behaviour and healthier chemistry. The authors stress the work is correlational, a map for future causal tests.
pmc-13501941:
Madsen and colleagues compared intimacy and relationship life between partnered cancer survivors and people without a cancer history in Denmark's nationally representative Project SEXUS cohort. Their 2026 study covers 47,718 partnered adults, including more than three thousand survivors. Cancer is well known to damage sexual function, but whether it changes how much people value intimacy, why they have sex, and how their relationships feel was less clear.

Madsen found survivors rated the importance of various kinds of intimacy, their reasons for having sex, and their relationship characteristics the same as peers without cancer. This held after demographic weighting and adjustment. The similarity held for both sexes and for survivors within five years of diagnosis as well as longer-term ones. The authors argue that survivorship care should treat sexual health holistically, recognizing that intimacy and relational strengths often survive cancer intact and can buffer the functional difficulties that do occur.
pmc-13502141:
Linrong Li leads a five-author team with a 2026 review of antibody-encapsulated drugs, a proposed successor to antibody-drug conjugates in cancer therapy. Conjugates weld a poison to an antibody, but the welding is uneven: drug-to-antibody ratios vary, linkers can leak early, and production is complex. The new platform instead tucks a fixed number of drug molecules inside an antibody without a covalent bond, using a technique called single protein encapsulation. That promises exact dosing, less premature release, and simpler production.

The proof-of-concept pairs trastuzumab, a HER2-targeting antibody, with actinomycin D sealed inside it. Across cancer models with varying HER2 levels the construct killed tumours while showing a friendly toxicity profile in animals. Parallel trials of albumin-encapsulated medicines support the wider platform. The authors position the approach as a way past conjugate resistance and limits, widening which payloads and proteins can be used.
pmc-13502641:
Liang-Ting Wu leads a four-author team with a 2026 study of why fluorinating an ether solvent makes lithium-metal battery electrolytes resist oxidation. Fluorinated versions of an ether had shown excellent stability in tests, but solvent design remained guesswork. The team attacked the question at three scales. Density functional theory covered electronic structure, ab initio molecular dynamics covered short-time behaviour, and a machine-learning force field covered longer interfacial simulations at the cathode surface.

Three fluorine effects emerged. Beta-fluorination stabilizes the ethoxy carbon-hydrogen bonds through an inductive effect. Shifted electrons weaken the solvent's grip on the nickel-rich cathode surface, discouraging oxidation and carbon-carbon bond activation there. The fluorinated molecule's dipole moment makes it line up one way, shielding its methoxy group from the surface. Together the three explain the stability jump, and the authors offer the dissection as a template for electrolyte design.
pmc-13503841:
Hadil Faris Alotaibi leads a team that uses machine learning to predict how well drug cocrystals will dissolve, in a 2026 study. Cocrystals pair a drug with a partner compound to help poor drugs mix with water. Picking the right partner depends on how the two parts interact.

The team fed 181 samples, each with 86 traits from two descriptor methods, into three tree-based models. A search method modeled on dragonflies tuned each model. One model, Extra Trees, beat the rest on all three solubility outputs, with fit scores above 0.86. Traits from both descriptor sources mattered. The authors say the tool can speed the screening of partner compounds before lab work begins.
pmc-13504141:
Jintao Cui leads a team building a breast cancer outlook score from genes tied to a contact zone between two cell parts, in a 2026 study. The zone links the energy factories to the protein-folding workshop, and its faults can steer tumor growth and immune response. Its value for forecasting care was not yet clear.

From 83 such genes, the team distilled a four-gene score that split patients into high and low risk across several cohorts. Low-risk tumors held more immune cells and were tipped to answer better to immune therapy. High-risk tumors looked more open to chemo and targeted drugs. Single-cell maps showed where each gene acts in the tumor. Lab tests confirmed three of the four genes run high in breast cancer cells.
pmc-13505141:
Emad Shamsan and co-authors studied a severe parasitic liver disease caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, which grows into liver tissue and scars it over time. They focused on a signalling pair, the protein IL-33 and its receptor ST2, and asked whether blocking ST2 changes the course of infection. Work combined liver tissue from patients with a mouse model of the disease.

Patient tissue showed raised IL-33 and ST2 alongside markers of immune activity and scarring. In infected mice, blocking ST2 shrank parasite lesions and reduced liver invasion. Treated livers carried less scar tissue, fewer gathered immune cells, and lower levels of several inflammatory signals in the blood. Because parasite burden also fell, the authors note that further work must separate direct anti-scarring effects from effects that follow from controlling the parasite.
pmc-13505741:
Minji Jeong and co-authors improved how perovskite solar films are grown by vacuum deposition, a route valued for even coatings. The weak point is the start of growth: one ingredient lands first and clumps into islands, leaving pinholes and defects where the film meets the electron-transport layer. Their fix pre-lays an extremely thin lead iodide layer that acts as a seed bed.

That seed layer converts fully as the remaining ingredients arrive, so grains start evenly and grow sideways into a coherent film. Grains ended up larger, defect counts in the bulk and at the interface fell, and charge carriers lived nearly twice as long before recombining. Cells built this way reached a stabilised efficiency close to twenty percent. The authors offer the seeding trick as a general recipe for cleaner vacuum-grown films in future optoelectronic devices.
pmc-13508041:
De Manincor and colleagues ran an experimental warming study on plant and pollinator communities to see how climate warming breaks their partnership, in a 2026 ecology paper. The usual suspect is timing mismatch, flowers and bees shifting seasons at different rates, but direct experimental evidence was missing. The team warmed whole spring communities and tracked timing, traits, behavior, and the fitness of both partners.

De Manincor found warming shifted both flowering and bee activity yet kept the partners in step with each other, so timing mismatch was not the culprit. Instead warming cut flower numbers, lowered the nectar and pollen rewards, reduced bee visits, and depressed bee survival, weakening the mutualism through body condition and behavior rather than calendars. Both plant and bee fitness fell as a result. The authors argue conservation attention should move from phenology alone toward the physiological and behavioral pathways that quietly erode species interactions.
pmc-13508341:
Ju Chang and seven co-authors test whether spraying tiny silica particles on bamboo leaves improves seedling nutrition, in 2026 work. Bamboo locks away carbon and guards forests, yet how nano-silica shapes its nutrient balance was unclear. Seedlings of a large bamboo species received six spray strengths, from none up to the highest dose. The team measured leaf greenness, silica content, and the levels and ratios of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium in the plants. Patterns were checked with correlation and grouping analyses.

A middle dose gave the best overall result. It raised leaf greenness and boosted silica, phosphorus, and potassium stores while keeping nitrogen high. The top dose backfired, cutting greenness and nutrient stores. Greenness tracked closely with silica, nitrogen, and phosphorus levels. The authors suggest a moderate spray can sharpen seedling quality for planting programs, while warning that more is not better with these particles.
pmc-13508441:
Meryem Bekmezci and Mehmet Semih Demirtas compare blood inflammation scores in pregnancies exposed to methamphetamine and in matched controls, in 2026 work. The drug is known to harm birth outcomes, and simple blood ratios may flag that risk. Records covered 52 exposed pregnancies and 93 controls at a university hospital. Inflammation indices were built from admission blood counts for mothers. For babies, counts existed for only 28 exposed newborns, drawn when doctors judged them needed. Paired tests compared mother and baby scores.

Mothers in the exposed group ran higher on every inflammation measure, including cell counts and combined indices. Their scores were far above controls by clear statistical margins. Mother and baby scores also differed from each other in paired checks. The authors suggest cheap blood indices could help flag exposed pregnancies needing closer watch, while noting the small newborn set limits how far the baby findings stretch.
pmc-13509841:
Fernanda Carvalho and Joana P. Costa survey metal compounds built around camphor-based parts as possible cancer and germ fighters, in a 2026 mini-review. Camphor comes from a familiar plant source, and chemists can reshape its structure and attach different metal centers to tune how the resulting compounds act on cells. The review draws together lab findings on these compounds and their effects.

Choosing the right metal and shaping the camphor part can strengthen killing of cancer cells while also adding action against bacteria or fungi. That double action makes the compounds attractive for settings where infection and cancer risks meet. The authors point to a next step of loading such compounds into body-friendly materials, such as mineral coatings or gels, to make wound dressings and other composites that treat as they cover.
pmc-13510841:
Pampalakis and Pontiki profile an obscure family of nerve agents entirely by computer. Their 2026 paper studies the phosphonate esters of alkyl acetoacetates. These little-known members of the V-agent class, which includes VX, exist as two geometric forms. The E and Z isomers have largely unmeasured properties. The authors applied computational tools to predict absorption, chemical behaviour, and structure-related toxicity.

The models predict these agents penetrate skin, making them contact hazards, and also cross the gut wall and the blood-brain barrier. Certain liver enzymes were predicted to handle the two isomers differently, which may explain reports that the E forms are far more toxic than their Z counterparts. Stability analysis likewise supported the reported fragility of the Z forms. The authors present this first detailed in-silico description as groundwork for countermeasures, requiring targeted laboratory validation.
pmc-13511541:
Pan Tang and eight co-authors build a nanoparticle vaccine against a pig diarrhea virus that costs the swine industry heavily, in 2026 work. Current shots give weak immune responses, poor gut-level protection, and short cover. The team mounted the virus's S1 spike part onto ferritin protein shells using a snap-together tag system, then checked particle shape and size before testing in mice and piglets.

After two doses, piglets made strong antibody levels that topped those from a standard killed-virus vaccine, alongside higher virus-blocking titers and higher immune signal levels. When challenged with the live virus, vaccinated piglets were fully protected and showed far milder diarrhea and gut damage than unprotected animals. Mice also mounted strong body-wide and cell-based responses. The authors call the candidate promising while noting this is an early step before farm rollout.
pmc-13511741:
Marci K. Sontag and Susanna A. McColley introduce a special issue on newborn screening for cystic fibrosis, a testing practice now nearly fifty years old, in 2026 work. Screening methods, teaching approaches, and treatments have all advanced since the first programs. The issue spans lab testing, screening accuracy, hard diagnostic cases, and the effect of newer modulator drugs on the screening picture.

One anchor piece sets out United States consensus guidelines for the best screening setup, drawn up to catch as many affected infants as possible. A companion commentary weighs the load those aims place on public health programs. State programs also report their own fixes, including seasonal cut-off tuning in California and a full pathway review in Georgia. Wide variation between programs drives the push for shared standards that still fit local limits.
pmc-13512541:
Mingyuan Yuan and Fei Zhou propose a shared control frame for boosting artemisinin output in the plant Artemisia annua, in 2026 work. The compound, a frontline malaria drug ingredient, is made and stored in tiny hair-like glands on the plant. Yield is capped by a tug-of-war among gland number, chemical flow through the pathway, and total plant growth. The review centers on a family of switch proteins called bHLH factors that tie those threads together.

One family member merges two hormone signals to switch on core production genes. Another links gland birth to pathway flow and teams with partners to amplify key enzymes. A third stretches the control to the whole plant, matching gland formation with photosynthesis and carbon use. The authors argue that editing several hubs at once, guided by multi-layer data, could break the growth-versus-defense trade-off that breeding alone has not.
pmc-13513141:
Huang and colleagues compared a 2026 cohort of older patients given indobufen or aspirin after heart bypass surgery for unstable angina. Patients aged seventy and above face a fine balance between preventing clots and causing bleeding. Indobufen blocks the same enzyme as aspirin but is less studied after bypass operations.

The single centre study covered operations from 2017 to 2021 and kept seventy-nine patients after screening, forty-nine on aspirin pathways and thirty on indobufen. Huang weighted the groups statistically to balance sixteen baseline traits before comparing two year outcomes. No significant difference appeared in major heart and brain events, serious bleeding, or the combined outcome. Graft checks were available for most patients at one and two years, and the authors call for larger prospective trials.
pmc-13513941:
Ahmed and Cao published a 2026 study on steering a blood protein's shape on titanium implants. Fibrinogen, a clotting protein, is among the first to coat any implant. Its shape on the surface steers how tissues accept the device later. The team coated titanium with chalk-like calcite using electric deposition.

Longer coating times thickened the layer to near-full surface coverage overall. Calcium leaking from the coat reshaped fibrinogen into sponge-like clumps. A three-hour coat produced the strongest sponge effect in their tests. Surface scans confirmed the protein's new bonding pattern after reshaping. Guided protein shaping could help implants knit with tissue better. Calcium release rose with coating time in a steady climb. Coverage neared 99.8 percent after the longest coating run in tests.
pmc-13517041:
Zuzana Hudáková and four colleagues link long non-coding RNAs to drug resistance in glioblastoma in a 2026 cell study. The standard drug temozolomide fails often against this brain tumour. The A172 line proved most sensitive and the T98G line most resistant. Sensitive cells jammed in the run-up to division, while resistant cells barely reacted and carried far more MGMT. RNA patterns split the lines clearly: MALAT1 fell across the board, while NCK1-AS1 surged, above all in the resistant line. pmc-13518841:
Vladimir Nikora, Hongwei Fang, Guojian He, and Lei Huang argue in 2026 that flowing surface water helped life make the leap from single cells to multicellular forms. Bigger, many-celled organisms burn far more energy, so they need faster nutrient supply. Rising oxygen in the Neoproterozoic era gets most of the credit in standard accounts.

Nikora and colleagues propose that widespread water movement boosted nutrient delivery to microbes, acting as a necessary partner to oxygen. They define three testable flow regimes governing uptake for both attached and free-floating microbes. Streambeds, where water meets the bottom, may have been breeding grounds for early multicellularity. Their framework yields predictions linking organism size, flow, and habitat.
pmc-13520241:
Ming Wang leads a large team in 2026 building turmeric-derived nanovesicles to calm the runaway immune response that erodes bone in gum disease. Single-cell data from public sets flagged faulty trap formation as a treatment target.

The tiny plant vesicles, loaded with turmeric's own active compounds, were eagerly taken up by neutrophils. Treated cells cast far fewer traps, showing lower oxidative stress markers and less expelled DNA. Gene profiles confirmed quieter trap pathways alongside stronger antioxidant defenses. In mice with periodontitis, vesicles gathered at inflamed sites, slowed bone loss, and preserved bone structure.
pmc-13522441:
Kedziora and co-authors demonstrate in 2026 a way to steer the spin of light inside perovskite microwires, thin crystal channels that guide light like optical fibers. They worked with exciton-polaritons, hybrid particles that are part light and part matter excitation, which can condense into a coherent state. Controlling the polarization, or spin, of such signals is a step toward photonic circuits that encode information in spin.

Above the condensation threshold, the microwires emitted polarized light from their edges in a pattern matching the optical spin Hall effect, where opposite spins travel to opposite sides. The emitted light showed chirality exceeding eighty percent, meaning one spin direction strongly dominated, and the spin-polarized signal propagated over tens of micrometers along the wire. The crystals form a natural cavity without mirrors. The authors present these CsPbBr3 waveguides as a platform for spin-coded information transport on a chip.
pmc-13522541:
Guo and colleagues identified in 2026 a receptor for a bacterial signal molecule in Lactiplantibacillus plantarum, a gut-friendly bacterium. The signal, c-di-AMP, is a small ring-shaped messenger that shapes how bacteria interact with their host, but its role in this species was unclear. It blocked one gene whose product helps the bacterium grip fibronectin, a surface protein of gut lining cells, and boosted a gene for an enzyme that breaks down matrix. pmc-13523241:
Toshiyuki Suzuki and colleagues identify tissue features tied to pancreatic leakage after surgery in a 2026 study. A fistula, an abnormal leak of pancreatic fluid, is a serious complication after removal of the body and tail of the pancreas. One hundred eighty-six patients were studied, with thickness measured on preoperative scans and the cut surface examined under a microscope for small duct branches and scarring.

One third of patients developed a clinically relevant leak. Risk rose with a thicker pancreas at the cut site, a higher density of branched small ducts, and a lower share of fibrous scarring. Thick glands also tended to show denser branching and less scarring, suggesting the features travel together. The authors propose that gland anatomy and tissue makeup jointly shape leak risk and could guide surgical technique.
pmc-13523341:
Fanny Iafrate-Luterbacher and colleagues track a heart risk marker over time in young people with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Lipoprotein(a) is a genetically set blood fat particle usually measured once in a lifetime, yet its behavior in childhood was poorly known. Annual fasting measurements from two hundred eighty-six patients at a Geneva hospital between 2012 and 2023 were analyzed.

More than fourteen hundred measurements were available. At first testing, about one quarter of participants had elevated levels. Among those measured repeatedly, nearly one third fluctuated by more than half of their personal maximum, and about one in eight crossed the clinical risk threshold at some point. Levels peaked in late childhood and varied modestly by season. The authors challenge the single lifetime measurement approach for this group.
pmc-13523441:
Hilda Machika Kanjedza, Ditress Nyirongo, and Genesis Chorwe-Sungani report a 2026 validation study from postnatal clinics in Lilongwe, Malawi, for a Chichewa version of the City Birth Trauma Scale.
