A structured medical interview put prevalence near one in five mothers, while the scale itself gave a lower figure. Reliability and accuracy measures were acceptable, with an optimal cut-off above 23. The authors conclude that the translated scale can support screening in Malawian postnatal care.
pmc-13524941:
C. Kishor Kumar Reddy and others propose, in a 2026 study, a sonar system that copies echolocation principles and pairs them with machine learning for underwater detection and navigation. Standard sonar uses much energy, suffers noise, and weakens in changing water conditions. Their model adjusts the pulses it sends on the fly in response to the environment.

Its signal steps include special filtering, wavelet decomposition, and adaptive thresholding to clean echoes. A convolutional network and a memory network then sort the echoes. In simulation tests tuned to real ocean data, the system reached 92.7 percent classification accuracy against 85.4 percent for standard methods. Energy use fell by about a fifth, signal clarity rose, false alarms dropped, and depth readings grew sharper through a sound speed fix. Trials stayed in simulation rather than open water.
pmc-13526741:
Hui Yu and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether a cell adhesion protein called ITGA7 restrains thyroid cancer by binding fibronectin and quieting a growth pathway. Thyroid cancer is the commonest endocrine malignancy and usually curable, yet some patients relapse. ITGA7 levels were compared between tumor and neighboring normal tissue.

Expression of ITGA7 was lower in cancers at both message and protein levels, including in cell lines. Removing ITGA7 made cancer cells grow, divide, migrate, and invade more, while resisting cell death. Binding tests confirmed a physical partnership with fibronectin, whose levels rose in tumors and moved opposite to ITGA7. Silencing fibronectin impeded tumor behavior, and pathway blots plus a mouse graft model supported the proposed chain through the PI3K and AKT signaling route.
pmc-13527141:
Diksha Arora, Jhilik Bhattacharya, and Chinmaya Panigrahy present, in a 2026 study, a deep learning method that reads rice leaf nutrient levels from drone multispectral images, instead of slow wet-lab chemistry. Knowing leaf nutrient levels guides fertilizer choices and yield. Their system searches for a good network design while using polynomial approximation functions and adaptive activations to cope with small training sets.

Error ranges came with the predictions, and feature maps showed leaves with similar nutrient values grouping together. Ablation and cross checks by treatment and plot confirmed each part's role, and the method beat standard deep and machine learning baselines.
pmc-13528041:
Zina Bai and ten colleagues published this 2026 study on irisin, a hormone released from muscle during exercise, as a treatment for flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The team measured irisin and its receptor, integrin αVβ5, in lung tissue, then modelled smoke and toxin lung injury in mice and cells to trace how irisin acts.

Blocking the receptor with the drug cilengitide abolished those benefits, and silencing the receptor in cells did too. The authors propose the receptor pathway as a treatment direction for COPD.
pmc-13528141:
Masayuki Kaneda and three colleagues study which Japanese hospitals claim an advanced ward pharmacy fee in a 2026 paper. The fee signals pharmacists doing deep ward-based care. National open data for 2021 to 2023 covered about 5,800 eligible hospitals each year. Only about a third filed the fee. The team linked staffing counts and hospital traits to filing.

Pharmacists per hundred beds showed the strongest tie. Filing hospitals had a median near 5.2 pharmacists per hundred beds. Non-filers sat near 2.6. A cutoff around four separated the groups well. University and high-function hospitals filed at rates near ninety percent. Long-term care hospitals filed at only about three percent. Sparse regions filed least. The authors read the pattern as uneven spread of pharmacy staff.
pmc-13528541:
Anastasia Louka and ten colleagues build light-switchable blockers for an inflammation enzyme in a 2026 study. The enzyme, 15-LOX-1, feeds gut inflammation and a cell death route called ferroptosis. Three families of switches were designed from known blocker shapes. Sunlight-style flashes flip each molecule between two forms. Crystal checks and computer models confirmed the flipping.

Two families turned off in one form and on in the other. The third family showed the reverse pattern. That mix lets users program the direction of control. In cells and in mice with colon inflammation, blocking the enzyme cut the signal IL-8. Light form decided how strong the cut was. The authors present a recipe book for photoswitch drugs. Gut disease is their first proving ground.
pmc-13529841:
Lan Lei and seven colleagues review new attacks on a growth pathway in the commonest breast cancer type in a 2026 paper. The cancer feeds on hormones and lacks HER2. Drugs blocking cell cycle gears work at first, then resistance grows. The PI3K to AKT to mTOR pathway often drives that escape. About forty-five percent of tumors carry a PIK3CA fault.

Narrow PI3K blockers help patients with that fault. One newer drug pairs benefit with gentler side effects. Broad blockers stumbled on toxicity. AKT blockers earned a place, with one approved in the United States. The mTOR blocker everolimus helps regardless of fault status. A dual blocker shows promise even without the fault. Next-wave drugs aim only at mutant forms. Choosing order and partners stays the open puzzle, the authors say.
pmc-13530241:
Taghi Shirzad and colleagues image underground fractures in 2026 at the Geysers geothermal field in California using tiny earthquakes as their light source. Steam-driven fields need clear maps of cracks and fluid paths to produce power well. The team selected 1,276 small induced quakes recorded between 2006 and 2015.

Wave speeds measured between quake pairs built a layered three-dimensional picture at fine spacing. Slow zones fell into three kinds: fault damage with altered rock, boundaries near the steam cap, and patches tied to injection work. Combined with quake locations, the map tracks fluid movement and stress change.
pmc-13531741:
Ahmed Abdelaziz leads a 2026 pooled analysis on spinning drill treatment for fully blocked heart arteries. Rotational atherectomy grinds hard calcium so stents can pass, yet safety inside chronic total blockages was uncertain. Four studies with 1,925 patients compared blocked versus unblocked lesions.

Vessel puncture occurred more often in blocked lesions, roughly three and a half times the odds. Death, heart attack, repeat treatment, and technical success otherwise matched between groups. The authors judge the drill approach workable for total blockages while urging respect for the puncture risk and more study of case severity.
pmc-13532241:
Victor M Gonzalez Ramos and co-authors characterize in 2026 a new gene switch that tells a white-rot fungus when to make wood-digesting enzymes. The switch, Bhr1, oddly fuses an energy-using motor fold with zinc-finger DNA grips. Gene editing knocked it out in the fungus Dichomitus squalens to test its role on mannose-rich foods.

Mutants faltered in enzyme output on mannose and guar gum while wild types thrived. Gene readings showed the switch turns on specific digesting enzymes without touching sugar transport or metabolism genes. The regulator appears only in mushroom-forming fungi, a lineage-specific invention.
pmc-13533041:
Gamze Babur Guler and colleagues reply in 2026 to comments on their single-centre study of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a thickened heart muscle condition. They clarify that the work aimed to describe traits, background, and imaging in a large group in Turkiye, not to predict outcomes. Follow-up had a median of 13 months, which they call short for a slow disease.

They agree that an apical form may carry higher risk than once thought, citing strong scar signals on scans. They also accept limits from a 32 percent genetic testing rate and plan deeper work on blocked mid-chamber flow and burn-out forms.
pmc-13533841:
Trang Cao and twenty colleagues published this 2026 analysis asking whether MRI studies of psychiatric disorders can ever agree on a brain phenotype. They tested how consistently research sites reproduce the same maps of gray matter differences. Pooling five disorders, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, autism, major depression and bipolar disorder, across 59 study sites, they correlated each site's brain-wide volume and thickness maps against the rest. The pool held 2,437 patients and 2,065 controls.

Consistency was dismal: the median cross-site correlation was at most 0.16, far below the 0.54 achieved in Alzheimer's disease, and the gap was not explained by demographics, scanners or analysis choices. Bootstrapping suggested schizophrenia maps might stabilise with at least 200 people per group, while other disorders would need much larger samples. The authors conclude that today's standard practice, many small independent studies, is unlikely to converge on MRI phenotypes for these disorders, and the field's methods need rethinking.
pmc-13534741:
Fuad S Al-Duais and colleagues propose in 2026 an uncertainty-aware framework that reads chest X-rays for pneumonia, lung scarring, and fluid build-up. Many image models give overconfident answers, which is risky in high-stakes diagnosis. Their system joins a vision transformer, a two-way sequence module, and a Bayesian fusion layer.

Training used two large public chest image collections after lung outlining and heavy augmentation. The model reached high accuracy with a top ranking score and very low calibration error. Calibrated confidence helps clinicians tell safe calls from risky ones that need human review.
pmc-13535741:
Juan Li and colleagues analyse in 2026 the spread and drivers of human brucellosis in Zhejiang Province, China, from 2018 to 2023. The animal-spread disease has risen even in developed regions with little livestock farming. Case data from 11 city areas fed Bayesian space-time models plus checks for clustering and risk factors.

Cases clustered clearly, with higher risk in four areas and lower risk in five coastal or urban areas. Live sheep imports and slaughter volume were the dominant drivers, each tied to higher incidence. Tighter control of sheep transport and slaughter in high-risk areas is recommended.
pmc-13536841:
Qiuxian Ye and colleagues examine why nurses speak up with ideas to improve care in a 2026 three-wave survey in China. Nurses caring for vulnerable patients face heavy pressure, so the study tests whether a trauma-aware workplace climate encourages constructive suggestions. A total of 508 matched replies came from nurses in six hospitals and related sites in two provinces, spaced two weeks apart. Models traced links through felt empowerment and cultural humility.

A stronger trauma-aware climate tracked with more speaking up and stronger felt empowerment. That feeling in turn tracked with speaking up and carried part of the climate link. The indirect path grew stronger when cultural humility, meaning openness to other backgrounds, ran high. The authors stress that the patterns show association rather than proof of cause, and they highlight supportive conditions for nurse voice.
pmc-13538641:
Xiaona Sun and colleagues uncover a protective metabolic enzyme in stroke injury in a 2026 mouse and cell study. When blood flow returns after a blocked brain artery, a second wave of damage follows, and metabolism may steer it through gene switches. The enzyme, which makes a key building block from citrate, rose after vessel blockage and reperfusion in mouse brains. Blocking or silencing it in animals and cultured neurons was tested.

Blocking the enzyme worsened brain injury in living mice and cut neuron survival after oxygen and sugar deprivation. The enzyme raised the building block supply, boosting gene switch tags on the promoter regions of power unit chain genes, which improved power unit function and curbed oxidative stress. The authors nominate the pathway as a fresh stroke treatment target.
pmc-13538741:
A Rumanes and colleagues examine foot ulcers as a warning marker in people with both diabetes and heart failure in a 2026 Dutch cohort study. Records covered 4,937 adults treated at one large center over two decades, split by whether a foot ulcer had occurred. Death and heart failure admissions were tracked over three years, with five-year death checks and bias-aware models.

Patients with ulcers carried more kidney disease and nerve damage. Death gaps looked modest over three years from heart failure diagnosis but widened clearly by five years. When timing started at ulcer diagnosis, one-year death rates ran dramatically higher in the ulcer group. A time-aware model tied ulcer occurrence independently to nearly triple the death hazard. The authors cast ulcers as a marker of advanced disease meriting intensified team care.
pmc-13540341:
Yifan Han leads a large 2026 trial of a lab-made hormone copy. The hormone, thrombopoietin, tells the body to make platelets. The patients had chronic liver disease and very low platelet counts. Low counts force delays to planned procedures. They can also force risky platelet transfusions.

One hundred twenty Chinese adults joined the phase three trial. Two thirds got the hormone and one third got a placebo. Dosing ran for up to a week before a planned procedure. Eighty-five percent on the drug kept counts above target. That held through a week after the procedure. Most treated patients avoided transfusion, and side effects matched the placebo group.
pmc-13540841:
Ece Erdem Altınyürek and Veli Özgen Öztürk study the mouth in a 2026 project. They asked whether stomach inflammation reshapes mouth bacteria. The condition is called gastritis. The mouth and gut form one connected system. Gum health was part of the question too.

Fifteen gastritis patients gave saliva samples for the study. Fifteen healthy volunteers did the same. All had gum examinations as well. The team sorted each person by gum state. States ran from healthy gums to early periodontitis. Bacterial diversity ran higher in women. It also rose in the group with both gastritis and early gum disease.
pmc-13541641:
Yu and colleagues review live-attenuated vaccines against respiratory syncytial virus, the leading cause of severe chest infections in small children. It causes millions of illnesses and around a hundred thousand deaths under five each year worldwide. Older children past six months still lack any approved vaccine. Weakened-virus designs must walk a line between too feeble to protect and too strong to be safe, and early vaccine history left a shadow of enhanced disease. Their 2026 review tracks how reverse genetics changed the craft.

By editing the viral genome deliberately, developers can now tune weakening precisely and stack safeguards. Trials in children who have never met the virus show no sign of the vaccine-enhanced respiratory disease that haunted the field. The authors weigh newer platforms honestly: shots that protect newborns through their mothers fade within the first year.
pmc-13542441:
Lien Creytens, Sofie Piepers, and Sarne De Vliegher checked two rapid culture tests in 2026 that veterinary clinics can run on site when judging whether a mastitis case needs antibiotics. Selective treatment rests on a quick distinction: infections from gram-positive bacteria mostly benefit from antibiotics, while gram-negative cases often clear on their own. Standard laboratory culture is too slow for that decision, so the MicroMast and VetoRapid kits were checked against full lab bacteriology.

Both kits sorted gram-positive from gram-negative infections well in practice hands, with VetoRapid the stronger of the two. That distinction is exactly the one the treatment call needs. Naming the precise pathogen was another story: naming at species level was limited for both systems. The authors therefore endorse the kits for guiding selective treatment, while warning against leaning on them for wider udder health care.
pmc-13543341:
Xile Wang's team studied in 2026 how the body can neutralise adalimumab, a biologic drug used for rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. Some patients develop anti-drug antibodies that lower drug levels and blunt benefit. The team tracked 78 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis and 59 with active ankylosing spondylitis for 24 weeks, checking drug levels and antibodies with lab assays, with healthy volunteers set beside them.

By 24 weeks about one in five patients had gained anti-drug antibodies, nearly all of them neutralising, and the rate ran higher in ankylosing spondylitis than in rheumatoid arthritis. Patients with antibodies carried lower drug levels and were more likely to remain highly active in their disease. Early antibody arrival pointed to worse status, while higher drug levels guarded against it. Tracking drug and antibody levels could help doctors decide when to adjust or switch treatment.
pmc-13543641:
Yuyuan Ma and colleagues published a 2026 study of how rootstocks change the flavour and nutrition of tomato fruit, using the cultivar HZ504 grafted onto three rootstocks with self-grafted plants as control. Grafting is routine for vigour and disease resistance, yet its grip on fruit quality runs through poorly mapped molecular routes. The team paired harvest traits with full gene-activity and metabolite profiling of the ripe fruit.

One rootstock, called JZ, stood out: it raised fruit number per plant and soluble solids, and it broadly rewired the fruit's chemistry. Phenolic acids, flavonoids, terpenoids, and amino acids all climbed. At the pink ripening stage, JZ switched on the flavonoid production line in step with ripening, matching the chemical build-up. Choosing a rootstock, the authors conclude, is also choosing a flavour and nutrition programme, not merely a stronger root.
pmc-13547241:
Leilei Chen, Yanyan Lin, and Hongfei Xiao addressed in 2026 a stability problem in clusters of small DC power grids linked together. Power exchange at the shared connection point can swing and disturb voltages across the cluster. Their control design lets the converters between sub-grids cooperate with local generators, balancing active power across the whole cluster while handling reactive power locally inside each sub-grid.

A detailed small-signal model, the standard tool for checking whether small disturbances die out, was built for this exact control arrangement. Simulations under light loading, heavy reactive loading, and heavy active loading all behaved as intended. The converters tracked their power targets while the connection voltage stayed stable, which the authors offer as evidence the split-level design works.
pmc-13548641:
Xinxiu Liang and colleagues follow a gut microbe product in the blood to see how it relates to coronary heart disease, diet, and the microbiome, in a 2026 prospective study. The compound, imidazole propionate, is made by bacteria from the amino acid histidine and can disturb sugar metabolism. Big American health cohorts supplied over seven thousand participants for the risk analysis, with smaller groups providing stool and diet records.

People with the highest blood levels faced roughly eighty percent higher heart disease risk than those with the lowest. Eating more histidine alone showed no clear link, and fiber, especially pectin from fruit, predicted lower compound levels. Seventeen bacterial species predicted production, and levels rose from histidine only when fiber intake was low and producer microbes were abundant. The authors highlight fiber and the microbiome as levers on this pathway.
pmc-13548941:
Simone Finizio and colleagues describe a way to keep X-ray microscope images sharp despite the trembling of the laboratory, in a 2026 instrumentation paper. Scanning transmission X-ray microscopy maps chemistry at nanometer scale, but the sample must sit still relative to the focusing lens, and vibration plus slow repositioning waste beam time. Their method, supersampled scanning microscopy, records the sample's true position far faster than the vibrations occur.

Each detector count is logged with the position measured at that instant, and the image is rebuilt afterward from that list rather than from where the sample was supposed to be. Proof-of-concept experiments delivered high-resolution images while cutting the overhead that precise positioning usually demands. The authors argue the trick matters most at the new, brighter synchrotron sources, where fast scans make positioning the bottleneck.
pmc-13550541:
Amir Alambeigi and colleagues ask why greenhouse growers in Iran hesitate to adopt safety tools that protect workers, consumers, and the environment, in a 2026 survey study. Productivity gadgets spread fast, while safety tools lag. Building on a classic persuasion model, the team added perceived risk as the spark and surveyed 119 owners and managers of automated or semi-automated greenhouses, modeling their answers with statistics.

Attitude toward the technology proved the strongest predictor of intending to adopt it. Perceived risk did not push intention directly; instead it raised motivation and confidence to think things through, which switched on careful, central weighing of the arguments. Side cues like endorsements still swayed the less engaged, though strong motivation shrank their pull. The authors prescribe packages mixing risk briefings, skills training, credible champions, and supportive policy.
pmc-13550641:
Alba Garrido, with four colleagues, published a 2026 paper on a deep learning system for cancer survival. The system takes in many kinds of patient data at once. It uses clinical facts, four molecular profiles, and tissue images. Older models used one data type and missed much of the tumor's story. The new system, called SAMVAE, maps all inputs into one shared space.

Tests used breast cancer and a brain tumor group. The system matched top rival models on survival calls. It can also split risks, such as death from cancer versus other causes. Its design yields a personal survival curve for each patient. Clinicians can read clear summary numbers from those curves. The team calls it an early public tool of its kind.
pmc-13551841:
Xi Chen, leading four colleagues, published a 2026 qualitative study of how Chinese culture shapes nursing students' views of schizophrenia. Stigma among future nurses can block patient recovery, and Chinese emphases on face-saving and Confucian values may color it differently from Western settings. Thirty students aged 19 to 22 joined online focus groups in mainland China in 2022, analyzed by conventional content analysis.

Five themes covered knowledge gaps, misconceptions, cultural influence on attitudes, intended behavior toward patients, and pity mixed with awareness of injustice. Family and community attitudes, religious interpretations, and contact with mental health services all fed perceptions in the reported themes. The authors say anti-stigma programs for nursing students must work with these cultural factors rather than import generic material.
pmc-13555641:
Qiaoqiao Guo leads a six-author team showing how one letter change in DNA can rescue E. coli bacteria missing a vital fat-making gene in a 2026 study. Without that gene, cells stay tiny and shrink from antibiotics. A helper gene can bypass the gap, but only when present in many copies. The team selected rare survivors that resisted a strong antibiotic.

One survivor carried a single letter swap inside a neighbouring gene. That swap accidentally created a new promoter, a start switch, which cranked up the helper gene's output. Growth, fat making, and drug resistance all returned to normal levels. The finding warns drug hunters that bacteria may hide escape routes behind dormant genes, ready to wake with one small change.
pmc-13555941:
Diya Dou leads a six-author team pooling studies on how social-emotional learning programmes affect the teachers who deliver them in a 2026 analysis. Most reviews judge such programmes by student gains alone. Eighteen studies covering 3,465 teachers entered the pool. Effects on positive and negative sides of well-being were separated by a two-path model.

Programmes lifted teacher well-being overall by a modest, firm margin. Positive well-being, such as energy and satisfaction, rose more than distress fell. Study design, extra coaching, and mindfulness content each changed how strong the effect ran. Coaching mainly boosted the positive side, while mindfulness mainly eased the negative side. Time and dose did not matter clearly.
pmc-13556241:
Rachel Kratofil and colleagues filmed Staphylococcus aureus biofilms inside living tissue to see how a sugar coating shields the bacteria from immune attack. Biofilms are bacterial cities glued together, and this coating, called PNAG, is a slime the bacteria secrete.

Using a foreign-body infection model in mice, the team watched white blood cells called neutrophils try to reach bacteria clusters. The PNAG layer worked as a physical wall, keeping neutrophils out and delaying clearance of the infection. Strains unable to make PNAG let more neutrophils in and were cleared faster by the body. Enzymes that chew up PNAG broke the wall open, restored neutrophil access, and sped bacterial clearance.
pmc-13558641:
Ruhama Ilyas and two colleagues settled in 2026 a practical question for wind farm planning: which probability curve best describes wind speeds at tropical sites. Most assessments default to one familiar curve, yet wind character shifts with place and season. The team fitted ten candidate distributions to records from ten South Pacific island sites. They scored the fits with ten criteria. Four ways of estimating each curve's parameters were compared, and a decision procedure ranked the estimation methods.

A three-parameter version of the classic Weibull curve fitted best at the largest share of sites, and a maximum goodness-of-fit estimation method won most often. The traditional two-parameter curve, plus two other families, still prevailed at particular sites. Wind power densities were calculated from the winning fits. The authors' message is procedural: test several curves and estimators rather than trusting one habit.
pmc-13558741:
Nima Omidi, Seyed Ali Hosseini Tafreshi, and Mohammad Reza Zoghi showed in 2026 that an ordinary camera image can stand in for laboratory assays when growing the microalga Dunaliella salina. Measuring biomass and pigments normally destroys the sample and takes time, blocking live control of cultivation. Their framework reads colour through five colour spaces. The numbers feed two modelling platforms, neural networks and response surface fits. Growth density and three pigments are predicted at once, in cultures stressed by salt and light.

Networks handled the nonlinear, stress-shaped responses best: one colour space led for total carotenoids, another for the main chlorophyll, while the simpler statistical model sufficed for the second chlorophyll. Error tracking across the whole growth cycle showed the networks stayed steadier over time. The authors offer the low-cost imaging method for bioprocessing and smart farming.
pmc-13559141:
Guangbo Li and four colleagues studied early warning signs that a child with immunoglobulin A vasculitis will go on to develop kidney involvement, the illness's most serious complication. Their 2026 retrospective analysis covered 100 children treated at a Fudan University children's hospital branch between January 2023 and June 2025. Thirty-two children developed the kidney complication and 68 did not.

Three laboratory measures differed between the groups: C-reactive protein, the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and fibrinogen degradation products. In multivariate analysis, the ratio and the degradation products each stood as independent risk factors on their own. Used together, the two markers predicted kidney involvement with an area under the curve of 0.882 in the group's results. Sensitivity and specificity both sat near 87 percent at the chosen cutoffs. The authors present the paired test as a practical aid for spotting children who need closer kidney monitoring.
pmc-13560141:
Qianhui Yang and four colleagues quantify dye leakage around the pupil's edge on iris angiography to grade diabetic eye disease. Their 2026 observational study enrolled 66 healthy volunteers and 185 patients with diabetes, sorted into no retinopathy, non-proliferative, and proliferative groups. Custom software measured how long leakage took to appear and how many degrees of the pupil's rim it covered.

Young healthy eyes showed no leakage at all, while older healthy eyes leaked mildly and briefly. Leakage range widened steeply with disease stage, roughly tripling from the earliest diabetic group to the proliferative group in the reported means. Leakage also began sooner in advanced disease. Both measures separated diabetic patients from age-matched healthy subjects. The authors propose the iris measurement as extra information about front-of-eye vessel involvement, handy when the retina itself is hard to examine.
pmc-13560241:
Ching-Han Liu and colleagues test finerenone, a newer mineralocorticoid receptor blocker, against acute alcohol injury to the heart. Their 2026 study works in rat heart cells exposed to ethanol and in mice given three days of alcohol. No curative drug exists for alcoholic cardiomyopathy, and alcohol raises aldosterone, the hormone this drug class counters.

In cells, finerenone blunted ethanol's effects: fewer cells died, mitochondria stayed less fragmented, and inflammatory signaling quieted. The drug also curbed ethanol's upregulation of the mineralocorticoid receptor itself. In mice, it lowered the blood injury marker CK-MB and reduced heart cell death and tissue damage. Inflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction all eased with treatment. The authors propose finerenone as a protective candidate for acute alcoholic heart injury, while noting that clinical evidence must follow this preclinical work.
pmc-13560441:
Musa Acartürk, Seda Gürsoy, and Ibrahim Filazi ask whether metals from dental amalgam fillings linger in tooth structure after the fillings are removed. Their 2026 ex vivo study examines sixty extracted molars: intact controls plus teeth that carried one-, two-, or three-surface amalgam restorations stored in artificial saliva. After removal and acid digestion, mass spectrometry measured nine metals.

Every metal appeared in every group, including untouched teeth. Seven metals, mercury among them, ran higher in restored teeth than controls, while silver and lead ran higher in controls. Only chromium and nickel climbed consistently with restoration size; the rest showed no tidy surface-count pattern. The authors conclude amalgam metals do persist in tooth tissue after removal, in element-specific ways that size alone cannot explain. They leave the clinical meaning open, calling for further investigation before health claims attach.
pmc-13560541:
Alvaro Rodríguez-Mora and colleagues present ANGOSAP, an implementation protocol for building psychological support services inside four Angolan universities. Funded through Erasmus+, the project answers rising student mental health demand in a system short on specialists. Its model shares tasks beyond specialists and steps care up or down by need.

Each campus will run standard procedures for intake, triage, risk assessment, safeguarding, and referral, backed by competency-based training and supervision. Students get psychoeducation, brief interventions, and digital resources, with formal pathways into outside care. Early success will be judged by reach, waiting times, first-appointment uptake, and care-plan completion, plus symptom change on standard questionnaires. No clinical outcome data appear yet; the protocol's outputs are the pathway itself, a minimum monitoring dataset, and equity dashboards. The authors aim the design at national scale-up talks.
pmc-13561241:
Dahir and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare case combining three dangerous problems in a 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease that inflames many organs. She also had lupus kidney disease, was on dialysis, and took her immune-suppressing drugs irregularly. She arrived with fever, chest pain when breathing, a productive cough, and confusion.

Dahir's scans showed many hollow lung nodules and wedge-shaped shadows that fit septic pulmonary embolism, infected clots lodged in the lungs. Blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus, a common severe infection bacterium. She then weakened on her left side, and brain scans revealed a large bleed plus clots in two brain veins. Antibiotics and intensive support were given, but blood thinners were withheld because of the active bleeding. She improved steadily and left hospital in stable condition.
pmc-13561741:
Kwang Jin Ko and Jae Hoon Chung report early bladder function findings after single-port transvesical robot-assisted prostate removal, an approach credited with fast continence recovery. Their 2026 prospective case series studies eleven prostate cancer patients of one surgeon, all without spread on imaging. Full urodynamic testing and questionnaires were completed three months after surgery.

Bladder storage looked favorable: median capacity reached 450 milliliters with healthy compliance in the pressure studies. Leak testing provoked no leakage in nearly three quarters of patients. Continence climbed steeply, with zero-pad rates reaching 90.9 percent by three months in the small series. Cancer control lagged, though: positive margins hit 45.5 percent of specimens and PSA persisted in two patients in the reported outcomes. With no preoperative studies or control group, the authors refuse claims of superiority and urge careful patient selection.
pmc-13562541:
Vahid Parvaz and Jabbar Ganji build a tool that estimates how severe electricity losses from theft, faulty meters, and billing errors are, rather than flagging them. Utilities lose money on such non-technical losses, and inspectors need to know where the damage is biggest. Their 2026 framework defines an index of abnormal deviation: the gap between a customer's measured use and a baseline model of expected demand. A boosted-tree regression model, pruned by a feature-elimination routine, predicts that gap from smart-meter data.

On a public dataset the tuned model fit tightly, reaching a score of 0.9869, and beat ensemble and deep learning rivals. Its uncertainty bands behaved well, catching about 94 percent of cases inside the nominal 95 percent range. Load-related features drove the deviations most. The authors frame the output as a ranked risk guide for inspections, never as proof that a given customer stole power.
pmc-13562641:
Gongyu Zhang and seven colleagues build a score that predicts which patients will still hold titanium clips in the stomach six months after an endoscopic procedure. Clips close the wound left when early stomach lesions are cut out through a scope. Most fall away as healing completes, yet lingering clips may cause trouble. The 2026 study reviewed 1,055 patients, split into training and two validation groups. Regression analysis searched their records for traits tied to clips staying put.

Overall, 132 patients, 12.5 percent, kept clips at six months. Three traits predicted it: a tumour in the upper third of the stomach, worth two points, plus diabetes and the use of eight or more clips, worth one point each. Scores sorted patients into risk bands whose rates climbed from a few percent to over half. The score held up on fresh data, and clinicians could use it to plan follow-up where need is likeliest.
pmc-13562741:
Oluwakemi O. Onabanjo and six colleagues turn discarded banana flowers into a sponge for a stubborn synthetic dye in wastewater. Methylene blue lingers in water and threatens people and aquatic life, while treatment plants need cheap capture materials. The 2026 team dried banana flower waste, used part raw and part treated with acid to sharpen its surface chemistry. Imaging, diffraction, and surface-area tests confirmed a spongy, unordered solid rich in oxygen-bearing groups that can grip dye. Batch trials varied heat, acidity, time, and dose.

Uptake peaked under alkaline conditions. The acid-treated material held 48.6 milligrams of dye per gram, against 29.9 for the raw waste, a clear gain from a cheap step. Its surface measured 106.3 square metres per gram with pores near 6.1 nanometres wide. Heat calculations showed the capture runs spontaneously and absorbs warmth. The authors offer farm waste as a low-cost candidate for dye cleanup.
pmc-13563741:
Hongliang Gao and eight colleagues test whether stimulating two acupuncture points beats one alone at preventing sickness after womb-scope surgery. Nausea and vomiting trouble many patients after hysteroscopic procedures. Their 2026 trial enrolled 90 women and split them three ways: thumbtack needles at both the Neiguan wrist point and the Zusanli leg point, Neiguan alone, or a sham device as control. Nausea and vomiting were tracked across the first day after surgery, along with pain scores and gut restart time.

Both real-needle groups beat the sham for nausea in the first six hours and for vomiting across the first twelve. The combined group pulled ahead of everyone: its pain scores at six, twelve, and twenty-four hours were the lowest, and its bowels woke soonest. Single-point treatment helped, but the pairing did more. The authors recommend the two-point routine as a cheap layer of protection for these operations.
pmc-13563841:
Yuchen Pan and four colleagues pool published findings on a failure mode of hepatitis B prevention: babies protected at birth who still catch the virus. Their 2026 review, registered and run to reporting standards, searched five databases for people born to infected mothers, and forty studies qualified. Breakthrough was defined as turning positive for the surface antigen, or for a core antibody that marks infection, at age two or later.

True surface-antigen breakthrough was rare, at a pooled 0.24 percent of cases. The exposure marker told a story at 4.57 percent, climbing with age and running far higher when mothers carried the virus's e-antigen: 6.81 percent against 0.64 percent in other mothers. Protection improved with booster shots, with a ten-microgram rather than five-microgram dose, and with yeast-made vaccines. The authors argue for optimised schedules and follow-up in this group, since exposure accumulates even when disease stays rare.
pmc-13571241:
Isabelle Fleury leads a 2026 letter reporting real-world evidence on fixed-duration venetoclax treatment for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The question is what works after the disease progresses on a covalent BTK inhibitor, a common first targeted drug. Venetoclax, which blocks a survival protein in leukemia cells, can be given for a set period with an antibody partner.

Earlier trials and records showed durable responses after BTK inhibitor exposure, yet few patients in those analyses had truly progressed on the drug rather than stopping for side effects. The letter introduces an analysis from a large joint real-world study focused on exactly that progression group. Clinicians get evidence aimed at the hardest ordering question in this leukemia.
pmc-13574141:
Xingchi Chen, with 11 colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of a drug bath that makes immune cells better at killing leukaemia. The cells are gamma delta T cells, a type that can attack cancer without matching tissue types, which suits off-the-shelf use. A short bath in venetoclax, a drug that primes cell death pathways, had boosted a sister cell type before.

Pre-treated cells killed acute myeloid leukaemia cells harder and grew faster, with fewer signs of exhaustion. They held more cell powerhouses and burned fat for fuel, a profile tied to stamina. In mice, the treated cells held the disease down over time. The same bath also lifted engineered CAR versions of the cells. The authors propose adding the step to cell manufacturing for this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13574841:
Ji-Hyun Seo and Sang-Jin Shin report a 2026 study of keyhole repair for shoulders that are both loose and stiff. A dislocated shoulder can heal into frozen stiffness, a rare clash that stalls surgery plans. The team reviewed patients who had both faults and still went ahead with a scope repair of the torn rim.

Of 442 repair patients from 2019 to 2022, nineteen met the stiff-and-loose bar, and they were followed for near three years. Seventeen of the nineteen regained full motion. Forward reach, outward turn, and inward reach all rose sharply, while pain fell to near none. Two standard shoulder scores climbed into the top range. No patient needed a second operation or met a complication. The authors back scope repair for this mixed picture.
pmc-13575241:
Clara D C Claveau, Lauren Human, and Francesca Capozzi study eye contact during live conversation in a 2026 paper. Eye contact is widely believed to sharpen first impressions and shared attention, yet most past work used photos or videos on screens. Their study used real face-to-face meetings instead.

Participants met four people one at a time, rated each person's personality, then did a gaze-cueing task that measures joint attention. People mostly looked at their partners' eyes, more so when the eyes were easy to see. Eye contact barely predicted how accurate the personality ratings were. Early links did appear between gaze during the meetings and joint attention afterwards. The authors argue eyes carry real social weight in daily life, with effects that are subtle rather than sweeping.
pmc-13576141:
Chendi Qin leads a 2026 study building a quick sensor for a key tuberculosis drug, isoniazid. Knowing a patient's drug level helps set the dose and cut side effects, yet lab testing is slow. Their sensor uses a nanozyme, a nanomaterial that acts like an enzyme, whose colour reaction fades as drug levels rise.

Two readouts were built: a bench instrument and a smartphone method that reads colour values from photos. The bench method measured levels from 1 to 30 micromolar units, the phone method from 3 to 30 in the same units. Spiked samples of tablets and rat serum recovered close to the true amounts. Among three learning models, a convolutional network read phone photos best and stayed accurate under room light. The authors pitch the platform for routine drug monitoring.
pmc-13578441:
Habib Amiri Savadroodbari and colleagues tune a cotton yarn process by running a trained neural network in reverse, in a 2026 study. Factories set twist levels by trial and error to hit a target yarn strength. Their network first learned how settings map to strength from plant data. Then the settings themselves were nudged, step by step, until the network forecast the wanted strength.

Twist direction proved the biggest lever on strength, ahead of twist amounts. The best recipe used matching high twists in each single strand, a slightly lower combined twist, and a Z direction wrap. Strength rose by about a quarter over the starting yarn. A rival genetic search matched the cost score yet needed nearly four times the computing tries.
pmc-13578841:
Jennifer McNeely and a large trial team test a team based care plan for risky opioid use in primary care, in a 2026 trial across five United States sites. Patients who used opioids in risky ways, without severe addiction, often get no preventive help. Clinics were assigned by chance to the new plan or to boosted usual care, covering 202 patients in all.

The plan paired brief doctor advice with a nurse care manager in the clinic for a year, plus phone health coaching. Both groups kept normal care and got overdose safety materials. Most patients carried heavy pain loads and below average health at the start. At six months the plan group averaged fewer days of risky use than the usual care group, a gap the authors weigh with care given wide spread in the numbers.
pmc-13579741:
David M Ndetei and colleagues survey anxiety symptoms among young people in the Nairobi region of Kenya, in a 2026 study. Close to two thousand participants aged fourteen to twenty five came from colleges and neighborhoods across city and fringe areas. Standard questionnaires covered anxiety, depression, trauma, and drug use, along with family wealth and background facts.

Worry and nervousness were the most common complaints. Women and city dwellers scored clearly higher than men and fringe residents, across every score type. Poorer youth scored higher as wealth fell. Anxiety traveled with depression most strongly, and also with trauma symptoms, psychosis signs, mood swings, and alcohol or cannabis use. The authors call for joined up youth mental health plans that tackle poverty gaps and treat linked conditions together, with longer tracking to come.
pmc-13584341:
Arpan Mohanty and colleagues weigh whether antiviral drugs cut liver cancer risk in people with long-term hepatitis B who do not yet have cirrhosis. Hepatitis B affects close to 300 million people, and liver cancer can arise even before the liver scars badly. Their 2026 review screened more than two thousand records and kept 61 papers that covered 50 studies of treated and untreated patients.

In the four studies that could be compared head to head, treated patients developed liver cancer at a rate about forty percent lower than untreated patients. Cancer rates rose with longer follow-up in both groups, so the gap matters more over time. The authors say the findings support widening treatment rules to reach non-cirrhotic patients sooner, while calling for studies on when to start.
pmc-13586641:
Jezek and colleagues published a 2026 study on spotting hungry maize plants by leaf glow. Chlorophyll fluorescence sensors read how leaves handle light, hinting at plant health. Nitrogen and magnesium shortages both yellow leaves, so telling them apart is tricky. The team grew maize seedlings with each shortage and tracked leaf signals.

Both shortages cut the greenness index and nudged a protective compound index up. The protective index rose far less under magnesium shortage than nitrogen shortage. Nitrogen shortage marked young upper leaves first in their time-lapse tracking. Magnesium shortage began at the tips of older, lower leaves instead. Leaf age, they stress, must guide any sensor-based feeding decision. Sugar buildup inside leaves differed sharply between the two shortages too.
pmc-13589941:
Jiaqian Miao leads a 2026 study of alpha-mangostin, a natural compound from fruit rind that switches on STING, a protein that alerts the immune system. Turning STING on inside tumors can rouse immune attack, yet most such drugs spread through the body and miss the tumor. Miao and the team let the compound build its own tiny particles, with no carrier at all. Each particle held only the drug itself.

The particles stayed stable, released drug faster in acid, and entered cells well. In mice with skin cancer they reached tumors and woke STING there. Immune attack grew strong after shots into the tumor or into a vein. The team says a carrier free design also avoids harm from carrier stuff.
pmc-13591641:
Qi Qu leads a 2026 letter on lithocholic acid, a bile acid that rises when calories are cut and seems to copy some gains of eating less. Prior work in mice tied it to stronger muscle and longer life. Yet very high doses have harmed the liver in other studies, so safe dosing is an open worry. Qu and the team test the acid against fatty liver in mice made obese on a high fat diet, and in macaque monkeys.

Doses were set to match blood levels seen after calorie cutting, well below harmful ranges reported before. The letter lays out the safety question in full: which dose keeps the benefit without liver harm, in young and old animals alike, and whether mouse gains extend to primates. That framing guides the tests the team reports.
pmc-13595641:
H Bindels and colleagues listened to parents in German psychosomatic rehabilitation describe the grind of work-family conflict, captured in one patient's image of a hamster wheel. Their qualitative study reanalyzed thirty-two interviews with parents who had mental disorders, sorting their accounts into recurring inner patterns and story lines.

Eight distinct ways of living the conflict emerged. Their names include Self-Sacrifice, Invisible Loneliness, and Threat to Self-Identity. Thirteen narrative scenarios sat alongside them. The scenarios link job strain, family demands, and illness to the decision to seek rehabilitation. Some patterns resembled depression or burnout symptoms, yet patients insisted they named something distinct: the daily experience of failing two roles at once. The authors urge clinicians to assess work-family conflict explicitly, since naming it validates patients and sharpens treatment planning.
pmc-13598041:
Philip Xie and co-authors rethought assisted oocyte activation, the laboratory rescue used when sperm injection fails to fertilize eggs, by first asking which partner's contribution is missing. The missing spark is usually a sperm protein called PLC-zeta, and their 2026 case series of 135 couples measured its content to classify each failure as sperm-related or egg-related.

Activation then matched the diagnosis: a chemical ionophore, the recombinant protein itself, or both together. Each single approach rescued fertilization about as well as the other. The dual treatment transformed results, though. Fertilization rose from about a quarter to nearly three quarters of eggs. Ongoing pregnancy rose from none to nearly two thirds of couples. This held even with testicular sperm. The authors advocate replacing one-size-fits-all rescue with this individualized, more physiological strategy.
pmc-13598141:
Despina Antypa, Patrik Vuilleumier, and Ulrike Rimmele suppressed the morning cortisol rise with a drug. They did so in a double-blind, placebo-controlled brain imaging study. The aim was to test how the stress hormone shapes recall of emotional memories. Volunteers recalled charged material right after suppression and again four days later.

Blocking cortisol hurt recall on the spot and broke up the shared work of the brain regions that normally serve emotional recall. The change was not brief: brain patterns of those memories, measured days later under a normal hormone state, stayed altered. The authors read that lasting mark as proof that one recall under suppressed cortisol can rewrite how a memory is stored. They suggest the process deserves study as a possible route to easing painful memories in care.
pmc-13600941:
Li and co-authors imaged a 2026 set of plant photosystem structures inside living rice chloroplasts, rather than after lab cleaning. Photosystems I and II work side by side in membranes to turn light into chemical energy, but their native layout was unknown. In situ cryo-electron microscopy let the team picture them in place.

They resolved a large photosystem II supercomplex carrying four antenna trimers that cleaning usually strips away. Energy transfer figures from that shape closely matched readings in living tissue, backing its real-world fit. Li also found lopsided photosystem II pairs in several layouts and stacks of three and four units. The structures suggest the complex forms a skeleton across membrane layers that shapes the chloroplast's stacked membranes.
pmc-13601541:
Lisa Quadt and eight colleagues ask in 2026 whether the number of connective tissue quirks in flexible joints predicts neurodivergent traits. Joint hypermobility and conditions such as hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome often travel with autism and ADHD, for reasons not yet settled. The team assessed 99 adults with anxiety for hypermobility features, then screened them for autistic and ADHD characteristics and measured autonomic reactivity, the body's arousal system.

Nearly all participants, 99 percent, met criteria for generalized joint hypermobility, and 57 percent for hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Screening thresholds were crossed by 47 percent for autism and 20 percent for ADHD. Every measure correlated with the others. Mediation analysis showed autonomic reactivity carried the link between feature count and neurodivergence, with anxiety held constant. The authors read this as a possible mechanism: the arousal system may link variant connective tissue and neurodivergent traits.
pmc-13601641:
Annika Barzen and Dylan Göpfert study how telepathic animal communicators make their services sound credible online. People who claim to talk with animals telepathically sell a service no client can verify, which makes the case revealing for the study of knowledge claims. Using grounded theory methods, the pair analyzed German websites offering this service and built an account of the credibility strategies on display.

Three mechanisms stood out. Practitioners present themselves professionally, with structured services, therapy-flavored terms, and life stories that vouch for their gift. They also work the emotional register, stressing personal attention, care, and closeness with the client. Most distinctively, the impossibility of checking their claims is turned into a shield: flexible interpretation keeps any outcome compatible with success, so claims cannot fail. The authors conclude that credibility here is stabilized by professional, relational, and epistemic moves working together, with no proof behind the service itself.
pmc-13602441:
Moea Nimmo, Kari A Clifford, and John C Woodfield study in 2026 who develops a hernia beside a permanent colostomy. A parastomal hernia bulges through the abdominal wall next to the stoma opening, spoiling appliance fit and sometimes blocking the bowel. The team reviewed adults who received an end colostomy at Dunedin Hospital, New Zealand, between 2009 and 2022, all with at least one abdominal CT scan. Records were combined with scan measurements.

Of 217 patients, 64, or 29 percent, developed a parastomal hernia, about half of them with symptoms. Single-factor analysis flagged six risks, including body mass index and diabetes. After adjustment, three stood out: a wider fascial opening raised risk sharply, a higher muscle-to-fat ratio lowered it, and a stoma placed toward the side of the rectus muscle raised it. Scan-based measures before surgery, the authors suggest, could flag high-risk patients and guide stoma placement and prevention.
pmc-13609841:
Violetta A. Ionova and five colleagues report an odd fork in a classic reaction: attaching amines to the ligand 1,10-phenanthroline. This ring system anchors countless catalysts and complexes, and amino versions are prized. Aminating its 2-chloro form with aliphatic amines took two roads depending on conditions. Without any catalyst, the reaction stopped at secondary amines, one phenanthroline per nitrogen, in 40 to 80 percent yields.

Adding palladium changed the destination entirely. Even with amine in excess, the products were tertiary amines carrying two phenanthroline units, opening a route to unsymmetric diamines with two different heteroaryl groups, in 44 to 50 percent yield. Switching to the bromo starting material raised those yields to 62 to 91 percent. Fully loaded diamines with four heteroaryl groups were also reached, up to 55 percent. The products are promising ligands, the authors note, and the divergence itself is a synthetic tool: one starting pair, two product families, selected by catalyst alone.
pmc-13612641:
Josefine Andreasson, Louise Bennet, Jonas Björk, and Dominik Dietler ask in a 2026 Swedish study whether catching SARS-CoV-2 can set off new type 2 diabetes in adults. They followed more than three million adults in Sweden who had no diabetes at the start of 2020. All had taken a virus test through the health service by early 2022. Each infected person was matched with up to five similar uninfected controls.

The design was built to guard against a simple trap: sick people see doctors more often, so their diabetes may just be found sooner. The team used test-negative matching and checked three other conditions, anaemia, kidney disease, and thyroid trouble, as controls for that bias. Readers get a careful test of cause and effect, plus a look at whether severe illness changed the risk.
pmc-13613141:
Ming Lu and colleagues present a phantom study on the power level at which wireless resonators in MRI scans switch off safely. These devices must cut out when the scanner sends its strong pulses. These small coupled devices boost image quality, yet they need to stop resonating at the right moment to stay safe. All tests used phantoms, model objects that stand in for a body in the scanner.

The team took a series of scans at rising flip angles and compared signal near and far from the device. Failed switch-off shows up as an L-shaped curve, and its bend marks the power threshold. The method held up across devices with different diode counts, two field strengths, and scanners from two makers. It offers labs a simple check for safety testing and routine quality control.
pmc-13614641:
Sean K. Whittier and colleagues examine the sorting platform of the type III secretion system in Shigella bacteria, the needle-like machine the bacteria use to inject proteins into human cells. A ring of pod parts, built from a protein called Spa33, anchors the platform to the cell membrane and links it to the motor that drives injection. How many copies of Spa33 each pod holds has been unclear, since images of the platform are fuzzy.

Earlier microscopy suggested a set ratio among the platform's parts, with four copies of the pod protein for each anchor. Combining structures of single parts with fresh tests, the team shows the pods can hold several copies of Spa33 at once. Settling the count matters because this machine is a prime target for new drugs that disarm bacteria without killing them outright.
pmc-13614941:
Anna Palmieri leads a large team reporting in 2026 on a water-loving ring molecule built to trap dye pollutants in water, a growing worry for city groundwater. The host molecule, a prism-shaped ring with sulphate groups at both rims, dissolves in water and grabs two common dyes, rhodamine B and methylene blue, with strong attraction. The team checked the binding with light, magnetism, size, and heat methods that agree with each other.

With rhodamine B, the host formed both single in-cavity pairs and a two-ring capsule holding one dye molecule, stitched together by water. Methylene blue formed only the simple one-to-one pair. A host that can catch a pollutant in water is a step toward sensors that spot contamination and materials that pull it out, both badly needed for clean water.
pmc-13618041:
Bar Ezra and two colleagues present a first-principles quantum simulation of photodissociation, the breaking of a molecule by strong light pulses, with molecular rotation treated in full. Exact simulation becomes impossible as the number of states grows, which is exactly the regime strong-field experiments reach. Their method uses random-phase thermal wavefunctions, statistical stand-ins that slash the cost while keeping the physics grounded in the underlying Hamiltonian.

The simulation produces measurable outputs directly, such as the angular spread of fragment momenta. The authors study how results converge at two field intensities, each at a different temperature, and validate the approach against exact calculations where those remain possible. Beyond the usual dependence on system size and number of realizations, they find convergence also depends on how sensitive each observable is to quantum coherence. The method is designed to open regimes where exact numerics fail.
pmc-13618941:
Bita Erfanifar and three colleagues publish a plan for a systematic review of risk and protective factors for non-suicidal self-injury among adolescents in Iran. Self-injury is a major adolescent public health concern, and while many factors are known worldwide, Iran-specific synthesis is notably missing, especially on what protects teenagers. The plan is registered with PROSPERO and follows standard reporting rules.

The planned review will cover Persian and English peer-reviewed studies from 2015 onward on adolescents aged ten to nineteen. It will span quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods designs across seven databases, including the Iranian indexes SID and Magiran. A standardized form will extract data, the Mixed Methods Assessment Tool will grade quality, and results will be synthesized narratively in categories such as psychopathology, individual, family, peer, and demographic factors. No findings are reported yet; the plan's value is its open, registered design.
pmc-13620241:
Firew Tekle Bobo and six colleagues measured who actually reaches mental health care in Australia, using the national wellbeing survey from 2020 to 2022, in a 2026 analysis. The dataset held 15,893 respondents, weighted to represent the whole adult population. The team looked at service use in the year before the survey among people reporting a mental disorder, then tested how money, schooling, age, sex, and remoteness combined.

Lifetime experience of a mental disorder ran high, yet under half the people with a recent disorder had used any service. Use climbed with university education and area advantage and fell in remote districts and poor ones. The two forces compounded: disadvantaged people in remote areas had the lowest use of all, while advantaged city residents had the highest. The authors call for place-based outreach and digital or community models shaped for the places and groups now left behind.
pmc-13620441:
Gendi Li and six colleagues report early experience combining two treatments for sunken acne scars in patients with medium skin tone, where dark marks after inflammation are a chief worry. Micro-plasma radiofrequency resurfaces the skin with tiny plasma points, while subcision frees the scar from below with a needle. Twelve patients finished three sessions each at their hospital.

Scabs separated within fifteen days for everyone, and redness cleared within two months for nearly all. One patient developed temporary darkening, the only complication. Graders rated most patients markedly improved, and the total effective rate topped ninety percent, yet only three quarters of patients called themselves satisfied. Nobody reached the top grade of cure. The authors highlight that gap between measured improvement and patient feeling, and they ask for larger studies in darker skin before wider use.
pmc-13620841:
Rana A Jawad and eight colleagues documented what the cattle tick Rhipicephalus annulatus does to sheep skin in Iraq's Kerbala Province. They examined 540 sheep across several rural localities between March and November 2023 and collected ticks from feeding sites for study under ordinary and electron microscopes. Attachment sites on the animals showed swelling and redness to the naked eye.

Under magnification, the ticks' mouthparts and outer surface showed the hooks and texture that let females lock in and feed for days. Skin samples from bite sites revealed thickened, damaged surface layers, patches of dead tissue in the deeper layer, and dense crowds of immune cells, mainly eosinophils and lymphocytes. Blood vessels at the sites sat swollen and congested. The authors say the integrated picture strengthens the case for organized tick surveillance and control programs in local sheep farming.
pmc-13623141:
Shannon Esher Righi comments on new research that flips a long-held belief about fungal biofilms. Biofilms are sticky communities microbes build on surfaces, and in the yeast Candida parapsilosis they were thought to help the fungus persist in hospitals and resist drugs. A study in PLOS Biology by Daneshnia and colleagues found the opposite pattern in outbreak strains.

The outbreak isolates, collected worldwide and often resistant to a key antifungal drug, made unusually weak biofilms. Gene activity tests showed broad reprogramming in these strains, favouring traits that help the fungus dodge the immune system and survive in the body. Making less biofilm, in other words, may be a trade that buys longer persistence in patients. Righi frames the result as a warning against assuming one trait always helps a pathogen, and as a prompt to study what outbreak strains give up, not only what they gain.
pmc-13624541:
Xiangning Chen and co-authors feed young gibel carp five diets that differ only in soybean oil, the single fat source, ranging from none to twelve percent of the feed. The twelve-week trial tracked growth, muscle makeup, blood fats, liver health, and gene activity in the liver-like organ of the fish. Starting fish weighed about twelve grams each.

Fish on mid to high oil grew faster and heavier, and the six percent diet used feed most efficiently. Muscle fat and helpful unsaturated fats rose with oil level, while blood fats climbed too, and liver tissue showed local damage at the top two levels. Gene readouts pointed to busy fat-making pathways, so the authors settle on six to nine percent as the workable range.
pmc-13624841:
Leah M Savitsky and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, test a simpler way to give insulin during labor. Their unit replaced routine intravenous insulin with shots under the skin for patients whose blood sugar rose past a set line, and it fixed one shared sugar target. The quality study covered 1,140 deliveries from March 2021 through December 2025, comparing care before and after the July 2024 switch.

Newborn low blood sugar, or nursery intensive care for that problem, struck about one baby in four under both systems, with no rise after the switch. Nurses liked the new routine far more, with approval climbing from under a third to over half of survey answers. Shots may thus spare families the drip without added risk.
pmc-13625041:
Yuewen Zhang and four colleagues compare two forces that reshape the bacteria living on young kelp, the seaweed Saccharina japonica. Farms raise its early life stage, called gametophytes, in tanks where germ balance can tip toward disease. One set of tanks got a penicillin and streptomycin mix, another set sat at varied temperatures, and the team profiled the surface microbes in each.

Antibiotics tore the community apart, halving the dominant group and letting two less welcome genera move in, which the authors call severe imbalance. Heat left the main groups in place, yet the germ Vibrio peaked at fifteen degrees, the very warmth where kelp grew fastest. Their advice splits by goal: guard seedlings strictly at that warmth, and store breeding stock colder.
pmc-13626641:
Jean-Jacques Temprado and Abdul-Fatawu Abdulai argue that exercise games meant to protect aging brains are built on the wrong recipe. A decade of trials shows exergames seldom beat plain combined exercise and thinking practice, and players drift away. In this viewpoint they blame structural habits: studies recruit patients instead of healthy elders, borrow drills from rehabilitation, and dress games in polished but culture-free virtual worlds.

Their alternative, MAGIC exergames, embeds movement and thinking inside art, heritage, and story-rich virtual places. Four pillars support the design: full-body sensing inside believable worlds, story and meaning to wake memory systems, emotional resonance to fuel learning and return visits, and reframing effort as pleasure. Culture, they insist, is not decoration but an active ingredient for prevention.
pmc-13629241:
Olof Leimar and five colleagues model how habits could evolve as a form of behavioural flexibility, published in 2026. Habits form when repeated actions become automatic, and the authors propose that offloading routine choices frees limited attention for other tasks, such as watching for predators.

Their simulated forager faces feeding options of unknown quality in an environment that occasionally changes. Exploring early, then letting successful options harden into habit, cut deaths from predation substantially in the simulations without much loss of feeding success, provided conditions stayed stable between changes. Predictable rewards encouraged habit formation. The authors argue that making and breaking habits deserves a place beside learning and fixed instinct in evolutionary accounts of behaviour.
pmc-13630541:
Y. Zhou and two colleagues review electron crystals in layered two-dimensional materials. Their review appeared in 2026. When electrons in an ultra-thin material grow sparse enough, their mutual push can outweigh their motion. They then freeze into an ordered crystal of their own. Wigner proposed the idea nearly a century ago. Modern materials finally let physicists watch it happen.

The review surveys where these states have been realised. They range from graphene stacks to atom-thin semiconductors. It also covers the sensing tricks that reveal them. Those include optical signatures and scanning probe images of the frozen patterns. Open questions remain. They ask how disorder, spin, and band structure interact with the freezing. The authors map the platforms most likely to answer them.
pmc-13633441:
Duarte and colleagues published a 2026 study on a scab disease of sheep in Brazil's Midwest. Orf virus causes contagious sores around the mouths of sheep and goats. It can also infect people who handle sick animals closely. The team gathered scabs from nine outbreaks in Mato Grosso state.

All 103 scab samples tested positive for the orf virus by DNA checks. The team grew the virus in lab cells from most samples they tried. Gene reading tied the local strains to others already known in Brazil. Close kinship with older Mato Grosso strains suggests steady local circulation. The authors urge stronger farm hygiene and control steps against spread. Since people can catch orf too, worker protection matters during outbreaks.
pmc-13635041:
Lorenzo Iuliano, Daniele Veritti, and Paolo Lanzetta published this 2026 review appraising iridology, the practice of diagnosing body-wide disease by inspecting the colored part of the eye. Practitioners claim that iris patterns map onto distant organs and reveal their disorders. The authors examine the practice from an eye specialist's viewpoint. They trace its origins, test its proposed logic against iris biology, and weigh the clinical evidence, including a recent government-commissioned evaluation.

Their verdict is uniformly negative. Studies show no diagnostic accuracy worth the name, results do not repeat between examiners, and no plausible pathway links iris markings to distant organ states. The iris is shaped mainly by genetics and development, with only limited disease-specific change. The authors warn that trusting such readings can delay real diagnosis and mislead patients. Their conclusion: iridology deserves no place as a diagnostic or screening tool in eye care or general medicine.
pmc-13635241:
Dandan Chen and eight colleagues published this 2026 study tracing psoriasis-related insomnia to inflammation inside the brain. People with psoriasis sleep badly at striking rates, and the usual explanation is itching. Quick sleep gains from immune drugs, arriving before skin clears, argue for a deeper route. The team combined clinical observations with a mouse model of psoriasis-like skin inflammation. The animals stayed wakeful and slept in fragments even when itching was removed from the picture.

A wake-promoting cell group in the front hypothalamus ran overactive in the sick animals. That same area showed local inflammation, with awakened immune cells and high levels of a signaling protein, TNF-alpha. Injecting a blocker of that protein into the area restored much more normal sleep. The authors name this skin-to-brain pathway a dermo-hypothalamic axis and nominate the protein as a treatment target for insomnia in psoriasis.
pmc-13638041:
Golia Shafiei and eighteen colleagues chart how the brain's processing tempo matures from childhood into adulthood. Each brain region integrates signals over its own time window, its intrinsic timescale, short in sensorimotor areas and long in association areas. The team estimated timescales in two youth datasets with well over a thousand participants aged eight to twenty-two, then checked an independent adult dataset for contrast.

Development followed the same ranking seen across the cortex. Timescale patterns changed along the very axis that runs from sensorimotor to association cortex, the same axis that structures the adult brain. Adult data showed the pattern settled, confirming the youth changes reflect growth rather than noise. Both youth samples agreeing strengthens the claim. The authors present the timescale as a principled sign of how the brain matures in ranked order, tying development directly to the cortex's geography.
pmc-13639641:
Ohnishi and colleagues replied in 2026 to comments on their image report of ultrasound-detected tuberculous pleurisy, a fluid and membrane inflammation caused by tuberculosis. The exchange weighs lung ultrasound, a bedside scan whose artifacts were once dismissed but which a French pioneer showed can carry diagnostic meaning. The authors accept the critic's core point: the method depends on the operator and cannot stand alone for tuberculosis diagnosis.

They note the scan is now being explored for monitoring treatment response as well as detection, which could help clinics with poor access to standard follow-up. Cited work found chest-wall nodules and lung consolidation the most sensitive ultrasound signs in adults, with sensitivity ranges running high, though data on ruling disease out stay thin. A recent pooled review found the scan sensitive but not specific enough alone. The authors back standardized protocols to raise its reliability.
pmc-13642441:
Keegan E Eveland and four colleagues present a 2026 study of how two fruit bat species steer through turns by sound. Bats must sense clutter ahead while they also plan where to fly next.

Bats flew an L-shaped, felt-lined hall while a set of thirty-two small mics and 3D cameras tracked their calls and paths. One species aims its sonar with tongue clicks. The other uses its nose and head. Both slowed before sharp turns and angled their sound gaze away from their heading. That gaze foretold the turn to come in most flights. The smaller species flew faster and pulsed more quickly.
pmc-13642941:
Julia Steinbinder and five colleagues present a 2026 frog study on how males grow cornified nuptial pads, the rough thumb structures used in mating. The work tests whether frogs reuse the same genetic program that builds claws and hair in other land vertebrates.

In Xenopus frogs, the pads' spines expressed a relative of mammalian hair keratin, called krt59, and the control gene hoxc13 was enriched in forelimb skin. Knocking out hoxc13 with gene editing erased both krt59 expression and pad cornification. The authors conclude the frog pads evolved in parallel with hair by adapting an ancient skin-appendage program.
pmc-13645741:
Wei Zhang and six colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on a little-studied brain receptor part called GluN3A and its role in coping with social stress. The receptor sits in a middle stretch of the hippocampus, a brain area central to memory and emotion. The team used a social defeat stress routine, gene knockout mice, and circuit tracing tools. They asked whether losing this receptor part changes how animals respond to defeat.

Stress lowered GluN3A in that hippocampal stretch, and mice lacking it coped passively rather than actively. Restoring the protein in that one region reversed the pattern. Brain recordings showed the protein is needed for local neurons to fire during coping, and a natural chemical called D-serine quickly shifted mice toward active coping when the protein was present. The findings mark this receptor part as a possible target for stress-related illness research.
pmc-13646141:
Haoyang Zhou and thirteen colleagues refine a method for building three-dimensional models of rice plants from photos taken at many angles. Rice canopies are dense and tangled, which makes accurate modeling slow. Their workflow pairs a self-built imaging platform with an attention-guided segmentation network that cuts the plant out of cluttered backgrounds. Camera positions were then trimmed by testing combinations of placement strategies.

The segmentation model beat three rival approaches and yielded fuller point clouds. A chosen six-camera setup kept about three quarters of the points while cutting rebuild time by roughly seventy to eighty percent. Heights and canopy widths measured from the models matched hand measures closely. The authors present the trimmed setup as a practical balance of accuracy, completeness, and speed for high-throughput crop measurement, with lessons for other rotating imaging rigs.
pmc-13648141:
Sangjun Choi and six colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare work safety law in Korea, Britain, the European Union, and the United States. They ask how each place links three tools: risk checks, exposure tests, and health watch for staff. They also ask if the rules let a worker's past exposure be rebuilt years later.

British and EU law make the risk check the start point that drives the other two tools. US law orders tests and health watch for a set list of high-risk substances. Korean rules run the three tools side by side, with no tight link, and lack key data fields for adding up past exposure. The authors urge Korea to join the tools up and keep records far longer.
pmc-13649741:
Jawaher Ibrahim Alahadeb and three colleagues mapped where a crown gall bacterium, a germ that swells the stems of many crop plants, can live now and where climate change may push it. They fed 415 checked sighting records and five climate traits into a mapping model.

The model scored the fit as excellent. Prime zones today cluster in Europe's west and centre, in eastern China and northern India, and in the eastern United States. Yearly mean warmth drove the map most. Future runs pushed good habitat toward the poles and shrank the best zones in today's core areas, with the shift far worse under high emissions by 2070. The authors offer the maps to guide plant health watch work.
pmc-13650141:
Xinghua Chen and twelve colleagues, publishing in 2026, develop a pig vaccine against Seneca Valley virus, which causes blistering disease and heavy losses in young piglets. Their approach inserts premature stop signals into the viral genome, so the virus can only copy itself in cells supplied with special transfer RNA molecules that read through those stops.

The engineered virus carried three stop signals in a key gene and stayed stable while growing well in the helper cells. In mice and pigs, the vaccine raised strong antibody levels within two weeks of the first dose and produced a stronger cell-based immune response than a killed vaccine. Pig trials showed full weakening of the virus, no spread between animals, and protection matching the commercial killed product. The authors propose the method as a general way to build live vaccines that cannot replicate in ordinary animals.
pmc-13650341:
NI Cherny and five colleagues, publishing in 2026, set out a clinical framework for hope and despair in cancer and other serious illnesses.
