Hope shapes how patients hear a prognosis, choose treatments, and plan, and when it is handled badly it can drive misunderstanding, burdensome overtreatment, and loss of trust.

The review treats hope as changing and layered. Early hopes for cure often shift toward comfort, function, closeness with family, dignity, or peace as illness advances. Hope for exceptional outcomes can live alongside realistic planning, yet rigid hope that clashes with reality can delay preparation for decline. Symptoms, mood, culture, faith, and social setting all feed hope's direction. The authors describe communication habits, meaning-centered work, dignity-preserving care, and spiritual support that keep hope realistic, and they present this skill as a core duty of serious-illness care.
pmc-13650741:
Muhammad Uba Abdulazeez and four colleagues analyze child passenger injuries in the United Arab Emirates, where road crashes are the leading killer of children and most young casualties ride inside vehicles. No dedicated national study had examined what drives injury severity for child occupants in over a decade of usable data.

National crash records from 2012 to 2023 for children up to seventeen were modeled in stages, adding groups of factors pillar by pillar under a safe system framework. The child's sex, age, and seating position mattered, as did posted speed, road and lighting conditions, and which emirate the crash occurred in. The authors recommend enforcing laws against underage driving and front-seat riding for young children, and lowering speed limits. They also urge behavior campaigns aimed at boys, higher public awareness, and faster emergency response.
pmc-13658041:
Yan Zhang and a large international team pool river DNA data from around the world to find what shapes fish diversity. Freshwater life is declining faster than monitoring can track, and environmental DNA, genetic traces shed into water, offers a quicker census. By unifying many separate eDNA datasets, the researchers could test which features of a drainage basin go together with richer or poorer fish communities across continents.

Common patterns emerged despite the many regions, methods, and species involved, linking biodiversity to drainage characteristics that river managers can actually measure. A shared global dataset also exposes where sampling is thin and methods disagree. For conservation groups with limited budgets, findings like these help decide which rivers to survey first and which basin features most deserve protection.
pmc-2018741:
Peirce introduces PsychoPy, a free software suite for psychology experiments written in Python. Most studies of vision run on computer screens, where precise timing and display control matter. Commercial tools for such tasks were costly and could be hard to adapt.

PsychoPy was built to make building display experiments easier, using current hardware and software advances. It runs across different computer platforms, so labs can share experiment scripts freely. Open tools of this kind lowered the cost of careful perception research and helped labs repeat each other's setups exactly.  Teachers adopted it for perception courses because student scripts could be shared freely.
pmc-3197541:
Wong reviews apoptosis in cancer, from how the disease begins to how it can be treated. Apoptosis is an ordered, orchestrated process by which cells dismantle themselves. It occurs in both normal physiology and disease, and it is among the most studied topics in cell biology.

Understanding its mechanism matters because faulty cell death plays a pivotal role in disease. Cancer cells often evade apoptosis, surviving when they should die. The review explains those escape routes and treatments designed to restore death in tumour cells, a strategy behind several modern cancer drugs.
pmc-3414841:
Nik-Zainal, Alexandrov, Wedge, and co-authors catalogue mutation patterns in twenty-one breast cancers. All cancers carry mutations acquired during life. Their patterns reflect the DNA damage and repair processes that cancer cells and their precursors endured over time.

To explore those mechanisms, the team generated full catalogues of somatic mutation from the twenty-one tumours. Distinct patterns point to distinct causes, from internal chemistry to outside exposures. Reading such signatures later became a way to infer a cancer's history and, sometimes, its likely weaknesses.  Later signature catalogues across many cancer types grew directly from this approach.
pmc-3964941:
Li and co-authors presented starBase version two in 2013, a web database for maps of how RNA pieces interact. Small RNAs called microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and other RNA types help set cell fate and play roles in disease. Yet the links among them were still poorly charted when this work appeared.

StarBase draws on large sets of CLIP-Seq data, which capture where proteins bind RNA. From those data it builds networks that connect microRNAs with competing RNAs, other non-coding RNAs, and proteins. Researchers can use the maps to form testable ideas about gene control in health and disease.
pmc-4384041:
The UniProt Consortium described UniProt in 2014 as a hub for protein information. UniProt collects protein sequences and adds notes on their function and features. In the past year alone, its holdings had doubled to a huge number of sequences.

That growth forced an expansion of the accession number space so each entry keeps a unique code. A rising share of entries now comes from automated annotation of new genomes. UniProt is the reference that countless tools link to for protein identity. Keeping it current and well organized underpins research from drug design to evolution.
pmc-4817141:
Page, Cummins, Hunt, and their colleagues introduced Roary in 2015. A typical study of a bacterial population can now include hundreds or thousands of isolates. Questioning such datasets can reveal the genetic structure of bacterial genomes in fine detail.

Roary rapidly builds the pan genome of a large set of bacteria, meaning all genes found across the group. It splits genes into the core set shared by all and the accessory set found in some. That split shows how a species adapts and which genes drive outbreaks. Speed is the point: pan genome work that once took weeks became routine.
pmc-4995441:
The Global BMI Mortality Collaboration, led by Di Angelantonio, Bhupathiraju, and others, pooled data in 2016 on body-mass index and mortality. Overweight and obesity are increasing worldwide. The team assessed how body-mass index relates to death from all causes in different populations.

They combined individual-participant data from a very large set of prospective studies across four continents. To limit confounding and reverse causality, they restricted the analysis, for example by excluding early deaths and smokers in key checks. The huge pooled sample gives precise estimates of risk at each weight range. Those figures inform public health guidance on healthy weight.
pmc-5551541:
Pizzino, Irrera, Cucinotta, and their colleagues reviewed oxidative stress in 2017, covering both its harms and benefits for human health. Oxidative stress arises when cells and tissues make and hold more reactive oxygen species than the body can clear. It also reflects how well the body can detoxify these reactive products.

Reactive oxygen species can play several physiological roles, including signaling and defense against germs. In excess, they damage proteins, fats, and DNA and contribute to many diseases. The review weighs both sides rather than treating these molecules as purely harmful. That balance matters for judging antioxidant supplements, which have often disappointed in trials.
pmc-6029841:
Claire McQuin, Allen Goodman, Vasiliy Chernyshev, and coauthors announced CellProfiler 3.0 in 2018. CellProfiler lets biologists build image analysis pipelines without writing code. It has served the field since the mid two thousands.

The new version handles three-dimensional images, both as whole volumes and plane by plane. That matters as microscopes now stack many slices into deep views of tissue. Pipelines can measure shapes and counts across the full volume. The release keeps the modular style users know while extending it to richer data from modern imaging. The release also improves speed, so larger three-dimensional stacks finish in reasonable time.
pmc-7203741:
Dengfeng Guan, Shane McCarthy, Jonathan Wood, and coauthors presented a tool for cleaning genome assemblies in 2020. Long-read methods now produce near-reference genomes quickly. In variable regions, assemblers often emit both parental copies as if they were separate loci.

Those haplotypic duplications inflate gene counts and break later analysis. The purge_dups tool spots duplicated stretches from read depth and self-alignment and removes the extra copies. It runs fast enough for large vertebrate genomes. Assembly projects for biodiversity programs adopted it as a standard cleaning step. The authors validate the tool on assemblies from the Vertebrate Genomes Project.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-1-a:
For the week ending August 14, 1841, Punch printed the third chapter of The Wife Catchers, a legend of my uncle's boots told in four chapters. The scene lies in the Irish village of Ballybreesthawn, in the corner shop of Matthew Tibbins.

Tibbins, a fair-haired haberdasher with a lisp, sells ribbons, toys, patent medicines, and compliments in equal measure. His gifts as poet, card player, and wit make him a dangerous rival to Terence, who wants the heart of Miss Biddy O'Brannigan. Readers get early Punch fiction: Irish courtship played for laughs, with boots as family treasure.

Punch for the week ending August 21, 1841, closes its tale The Wife-Catchers with a fourth chapter set on the night of a planned elopement in Ireland. Miss Biddy O'Brannigan has agreed to slip away with Terence before daybreak.

Guests staying at the lodge, a jug of strong punch at the door, and a horse ready to carry double set the stage. Terence waits in a chamber with a turf fire, troubled most by his soaked boots. The haberdasher rival sleeps under the same roof. Readers get the tale's comic knot tied tight before its ending.

A new serial opens in Punch for the week ending August 28, 1841: The Heir of Applebite, whose first chapter presents the Applebite family of Puddingbury. Isaac Applebite, member of Parliament, has died leaving a seat, a widow, a son, and fifty thousand pounds.

The widow takes two-thirds of the money, builds a monument praising the best of husbands, then marries a young dragoon officer and leaves for the Continent. Her son Agamemnon Collumpsion Applebite, the fat cherub of the monument, is left to his own care. Readers get the start of a mock pedigree told with grave nonsense.

Punch for the week ending August 7, 1841, prints the second chapter of The Wife-Catchers, the legend of a pair of family boots in Ireland. An uncle tells his nephew Jack how the topped boots, spurs, and red waistcoat came down from his grandfather.

The boots, he explains, were brushed up whenever a cousin went to court a landlord or a sweetheart, take a farm or a wife. Their luck in matchmaking earned them their name among the young men of the family. Talk flows over tumblers of punch, proving the old proverb that a drink is better than a story.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-1-d:
Punch for the week ending December 11, 1841, prints the eleventh part of The Physiology of the London Medical Student, following Mr. Muff as he ends his evening. Beer, measured in pots of half-and-half at fivepence, serves as the student's unit of money.

Muff tells how Rapp pulled lanterns from wood paving works in the Strand, claimed to be a watchman, and scattered paving blocks while the police closed in. A chase through alleys toward the Cider-cellars follows. Readers get a rowdy portrait of student life, where study ranks below drink, daring, and escape.

The twelfth and closing part of The Physiology of the London Medical Student fills Punch for the week ending December 18, 1841. Mr. Muff must grind once more before facing examination at the College of Surgeons in Lincoln's Inn Fields.

The grinder's room smells of tobacco smoke, varnished bones, and gin and water, with anatomical prints on the walls. Rapp, drawing little men in his anatomy book, answers a question on the eye with a muddle about the Paddington Canal. Readers get the series' last laugh at cramming, fear, and half-learned science.

Christmas week in Punch, ending December 25, 1841, brings a portrait of Mr. Chokepear, a respectable man who keeps a merry Christmas in his own hard way. He pays his rates at once, takes the sacrament, keeps the oldest port in the parish, and gives to good causes.

Yet his children greet him with lips of ice, and his charity stops where his comfort begins; for the starving he has Newgate and a hard-hearted alderman. The sketch follows the family to church and through the day. Readers get a sharp Christmas lesson on respectability without kindness.

Punch for the week ending December 4, 1841, claims to print the true draft of the official report on the fire at the Tower of London. The paper says the version in the newspapers was dressed up for the public eye, and offers its own neat copy instead.

Watchman Mr. Snooks testifies that he slept in his box through the alarm of October 30 and found himself barricaded inside it until morning. His wife confirms the lantern trimming, and a publican describes lights flickering like candles blown in and out. Readers get official language undone by comic witnesses.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-1-j:
Punch began on the week ending July 17, 1841, and its first number opens with The Moral of Punch, a statement of what the new London comic paper means to do. The writers take their puppet patron as a teacher, not a mere clown.

Crowns on base brows, gilded coaches, bought voters, and hollow demagogues pass in review as the cheats Punch means to face down. His way is to laugh, forget the tormentor, and sing. Readers get the founding promise of the weekly: mirth with a moral edge, aimed at pomp in church, state, and street.

A modest method of forming a new budget fills the lead of Punch for the week ending July 24, 1841. The writer whispers the plan to Mr. Punch as a secret too good for the Whig ministry that lately fell.

Since private vices can bring public benefits, the essay asks why public crimes cannot pay too. Every prisoner in Britain would be freed on payment of a fee set by a sliding scale, filling the empty treasury at a stroke. A second tax dodge, borrowed from dog and hair-powder duties, follows. Readers get finance satire with a straight face.

Punch for the week ending July 31, 1841, prints a letter urging poetry on an improved principle. The writer begins by mourning that verse no longer sells as a luxury, though doctors prescribe bad poems as sleeping draughts of rare strength.

His cure is a new invention in rhyme. Old pairs have worn the art out: mountain always finds fountain, sadness leads to madness, and the poor always enter at the door. The letter promises to close that door on stock rhymes for good. Readers get a comic patent for saving poetry from its own habits.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-1-n:
News of a royal birth leads Punch for the week ending November 13, 1841, written in the voice of a correspondent with exclusive intelligence. The Prince of Wales has been born, and the paper claims it was not premature in predicting him.

The report wonders what name the prince will reign under and regrets that twins were not provided, so both the outgoing and incoming lord mayors might gain baronetcies. The Princess Royal, meanwhile, is said to suffer a nose put out of joint by the new arrival. Readers get court news turned into cheerful impudence, one week into a reign that had not yet begun.

Punch for the week ending November 20, 1841, leads with a tale headed Myself, Punch, and the Keeleys. The narrator tells how he ran into an old schoolfellow on Cornhill after seventeen years apart and was asked to dinner the next day.

Jack Withers has grown stout and rich in trade. The narrator, a surgeon home from sixteen years with a native regiment in the Carnatic, has come back poor and yellow with jungle fever. Two months of Cheltenham water restored his colour. Readers get a contrast of fortunes told over an excellent dinner.

Part nine of The Physiology of the London Medical Student appears in Punch for the week ending November 27, 1841, covering what follows the Hall examination. Mr. Muff walks from the funking-room to the council chamber unsure whether he is on his head or his heels.

For an hour and a half he is questioned over pharmacopoeias, drug trays, and half-dead plants, puzzled, bullied, and caught out, until his good genius prevails and he may retire. Certificates follow, then a rush to the shop across the way with Jones, Rapp, and Manhug. Readers get examination dread played for comedy.

A day-dream at my uncle's opens Punch for the week ending November 6, 1841. A young man's parents debate how he should begin the world, discarding scheme after scheme, until the postman ends the argument with a letter.

The letter comes from uncle Ticket, the great Ticket, and offers the boy an apprenticeship. His trade, as the son blurts out, is pawnbroking, the greatest such business in London. The father defends the glorious money-making trade while the boy doubts. Readers get a family council where sense, pride, and profit pull three ways.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-1-o:
Punch for the week ending October 16, 1841, leads with a trade report from its own reporter, written as sober market news and meaning none of it. Feathers are heavy, lead is brisk, and flounders in the fish market are not so flat as they had been.

Tallow deliveries smooth the day's business, a glut of mutton checks the trade, and rain unsettles the milk market. Cotton is so dull that the only ball seen belongs to a basket-woman darning a stocking. Nothing is done in gloves. Readers get the language of the money page turned into pure wordplay.

The Tiptoes, a sketch of the would-be genteel, leads Punch for the week ending October 2, 1841. Morning and evening, young men stream between suburban villages and their city desks, the advanced guard of an army the sketch blames for spoiling English homes.

Parlours become boudoirs, rose patches become parterres, and centre tables fill with albums and wax flowers under the new rule of gentility. Comfort, the writer argues, is treated as cheap beside luxury, and showy thriftlessness passes for respectability. Readers get an early attack on suburban pretension, quoted from Vanbrugh at the head.

The Great Creature begins in Punch for the week ending October 23, 1841, introducing Mr. Horatio Fitzharding Fitzfunk, clerk to the attorneys Tims and Swindle of Thavies Inn. He earns a guinea a week carrying overdue bills through the streets.

His real passion is the stage. His few free hours go to Shakespeare, recited at full voice to the alarm of the lodger next door. Fellow amateurs who have pawned their watches to hire a private theatre take him in as a member. Readers get a clerk with sore boots and a burning wish to blaze as a star.

Punch for the week ending October 30, 1841, continues The Great Creature with a new figure in debt. Hannibal Fitzflummery Fitzflam's tailors, Moleskin and Corderoy, can find no receipt on his many bills, and the law is set moving against him. Their lawyers set a sheriff's officer on his trail.

Fitzflam keeps giving the officer the slip, leaves town, and arrives at the very inn where Horatio Fitzharding Fitzfunk is staying. A waiter then startles him with news of who else is in the house. Readers get debt, disguise, and pursuit mixed in the serial's broad comic style.

A manual of dénouements leads Punch for the week ending October 9, 1841, offering a recipe for ending a melodrama. Such a play, the writer says, is a dose in two or three acts, made of a villain, a lover, a heroine, a comic character, and an executioner.

Endings are sorted into the natural, the unnatural, and the supernatural. Natural ones include the villain hiding vital papers in the most visible spot on stage and loud confessions made in rooms full of closets. Readers get theatre craft mocked by a writer who plainly knew every trick in the house.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-1-s:
Chapter three of The Heir of Applebite fills Punch for the week ending September 12, 1841. Agamemnon Collumpsion Applebite has married Juliana Theresa, lately Waddledot, and the pair set off for Brighton in a yellow-bodied chariot with a sandwich basket.

Three days of honeymoon bliss follow, with an imaginary dinner party made real and walks along the Steine and the Chain Pier. Yet even honey cloys, and the narrator hints the sweetest moon can pall. Juliana passes her days on the sofa with a novel. Readers get married life sketched with tender mockery.

Punch for the week ending September 18, 1841, prints chapter four of The Heir of Applebite, which warns that it has much to say about someone besides the hero. Agamemnon's kindness leaves him defenceless before the troubles that follow a child's birth.

The narrator, claiming seventy-one years and a brown wig, warns bachelors against the flowery chains of love. Then Mrs. Pilcher the monthly nurse arrives, announced by her short cough on the door mat, a woman said to have borne eighteen lovely babes. Readers get domestic satire on marriage, nurses, and new fathers.

Chapter five of The Heir of Applebite appears in Punch for the week ending September 25, 1841, under a warning that many a slip lies between more things than cup and lip. The Applebite heir thrives, and his mother plans a grand evening party for his first tooth.

Cards go out for quadrilles at No. 24, Pleasant Terrace, and the house turns into a kitchen for a week. Mrs. Waddledot directs the decorations while old John runs errands and Agamemnon, a cipher in his own house, struggles to get fed. Readers get party preparations as domestic warfare.

The Gentleman's Own Book occupies Punch for the week ending September 5, 1841, turning from conduct to the cut, ornaments, and pathology of dress. The cut of a coat, the essay says, is to the garment what the royal head is to a coin.

Tailor and sculptor are paired as kindred artists: Phidias and Canova shaped marble gods, while Stultz with his shears shapes broadcloth into the nobility of the Blue Book and the Army List. Wool, loom, and pipe-clay each get their due. Readers get fashion philosophy written with mock learning and real admiration for the tailor's art.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol1-1841:
Jules Quicherat opened his great edition of Joan of Arc's trials in 1841 with the record of her condemnation. Procès de Condamnation et de Réhabilitation de Jeanne d'Arc, volume one, prints the Latin trial text of 1431. Joan was nineteen when a church court at Rouen sent her to the fire.

The volume gives the charges, the long questioning, and her answers as the court clerks wrote them down. Readers meet her voice under pressure, session by session. Quicherat's edition became the base for all later study of Joan. The first volume is where that study starts: in the courtroom itself.
raimundi-lulii-de-secretis-natur-siue-qu: Raimundi Lulii De Secretis Naturae is a Latin alchemy book whose opening pages are mostly repeated modern stamps, Early European Books and the Wellcome Trust, London, over a garbled title page. What the broken type allows to be read names Raimundus Lullius of Majorca. He is called most acute philosopher and famed physician. His two books on the secrets of nature follow. The subject is the quintessence. Five books of Albertus Magnus are added. They treat minerals and metals.
robert-boron-saint-graal-michel-1841:
Robert de Boron gave the Grail its Christian root in two romances of the years around 1200. Le Roman du Saint-Graal, in Francisque Michel's 1841 edition of the Old French, holds his Joseph of Arimathea and his Merlin. No earlier texts bind the Grail cup to the Passion.

Joseph tells how the cup that held Christ's blood came west and who kept it. Merlin tells of the prophet's birth, his gifts, and his hand in Arthur's rise. Every later Grail tale, from the great cycles to Malory, descends from these two. Michel's edition prints the founding texts in their first tongue.
se-quo-yah-from-harper-s-new-monthly-v-4:
Harper's New Monthly printed this life of Se-quo-yah in volume 41 in 1870. No writer is named in the piece. It opens in 1768, when German trader George Gist left the Savannah River settlement of Ebenezer with two pack horses and entered Cherokee country.

Early pages explain the fur trade that linked Augusta with distant Native towns. Licensed traders, pack trains, and river boats moved pelts to the coast for large profits. Governors and Crown officers fought over who could grant trade rights. That busy world of trade and rule forms the ground on which the Cherokee figure at the heart of the piece grew up.
sinceri-renati-samtliche-philosophisch-u:
Sincerus Renatus gathered his philosophic and chemical writings in this German volume, printed at Leipzig and Breslau in 1741. Worn Fraktur type and rough scanning leave many lines hard to read. Title fragments promise a theo-philosophy of divine and natural knowledge, and a golden work of nature and art built on trials and chemical handgrips.

An opening defense answers mockers of alchemy who sneer at each new alchemist. The writer presses on in an age he grants is hostile. German Pietist alchemy speaks here in its own dense tongue, joining prayer, furnace work, and the hope of hidden wisdom.
stanhope-epictetus-simplicius-1741:
Epictetus, a freed slave who taught in Greece under the Roman Empire, left a short handbook of Stoic life called the Enchiridion. George Stanhope turned it into English, and his version first appeared in 1694. The fifth edition of 1741 adds the long commentary of Simplicius, a scholar of the sixth century, plus a life of Epictetus from Boileau.

Simplicius works through the handbook line by line, drawing out its rules on what we can and cannot control. For generations this was the form in which English readers met Stoic ethics. It stays the only pre-modern English version of Simplicius on the handbook.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5041:
John F. Kennedy gives three yearly addresses, dated January 30, 1961, January 11, 1962, and January 14, 1963, parted by three stars. The first opens with a homecoming. It is a pleasure, Kennedy tells the Speaker and the members, to return from whence he came. They are among his oldest friends in Washington, and the House is his oldest home in the city.

More than fourteen years back, he took his first oath of federal office in that chamber. For fourteen years he drew knowledge and spark there from members of both parties in both houses, from wise and open leaders, and from famed speeches he can still clearly recall. He names the programs of two great presidents, the un dimmed force of Churchill, the soaring hopes of Nehru, and the firm words of General de Gaulle. To speak from that same stand is a grave thing, he says.
the-confessional-an-analysis-of-the-caus: A medical pamphlet called The Confessional survives here in badly garbled print, though its title page can still be read in fragments. It promises an analysis of the causes and cure of melancholy, nervousness, and mental and physical debility, and it carries a line from Hamlet about coming in a questionable shape. The London printer's line is only partly legible, and no author is named in what can be read. No body text follows in legible form.
tob-0041:
John Jacob Nutter, a political scientist, published The CIA's Black Ops with Prometheus Books in 2000. The book examines CIA covert action and its effects on foreign policy and democracy. Nutter writes as a critic with a scholar's apparatus.

Case by case, he argues that secret operations bend policy away from public control, prop up clients, and corrode democratic practice at home and abroad. Coups, paramilitary wars, and covert funding all come under his charge sheet. The book belongs to the post-Cold War reckoning with the agency's hidden hand, and it gives readers a sourced, prosecutorial account of covert action's costs.
tob-13141:
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras compress the whole path of yoga into 196 short sayings. Charles Johnston edited and translated them under the title The Book of the Spiritual Man. The sayings are terse, almost like notes, and each one rewards slow reading.

Johnston's commentary unpacks the eight limbs of yoga, from right conduct and posture through breath control to deep absorption, called samadhi. The goal is to still the movements of the mind so the true self stands clear. Students of yoga still treat the Sutras as their root text, and Johnston's edition remains one of the clearest doors into it.
tob-4041:
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel published the Phänomenologie des Geistes in 1807, presented here in the German original. The Phenomenology of Spirit traces consciousness climbing a ladder of forms, from simple sense-perception through self-consciousness, reason, and spirit, toward absolute knowing. Each stage collapses under its own contradictions and passes into the next.

Along the climb stands the famous master and slave dialectic, where work and recognition remake both parties, an idea Marx and later thinkers seized upon. Hegel finished the manuscript as Napoleon's army approached Jena. The German text is thought's most demanding mountain in this library; readers of the original meet Marx, existentialism, and much modern theory at one of their sources.
tob-4141:
Waite restored and enlarged the Hermetic Museum in 1893, and volume one of that fuller edition stands here. The famed tracts include the Golden Tripod, Sendivogius's New Light of Alchemy, and the Sophic Hydrolith, each a classic of the spagyric art. Waite edits and translates with his usual full apparatus.

Instructions for the disciples of the art mix laboratory hints with spiritual counsel, since Waite read alchemy as both at once. Checked from the 1919 printing, the volume improves on the older Latin collection it revives. Students of the old tracts still begin with Waite's Museum when they want the canon in English.
tob-4214-10741:
Arthur Schopenhauer, the great pessimist, surprised readers with the warm, practical essays of The Wisdom of Life. T. Bailey Saunders translated them into the English most readers still use. Schopenhauer divides human good into what a person is, what a person has, and what others think of him.

Only the first, he argues, truly counts toward happiness. Health, character, and a rich inner life outweigh wealth and fame, which rest on chance and opinion. His advice sounds like Stoic counsel in modern dress. The gloomy thinker turns out to be a shrewd, humane guide to getting through life well.
tob-9141:
Part two of Darmesteter's Avesta completes the Zoroastrian scriptures in the Sacred Books of the East form, verified from the 1919 scan. The Yasna liturgy, with its hymns and the Gathas at its heart, leads the volume. The Visperad and the lesser texts, hymns and fragments, follow in order.

Priests still recite the Yasna before the sacred fire, in words few now parse but all revere. Darmesteter's notes trace each rite and being to its roots. With part one, the set gives ancient Persia's worship entire in English. The Avesta's survival, through so many lost centuries, is itself remarkable.
un-ga-res-1541:
When does a colony stop being a colony for UN purposes? Resolution 1541, adopted by the General Assembly in 1960, lays down the guiding tests. Under Article 73 of the Charter, states that rule overseas lands must send facts about them to the UN. A team of six had spent a year working out when that duty ends, building on a list of tests from 1953.

The Assembly thanks the team and approves its tests, with a few changes. Those tests weigh whether a land has gained full self-rule, joined a free state as an equal, or linked itself to one by free choice. The list became the yardstick of the great wave of decolonization that swept the 1960s.
un-ga-res-41:
First principles for cutting world armaments were set down in Resolution 41 of the General Assembly, passed on 14 December 1946. Under Article 11 of the Charter, the Assembly claims its part in guarding peace. It states the need for a swift, general ordering and cut of arms and armed forces, across all states at once.

The Security Council is urged to draft the workable steps at speed, in the order of their weight. The plans would go to member states for debate at a special session of the Assembly. Pacts approved there would then go to states for ratification under Article 26. Arms given up by all at once, never by a few alone, is the rule at the heart of the text.
un-ga-res-41-41: General Assembly Resolution 41/41 survives in the catalog under the doubled form 41 (41), dated to 1987, with no subject named in the record. The numbering ties it to the Assembly's forty-first session, which spanned late 1986 into 1987. Beyond that, the honest account is of form: a formal decision of the whole Assembly, preserved as official record text. Its topic must be taken from the text itself, since neither title nor notes in this record supply one that can be checked.
un-ga-res-a-69-41:
Stalled talks on nuclear disarmament are pushed forward in Resolution A/69/41, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the vote of the year before on taking such talks ahead, toward a world free of nuclear arms. Deep concern runs through it at the ruinous toll any use of such arms would bring.

All the peoples of the world, the first disarmament session held in 1978, hold a vital stake in the success of arms talks. All states have the right to sit in them. The roles of the Conference on Disarmament and the Disarmament Commission are restated. The vote is one of a yearly set that keeps the goal of a nuclear-free world on the table.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1541 (XV) was adopted on 15 December 1960. It laid down the principles for deciding when a member state must report on a territory. The duty comes under Article 73 e of the Charter. It covers peoples who have not yet gained a full measure of self-government. The annex lists the tests for judging each case on its own facts.

The principles say a territory counts as self-governing in three cases. It may become a sovereign state. It may join an independent state on equal terms. Or it may freely link itself to one by an informed, free vote. A land that is apart in place and in its people's culture is presumed to fall under the duty. That holds until one of those ends is reached.

General Assembly Resolution 41, adopted on 14 December 1946, laid down principles for the general regulation and reduction of armaments. The Assembly held an early, shared cut in arms and forces to be needful. It asked the Security Council to draft workable steps, in order of urgency. All states would follow them, rather than a few acting alone.

A central aim was banning atomic weapons and all major weapons fit for mass destruction. It came with world control of atomic energy for peaceful ends only. The text calls for safeguards by way of inspection, to guard states that keep the rules. It urges troops stationed abroad without consent to be pulled back.

General Assembly resolution 69/41 (2014) tries to restart multilateral nuclear disarmament talks after more than a decade without concrete results. The Assembly welcomes the report of its Open-ended Working Group, which met in 2013 to develop proposals. It welcomes the Secretary-General's collection of member states' views. It calls on governments, international organizations, and civil society to keep building on those proposals. They should do so in United Nations and other forums. It decides to review progress at its seventieth session, if necessary through the Working Group again.
un-sc-res-1041:
Liberia's observer mission was extended as the Abuja timetable slipped on 29 January 1996. The Secretary-General's report of 23 January covered UNOMIL's work. Ceasefire breaches had grown, and ECOMOG troops had come under attack. Disengagement and disarmament lagged behind the Abuja Agreement's terms. ECOWAS won praise for its steady work to restore peace.

The Council extended UNOMIL's mandate until 31 May 1996. All Liberian parties were called to honor the Abuja Agreement in full and in speed, above all on the ceasefire, disarmament, and reconciliation. The armed attacks on ECOMOG staff were condemned. Condolences went to the governments and peoples of the fallen soldiers. Every faction was told once more to respect the status of United Nations and ECOMOG staff strictly. Member states were urged to give money, transport, and other backing to the peace process and to the trust fund for Liberia.
un-sc-res-1341:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo was the matter before the Council in Resolution 1341, adopted on 22 February 2001. The long war had swollen the ranks of refugees and the displaced. Atrocities hit civilians in the east, and child soldiers were still being recruited. The cease-fire was now broadly holding, and a plan for pulling forces apart existed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that Ugandan, Rwandan, and all other foreign forces leave Congo. The parties must carry out the disengagement plan within fourteen days from 15 March 2001. A full withdrawal timetable is due by 15 May 2001. The text backs the updated plan for the United Nations mission, MONUC, to watch the cease-fire and verify each step.
un-sc-res-141: The Republic of Somalia applied for United Nations membership as it gained independence in 1960. On 5 July 1960 the Security Council examined the application. It recommended to the General Assembly that Somalia be admitted. The decision was unanimous and fills a single sentence. Somalia took its seat days after independence. The new state joined a fast-growing wave of African members that year.
un-sc-res-1441: Preserved as Resolution 1441, this Security Council text carries a 2002 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1541:
Western Sahara's stalled peace process returned to the Council in April 2004. On 29 April 2004 the Council renewed MINURSO until 31 October 2004. It restated support for the peace plan backed the year before. The Secretary-General had reported on the dispute days earlier. The goal remained a settlement both sides could accept. That settlement had to let the territory's people choose their own future.

The Council called on the parties and nearby states to work with the Secretary-General. His envoy needed their full cooperation. The Secretary-General owed a report before the mandate ended. It would also cover talks on freeing remaining prisoners of war. The ceasefire held, but the political track stayed stuck.
un-sc-res-1641:
Burundi's peace operation received a six-week extension in late 2005. On 30 November 2005 the Security Council kept ONUB in place until 15 January 2006. The Council recalled its earlier Burundi texts, above all resolution 1545. It restated its commitment to Burundi's sovereignty and unity. It also noted that sources of instability remained. Those, it said, still threatened peace in the region.

The extension was made under Chapter VII of the Charter. That gave the mission its enforcement weight. The short term suggests a drawdown decision was near. Burundi had just finished a long transition with elections. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter while the mission's future was weighed.
un-sc-res-1741: Security Council Resolution 1741 survives in this collection through a Wikisource transcription of the UN's official record. The text follows the body's standard two-part design, findings before action. Because the Council's authority depends on agreed language, the language itself is the artifact, and this entry preserves it without abridgment or commentary.
un-sc-res-1941:
Sierra Leone faced the Security Council in Resolution 1941, adopted on 29 September 2010. The country was rebuilding after civil war and looking ahead to elections in 2012. Tensions could rise as the vote neared. The United Nations peacebuilding office there, UNIPSIL, helped with elections, jobs, and the rule of law.

The text extends UNIPSIL's mandate until 15 September 2011. The office should help prepare the 2012 elections and calm disputes between parties. It should also back the fight against graft and drug trafficking. The Council praises the Special Court's work and urges the government to press on with reform and national unity.
un-sc-res-241:
Mercenary attacks on the Congo angered the Council in November 1967. Foreign fighters had struck the country from bases abroad. Portugal had let them use Angola as a staging ground. On 15 November 1967 the Council condemned any interference in the Congo's internal affairs. It condemned Portugal in particular for breaking earlier resolutions. Support for the mercenaries, from recruitment to arms supply, ran through the text.

Portugal had to end all help to the mercenaries at once. Countries that received fleeing mercenaries had to stop them fighting again. Measures to block new attacks on any state were required. The mercenaries had just been beaten in eastern Congo. The text aimed to close the pipeline that produced them.
un-sc-res-341: As number 341 in the Council's series, the resolution is catalogued in this library under 1973. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-41:
A truce in Indonesia gave the Council reason for satisfaction in February 1948. The Netherlands and the Republic of Indonesia had signed the Renville Truce Agreement. Both sides also accepted principles for a political settlement. On 28 February 1948 the Council noted those steps with pleasure. Its Committee of Good Offices had helped the parties reach them. The committee's members earned formal praise in the text.

The Council kept its offer of good offices open. Both parties and the committee had to keep it informed directly. News on the political settlement was the key need. The same day, the Council asked the committee to watch two regions closely. The truce later broke down, but the framework shaped the final transfer of sovereignty.
un-sc-res-441:
UNDOF came up for renewal at the end of November 1978. On 30 November 1978 the Security Council extended the Golan force until 31 May 1979. The Secretary-General had supplied his report on the mission. The decision uses the standard three-part form. The parties must carry out resolution 338 at once. A report on the term is due at its end.

China did not take part in the voting. That abstention by absence was China's habit on this file. The force itself kept watch over the separation area. It had done so since the disengagement deal of 1974. The renewal kept that quiet arrangement alive for another half year.
un-sc-res-541:
Northern Cyprus's breakaway declaration was ruled void on 18 November 1983. The Turkish Cypriot leaders had declared a separate state on 15 November. Cyprus's foreign minister addressed the Council. The move clashed with the 1960 treaties that set up the Republic of Cyprus and guaranteed its shape. The Secretary-General had spoken on 17 November.

The Council deplored the purported secession of part of the Republic of Cyprus. It judged the declaration legally invalid and called for its withdrawal. Resolutions 365 (1974) and 367 (1975) had to be applied in full at once. The Secretary-General was asked to press his good offices toward the earliest progress on a just and lasting settlement. All states had to respect Cyprus's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. No state was to accept any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus. The declared state remains unrecognized abroad.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Liberia's civil war shapes Resolution 1041, adopted on 29 January 1996. The UN Observer Mission in Liberia, UNOMIL, worked beside the West African force ECOMOG under the Abuja Agreement. The Council praised ECOWAS peace work but deplored fresh ceasefire breaches, attacks on ECOMOG troops, and slow progress on pulling forces apart and disarming fighters.

The Council extends UNOMIL until 31 May 1996. It condemns the attacks on ECOMOG and on civilians and demands that they stop. It calls on all Liberian sides to keep the ceasefire, disarm, and work toward unity, and warns that world support depends on their will to settle matters in peace. States are urged to fund ECOMOG and the peace process, and the arms embargo on Liberia is recalled.

Congo's ceasefire gains ground in Resolution 1341, adopted unanimously on 22 February 2001. The Secretary-General reported that conditions for deploying MONUC were being met: the ceasefire was holding, disengagement plans existed, and Congo's president had pledged cooperation. Rwanda had promised to pull its forces from Pweto, and Uganda to cut two battalions. Atrocities, child soldiers, and illegal resource extraction still scarred the east.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that Ugandan, Rwandan, and all other foreign forces withdraw. It demands that the parties carry out the Kampala and Harare disengagement plans within the 14 days from 15 March 2001. It sets 15 May 2001 as the deadline for a full withdrawal timetable and for disarmament plans covering all armed groups. It endorses MONUC's updated deployment concept to monitor the ceasefire and disengagement, as the first step toward complete foreign withdrawal.

Two colonial lands joined hands to form one state in 1960. On 5 July, the Council adopted Resolution 141 without dissent. The Republic of Somalia had been born four days before. British Somaliland had just won its freedom. It then merged with the Italian-run trust land of Somalia. Somali nationalists had long demanded that union.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Somalia. The Assembly seated it that September. Somalia stood out among the new states of 1960. Two lands chose to join at the moment of freedom. The union aimed to gather most Somali speakers under one flag. Its loose ends shaped wars in later years.

A final chance to disarm under inspection is given to Iraq on 8 November 2002. The Council found that Iraq had failed to account fully for its banned weapons programmes and had blocked inspectors for years. It judged Iraq to be in material breach of the ceasefire terms set after the 1991 Gulf War.

A tougher inspection regime is set up, to complete the disarmament required since 1991. Iraq must declare all its weapons programmes at once and give inspectors from the United Nations and the atomic energy agency full, immediate access everywhere. False statements or any failure to cooperate would be reported to the Council, which warned of serious consequences.

Even the Sahara mission's size came under review in this text of 2004. On 29 April, the Council adopted Resolution 1541 without dissent. The Secretary-General's April report lay before it. The text restates Resolution 1495 from the year before. That text had backed the envoy's peace plan as the best deal-based path.

Support for the plan is voiced again here. All parties and states in the region must work fully with the envoy. MINURSO's mandate then runs to 31 October 2004. One new note stands out. The Secretary-General must weigh the mission size the tasks truly need. A cut is openly on the table. The vote the mission exists to run had still not come.

Burundi held landmark elections in 2005 after years of civil war. A UN operation, ONUB, had supported the transition since 2004. Its mandate was nearly finished. Resolution 1641, adopted on 30 November 2005, kept the operation alive a little longer. Members noted that pockets of instability still threatened the region.

ONUB's mandate now ran until 15 January 2006. The extension added only six weeks. It was a bridge, not a fresh commitment. The Council acted under Chapter VII, giving the decision binding force. Burundi's elected government was taking charge of security. The short renewal let the UN draw down in step with that handover.

Ethiopia and Eritrea's mission, UNMEE, is extended for six months on 30 January 2007, until 31 July 2007. The border remained undemarcated, and the mission's staff are praised for working in hard conditions. Eritrea had moved troops and equipment into the Temporary Security Zone, a step treated as a serious breach.

Eritrea is demanded to withdraw its troops and equipment from the zone at once. Both parties are also demanded to give UNMEE the access, help, support, and protection it needs, and to lift all restrictions without delay. Ethiopia is pressed over its own duties under the Algiers Agreements, and the Secretary-General and the wider world are called on to engage both governments to restart the stalled demarcation.

Sierra Leone's peacebuilding office is renewed by Resolution 1941, adopted on 29 September 2010. The UN Integrated Peacebuilding Office, UNIPSIL, was helping the government prepare for the 2012 elections, which carried a risk of rising tension. The government was carrying out its Agenda for Change, and the parties were keeping the 2009 joint communiqué that ended political violence. The Special Court's last trial was still running.

The Council extends UNIPSIL until 15 September 2011. Its work with the UN country team should focus on support for the 2012 elections. It covers conflict prevention and dialogue between parties, tackling youth unemployment and help with governance, anti-corruption work, and fighting drug trafficking. The government is called on to manage natural resources openly, strengthen the Anti-Corruption Commission, and act on the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's recommendations. Reports are due every six months, tracking benchmarks for a handover to a UN country team.

Mercenary attacks on the Democratic Republic of the Congo drew Resolution 241, adopted on 15 November 1967. Foreign fighters had struck the young Congolese state, and the Council was concerned that Portugal let them stage from Angola, which it still ruled. Support for the mercenaries, from recruiting to arms supply, kept flowing in from abroad.

The Council condemned any interference in Congo's internal affairs. It singled out Portugal for failing to stop the mercenaries from using Angola as a base, in breach of earlier resolutions, and told Lisbon to end all help to them at once. The text captures an early UN attempt to treat hired foreign fighters as a threat to the independence of new states.

A buffer force between the Egyptian and Israeli armies took legal shape on 27 October 1973. Resolution 340, passed two days earlier, had called for a United Nations Emergency Force to supervise the cease-fire. The Secretary-General reported the same day on how to set the force up. Resolution 341 is the Council's answer to that report.

The Council approved the report in full. The force would be established as the report set out, for an initial period of six months. After that, it would continue only if the Council decided it should. This decision gave legal form to the second United Nations Emergency Force. That force became the buffer that watched over the cease-fire after the October war.

A truce in Indonesia won rare praise from the Council in 1948. Dutch troops and republican forces had signed the deal weeks before. It rested on terms both sides had sworn to accept. The UN's good offices team had helped them reach it. Resolution 41 passed on 28 February 1948. Seven members voted yes. Four held back.

The Council voiced its joy at the truce. It praised the good offices team for its aid. The offer of UN help, first made in 1947, stayed on the table. Both sides and the UN team had to keep the Council up to date. News of the road to a full pact was required. The same day, the Council sent the team a fresh task on Java and Madura.

On 30 November 1978 the Council renewed a peacekeeping mandate in the Golan Heights. The vote was fourteen to none. China did not take part. The mission was the UN Disengagement Observer Force. It separates Israeli and Syrian troops. It also reports on the ceasefire line between them.

The extension covered six months, running to 31 May 1979. The Council called on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 from 1973. It also asked the Secretary-General to report at the end of the term. That report would describe events in the area. It would also list steps taken toward a settlement.

Resolution 541, passed on 18 November 1983, spurns a claim of statehood in north Cyprus. Three days before, the Turkish Cypriot side had declared a state of its own. Cyprus's foreign chief spoke in the hall. The Council judged the move a breach of the 1960 pacts. Those pacts had set up the Republic of Cyprus and pledged to keep it whole.

The Council deplored the claim. It held the bid to split off a new state void in law, and called for its recall. It told all sides to carry out its 1974 and 1975 Cyprus texts at once and in full. It asked the UN chief to press his good offices for the fastest path to a just peace. No state was to back any Cypriot state but the Republic.

A new flag rose over the desert in 1991. The land had been part of the Soviet Union. Now it stood on its own, rich in gas. Its leaders asked for a UN seat that winter. Resolution 741 was passed without a vote on 7 February 1992. The Council met as the Soviet map was being redrawn.

The members backed the bid. They told the General Assembly to admit the republic. The Assembly did so in March 1992. The state came in with a crowd of new states from the same fallen union. In time it chose a path of strict neutrality. This one short text marks its first step into world affairs.
versuch-einer-charakteristik-des-verhalt: Versuch einer Charakteristik des Verhältnisses der Alchemie zur Magie, 1841. The alchemy-magic relation. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
